10571-the-old-man-of-the-sea-ship-s-comp:
W. W. Jacobs published this comic tale as the eleventh part of Ship's Company, opening with George Wright asking old sailor Kemp to be his uncle. Wright wants a rich uncle from New Zealand, who will leave him all his money, to impress a young lady pursued by another man. Kemp, mystified over beer, agrees to play the part.

Wright must lend Kemp a little money, since a rich uncle needs brass to show, though Kemp admits he never yet paid back a loan. A letter calling Kemp home to New Zealand will end the game. Readers get a short, funny Jacobs tale of love, pretense, and a sailor's ready wit.
10791-double-dealing-sailor-s-knots-part:
W. W. Jacobs's "Double Dealing," the eleventh tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, opens on a seaside common where Fred Carter, a holiday Londoner, meets two hostile strangers. A strongly built man of fifty and his younger son eye Carter closely, declare "That's him," and demand what he has to say for himself. Carter, puzzled, waits for the charge.

The story unwinds a case of mistaken identity and double dealing, with Jacobs's trademark twists and dry humor. Seaside talk and suspicion carry the plot. Readers get a short comic mystery, complete on its own, from the author's popular riverside collection.
11481-dirty-work-deep-waters-part-11:
Near high water on a summer evening, the night-watchman sits aboard a lighter by the wharf, smoking and praising a job done alone from six at night to six in the morning. No foreman calls, no mates run into him with a loaded truck, and he is, as he puts it, his own master.

The story turns on a visitor who rings for a tanner, a sixpence, while the watchman has a purse of twelve pounds waiting in the dock. He pays to be rid of the man, and tells the tale with the same slow relish. Jacobs keeps the humour in the watchman's grumbling voice.
12131-a-golden-venture-the-lady-of-the-b:
Part 11 of Jacobs's Lady of the Barge stories, A Golden Venture, opens on the Tidger family at breakfast: Mrs. Tidger seated with knees wide apart, the youngest child nestled against her print dress, and Mr. Tidger holding a small child in a red flannel frock and a slipper on one moleskin knee.

The larger Tidger children take the solids of their breakfast up and down the room. This domestic scene sets up a venture in gold, speculation, or treasure, as Jacobs's sailors and villagers chase sudden wealth. The comedy lies in the gap between the Tidgers' crowded, ordinary morning and the golden dreams that will shortly unsettle it.
12211-a-spirit-of-avarice-odd-craft-part:
Mr. John Blows, a free-born Englishman, has been paid off at eleven in the morning for sleeping in a shed when he should have laid bricks. That dismissal opens A Spirit of Avarice, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft.

Blows, proud and lazy in equal measure, drifts home to a wife who thought him drowned, after a tale of falling in water and a rescue. He coughs, holds up his glass, and spins his absence into heroism, while his wife weighs belief against habit. Jacobs comedy rests on a man who turns every failure into a grievance and every return into a triumph. The story is short, sharp, and fond of its rogue.
15533-the-present-picture-of-new-south-w:
D. D. Mann, many years resident in official situations in New South Wales, published this picture of the colony in London in 1811, sold by John Booth. Four large colored views, drawn on the spot, show Sydney, the seat of government. A plan of the colony, taken from actual survey by public authority, heads the volume.

The first chapter runs from discovery and the arrival of a colony from England. It follows governors Phillip, Hunter, and King, with a printing press, a playhouse, numbered houses, a town clock, and a newspaper. Convicts, natives, lost cattle found wild, earthquakes, floods, and executions fill the chronicle. Mann writes as an insider, proud of progress yet plain about disorder, giving an early and detailed portrait of Australia's first colony.
15717-books-and-persons-being-comments-o:
Arnold Bennett gathered this book of comments on a past epoch, 1908 to 1911, in London in 1917, from Chatto and Windus. The contents were chosen from weekly articles that enlivened the New Age in those four years, under the pseudonym Jacob Tonson. A dedicatee read the whole series in four hours one Sunday afternoon, then demanded a volume.

Frank Swinnerton approved the selection and added slightly, Bennett suggested a few more, and the total amounts to one third of the original matter. Bennett's own works list fills pages. Novels run from A Man from the North and Anna of the Five Towns to Clayhanger and The Card. Fantasias like The Grand Babylon Hotel and belles-lettres like How to Live on Twenty-Four Hours a Day follow. The book is Bennett as critic: sharp, gossipy, and sure of his taste.
16394-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Charivaria leads the February 11, 1920 Punch, joking about burglars, Lady Beecham's telephone plan, and Miss Iris Hoey's plan to recite Shakespeare at an intruder. A libel case over a German cartoon of the ex-Crown Prince, food officials in Petrograd, and the Dempsey boxing row all get short, sharp jabs.

Cartoons, poems, and short funny pieces fill the rest of the number, all aimed at postwar London life. Each joke assumes a reader who follows the news, and the humor stays light even when the topics are grand. Set beside its February neighbors, this number is distinct in its own news jokes and its own cartoons.
17331-history-of-egypt-from-330-b-c-to-t:
S. Rappoport, a doctor of philosophy from Basel, wrote this eleventh volume of the Grolier history of Egypt. He was a scholar of Russian, German, and French oriental studies. It runs from 330 before the common era to the present time. It carries over twelve hundred coloured plates and pictures. The volume covers the Roman, Christian, and Arabic periods of Egyptian history.

Augustus remakes the government of Egypt, Christianity rises, the Arian controversy divides the church, monastic life grows, Alexandria declines, and Arab armies bring a new faith and new dynasties. Readers get a long sweep from Roman province to Arab land, told with the confidence of early twentieth-century scholarship. Its plates make the later history of Egypt unusually vivid.
18661-the-empire-annual-for-girls-1911:
A. R. Buckland edited this 1911 Empire Annual for Girls at London, with color plates and sixteen black-and-white pictures. Contributors include Lady Catherine Milnes-Gaskell, Mrs. Creighton, Mrs. Macquoid, Agnes Giberne, and Edith C. Kenyon, beside many more. The volume runs 384 pages in cloth gilt, uniform with a companion annual for boys.

Stories range from a Christmas child and a girl's adventure for her father's sake to a trooper of the North-West Mounted Police. A race for life on the frontier and a Christmas with Australian Blacks follow. Advice pieces cover golf for girls and girl life in Canada. The annual gives a warm picture of Edwardian girls' reading.
19081-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
The March 17, 1898 number of The Great Round World was a weekly paper for boys and girls. It mixed world news, travel notes, and book talk in short pieces. Young readers and their elders both could enjoy it. The paper came out each Thursday from New York.

One item touches on Mexico, where a house linked to Cortes and Maximilian still stands. Another notes new books from Germany, including doll-clothes patterns for girls. Short items keep the tone bright and instructive. Young readers get a window on the world of 1898, as a children's paper chose to show it.
2111-history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-:
Carlyle reaches Frederick's accession in Book Eleven, from June to December 1740, when the old king died on 31 May and Berlin closed its gates and stopped the post for days. On Thursday the regiments swore, and messengers shot forth. The accession closed the gates of Berlin for days, a mark of how seriously Prussia took a new king.

A young king talked of for talent and aspiration took the reins, and Europe watched with hope. Carlyle captures the buzz of a capital at a turning point, before the new king's first wars tested every promise. Frederick, at twenty-eight, had already read widely and dreamed of a philosopher's reign.
23548-the-raid-of-the-guerilla-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this Civil War tale in Tanglefoot Cove, a secluded nook among the Great Smoky Mountains, where judgment day seems to come early. A noted guerrilla, commanding a reckless troop, has declared his intent to raid the cove, and its few, feeble folk can only tremble.

Volunteering and conscription have already thinned the men, from the very young to the verge of the venerable, robbing cradle and grave alike. Only ancient weaklings, frail youths, women, and girls remain. Craddock writes the dread with mountain detail and a keen ear for cove talk, as a community of non combatants faces a warlike menace it did nothing to earn. Readers will find a tense, atmospheric tale of a small place under a great war's shadow.
23549-wolf-s-head-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this outlaw tale in a vast tract of dense mountain forest, craggy ravines, and swirling torrents, a country of panther, bear, catamount, and wolf. Like the beasts, ferocious and fugitive, fearsome and afraid, lives the man with a wolf's head. A price is set on him as the state sets a bounty on brute scalps.

One gloomy October afternoon, sportsmen camped in the wild learn the region's repute and the chance of serving on a sheriff's posse for the grimmest of duties. Seymour, prig and purist, bookish yet a good shot, argues the phrase wolf's head survives while the fact is obsolete. Craddock writes the wild with force and dialect, making a tense tale of law, legend, and men who hunt men in mountain country.
23550-una-of-the-hill-country-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this hill country tale at a silent sawmill on Headlong Creek, in the water gap of Chilhowee Mountain. Sawdust spread thick over a level open space marks the footing for a long heralded bran dance, destined to end strangely, while a barbecue roasts shoats underground to a turn.

Elder men and sun bonneted matrons discuss the feast on a shady slope by a crystal spring, as youths and maidens of nearby coves dance on, insensible to fatigue, hunger, or heat. Una, of the title, moves through this mountain gathering, where dance, custom, and faith tangle. Craddock writes the scene with rich dialect and mountain colour, making a vivid, if period bound, portrait of hill folk at play and at prayer.
23551-who-crosses-storm-mountain-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this winter tale on Storm Mountain, where wind stirs weighted pines and snow lies smooth and white. Footprints mark the woodland gentry abroad: pronged turkey claws, swift mink paces, padded wolf paws, and great hoof marks leading to a little log cabin crouched in winter, loneliness, and poverty.

Icy ranges ring the slope, rock ledges jut, crags beetle overhead, and a dark, starred sky arches above. Smoke steals from a stick and clay chimney, and a clapboard roof shelters a group within. Who crosses the mountain, and why, drives the tale, as law, sorrow, and the world seem far from so slight a thing. Craddock writes the winter with stark beauty, making a tense, atmospheric story of a cabin, a storm, and a crossing that matters.
23552-the-phantom-of-bogue-holauba-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this ghost tale on the Mississippi at midnight. Gordon stands beside the Mississippi at midnight and watches its flow pour sideways into Bogue Holauba, a bayou, as if the great river served as a tributary to the lesser waterway. Moonlight lies large and low, forests tower dark on either hand, and the river runs unshadowed, solitary, and silent.

Then Gordon's eye catches a singular sight on the bank of the bogue, and he gasps, seeking to explain it as illusion or trick of sense. Craddock builds the phantom from river lore, delta geography, and moonlit dread, letting the strange waterway do half the haunting. Readers who like a Southern ghost tale, slow and atmospheric, will enjoy the phantom's first appearance and the mystery it leaves on the bank.
23553-the-christmas-miracle-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this Christmas tale of Jubal Kennedy, a man of line and rule who yearns for a sign from heaven to confirm his faltering faith. Impervious to spiritual subtleties, he looks through a mountain gap at autumn splendour: amethyst haze, red and russet woods, a hunter's moon high in the east while a vermilion sun sinks west.

He knows sap sinks, growth fails, and snow will shroud all. Spring will quicken it again to bloom and fruit, and still he stays deaf to the lesson. The Christmas miracle of the title must speak in terms even Jubal can measure. Craddock writes the mountains with rich, slow colour, making a gentle tale of doubt, seasons, and a sign that comes, at last, in a form a practical man can trust.
23554-a-chilhowee-lily-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this short mountain tale around a single flower. It is a tall, delicate, stately Chilhowee lily, with the finished symmetry of a cultivated plant yet the fragility of an unheeded weed. Long familiar, the bloom now bears a special meaning, and its sight brings the hero to a sudden pause.

The cluster grows in a niche on a rocky verge above a rugged road on the ridge slope. Its great pure white bloom, trumpet shaped and crowned with a flaring, many cleft crown, stands bright against a deep blue sky. Moss, ochre water stains, ferns, and pendant vines heighten the whiteness by contrast. Craddock writes the flower as a sign of grace in rough country, and readers who love nature writing will enjoy the tale's slow, luminous focus.
23555-the-lost-guidon-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this Civil War tale on a stricken field at nightfall, where clouds shaken asunder by artillery give way to direful rain, the steady sequel of battle shock. Wounded men who might have lived face exposure through the night, awaiting tardy succour that must take its turn.

A surgeon at a hasty field hospital, sheltered under cliffs on a slope, pauses amid his grim scalpel work. His face is set and haggard, less from fresh horror than from its weary return. The lost guidon of the title, a small flag of a troop, becomes a sign of honour, loss, and rallying in the rain. Craddock writes war as weather, wounds, and waiting, making a sombre, powerful tale of a field after the guns fall silent.
23556-his-unquiet-ghost-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this ghost tale on a still mountain night, moon high and wind laid, where dew glints over a vast wilderness. Three men lurk in the shadow of a crag in a narrow pass, hearing for an hour only a rill tinkling far below in a black abyss. That sound is so slight it proves the quiet rather than breaks it.

At last a slow wheel and the clank of a tire on stone reach them from three miles down the winding valley road. The sound grows by slow degrees as horses' heads appear in moonlight between pines and sky. The driver of the vehicle, and the ghost that rides with him, give the tale its dread. Craddock writes the approach with patience and mountain detail, making the unquiet ghost a figure of guilt and night rather than of mere fright.
23557-the-crucial-moment-1911:
Charles Egbert Craddock wrote this tale of Walter Hoxer, a man whose years of labour, skill, and integrity seem nullified in a mere moment, as sudden and potent as lightning. Hoxer himself likens it not to angry skies but to a river trick. A mattress spur of woven willow wands, set at a crafty angle, turns the Mississippi's swirling current.

Waves like herds of wild horses hesitate at the spur, scour a new channel, and leave the old bank bereft, no longer the margin of the stream. That image stays in Hoxer's mind all afternoon, as he weighs how a trifle can divert a life. Craddock writes the crucial moment with river force and moral weight, showing how one small choice, or chance, can remake years of steady work.
25405-honey-bee-1911:
Anatole France's Honey-Bee, translated by Mrs. John Lane and illustrated by Florence Lundborg in 1911, is a fairy-tale romance. The Countess of Blanchelande was widowed when her husband fell in single combat with an Irish giant. A white rose left on her prie-Dieu warns her of a coming death in her house's line of countesses.

She weeps over her three-year-old son George, whose eyelashes shadow cheeks like flowers. Honey-Bee, the heroine, later rides beside a duchess in silver flowers and pearls, her gold circlet bearing three gold flowers. A tailor's grandson wonders whether she is alive or a wax image, so lovely is she.
25821-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Rossiter Johnson edits volume eleven of The Great Events by Famous Historians, a readable account of world history in eminent historians' own words, with associate editors Charles F. Horne and John Rudd. Imperial Austrian councillors thrown from a Prague castle window by Bohemian deputies front the book, precipitating the Thirty Years' War.

That defenestration scene, painted by Vacslav Brozik, marks the volume's early modern scope, from religious wars to revolutions and empires. Brief introductions by specialists connect celebrated narratives in chronological order, with indices, bibliographies, chronologies, and courses of reading guiding students through world history.
27796-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-december:
Joseph R. Buchanan's December 1887 Journal of Man, volume one, number eleven, leads with an essay on the world's neglected or forgotten leaders and pioneers. It celebrates the unveiling in Boston of a statue of Leif Ericson, the Norse discoverer of North America.

Other contents cover social conditions, expenses at Harvard, Edison's phonograph, autotelegraphy, Antarctic exploration, and capital punishment, with a continued chapter on the law of location in organology. The issue shows Buchanan's journal linking history, invention, and mind science in one monthly miscellany. Professor E. N. Horsford related the Norse history at the unveiling, drawing on an address quoted at length.
29558-boy-scouts-handbook-the-first-edit:
Printed as the first edition of 1911, the Boy Scouts Handbook served as the official guide of the Boy Scouts of America. Its pages teach camping, knots, first aid, woodcraft, and the Scout oath and law, with pictures of Scouts at camp. Notes in the text flag tips with serious consequences, such as using lead acetate to waterproof a tent, so readers learn care with every skill.

The handbook aims to build character through outdoor life: strength for work or play, readiness, and service. Its tone is earnest, practical, and boyish, in the manner of its age. Scouts, historians, and lovers of scouting lore will find the founding manual that shaped a movement.
3087-original-short-stories-volume-11:
The Umbrella opens volume eleven, where thrift turns comic and then cruel. Madame Oreille, a very economical woman, knows the value of a centime. She keeps a storehouse of strict principles about multiplying money, so her cook struggles for market pennies and her husband gets hardly any pocket money. The volume adds Belhomme's Beast, Discovery, The Accursed Bread, The Dowry, and The Diary of a Madman. Later tales include The Mask, The Penguins Rock, A Family, Suicides, An Artifice, Dreams, and Simon's Papa.

A railway scene has a woman left by her husband crying out in bewilderment while an inspector dismisses her trouble. The volume shows Maupassant's late manner, where thrift, madness, and family cruelty meet.
30870-the-works-of-robert-louis-stevenso:
Held here is volume eleven of the Swanston Edition of Robert Louis Stevenson's works, printed in London in 1912. The edition ran to twenty-five volumes, with two thousand and sixty copies printed and two thousand for sale. This volume holds one novel, Catriona, in two parts: The Lord Advocate, and Father and Daughter. A monument to Stevenson in St. Giles's, Edinburgh, fronts the volume.

Part one follows its hero from a beggar on horseback and a Highland writer to Pilrig and the house of Lord Advocate Prestongrange. Then he marches again with Alan, to Gillane Sands, the Bass, and Black Andie's tale of Tod Lapraik. Part two crosses to Holland in a voyage. Readers get a Jacobite adventure of law, loyalty, and young love, told in Stevenson's vivid Scots voice.
31761-wilson-s-tales-of-the-borders-and-:
Volume eleven of Wilson's Tales of the Borders and of Scotland, revised by Alexander Leighton and published in London and Newcastle-upon-Tyne in 1884, gathers historical, traditionary, and imaginative stories with a glossary. Contributors include John Mackay Wilson, Leighton himself, Professor Thomas Gillespie, Alexander Campbell, and Alexander Bethune.

Its contents run from The Dominie's Class and The Contrast of Wives to The Ghost of Howdycraigs, The Ghost of Gairyburn, and The Smuggler. They also include The Schoolfellows and The Red Hall, or Berwick in 1296. Readers get a rich Border miscellany of school, church, ghosts, smuggling, and medieval war, told in Scots-flavored prose.
3349-the-wandering-jew-volume-11:
Eugene Sue's serial reaches Book Eleven in this volume, near its end. The ruins of the abbey of St John the Baptist open it, with the calvary, the council, and happiness. Duty, the improvised hospital, and hydrophobia follow, with the guardian angel, ruin, and memories. The ordeal, ambition, and a letter to a socius, a socius and a half, lead to Faringhea's affection.

An evening at St Colombe's, the nuptial bed, and a duel to the death close the movement. Sue brings his wanderers, lovers, and conspirators toward a final accounting, in abbey ruins and sickrooms alike. Readers who have followed eleven volumes will find the long story gathering itself: happiness claimed, duty paid, and old debts settled at last.
3561-memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volum:
This eleventh volume of Bourrienne's memoirs covers Napoleon in 1812, the year of the invasion of Russia. Bourrienne, the emperor's former private secretary, writes from his knowledge of the government that planned and supplied the campaign, even though he no longer served at Napoleon's side. Supply, distance, and winter do more damage in these pages than any single battle.

The year moves from grand plans and a vast army marching east to retreat, cold, and ruin. Bourrienne records the confidence of the spring and the shock of the autumn, as the empire's strength broke on distance and winter. Readers following the series will find 1812 as the turning point, told with the detail of a man who knew the system from inside.
3578-recollections-of-the-private-life-o:
Constant's eleventh volume covers the last full years of the empire, when invasion reached France itself and the household faced its hardest choices. He describes a court preparing for siege and flight, servants packing and unpacking, and an emperor who refused to believe the end had come. Loyalty, in these pages, is tested by fear and by offers from the other side.

The volume shows the private side of a public collapse: families divided, papers hidden, and farewells said in haste. Constant writes as a man who stayed to the end of this phase of the story. Readers following the series toward its close will find a tense, personal account of an empire falling apart at home.
3591-essays-of-michel-de-montaigne-volum:
This eleventh volume of Montaigne's Essays gathers chapters thirteen through seventeen of Book Two. They treat judging the death of another, the ways the mind hinders itself, the growth of desire when difficulty increases, glory, and presumption. Montaigne opens the volume by warning that death is the most remarkable action of a life, yet we judge it badly, since men hardly believe in their own end.

The essays ask why we chase fame, why we value what resists us, and why we think too well of ourselves. Montaigne answers with stories from history and from his own conduct. The volume suits readers interested in pride, ambition, and the mind's tricks, written in Montaigne's plain, self searching style.
3911-the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rou:
Jean Jacques Rousseau's eleventh book opens with the triumph of Eloisa, his novel long in the press at the end of 1760. Madame de Luxembourg spoke of it at court, Madame de Houdetot spoke of it at Paris, and Saint Lambert read the manuscript to the King of Poland, who was delighted. Booksellers in the Rue Saint Jacques and the Palais Royal were beset by buyers asking when it would appear, and its success answered the impatience.

The dauphiness called it a ravishing performance, men of letters differed, and women of high life became intoxicated with book and author alike. Rousseau then turns to solitude, fearing the great machine of monarchy may fall in pieces. Readers who like Rousseau at his peak will find fame, flattery, and foreboding together.
5285-tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontain:
La Fontaine's eleventh volume opens with the author's preface to his second book of tales. He vindicates there the boldness and privilege he has assumed. He notes that he will write no more tales in this manner. He defends his rhymes, his run-on lines, and his licence, before offering Friar Philips Geese and Richard Minutolo.

The volume thus marks a turning point in the collection, as La Fontaine bids farewell to the manner of his tales. Readers get both the author's apology and two new stories, in which friars and lovers provide the usual comedy of desire and deception.
5527-the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-11:
Paula passes a fearful night in a small, frightfully hot prison cell in the eleventh volume of Georg Ebers's The Bride of the Nile, shut up with Betta. She cannot sleep. Whenever she closes her eyes, yells and clanking chains from the common prison wake her, along with the heavy step of another sufferer pacing overhead, even more restless than herself.

The volume centers on imprisonment, with Paula wondering about her fellow victim above. Ebers writes the cell's heat and noise as a form of torment. Readers get a harrowing stretch of the romance, where a young woman endures a night that will not end.
5540-a-thorny-path-volume-11:
Scarcely has Macrinus closed the door when Caracalla throws himself exhausted on the throne in the eleventh volume of Georg Ebers's A Thorny Path. He orders wine, and his gloomy gaze stays fixed on the ground. His physician notes with anxiety how his master's breast heaves and eyelids quiver, but when a soothing potion is offered, Caesar waves it away and commands the man to stop troubling him.

The volume shows the emperor at his most weary and unapproachable, with court attendants watching helplessly. Ebers portrays power as exhaustion and refusal. Readers get a dark, courtly stretch of the romance, centered on a ruler who will accept no comfort.
5913-the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1:
One chapter fills this Don Quixote installment: chapter twenty-nine, on the droll device adopted to free a love-stricken knight from his self-imposed penance. The chapter opens mid-tale, as a sad adventurer asks listeners to judge whether sighs, lamentations, and tears had sufficient cause, and whether consolation is idle where no remedy exists. All he asks is a place to live unharassed by fear of discovery.

Cervantes offers his plotting at its most theatrical, as friends stage a rescue for a knight who will not be rescued plainly. The single chapter favors speech, disguise, and comic persuasion over swordplay. It suits readers following Quixote in order, since the device here finally moves the penitent knight toward home, with Dorothea's part still to play.
618-codex-junius-11:
Translations from the Anglo-Saxon Junius manuscript fill this volume, covering Genesis A and B, Exodus, Daniel, and Christ and Satan. Written between the seventh and tenth centuries, these poems tell creation, the fall, the flood, and the harrowing of hell in stern, alliterative verse. Genesis B, set inside Genesis A, gives Satan's revolt its fullest early form.

An editor's note warns the poems are not one man's work, though once ascribed to Caedmon. The translations keep the old poems' gravity and music in modern English. The book serves as a key source for early English faith and poetry, where Bible tales wear a warrior's dress.
7596-the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume:
Part eleven of The Caxtons mixes travel humor with family conscience. At home, graver matters wait: the mother blames herself for what was, the narrator insists, his uncle's misfortune rather than his fault. He lays the blame on their horrible progenitor, William Caxton, whose defunct shoulders must carry it. The Caxtons reckon here with an inheritance that is moral as well as material.

The journey that frames that reckoning is bookish comedy from start to finish. On the Cambridge Telegraph, one outside passenger impresses his fellows with lore in dead languages, yet utters not a syllable in a live one from mounting to alighting. A joke about sleep as a better cover than a cloak, credited to Sancho, had already been said in substance by Tibullus. Learning travels badly, and Lytton enjoys the joke.
7669-what-will-he-do-with-it-volume-11:
Waife returns to his cottage in Book Eleven of Edward Bulwer Lytton's What Will He Do With It? He will not move into Lady Montfort's house, though she spends hours each day in his small parlor and garden plot. Sophy stays close by, and George promises to return soon to plan their future.

Later scenes show Sophy watching by Waife's sickbed as he gains strength, while Guy Darrell visits in private. Fairthorn's flute drifts from the woods where Sophy walks for air. Love, gratitude, and a good name long clouded shape this gentle, late volume.
7712-my-novel-volume-11:
Hate as a force in civilized life opens Book Eleven of Lytton's My Novel. Randal Leslie, clever and well taught, holds that roguery pays best. He shows the marks of a mind at war with the world: over-cunning, restless suspicion, and a belief that all conspire against him.

The volume follows his money schemes. A baron advises buying up a kinsman's bills while the young heir's father still lives in health. Post-obits on sound security cost dear, Randal notes. Through finance and family talk, the book shows ambition dressing itself as cleverness.
7725-the-last-of-the-barons-volume-11:
Warwick and Clarence escort King Henry in blue velvet to St. Paul's in Book Eleven of Edward Bulwer Lytton's The Last of the Barons, subtitled The New Position of the Kingmaker. On October 6 the restored king gives thanks in public, then lodges at the Bishop's Palace while a proclamation wins seeming assent across the realm.

No private revenge stains Henry's second reign, save Worcester's head on the scaffold. Master Adam Warner earns praise and advancement, as greatness tells wisdom their fates are joined. Yet Hilyard finds London traders call his plans for steady reform mere fanatic dreams. Triumph already sours.
7747-the-parisians-volume-11:
A meeting long planned in private goes wrong in Book Eleven of Lytton's The Parisians, when Graham sits beside Isaura in common company. Words rehearsed in the heart cannot be said, looks imagined in a magic glass give way to groups and chatter, and a chill tells him she has changed.

Her touch at greeting and the tone of her few words confirm it. Through the irony of chance, the volume shows how love can cool in silence and absence. It is a study of two people who meet again only to find the old closeness gone.
8481-life-on-the-mississippi-part-11:
As a backward glance closing the book, Part 11 of Life on the Mississippi opens with chapter 51, Reminiscences. Twain travels toward St. Louis aboard the City of Baton Rouge on a hot day. Town social life drew him in. So instead of the hundred steamboatmen he had hoped to interview, he managed only brief talks with a couple dozen of them.

This closing section gathers the book's backward glances, with old pilots, old boats, and a river changed by railroads. Readers get Twain taking leave of his subject, affectionate and a little rueful. It is a fitting end to a book that began with geography and became a memoir of a vanished working world.
9773-alice-or-the-mysteries-book-11:
Book eleven of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Alice, or The Mysteries, returns to Lord Vargrave at the height of his hopes. Evelyn Cameron's hand is pledged, the wedding day fixed, and in less than a week she will give a ruined peer a splendid dowry. Deeds to transfer the Maltravers baronial estates near completion, and Lisle Court awaits the pair. Politics, too, seems to favor him.

The final book tests whether Vargrave's triumph can hold, as old deeds and loves press their claims. Lytton's prose favors high, moral drama. A reader gets the closing book of a Victorian mystery romance, where ambition meets its reckoning.
a-general-history-and-collection-of-voya: Volume fifteen of Robert Kerr's voyages continues James Cook's voyage toward the South Pole and round the world. Its chapters follow Cook from leaving New Zealand toward his return home. The Resolution and Adventure carry the story through southern seas. Kerr's volume completes the Cook account begun in the fourteenth volume.
a-golden-venture-the-lady-of-the-barge-a: William Wymark Jacobs tells a golden venture in this part of The Lady of the Barge and others. Its scenes follow the Tidger family at breakfast in a stone flagged court, with weak tea and small pieces of bloater. Mr. Tidger urges his wife Ann to peg away at her work. Jacobs writes comic domestic life with his usual Thames side humor.
a-spirit-of-avarice-odd-craft-part-11: William Wymark Jacobs tells a comic story of avarice in which Mr John Blows, a free-born Englishman, is summarily paid off at eleven in the morning. The foreman, who caught him dozing in a shed instead of laying bricks, tells him to take his ugly face home and bury it in the backyard. Blows answers with fluent reflections on the foreman's ancestors, and the tale follows greed meeting its match in plain speaking.
a-thorny-path-volume-11:
Georg Ebers brings A Thorny Path near its climax in Volume 11, with Emperor Caracalla alone on his throne. Ebers shows the ruler worn out, calling for wine and waving away the soothing draught his anxious physician offers. Macrinus, his prefect, has just left the room, and reports arrive that the city's youths are gathering on the race course in a loud, unruly mood.

Chapter XXX listens to the songs the young men keep demanding, each one aimed at Caesar himself. Caracalla lets them sing, comparing their sport to a last meal granted before a final journey. His talk turns to a prison, and his smile tells the high priest of Serapis that the threats are meant in earnest. A ruler nursing insult and pain is the most dangerous figure in the book here.
alchemy-ancient-and-modern-being-a-brief:
Alchemy: Ancient and Modern, published in 1911 by H Stanley Redgrove, is a brief account of the alchemistic doctrines. Redgrove sets out to explain what the alchemists taught and how their doctrines connect in two directions. On one side they relate to mysticism, and on the other to recent discoveries in physical science, which in his day were reviving old questions about the elements.

Alongside the doctrines, the book gives particulars of the lives and teachings of the most noted alchemists. That mix of history and comparison made it a standard short introduction of its time. Readers get both the old art's ideas and its famous practitioners, surveyed by a chemist writing when radioactivity had made transmutation thinkable again.
alice-or-the-mysteries-book-11: Edward Bulwer Lytton finds Vargrave's hopes realised in the eleventh book of Alice, or the Mysteries, with Evelyn Cameron's hand pledged and the wedding day fixed. A splendid dowry promises to smooth the ruined peer's climb, while deeds transferring the Maltravers estates near completion. Triumph seems within reach, yet the very completeness of his success sets up the novel's reckoning.
andreyev-king-hunger-1911:
King Hunger, Leonid Andreyev's allegorical play, appeared in English in Poet Lore in the winter of 1911. Eugene M. Kayden made the translation. King Hunger, a gaunt personified power, rouses the starving poor of a great city to rise against the rich who feast above them.

Bells, judges, and workers people the stark, symbolic stages of the play. The rising swells toward a climax that Andreyev shapes as vision rather than report. He called such works dramas of ideas, meant to stage the forces that move crowds. Of all his plays, this one presses revolution most directly. The Poet Lore printing gave American readers an early taste of his radical theater.
arxiv-2509-00111:
Duncan A. Lockerby, working alone, presents a new drag correction for slow particles of any shape in 2025. The Cunningham correction factor adjusts drag laws when a particle is so small that gas no longer acts like a smooth fluid. Past forms need fits to test data and assume a sphere.

Lockerby gives a form that needs no such fitting and extends it to non-spherical shapes through a correction tensor, a grid of values that varies by direction. Checks cover test data and kinetic theory for spheres, plus computer solutions of the Boltzmann equation for spheroids of varied shape. The tool offers a simple, general way to gauge transport of tiny particles in gas. It suits aerosol and dust studies alike.
arxiv-2509-00311:
Hikmat Khan leads a team of seven authors who present MorphGen in 2025, a method to make cancer classification from tissue slides robust across hospitals. Whole slide images vary with tissue preparation, staining, and imaging gear, which shifts the data a model sees. Pathologists instead rely on morphological cues that stay diagnostic across settings, such as nuclear size, contour, and chromatin texture.

MorphGen models nuclear morphology and spatial organization explicitly. It joins slide images, augmentations, and nuclear segmentation masks in a supervised contrastive setup, which pulls same-class samples together. The hypothesis is that biologically robust cues yield features that resist domain shift. Single-domain generalization is the test: train at one site, perform at unseen ones.
arxiv-2509-00511:
Heikki Mantysaari, with three co-authors, Bjorn Schenke, Chun Shen, and Wenbin Zhao, tests how starting shape shapes flow in heavy-ion collisions. A deuteron, a light nucleus, changes its wavefunction shape, its quantum state description, with its polarization state, its spin alignment.

Mantysaari and his co-authors model lead plus polarized deuteron collisions with hydrodynamics, fluid-like equations, plus a hadronic transport step for late particle interactions. Response to the starting geometry predicts a clear sign for elliptic flow, the oval-shaped spread of particles, tied to deuteron polarization. That clean split offers a test of whether collective flow, shared motion, truly explains behavior in small collision systems.
arxiv-2509-00711:
Junghoon Justin Park leads a team of seven authors who analyze resting-state brain scans. They use a quantum transformer for the task. Resting-state scans reveal intrinsic brain networks at work. They can also show markers of mental conditions. Classical transformers are strong but costly and data-hungry.

Their Quantum Time-series Transformer uses two quantum algorithms. Together they give a cost that grows very slowly with input size. Tests use large datasets from two major studies. One is the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. The other is the UK Biobank. The quantum model matches or beats classical transformers on prediction. Gains are largest when samples are few. Explanation analysis also finds meaningful neural markers for ADHD.
arxiv-2509-00811:
Samuel Punch and one co-author, Krishnendu Guha, present MaestroCut, a framework for quantum circuit cutting on near-term hardware. Circuit cutting splits a large quantum circuit into smaller pieces that fit limited devices, but device drift and changing workloads can degrade accuracy after the cut is fixed.

MaestroCut closes the loop: it tracks a variance proxy in real time, triggers re-cutting when accuracy degrades, and routes shots, repeated circuit runs, using topology-aware priors. An estimator cascade combining maximum likelihood, Bayesian, and Gaussian process methods selects the lowest-error reconstruction within a fixed budget. Simulations show variance contraction and lower error than uniform baselines, while emulation with realistic queueing and noise shows stable latency and about one percent software overhead.
arxiv-2509-01011:
S M Rafiuddin, writing alone, ranks Bangla words using graph-based ranking algorithms. Ranking words helps summarize text and retrieve information, and a word graph represents words as vertices with relationships as edges, revealing each word's relative importance within the text.

Lacking a standard Bangla word database, Rafiuddin uses the Indian Language POS-tag Corpora, a rich collection of Bangla sentences with parts of speech tags. Standard preprocessing steps are applied to each word graph before running several graph-based ranking algorithms, allowing a comparison among them. The paper illustrates the entire procedure, from constructing the word graph from text to calculating rankings, and experimental analysis on real data reveals each algorithm's accuracy in terms of F1 measure.
arxiv-2509-01411:
Judging how good an image looks to human eyes is central to image processing, but heavy quality metrics are slow and human labels are scarce. Ugur Cogalan, with four co-authors, presents MILO, a lightweight perceptual metric for full-reference quality assessment, where a clean original is available for comparison. It works at several scales and runs fast enough for real-time use.

MILO is trained with pseudo scores: set distortions are applied to varied images, and an ensemble of recent metrics, accounting for visual masking, supplies the grades. That avoids large human-labeled data sets. Despite its small size, MILO beat existing metrics on standard benchmarks. The team also uses it as a perceptual loss for optimizing images and for latent representations inside a diffusion model, aligning results with human vision.
arxiv-2509-01511:
Program testing needs generators that cover the cases they claim to. Proving that point calls for must-style reasoning. One must show what a program has to do, not just what it may do. Zhe Zhou, Benjamin Delaware, and Suresh Jagannathan explore a link between two tools. One is coverage types. The other is incorrectness logic.

Coverage types extend the refinement types of functional languages. They add must-style, underapproximate reasoning, reasoning that understates on purpose. Incorrectness logic reasons in a like style about real bugs. The authors propose to merge the two inside one type system. Such a union could let programmers verify test generators in one place. Both their safety and their completeness could be checked. The talk maps what this merge offers to programmers and tool builders.
arxiv-2509-02411:
Honghui Xu and five co-authors wrote a 2025 survey of privacy and security for large language models running on phones and edge devices. Mobile models bring language skills to health, finance, and education apps, but they handle sensitive data on limited hardware.

The survey organises known defences such as differential privacy, which adds noise to protect individuals, federated learning, which trains without centralising data, and prompt encryption. It also catalogues attacks aimed at mobile models, including adversarial inputs, membership inference, which tests whether data was in training, and side-channel leaks. Comparing defences shows a persistent trade-off between safety and efficiency. The authors close with open problems and directions toward trustworthy mobile systems.
arxiv-2509-02911:
Guanglu Shi and 4 co-authors used the 2024 total solar eclipse in a 2025 study of the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona. During an eclipse, the Moon blocks the bright solar disk, so the faint corona becomes easy to photograph. The team asked how unseen regions on the Sun's far side shape that corona.

Routine maps of the solar surface only show the side facing Earth. The authors repaired that blind spot using full-disk magnetic maps taken a few days later, once rotation had brought the hidden region into view. Their computer simulation then matched eclipse photos and spacecraft readings more closely. A single active region far away had shifted the sheet of current flowing outward and changed plasma, meaning hot charged gas, even near the poles.
arxiv-2509-03011:
Alexis Ivan Lopez Escamilla, Gilberto Ochoa, and Sharib Al built a 2025 system that writes captions for endoscopy images of ulcerative colitis. Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammation of the colon, and endoscopy lets doctors view its lining directly. Written reports need to note severity and visible damage in a consistent way.

Their model joins image features from a standard vision network with heatmaps that show which areas drove its decisions. Clinical details, such as a severity score and signs like bleeding or redness, are fed in as text prompts. An attention step and a language decoder then produce structured descriptions with lesion tags. Compared with baseline systems, theirs gave better captions and more accurate severity calls.
arxiv-2509-03411:
Michael Albert, Samuël Borza, and Maria Gordina classified shortest paths on Grushin spaces in a 2025 geometry paper. Grushin spaces are geometries where movement is restricted in certain directions. They generalize a classic singular plane. Geodesics, the length-minimizing curves, are the objects of study. Finding every minimizer from each point is called optimal synthesis.

The authors solve Hamilton's equations for these spaces. Their tools are generalized trigonometric functions, adapted to the setting. For geodesics starting at a regular point, they obtain explicit conjugate times. Those are the moments when a path can stop being shortest. A conjectured cut time takes the minimum of several symmetry-based candidates. It is proved to lower-bound the first conjugate time. In three dimensions, a density argument completes the conjecture and the full synthesis.
arxiv-2509-03511:
Danilo Triggiani and one co-author wrote a 2025 physics paper on telling apart faint optical sources closer together than the usual imaging limit. That limit, set by diffraction, blurs nearby glowing objects into one spot. It hampers astronomy and biological imaging alike, where sources shine incoherently, without a shared phase.

A technique called SPADE sorts incoming light by spatial pattern before counting photons, beating direct imaging. The authors model incoherent light of any brightness pattern and compute the best possible discrimination rate, given by a quantum Chernoff exponent. SPADE reaches that ultimate rate only when certain compatibility conditions hold. Otherwise collective measurements across photons may be needed. They also show how rotating the SPADE setup suits each task, and test a simplified decision procedure in simulation.
arxiv-2509-03611:
A 2025 research paper by Danielle Sponseller and three co-authors tests whether small carbon-rich dust grains trace anomalous microwave emission. It is an extra glow in microwaves from interstellar space. The candidate grains are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, ring-shaped molecules whose infrared features might mark where the glow originates.

Using archival DIRBE satellite data, they map the grains' 3.3 micrometre feature across 98 compact sources listed by the Planck collaboration. Far-infrared dust glow still tracks the microwave glow better in most regions. Even so, about seventeen percent of sources match better with the small-grain signal. Among the 27 strongest microwave detections, over a third prefer the grain tracer. Local interstellar conditions may be shaping the grain signal, and more work is needed to find the true carriers.
arxiv-2509-03711:
A new way to hunt software vulnerabilities, called Reactive Bottom-Up Testing, occupies a 2025 research paper by Siddharth Muralee and four co-authors. Dynamic testing runs programs to provoke failures, but most tools work top-down and struggle to reach functions buried deep in the call graph. Bottom-up testing starts at single functions instead, yet often floods analysts with false positives or unrealistic inputs.

Their three-stage scheme first flags likely vulnerable functions and builds test harnesses aware of types and program context. Fuzzing, feeding randomised inputs, then hunts for crashes, while symbolic execution extracts the conditions each crash needs. Finally, combining constraints across stages verifies which crashes are truly reachable and triggerable in the full program. Their prototype, Griller, found 28 of 48 known vulnerabilities in a controlled benchmark across five open-source projects. On real applications, including the Pacman package manager tooling, it uncovered six previously unknown vulnerabilities.
arxiv-2509-03911:
Divya Acharya and two co-authors' 2025 mathematics paper determines the Lee distance of a family of cyclic codes. Cyclic codes are a structured family where rotating a codeword gives another codeword. Their codes have length a power of two and live over a three-layer ring built from a finite field with an added nilpotent element.

Lee distance measures how far apart codewords sit under the Lee weight, a notion tuned to certain error patterns. The Gray map, which sends codes over a related ring to binary codes while preserving weight, frames why Lee distance matters for applications. Algebraically, these cyclic codes are exactly the ideals of a quotient polynomial ring, which gives a handle on their structure. The Lee distance is computed for the whole family. Exact distances let designers predict error-correction performance without exhaustive search, completing a picture Hamming-distance studies leave open.
arxiv-2509-04011:
A 2025 research paper by Or Shachar and three co-authors covers NER Retriever, a zero-shot system retrieving documents that mention entities of a user-described type. Here types are not given beforehand: the user describes a type in open-ended words, and the system finds mentions with no fine-tuning for the type.

The method embeds mentions and type descriptions in one semantic space, using representations drawn from inside a large language model. A key finding guides the design: value vectors from middle transformer layers encode fine-grained type information better than the top-layer embeddings. A contrastive projection network refines them, pulling type-compatible entities together and pushing unrelated types apart. The compact, type-aware embeddings suit nearest-neighbour search. On three benchmarks the system outperforms lexical retrieval and sentence-level baselines. The codebase is public, and the authors argue the findings inform representation selection in language models.
arxiv-2509-04111:
Dan Saattrup Smart, writing alone, builds a reading test that spans more than three hundred languages in a 2025 research paper. The data set, MultiWikiQA, holds over a million question-and-answer samples. Each sample grows out of a Wikipedia article, which also supplies the passage to read. A language model drafted the questions, making sure each answer appears word for word inside its article. Questions were then reworded so simple word matching cannot cheat.

Human judges in thirty languages rated the questions as mostly natural or better. Six language models were benchmarked, with scores varying widely by language. The test is hard even for strong systems, Smart reports. Both the data and the judge surveys are public.
arxiv-2509-04211:
Mikkel Abrahamsen and three co-authors ask how little of a polygon must be revealed before it can be boxed in, in a 2025 research paper. A polygon arrives as a list of corners in counterclockwise order. Knowing a corner means knowing both its place in the list and its coordinates. The goal is to name a bounded region guaranteed to contain the whole shape, while learning as few corners as possible.

Some polygons can be bounded after seeing only about four times the base-two logarithm of their corner count. Yet other shapes force any method to inspect at least a base-three logarithm's worth. The two bounds match up to a constant factor, settling the question. Packing and containment algorithms inherit this limit.
arxiv-2509-04311:
Sara Najem and two co-authors import geometry tools from quantum physics to describe group interactions in networks in a 2025 research paper. Ordinary networks only link pairs, but real systems involve groups acting together. Simplicial complexes capture those higher-order groupings as triangles, tetrahedra, and beyond. Because the algebra behind their matrices does not commute, meaning order matters when combining them, a framework by mathematician Alain Connes becomes applicable.

That spectral triplet machinery yields notions of dimension, curvature, and distance for these complexes. Such geometric features can sit beside classic topological summaries when characterizing a system. Community detection and data analysis may gain sharper fingerprints for the higher-order structures now common in network science.
arxiv-2509-04411:
J Jobst and six co-authors map the empty energy bands of three molybdenum-based layered crystals in a 2025 physics paper. The materials, the metal paired with sulfur, selenium, or tellurium, belong to a prized family of layered crystals used in electronics. Empty bands, the energy levels electrons visit only briefly, govern tests where light or impacts knock electrons out. The team measured reflected electrons at many angles for single layers and bulk stacks, producing precise spectra.

Theory for both band structure and scattering matched the data well, mainly at lower energies. A series of resonances between layers appeared, dominated by empty states of the chalcogen atoms. Tracking the series from sulfur to tellurium shows how chemistry tunes these fleeting states.
arxiv-2509-04611:
Swapping one cation for another can slow the loss of excited charge carriers in a solar material. Sanchi Monga and one co-author report that finding in a 2025 study of inorganic antiperovskite nitrides, compounds studied for photovoltaic use. They compare calcium, strontium, and barium versions, which differ in crystal structure.

Their calculations show strontium narrows the band gap and extends carrier lifetimes by reducing coupling between electrons and nuclei. A hexagonal form of the strontium compound gives the longest lifetime in their comparison. The work points to cation choice and crystal symmetry as practical levers for better solar materials.
arxiv-2509-05011:
When an electron scatters off a nucleus and emits a photon, polarisation can pass from electron to photon. Yu. M. Bystritskiy and one co-author calculate those polarisation observables exactly for the Bethe-Heitler process in a 2025 physics paper. Their calculation avoids assuming the electron mass is negligible, an approximation in earlier treatments.

They compare in detail with well-known previous works and comment on issues caused by dropping the electron mass. The results apply to modelling polarised cross sections at low energies, even down to a few electron masses. That regime matters for precision experiments where the mass cannot be ignored.
arxiv-2509-06111:
Choosing how many past values a forecast model should look at is the practical problem behind a 2025 paper by Juan Pablo Montaño and Mario E. Arrieta-Prieto. Treating lag count as a tunable knob is expensive, so the authors test association measures that need no model at all. Their focus is an adaptation of CODEC, a conditional dependence coefficient, inside a feature-ordering algorithm.

Extensive simulations across linear, nonlinear, seasonal, and unstable processes compare CODEC with Pearson and Spearman correlations. CODEC wins in nonlinear and nonstationary settings, especially with large samples, while Pearson stays better for purely linear models. On benchmark datasets the method recovers lag structures matching the literature, supporting CODEC as a handy exploratory tool for time series work.
arxiv-2509-06511:
Judging whether a brain tumor is shrinking under treatment is automated in a 2025 medical imaging paper led by Daniil Tikhonov, with nine co-authors. Glioblastoma care depends on such judgments, and standard criteria exist, but applying them is complex and readers often disagree. The method was built for the BraTS 2025 challenge.

A fine-tuned ResNet-18 network reads regions of interest from four kinds of MRI scan. Its learned features are fused with more than four thousand eight hundred radiomic and clinical features, including tumor growth and shrinkage masks, volume change, and shifts in the tumor center. A CatBoost classifier then sorts cases into complete response, partial response, stable disease, or progression. The hybrid design scored well, which the authors take as evidence that learned and hand-picked features work better together.
arxiv-2509-06911:
Readable patterns, written as regular expressions, that flag strange events are synthesized by Margarida Ferreira and six co-authors in a 2025 anomaly detection paper. In a stationary system, any deviation from past behavior may signal malicious activity. Deep learning detectors work, but their alarms are hard to explain.

Their algorithm, HyGLAD, first infers groups of entities that behave alike, using a hypergraph view of the events. It then builds regular expressions capturing the values those entities take. Because the patterns are readable, the anomalies they catch are interpretable too. Against seven unsupervised deep-learning detectors from a standard library, across five real-world datasets, HyGLAD improved precision and recall over the second-best method. It also trained and ran about ten times faster, on a single CPU rather than a graphics processor.
arxiv-2509-07111:
Zexin Hu and 6 co-authors pull out the ringdown signals of charged binary black holes in a 2025 paper. After two black holes merge, the new one settles down in a phase called ringdown. That phase offers a clean window onto gravity where the field is strongest. In theories that change gravity, the tones of this ringing, and their sizes and phases, may shift away from what general relativity predicts.

Charged black holes in Einstein-Maxwell theory are one concrete case beyond the standard Kerr picture. The team ran full general relativistic simulations, with charge-to-mass ratios up to a stated bound. From those runs they extracted the amplitudes and phases of the ringdown modes. Charge can speed up or slow down the long inspiral before the merger, they find. Yet the ringing itself, once excited, changes only a little.
arxiv-2509-07311:
Fine-tuning a large language model works best with the right training examples, but picking them is costly and unclear. Sihyun Park proposes KAMIR in a 2025 research paper. KAMIR judges training data by the model's internal representations, the number patterns inside its layers, rather than by its written answers. It compares each layer's hidden states with the final layer's states for a given input.

That comparison measures how familiar the model already is with each example. Earlier knowledge-based methods leaned on prompt engineering and mostly fit multiple choice tasks. KAMIR also works for reading comprehension and summarization. Experiments across several task datasets show a clear pattern: training on less familiar data generalizes better. The method needs only a small dataset and a simple classifier, which lowers the cost of data selection.
arxiv-2509-07411:
Yijun Lu and 2 co-authors propose an evolutionary game framework in 2025 for how self-driving cars interact on the road. With no central controller, each car must balance its passengers' demands against overall traffic flow and safety. Rule-based methods adapt poorly, optimization methods are costly, and classic game methods can be rigid or inefficient when cars should cooperate.

Evolutionary game theory lets strategies spread or fade based on how well they perform, mimicking natural selection across repeated encounters. A causal evaluation module tunes how fast strategies evolve by learning from past interactions, balancing change against stability. Simulations are reported to show gains over the older approaches the authors criticize. The framework aims at traffic that organizes itself safely without a traffic brain, a need that grows as autonomous fleets multiply.
arxiv-2509-07611:
Karen M. Leighly heads a 7-author analysis in 2025 of rare Balmer absorption in iron low-ionization broad absorption line quasars. Quasars are brilliant galactic centers whose spectra often show broad absorption from outflowing gas; the iron low-ionization class is unusual, and Balmer lines, from hydrogen, are among the rarest absorbers seen. The sample holds fourteen such quasars, eight newly identified.

The team measures velocity offset, width, and apparent optical depth for the absorption. Partial covering of the light source distorts the Balmer depth ratios, and correcting for it yields the true column density of excited hydrogen. The expected link between Eddington ratio and outflow speed appears but weakly, since most objects are slow, loitering outflows with low accretion rates. The strongest absorption sits at the lowest speeds in the least luminous objects, a pattern that constrains how these winds are launched.
arxiv-2509-07811:
Raphael Picard and 3 co-authors examine the faint background of gravitational waves in a 2025 cosmology paper. Gravitational waves are ripples in space itself. Some may arise when small early-universe fluctuations grow strong, a process called induction. The authors study extra source terms that appear at third order, a deeper level of the calculation than earlier work used.

Computing spectral densities for a radiation-filled early universe, they find these new terms lower the expected signal at the scales studied. Some terms grow stronger when the starting fluctuation spectrum is not sharply peaked. The finding matters because future detectors hunting this background need accurate predictions, and third-order effects can change what observers should expect to see.
arxiv-2509-08311:
Chest CT scans and their written reports are aligned at several scales by Rongsheng Wang and 10 co-authors in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Vision-language pretraining learns strong features from paired images and text, but CT lesions are small, sparse, and structurally intricate. Reports add another difficulty: each sentence's pathology may correspond to a small sub-region, with the mapping left implicit.

Their SimCroP framework combines similarity-driven alignment with cross-granularity pretraining, tying whole scans to reports and sub-regions to phrases together. Learning those links should produce representations that transfer better to diagnosis tasks with little labelled data. Hospitals hold millions of scan-report pairs; methods that mine them faithfully reduce dependence on scarce expert annotation.
arxiv-2509-08411:
Topological materials promise devices that shrug off local defects, but the flagship Haldane model usually demands deep cold. Jiefei Wang and 9 co-authors report realizing it at room temperature in a 2025 research paper. Their platform uses groups of warm atoms set in momentum-space lattices. Such lattices resist thermal noise by nature.

The team revealed the phase transition through emission contrast between two timed quantum states of the lattice. Working warm also unlocked a deep tuning regime that cold setups rarely reach. There, phases with high Chern numbers appeared, going beyond the traditional Haldane model. Chern numbers are the labels that classify topological phases. A warm, reconfigurable platform like this brings this physics closer to real quantum tools and to tests that deep cold priced out.
arxiv-2509-08511:
Chiang-Mei Chen and 2 co-authors show that fermions stay calm near a charged black hole where bosons run wild in a 2025 paper. The black hole is a near-extremal charged Nariai hole. Its near-horizon space is a product of a two-dimensional de Sitter part and a sphere. The team solves the Dirac equation there for a heavy charged fermion.

Emission in the thin zone between the two horizons hits the Pauli cap and stops. There is no runaway growth. An earlier study by the same group found runaway emission for spinless bosons in the same setting. A swap rule extends the fermion result to Schwinger pair creation. Spin, it turns out, polices how fast such a black hole can shed its charge.
arxiv-2509-08611:
Heat exchangers with stacked tube rows do not perform uniformly: each row lives in a different flow. Mateusz Marcinkowski and Kacper Korab quantify that row-by-row behavior in a 2025 research paper. They simulated an eight-row plate fin and tube exchanger with offset tubes and flat fins. Computational fluid dynamics revealed the flow and temperature fields in detail.

The first, second, and eighth rows transferred heat far more efficiently than the exchanger average. Which rows led depended on air speed: early rows won at low speeds, the last row at high speeds. The authors fitted a separate heat transfer correlation for each row. They traced the patterns to boundary layer growth, wake interference, and vortex shedding. Designers can use row-resolved correlations to cut exchanger size and fan power at once, trimming both purchase and operating costs.
arxiv-2509-08811:
Andrew Jun Lee and 4 co-authors propose a Bayesian model of joint action and coordination in a 2025 paper. Teamwork depends on how people influence and adapt to each other over time. Older measures capture either synchrony or direction of influence, but not both together.

Their context matrix records how much each person's current act follows their own past versus others' past. A sequential Bayesian model infers these matrices from time series data. Simulations recover them well under noise. On human eye tracking data, summary features match expected task differences and predict accuracy. The work aims for a fuller picture of interpersonal dynamics.
arxiv-2509-09311:
Illia Volkov and 3 co-authors evaluate image recognition with vision and language embeddings of vision language models in a 2025 paper. Such models enable zero shot classification through image text alignment. Their purely visual inference ability, by contrast, remains under explored.

Language guided and vision only classification are compared across many dual encoder models, including recent ones. Tests use the ImageNet validation set and a label corrected variant. Prompt design, class diversity, neighbor count, and reference set size all affect accuracy. Some classes favor text prompts, others favor visual similarity. A simple learning free fusion based on per class precision improves performance by exploiting that complementarity.
arxiv-2509-09511:
Devanshi Arora's 2025 thesis tests chromatic calorimetry, a detector idea that reads particle showers by colour of light. Layers of scintillator are stacked so each emits at a shorter wavelength than the one before. Watching how a shower's energy spreads along that stack, through amplitude shares and a centre of gravity, should sharpen both energy measurement and particle identification.

Arora reports beam tests run at CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron in 2023 and 2024, alongside GEANT4 simulations of a design based on quantum dots. Together the results check whether the approach can deliver its promised resolution and separation. The work is aimed at detectors for future machines such as the Future Circular Collider.
arxiv-2509-09811:
Evan Scannapieco and 3 co-authors refine a standard formula in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The formula describes how gas density spreads inside supersonic turbulence. That spread feeds models of star-forming clouds and other churning systems. Most fits use a lognormal curve. Its width depends on Mach number. It also depends on how the flow is driven. The usual fit skips one point. It ignores how long the driving stays in step.

The team ran simulations across many Mach numbers and driving styles. They also varied the time the driving stays in step. Squeezed flows break the old pattern, they find. Their width grows in step with Mach number instead. It also leans on that driving time in a clear way. Mixed driving barely notices the time. Swirling flows follow a rule of their own.
arxiv-2509-10111:
Dominik Sidler and 5 co-authors present a computing framework for light-matter coupling in this 2025 paper. Shining light inside optical cavities can change how molecules behave, but the reasons are still poorly understood. The problem spans scales: a cavity affects huge numbers of molecules at once, while each molecule's details feed back into the shared coupling.

Their method joins a quantum chemistry scheme, density-functional tight binding, with grid-based simulations of Maxwell's equations, treating both sides self-consistently. They use it to compute two-dimensional spectra that match laboratory protocols, to inspect single molecules inside a coupled crowd, and to test better cavity designs. Planned extensions cover warm, condensed, and more strongly quantum settings.
arxiv-2509-10311:
Marco Artiano and three co-authors develop careful numerical methods for the equations of compressible air flow in this 2025 paper, aimed at atmospheric modeling. Their formulation tracks potential temperature directly, and the challenge is to simulate storms and weather without the code slowly inventing or losing energy and entropy.

Within a discontinuous Galerkin framework on curved meshes, they construct three numerical fluxes that conserve both entropy and total energy. They extend kinetic-energy preservation to flows under gravity by treating the source term with a flux-differencing approach. The schemes stay balanced on still background states, a property weather codes need. Tests across classic atmospheric scenarios compare the new formulation favorably with the traditional equations.
arxiv-2509-10611:
Sukrit Ranjan and nine co-authors ask a pointed question in this 2025 planetary science paper. Could warm versions of Titan exist around red dwarf stars? A warm exo-Titan would carry a nitrogen-methane atmosphere, like Saturn's moon Titan. It would sit closer to its star. The James Webb Space Telescope now reads small planets' spectra, but the readings are ambiguous. Theory like this sets how much proof a claimed detection needs.

The team uses photochemical modeling, with TRAPPIST-1e as the test case. Stronger starlight destroys methane far faster on a warm exo-Titan than on Titan itself. Its lifetime shrinks to at most a tenth, and most likely a fiftieth. The chance of catching such a world is under one in ten, and likely under one in a hundred. A real claim needs support, they argue, such as oxidized carbon gases.
arxiv-2509-10711:
Subhajit Pramanick and three co-authors study a strange gathering problem for robots in this 2025 paper. Faulty robots cannot move. In the indulgent version of gathering, healthy robots must come to a faulty one's location. Meeting somewhere new is not allowed. The robots are opaque, so they block each other's view. They follow no shared clock. They signal with colored lights, in the LUMI model.

The authors first prove a negative result. Gathering is impossible for a two-robot, one-fault system with two colors. They then give an optimal three-color solution. Larger systems get two deterministic algorithms. One runs in linear time with seven colors. The other is faster, keyed to the layers of the starting formation, with twenty-six colors. Both handle unknown numbers of robots and faults. Their algorithms are the first for this setting with analyzed running times.
arxiv-2509-10911:
Stavros Garoufalidis and four co-authors study the colored Links-Gould polynomial in this 2025 paper. It is a knot invariant. Knot polynomials assign algebraic fingerprints to tangled loops. The colored versions use higher-dimensional representations to extract finer information. Here the representations come from the quantum superalgebra for sl(2|1).

The authors give a cabling formula. It covers knots colored by a family of irreducible representations. They identify the result with the V_n-polynomial, for n equal to two. From the formula flow bounds on genus. A route that specializes to the Alexander polynomial appears, too, and it does not depend on n. Those consequences settle conjectures from earlier work by two of the authors. They extend the n equal to one case. Their genus bound for the second Links-Gould polynomial is sharp. It holds for every knot up to sixteen crossings.
arxiv-2509-11311:
Social scientists increasingly use language models as stand-ins for human survey respondents, and Bingchen Wang, Zi-Yu Khoo, and Jingtan Wang test how faithful those stand-ins can be in this 2025 paper. Their framework, preference reconstruction theory, treats matching a population's tastes as a representation problem.

The system they built, Prompts to Proxies, works in two stages. First, structured prompting with adaptive sampling creates a varied pool of synthetic agents spread across the space of possible preferences. Then a regularized regression picks a small weighted ensemble whose combined answers match real survey data, with no model fine-tuning and no sensitive demographic inputs. Tested on fourteen waves of a major American survey panel and on the World Values Survey, the ensemble reproduced population answers closely at a cost of under a dollar per survey.
arxiv-2509-11411:
Nikolaos Zioulis and four co-authors fix a deformation glitch in Gaussian avatars in this 2025 computer graphics paper. Human avatars built from three-dimensional Gaussians render fast and animate by forward skinning, but the standard linear blend skinning used to move them mishandles how each Gaussian should rotate.

Earlier fixes borrowed mesh properties to rotate the Gaussians or trained networks to predict corrections. Zioulis and colleagues instead blend rotations directly, using quaternion averaging, which keeps the Gaussians simple and vertex-based. Only the skinning step changes; any standard Gaussian rasterizer can then animate the result, so the avatars drop into existing engines with little fuss. The approach trades a layer of machinery for a cleaner mathematical treatment of the same problem.
arxiv-2509-11811:
Mehwish Mehmood and four co-authors present a featherweight network for tracing retinal vessels. This 2025 medical imaging paper treats vessel segmentation. It underpins early diagnosis of diseases that threaten sight and more. The best deep models are heavy. The clinics that need them most have the least computing power.

Their LFRA-Net puts its focal modulation attention right where encoder meets decoder, at the bottleneck. Region-aware attention sits in selected skip connections. Local detail and global context both sharpen. The parameter count stays well under a fifth of a million. On the DRIVE, STARE, and CHASE_DB sets, the network beat many state-of-the-art models. It led on overlap scores in each. The gain per unit of compute is the real advance.
arxiv-2509-11911:
Antonin Sulc teaches a neural network the equation governing a noisy quantum system. This 2025 quantum computing paper is a solo effort. Characterizing how a quantum device interacts with its environment is a bottleneck. Traditional tomography is data-hungry and scales poorly.

The framework performs Lindblad tomography with physics-informed neural networks. The Lindblad master equation sits directly in the network's loss. Sparse time-series measurements train it. The state's evolution is rebuilt. The unknown dissipation parameters are inferred at the same time. Even their functional form comes out. The result is a fully differentiable digital twin of the noisy system. Little data is needed. The method offers a sample-efficient, scalable route to characterizing real quantum hardware.
arxiv-2509-12011:
Robots that run a whole materials synthesis line, not just one instrument, are the subject of a 2025 report by Wei-Sheng Wang and two co-authors. Their target is bulk intermetallic compounds, alloys whose experimental checking has lagged behind computer predictions of promising new materials.

The team built an automated arc melting system orchestrated through ROS2, the robot operating system, chosen because it lets one controller coordinate several different machines at once and accept new ones later. The setup repeats a chosen procedure unattended and can also switch among multiple elements to produce different compounds. By removing repetitive manual work, the authors expect fewer human errors and much faster experimental testing of candidates that data-driven searches propose.
arxiv-2509-12111:
Black holes that absorb and emit quanta, Hawking radiation included, are rebuilt from on-shell scattering amplitudes by Katsuki Aoki and four co-authors in 2025. The point of the on-shell program is to skip gauge-dependent middlemen and speak only in physical processes.

Starting from quantum field theory on a Schwarzschild background, the authors set up the Boulware and Unruh vacuum states and their S-matrices. Absorptive amplitudes for a hole changing mass by swallowing or emitting a quantum follow to all orders in the gravitational coupling, with each black hole's identity carried by the amplitudes' discontinuities. Hawking's thermal spectrum emerges from simple three-point processes. In a binary, a companion's motion shifts the hole's mass; the average shift is classical, while its spread depends on the vacuum.
arxiv-2509-12211:
Small language models still cost too much memory and time when they answer one token at a time, because each step rereads a growing cache of past keys and values. Dong Liu and one co-author present TinyServe in 2025, a serving system built for tiny models on modest hardware.

TinyServe skips most of that cache. A query-aware method scores blocks of the cache by how relevant they look, loads only the useful ones, and runs the attention math in a single fused graphics kernel. Tests report speedups above threefold and memory savings above twofold, with almost no loss in accuracy, plus checks on cache reuse and multi-card scaling.
arxiv-2509-12611:
Anmol Singhal and Navya Singhal propose a prompting method for financial sentiment study in a 2025 paper. Judging whether financial news is positive or negative helps anticipate market movements. Language models understand text well, but current methods often miss complex economic context and lack transparent thinking, which undermines reliability.

Their system, Analogy-Driven Financial Chain-of-Thought, guides a model to draw parallels between a new event and relevant historical scenarios with known outcomes. Those analogies are embedded into a structured, step-by-step thinking chain before predicting sentiment. The approach works purely through prompting, with no extra training data or fine-tuning, and draws on the model's internal financial knowledge. The authors present it as among the first to combine analogical cases with chain-of-thought thinking in finance.
arxiv-2509-12911:
