Abdellah El Mrini, Sadegh Farhadkhani, and Rachid Guerraoui propose a safer way for many machines to learn together in a 2025 arXiv paper. In collaborative learning, groups train one shared model by exchanging updates. Some participants may act as adversaries and send poisoned updates on purpose. Older defenses need a central server or force every node to talk with every other, which grows costly fast.

Their method, RPEL, drops the central server and uses pull-based epidemic spread. Each node pulls model parameters from a small random subset of peers, then updates its own copy. Message counts grow far slower than with all-to-all exchange as networks expand. The authors prove convergence still holds with high probability under attack. Experiments showed RPEL stayed robust in adversarial settings and matched all-to-all accuracy. It also scaled well across large networks in their tests.
arxiv-2510-08611:
Jason Hawkins estimates how land use shapes fossil fuel carbon emissions across the United States in a 2025 arXiv paper. Emissions vary with development patterns, climate, economic mix, and energy sources, many of which planning and policy can influence. He uses the Vulcan version 3.0 data set, which estimates fossil-fuel carbon dioxide on a one-kilometer grid nationwide. Analysis runs at neighborhood and metropolitan scales to expose scale effects.

A data-driven propensity score approach builds doubly robust causal estimates for several land use features, by sector. Preliminary results suggest local density alone does not significantly change per-capita transport emissions, once metropolitan density is controlled. Hawkins cautions this may reflect how the Vulcan data set allocates transportation emissions across the grid. Results for residential electricity, called scope 2, and non-electricity energy are also examined. The study links climate flux data with causal inference tools.
arxiv-2510-08711:
Jiachen Jiang, Zhen Qin, and Zhihui Zhu teach wireless equalizers to adapt on the fly with in-context learning in a 2025 arXiv paper. Equalization undoes channel distortions like frequency-selective fading and inter-symbol interference in MIMO systems. Supervised equalizers need retraining for each new channel, which is costly. In-context learning adapts at inference from a few examples instead, but prior work assumed static channels.

Real channels vary within the context window itself, a non-stationary setting theory had not covered. The authors design attention mechanisms guided by classical adaptive signal processing algorithms. Variants derive from the Least Mean Square algorithm, a robust root-mean-square version, and multi-step gradient updates for long-term tracking. Experiments show in-context learning holds strong promise for time-varying MIMO equalization. Attention inspired by adaptive algorithms substantially improved adaptability and performance in dynamic environments.
arxiv-2510-09011:
Qu and colleagues build a benchmark that grades AI travel plans the way a seasoned traveler would, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Planning a trip mixes budgets, opening hours, distances, and taste, and even strong language models produce plans that collapse on contact with reality. Existing tests score plans too coarsely to catch infeasible legs or joyless itineraries. TripScore folds fine-grained criteria into one unified reward, so plans can be ranked directly and the reward can train models.

Their automated evaluator agreed moderately with human travel experts and beat several judge-model baselines. The released dataset holds nearly five thousand planning queries, including over two hundred genuine free-form requests from real users. The team then compared prompting tricks, symbolic hybrids, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning across many models. Reinforcement learning generally improved feasibility most, lifting unified reward above both prompt-only and supervised approaches.
arxiv-2510-09211:
Li and co-authors fix a common frustration with big language models: they reason well, then ignore the strict output format the user demanded, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Retraining the big model is costly and often impossible, since its parameters may be closed. Their framework, DICE, splits the job in two. The large model first answers freely in natural language, keeping its knowledge and reasoning. Then a small language model, cheap to train, inspects and repairs the answer.

The small model is fine-tuned on specially built datasets and works in an analyze-then-answer pattern. In experiments, DICE lifted the average format accuracy of large-model outputs by about thirty-five percent and their content correctness by about twenty-nine percent. Those gains topped the competing baselines the team tested. It offers structured outputs from powerful models without touching the big model's weights.
arxiv-2510-09411:
Amir Bahador Javadi and Philip Pong compare two data-driven ways to model a power grid device in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their system is a grid-forming converter tied to an infinite bus, a device that helps renewable sources feed a stable grid. Knowing its dynamics, meaning how it reacts to disturbances, is critical as renewables spread.

The authors generate synthetic data simulating disturbances in active power, in reactive power, and in voltage settings. On that data they train two methods that learn equations from measurements: sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics, or SINDy, and deep symbolic regression. Symbolic regression captured the complex behaviour more accurately, but it needed far more computing time. Sparse identification ran much faster with somewhat lower fidelity. The authors conclude that the faster method suits real-time grid use, while symbolic regression offers accuracy when time allows.
arxiv-2510-09711:
Wenbin Guo, Xin Wang, Jiaoyan Chen, Lingbing Guo, Zhao Li, and Zirui Chen connect knowledge graphs with language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Knowledge graph completion predicts missing links between entities, and language models bring strong reasoning to the task. The mismatch is representational: graph embeddings live in a continuous space, while language models read discrete tokens, so the structured knowledge transfers poorly.

Their framework, ReaLM, discretises pretrained graph embeddings through residual vector quantization, a staged compression that turns each embedding into a short code sequence. Those codes enter the language model's vocabulary as learnable tokens, fusing symbolic and contextual knowledge. Ontology-guided class constraints further refine predictions by checking class-level compatibility. On two widely used benchmark datasets, ReaLM reached state-of-the-art performance. The authors present it as confirmation that quantised embeddings can align structured knowledge with large-scale language models.
arxiv-2510-09811:
Ogievetsky and Pavel Pyatov study quantum matrices in this 2025 arXiv paper in algebra. A quantum matrix algebra is a deformed version of the algebra of matrices, where the entries obey rules set by a parameter q. The authors look at the orthogonal family of these algebras and at one special part of each algebra, its characteristic subalgebra.

That part is commutative, meaning its elements can be multiplied in any order. The team shows that the basic sums that build this part are not free of each other in the orthogonal case, unlike the symplectic case. They obey a set of square-law relations, which the authors call reciprocal relations. The pair then solves these relations and works out how the quantum determinant interacts with the other generators.
arxiv-2510-09911:
Meng, David Salvador Novo, Albert H. Werner, and Samir Bhatt give a quantum algorithm with a full end-to-end analysis in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such complete analyses are rare for problems of practical interest. Their target sits in bioinformatics: the Binary Near-Perfect Phylogeny Problem, which asks for an evolutionary tree that almost perfectly explains species traits.

The team first presents the quantum algorithm for that phylogeny problem, with an explicit complexity bound. They then connect it to the Minimum Steiner Tree problem, a classic network design problem where extra junction points may shorten the tree. The link lets the phylogeny result speak to a broader class of problems. The paper stresses practical relevance over asymptotic promise alone.
arxiv-2510-10611:
Heng Zhang and seven co-authors redesign how language model agents talk to each other, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Most multi agent systems model communication as pairwise links, like edges in a graph. That misses group collaboration, where several agents work one subtask together. Fixed communication patterns also waste effort on simple tasks and under-coordinate on hard ones. The team's framework, HyperAgent, uses hypergraphs, where one hyperedge can join many agents at once.

Hypergraph convolutional layers then aggregate information across a whole group in a single step. A variational autoencoder with sparsity pressure adjusts the communication topology to match task complexity. On the GSM8K math benchmark, HyperAgent reached 95.07 percent accuracy while cutting token consumption by 25.33 percent compared with the baselines studied. The authors argue that hypergraph based topology design gives multi agent systems both better performance and better efficiency as they scale.
arxiv-2510-11011:
Farzaneh Zirak, Farhana Choudhury, and Renata Borovica-Gajic teach a database to fetch data before it is asked for, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Prefetching loads data into cache ahead of requests, cutting wait times. Pattern based prefetchers miss complex access behavior, and learning based ones often need the full dataset and frequent retraining, which privacy rules may forbid. Their GrASP prefetcher learns from samples instead. It models the gaps between logical block addresses and mixes query representations with encodings of past results.

Prefetching is framed as context aware multi label classification, with stacked LSTM networks predicting the gap patterns. In experiments on real datasets and industrial benchmarks, GrASP generalized to datasets 250 times larger than its training data. It reached up to 45 percent higher hit ratios, 60 percent lower input output time, and 55 percent lower query latency than existing baselines. Its average hit ratio was 91.4 percent.
arxiv-2510-11211:
Today's largest language models are so big that hardly any single computer can train or even run them, so the field splits the work across many machines. Sheikh Azizul Hakim and Saem Hasan survey that distributed computing landscape for language models in this 2025 arXiv explorative study. They examine the techniques from two angles: making big models accessible, and serving them efficiently once trained.

On the accessibility side, they study how large models can run on consumer-grade computers, and they implement a novel modification based on metaheuristics to an existing system of that kind. On the serving side, they carry out a comparative study of three state-of-the-art techniques for running language model inference at scale. The paper maps the trade-offs between democratizing access to large models and operating them as services, a practical orientation for researchers choosing infrastructure under tight hardware budgets.
arxiv-2510-11311:
Thomassen's conjecture from 1983 says that any graph with high enough minimum degree contains a dense subgraph whose shortest cycle is long. Micha Christoph, Barnabás Janzer, Kalina Petrova, and Raphael Steiner ask what happens for directed graphs in this 2025 arXiv combinatorics paper. Replacing degree by out-degree, they study which directed patterns are avoidable, meaning a high-out-degree subdigraph free of that pattern always exists inside any sufficiently dense host.

Their main results split the landscape. All orientations of the triangle and of the five-cycle turn out to be avoidable. In contrast, one-directed orientations of complete bipartite graphs and all oriented trees are not avoidable, so the most direct extension of Thomassen's conjecture to digraphs is false. The authors fully characterize which digraphs are avoidable when the host graphs are regular. They close with open problems to spark further progress on the directed theory.
arxiv-2510-11411:
Approximating a function that decays rapidly on one side of the real line but not the other is a classic numerical headache. The efficient Sinc approximation wants decay in both directions. Tomoaki Okayama improves the standard remedy in this 2025 arXiv numerical analysis paper. The remedy is a change of variables that makes the function decay on both sides; earlier transformations by Stenger and successors achieved only root-exponential convergence for such one-sided functions.

Okayama proposes a new transformation of double-exponential type, layering hyperbolic sine and logarithm functions so the transformed variable squeezes the line far harder. He derives an error bound for the resulting approximation formula. The bound shows the method achieves almost exponential convergence, a big improvement over the root-exponential rate of earlier methods. Numerical tests confirm the theory, validating the new transformation for one-sided rapidly decreasing functions.
arxiv-2510-11511:
The Tate-Shafarevich group measures how badly an abelian variety fails a local-to-global principle, and Iwasawa theory predicts how it grows across towers of number fields. Erman Işık and Antonio Lei extend that theory to a harder case in this 2025 arXiv number theory paper. Their case is p-supersingular abelian varieties of GL2 type with real multiplication, over Zp-extensions.

Building on Iovita and Pollack's work on elliptic curves, and under precise ramification and splitting conditions on the prime, they construct systems of local points using Lubin-Tate groups. From those points they define signed Coleman maps and signed Selmer groups, a plus-minus splitting. Assuming the signed Selmer groups are cotorsion, they prove the Mordell-Weil rank stays bounded over all subextensions of the tower. They also give an asymptotic formula for the growth of the prime-above-p part of the Tate-Shafarevich group.
arxiv-2510-11611:
Primordial black holes, a dark matter candidate, are usually explained by dense regions collapsing under their own gravity. Cristian Joana and Zi-Yan Yuwen study the opposite starting point in this 2025 arXiv cosmology paper: primordial voids, regions of negative curvature perturbation emptier than their surroundings. Using numerical relativity simulations, they ask whether a deep enough void can still end as a black hole.

The simulations show it can. A deep void rebounds at its center, and the rebound piles matter into an effective overdensity that collapses into a primordial black hole. The authors find the critical depth threshold for this process across equations of state. The black holes born this way obey a scaling relation analogous to the standard overdensity case. The results establish primordial voids as a new formation channel, with consequences for predicted black hole abundances.
arxiv-2510-11811:
Matilde Gianocca studies minimal surfaces inside spheres, a classic topic in differential geometry. A minimal surface is a critical point of both area and energy, meaning small deformations change neither to first order. The two viewpoints diverge at second order, where the energy index counts unstable directions. It is known that when a surface's first eigenvalue is at least two, inside the three-sphere its energy index stays at most four.

Gianocca proves a partial converse in this 2025 arXiv note. If the first eigenvalue for a minimal surface in the three-sphere drops below one sixth, she constructs a deformation field with negative second variation. The field is chosen perpendicular to the four special Möbius fields, so the instability is genuinely new. She also proves a version in spheres of any dimension and any codimension. There the threshold becomes a dimension-dependent fraction.
arxiv-2510-12011:
Bei Zhou and five colleagues move heart simulations from supercomputers onto graphics cards. Cardiac electrophysiology models trace electrical waves through heart tissue to explain arrhythmias and guide treatment. The finite element versions are accurate but traditionally demand large CPU clusters, shutting out many clinics and labs. Their paper, published in SoftwareX and posted on arXiv in 2025, presents TorchCor, a Python library built on PyTorch that runs these simulations on GPUs.

TorchCor accelerates the calculations significantly, especially for large three-dimensional meshes of heart geometry. The team verified the solver's accuracy two ways: against manufactured analytical solutions with known answers, and against the community's N-version benchmark problem. Both checks passed, so the speed does not come from cutting physical corners. The library is free for academic and commercial use without restrictions. Its aim is heart modeling within reach of ordinary groups.
arxiv-2510-12111:
Aakash Lahoti, Tanya Marwah, Ratish Puduppully, and Albert Gu build one model that reads sequences, images, and graphs natively. Transformers dominate all three, but attention treats data as an unordered set, so topology must be smuggled in through position embeddings or random walks. Their 2025 arXiv paper, Chimera, instead generalizes state space models, which need no position embeddings, to arbitrary graph topology.

The results span modalities. Chimera beats BERT on the GLUE language benchmark by zero point seven points, and the Vision Transformer on ImageNet by two point six percent. On the Long Range Graph Benchmark it outperforms every baseline. Efficiency gets attention too: on directed acyclic graphs the model runs as a linear-time recurrence. For general graphs, a mathematical relaxation matches the transformer's quadratic cost without domain-specific biases. The authors read this as vindication of an old belief in topology as bias.
arxiv-2510-12311:
Marks, Wang, and Akyildiz develop particle based algorithms for training latent variable models whose prior is an energy based model, in a 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Latent variable models explain data through hidden factors, and an energy based prior assigns low energy to plausible hidden states. Training such models by maximum marginal likelihood, which scores only the observed data, is difficult because the hidden factors must be averaged out.

The authors build on recent particle methods for maximum marginal likelihood estimation. They define stochastic differential equations, continuous time random processes, whose solutions provably solve the fitting problem for latent energy based models. Discretizing these equations gives a practical interacting particle Langevin dynamics algorithm, in which many particles move together and share information. They prove the algorithm converges. Experiments on synthetic and image data sets show it learns such models well.
arxiv-2510-12411:
Marques-Chaves and a large team study extremely bright star forming galaxies shining near the end of cosmic reionization, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Their sample holds twenty seven very bright galaxies at redshift around six, drawn from the SHELLQs survey of faint quasars. Such bright systems efficiently produce ionizing photons, the radiation that reionized the early universe.

Stacking their ultraviolet spectra reveals a prominent nitrogen feature consistent with very young stellar populations, about six million years old. Their average ionizing photon production efficiency is high. For one galaxy, telescope data show a compact young starburst with mass and star formation surface densities about one hundred times typical values. Spectroscopy reveals strong nebular emission, high electron density, and a super solar nitrogen to oxygen ratio. Broad line components signal powerful outflows that appear heavily dust obscured, while the stellar continuum is nearly dust free.
arxiv-2510-12711:
Talha, Smida, and González study systems that sense radar targets and carry communications on the same hardware, when targets smear across both angle and range, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Integrated sensing and communication is a design goal for future wireless networks. Each target is modelled as a cluster of rays described by a density function whose parameters must be estimated.

The authors propose a truncated version of the MUSIC spread algorithm, a classical direction finding method, which limits the signal subspace rank using the eigen decomposition of the received signal's autocorrelation. A second, Fourier transform based algorithm estimates each target's distance and range spread. With these estimates they build a dynamic transmit beamforming scheme that illuminates several targets while serving several downlink communication users at once. Simulations show the proposed algorithms beat baseline schemes at low and high signal to noise ratios.
arxiv-2510-12811:
Karbab and Debbabi present TrapNet in this 2025 arXiv paper, a system for sorting malware without human labeling. Hundreds of thousands of new malicious programs appear daily, far too many for analysts to inspect one by one. A practical first step is grouping samples by semantic similarity, meaning similarity in what the code actually does, so known families can be recognized quickly.

TrapNet first unpacks disguised binaries, then builds a short numerical fingerprint for each sample from its ordered assembly instructions using a new fuzzy hashing method based on principal component analysis. Those fingerprints let it build a similarity network across many samples at once. Community detection algorithms then carve the network into dense groups matching malware families, and evaluations showed strong coverage and purity with faster runtimes than leading alternatives.
arxiv-2510-12911:
Simsek uses candlestick data to estimate spot covariance in this 2025 arXiv paper. Spot covariance measures how assets move together at a moment in time. It is usually estimated from high-frequency returns over short windows. That forces a trade-off between statistical accuracy and staying local in time. Candlesticks instead record open, high, low, and close prices, carrying extra information standard returns discard.

Simsek's framework exploits that extra range information to improve accuracy while preserving local structure. He adds a statistical test for spot covariance with good size control and notably higher power in small samples. Applying one-minute candlesticks from the full year 2024 to a large Bitcoin trust fund, he found systematic deviations from market neutrality, especially during market stress. An event study around Federal Reserve announcements showed the method detecting subtle shifts after mild news.
arxiv-2510-13011:
Qian and colleagues present Deliberate Lab in this 2025 arXiv paper, an open-source platform for running real-time social experiments with humans and AI agents together. Behavioral scientists increasingly want to study how people interact and decide alongside artificial intelligence. Few platforms support live multi-party studies at scale, though. Most deployments need custom engineering, and existing tools rarely treat AI agents as first-class participants.

Deliberate Lab lets experimenters create, facilitate, and intervene in live online experiments mixing human participants with language model agents. The authors report a twelve-month public deployment involving dozens of experimenters and more than nine thousand participants. They also analyze usage patterns and workflows from that deployment. Case studies and interviews with experimenters round out the report, which argues the platform lowers technical barriers and standardizes hybrid human-AI work on collective decision-making.
arxiv-2510-13511:
Svintradze presents a new geometric route toward the Poincaré conjecture using the calculus of moving surfaces. His 2025 arXiv paper reformulates the famous problem through evolving hypersurfaces in space. A compact surface moves under a velocity field tied to its own curvature. Smooth flow preserves the surface's topology the whole time, by construction.

A variational energy principle singles out constant mean curvature surfaces as the unique resting states. Any compact simply connected surface therefore relaxes toward such an equilibrium, he argues. In the symmetric case, that equilibrium is the round sphere, by a classical theorem. Unlike Ricci flow, the approach claims to work in all dimensions without surgery. Ricci flow needed cuts to handle singularities in its celebrated proof. Svintradze frames the method as one analytic framework joining dynamics, topology, and equilibrium geometry.
arxiv-2510-13811:
Witte and co-authors test whether a fine-tuned chatbot can help heritage professionals write clearer public guidance. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds HAZEL, an assistant tuned on heritage conservation and interpretation documents. Guidance from bodies like Historic England must be accurate yet readable by everyone. Generative AI might speed the drafting, but its limits need mapping first.

The team scores HAZEL against plain ChatGPT, built on GPT-4, across guidance-writing tasks. Quantitative assessments give HAZEL a slight edge over the general model. Fine-tuning on domain material, they conclude, does help with this specialist writing. Serious limits remain in areas needing cultural sensitivity or deep technical expertise. The authors are clear that AI cannot replace heritage professionals for technical authoring. Still, automating routine drafting steps could help resource-stretched organisations. The study is among the first to probe generative AI inside professional heritage practice.
arxiv-2510-13911:
Zhang and co-authors diagnose mouth diseases and describe them in words with OralGPT, a two-stage vision-language model. Their 2025 arXiv paper addresses oral mucosal diseases whose look-alike appearances confuse non-specialists. Leukoplakia, lichen planus, and recurrent ulcers overlap visually in frustrating ways. No large annotated dataset existed for this corner of medicine.

Stage one teaches the model visual concepts from classification labels alone. Stage two builds fluent description skills from long expert-written captions. A similarity-guided augmentation spreads those captions from expert-labelled images to weakly labelled look-alikes. The team also assembled the first benchmark dataset for oral mucosal diseases. It merges multi-source images with structured and free-text annotations for training and testing. On four common conditions, OralGPT matched competitive diagnostic accuracy. Its generated descriptions stayed fluent and clinically meaningful, the authors report.
arxiv-2510-14011:
Saman Hosseini and co-authors build a forecasting model for West Nile virus that deliberately needs very little surveillance data, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Many existing forecasts lean on mosquito or bird monitoring, which some regions simply do not collect. West Nile virus spreads from birds to people through mosquito bites, and predicting when outbreaks start and how severe they become guides spraying and public warnings.

Their model couples a temperature-driven compartmental simulation, which tracks the infection cycle, with statistical density estimation that needs no fixed formula. Together these produce a probability surface over mosquito abundance and accumulated warmth. Calibrated only on records of human cases, the model issues reliable forecasts months before the transmission season. Tested across six counties in California, Texas, and Florida with very different climates and ecology, it agreed strongly with observed outcomes on multiple performance measures.
arxiv-2510-14611:
Klar and co-authors present, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a computer model of how people point and click with a mouse. Most pointing models are built on optimal feedback control, a theory of how the brain corrects movement. The authors instead use active inference, a framework where an agent acts to make its observations match its preferences, such as seeing the cursor land on a button.

Their agent works with continuous states and a realistic delay in perception, and it plans by minimizing a quantity called expected free energy. In simulation, the agent produced believable pointing movements and clicked once the cursor was over the target. Its end-point spread matched that of human users. The agent also adjusted to easier and harder targets without retuning. Its delay handling is fully probabilistic, unlike earlier models. The authors discuss how hard such agents are to configure for continuous tasks.
arxiv-2510-14711:
Glaser, Widmann, Lindsten, and Gretton introduce, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a statistical test for whether a probabilistic model's stated confidence matches reality. A calibrated model that says seventy percent should be right about seventy percent of the time. Checking this for models with well-defined scores has usually required expensive approximations of expectations, which muddies the test's reliability.

Their test, KCCSD, is non-parametric and kernel-based, built from Stein's method for goodness of fit. Two ideas make it fast. A new family of kernels for score-based probabilities can be estimated without ever sampling from a probability density. And the test statistic uses a conditional criterion that keeps control over the type-I error, the rate of false alarms. The authors demonstrate the test's behavior across a range of synthetic settings. It offers a calibration check for probabilistic models used in forecasting and machine learning.
arxiv-2510-15011:
Serafin and Nitka bring, in a 2025 arXiv paper, two old forecasting tricks to a market where they had been oddly neglected: electricity prices. Choosing which historical window calibrates a model, and combining several models' forecasts, are simple, cheap tools repeatedly proven elsewhere. The authors apply the Autoregressive Hybrid Nearest Neighbors method, which uses both, to long price series from three markets: Germany, Spain, and New England.

The method beat popular literature benchmarks on forecast accuracy by up to ten percent. Two simplified variants the authors propose cut computation time vastly, with only minor losses in accuracy, making the approach practical for daily operations. A case study tests whether the forecasts earn money. A battery storage system trading on them, buying low and selling high, captured up to eighty percent of the theoretical maximum profit. The authors read this as demonstrated business value, not just statistical improvement.
arxiv-2510-15111:
Yunchao Zhang and T. Senthil explore a strange boundary between two seemingly boring phases of quantum matter in their 2025 arXiv paper. Both phases are atomic insulators, materials with no topological order, no protected edge behavior, and no exotic features. They still count as distinct, because in one the electron clouds center away from the actual atomic sites, blocking any smooth path between the two.

At the transition point itself, the authors find something far richer: an emergent form of quantum electrodynamics, the theory of electric charges and light, arising on its own. Whether that delicate state survives depends on how the crystal's symmetries restrain magnetic monopole defects, which would otherwise destroy it. Using anomaly matching, a consistency check between microscopic and large-scale descriptions, they confirm the state can genuinely arise from a local lattice model.
arxiv-2510-15211:
Yongchan Kwon and four colleagues at Stanford test a blind spot in reasoning models: whether they obey user instructions inside their own thinking, not just in final answers. Their 2025 arXiv paper argues that hidden reasoning traces that ignore instructions are harder to control and easier to misuse for shortcuts or fabricated steps. They built ReasonIF, a benchmark covering six kinds of instructions, from reasoning in a chosen language to limits on format and length.

Across open models including GPT-OSS, Qwen3, and DeepSeek-R1, fewer than a quarter of reasoning traces followed the given instructions, even for the best model. Compliance got worse as the underlying tasks grew harder. The team tried two fixes: letting models reason over several turns, and finetuning on synthetic instruction data. The finetuning raised one model's score from 0.11 to 0.27, a real gain the authors say still leaves much room to improve.
arxiv-2510-15411:
Jun Nian, Leopoldo A. Pando Zayas, and Cong-Yuan Yue repair a broken corner of the theory linking fluids to black holes. Their 2025 arXiv paper works on the fluid-gravity correspondence, which translates black hole physics into fluid equations. At very low temperatures the translation produced logarithmic terms that made the fluid description nonlocal in time, signaling a breakdown.

The fix imports recent quantum insights from near-extremal black hole physics, where a low-dimensional gravity theory captures quantum fluctuations in the black hole's throat. Averaging those quantum modes into the fluid adds a new length scale and restores a consistent local description. With the limits taken in the right order, the troublesome logarithmic divergence disappears. The authors then work out how every relevant fluid mode disperses. One striking result revisits a famous bound on viscosity relative to entropy, which the quantum corrections violate at the lowest temperatures.
arxiv-2510-15511:
Giorgos Nikolaou and five colleagues prove a surprising fact about language models: no two different inputs ever produce the same internal representation. Their 2025 arXiv paper challenges the intuition that nonlinear layers and normalization should sometimes collapse distinct inputs together. If representations never collide, the exact input text can in principle be recovered from a model's hidden activations.

The team proves injectivity for transformer models, showing the property holds at initialization and survives training. They then ran billions of collision tests on six leading models and found not a single collision. To make the property usable, they built SipIt, an algorithm that reconstructs the exact input from hidden activations with a proven linear-time guarantee. Tests confirmed exact recovery in practice. The authors point to consequences for transparency and interpretability. They also flag a deployment risk, since private prompts cannot hide inside activations.
arxiv-2510-15611:
Biomedical images need noise removed, yet clean reference images are often impossible to obtain. Tomáš Chobola, Julia Schnabel, and Tingying Peng present a lightweight denoiser in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their model, Noise2Detail, trains under the Noise2Noise idea, which needs no clean targets or noise models. At inference it first smooths the image by breaking up noise patterns, then restores fine detail. The final detail comes straight from the noisy input itself, keeping real structures intact.

Wide testing shows the method beats other dataset-free approaches on image quality. It does so while using only a fraction of their computing and memory resources. Fast, cheap inference makes it practical for everyday biomedical imaging use.
arxiv-2510-15811:
Vaibhava Srivastava, Jason Rohr, and Rana Parshad wrote a 2025 paper on farming and ecology. It addresses the paradox of enrichment. The paradox predicts that added nutrients destabilise crop and pest populations. Boom-and-bust cycles should follow. Crop failure risk should rise during shocks. Yet fertiliser use has soared since the Green Revolution. Widespread yield instability has not appeared.

The authors propose that insecticides resolve the paradox. Insecticides are often applied together with fertilisers. They may act as stabilising agents. The team tested this in a modified model. Three crop-pest systems were used. They were soybean with aphids, wheat with aphids, and cabbage with diamondback moth. Fertiliser raised yields but destabilised the dynamics. Insecticides restored stability and kept harvests predictable.
arxiv-2510-15911:
Ben Abramowitz, writing alone, settles how the Sleeping Beauty puzzle interacts with smart betting under the Kelly criterion. Sleeping Beauty is a classic problem of imperfect recall: a subject wakes without knowing how many times she has woken. One route to resolve it lets Beauty bet money on her beliefs, assuming she wants to grow wealth rather than lose it.

That route often assumes, wrongly in Abramowitz's account, that she should maximise expected value. He shows two things. First, her best betting plan judged before the experiment and her best plan judged from inside a waking coincide. Second, under an asymptotically optimal plan, Beauty as a Thirder, who assigns one third to heads, cannot be trapped by diachronic Dutch books, while as a Halfer she still can be. The betting lens thus separates the two classic answers.
arxiv-2510-16111:
A L Faisst leads a team of eighty-two co-authors presenting the core survey paper of ALPINE-CRISTAL-JWST. The survey blends sharp images and spectra from three great observatories, Hubble, Webb, and ALMA, for eighteen normal galaxies. These galaxies shine as they were when the universe was young, between one and two billion years old.

The data trace stars, hot gas, cold gas, and dust in each galaxy at fine scales. The galaxies prove fairly rich in heavy elements, from a tenth to seventy percent of the Sun's level. Star birth rates from unlike methods agree well. Six galaxies show hints of a feeding black hole at their core. Later papers will mine this matched data set, a rare bench mark for tests of galaxy growth theory.
arxiv-2510-16411:
Minh-Khoi Nguyen-Nhat leads five co-authors in a 2025 study on a lean way to scale AI models. The design is called Sparse Mixture of Experts. Only a few expert parts wake for each input, so size can grow cheaply. But these models cope badly when data shifts or turns dirty. Their fix adds a social graph among the experts.

Named SymphonySMoE, the graph guides which experts get each input chunk. The add-on is light and fits known models of this kind. Tests on language tasks and image tasks show clear gains. It also held up when scaled to models with billions of weights. The graph helps experts share work and stay robust.
arxiv-2510-16711:
Nishat Fiza and three co-authors explore a new use for the proton beam of the Electron-Ion Collider, a future machine built mainly to probe the inside of protons and neutrons. They ask whether a one-megawatt share of that beam could make a strong neutrino beam for long-baseline oscillation studies, with detectors placed far away.

Their simulations send the beam toward water-based scintillator detectors at two distances, nine hundred and twenty-nine hundred kilometers. Longer paths reveal more oscillation peaks and sharpen sensitivity to CP violation, a key unknown in neutrino physics. The authors note their setup uses simple error assumptions and no backgrounds. They present the plan as a physics reach estimate, not a finished design.
arxiv-2510-16911:
Sarah Al-Shareeda and three co-authors forecast home power use in a 2025 paper. Their work came from a 2025 forecasting competition on electric energy use. Sensor data there was noisy, patchy, and missing context. The task was predicting the next day of power demand.

The team shrank hourly data and filled gaps in two different ways. Missing values were replaced by averages or by fitted curves. A compact model then combined two memory-based network designs. It scored about eighty-four percent accuracy on the test data. Heat maps showed predicted demand tracking temperature trends closely. The result shows careful data cleaning can rival bigger models. It also keeps the model fast enough for live use.
arxiv-2510-17011:
Ya-Jie Wu, Tong Li, and Junpeng Hou announce a new topological state of matter in a 2025 paper. Hall effects describe sideways currents appearing in magnetic materials. Larger-spin systems can carry higher-rank spin-tensor currents too. Those currents generalize ordinary spin flow in a precise way.

The authors find insulators with a quantized spin-tensor Hall response. In these states, charge and ordinary spin currents both vanish. A special pseudo time-reversal symmetry protects the state. That protection works even though ordinary time-reversal symmetry is broken. The team fully characterizes the state's topological properties. They also explain its links to the known quantum spin Hall effect. The discovery widens the famous Hall family considerably.
arxiv-2510-17111:
Weifan Guan and three co-authors review fast vision-language-action models in this 2025 survey. Such models turn words and camera views into robot moves. They work well but need huge compute and memory. Small robots on site need quick replies with far less power.

The survey sorts fixes into four groups for clear review. One group changes the model shape itself. Others trim what the eyes feed in, how moves are made, or how training runs. Each group gets key methods and trade-offs summed up. The authors close with open problems and next steps. Builders of real robots can use the map to pick lean designs.
arxiv-2510-17311:
Public code libraries for serverless computing promise fast building, yet Eduard Marin and four co-authors find that their safety has barely been checked. Serverless computing lets builders write program logic without running their own servers, and shared repositories supply ready made parts. Marin and his co-authors give the first broad security study of these shared parts.

The team examined thousands of serverless components from five public repositories and a far larger set of setup templates from three frameworks. They found old software packages, careless handling of sensitive settings, risky setup choices, and names that invite typo based tricks. Their report closes with practical steps that builders and repository operators can use to lower these risks.
arxiv-2510-17611:
Factories need software that spots defective products, but training a separate detector for every product and every camera setup has fragmented the field. Jia Guo, leading a team with eleven co-authors, presents Dinomaly2, a single framework meant to cover image anomaly detection across products, sensors, and data types. Its guiding slogan is that less is more: simple parts, carefully arranged inside a standard reconstruction based design, beat specialised complexity.

On fifteen benchmarks, the unified model posted near perfect detection scores on two major industrial data sets and stayed strong on collections with hundreds of categories. Guo and her co-authors also show it can learn from only a handful of normal examples per class and still pass earlier fully trained models. Light adaptations extend the same core to multi-view and multi-sensor inspection.
arxiv-2510-18011:
Yu-Hsiu Huang, with six co-authors, simplifies a method that sharpens maps of cosmic shear, the slight bending of galaxy light by dark matter. Kinematic lensing adds motion data to images and cuts shape noise, but the full version needs heavy observing effort. The one-component version keeps much of the gain with less work.

Simulated forecasts test the method for future radio surveys. There it is not yet competitive, because the radio galaxies sit too shallow in distance. Deeper surveys with strong emission lines could flip the result. Survey planners get a clear rule for where this cheaper lensing route pays off.
arxiv-2510-18311:
Shadmaan Hye, with Matthew P LeGendre and Katherine E Isaacs, redesigns disassembly viewing in a 2025 paper. Disassembly is the raw instruction listing produced from a compiled program. Developers read it to see how the compiler changed their code and where speed was lost.

Their tool, DisViz, groups instructions into basic blocks while keeping execution order visible. Basic blocks are straight runs of instructions with no branches inside. A block-based mini-map gives context across thousands of instructions at once. In sessions with ten participants from four institutions, users completed analysis tasks and formed hypotheses about compiler choices. The integrated view helped them navigate large listings.
arxiv-2510-18911:
Andrew Medford and his four co-authors survey AI prospects in catalysis kinetics. The topic is intrinsic kinetics of heterogeneous reactions. Those are the rates on a catalyst's surface, before transport effects blur them. AI already speeds simulations and materials discovery. Linking surface rates to observed data is a many-to-one problem, though. It remains a key frontier.

Machine-learned force fields now explore chemical spaces quickly. Microkinetic and reactor models help as well. Operando and transient data give richer insight than before. Data quality is inconsistent, and models are complex. Those factors limit mechanistic discovery. The authors see generative and agentic AI closing the loop. Such tools can automate model building and quantify uncertainty. They can couple theory with experiment into self-driving models. The goal is understanding that is interpretable, reproducible, and transferable.
arxiv-2510-19111:
Andreas Winter gives a very simple proof of Hayashi's pinching inequality, a matrix result widely used in quantum information theory. The inequality compares a positive matrix with a scaled version of its pinched form, where parts of the matrix are removed by a projective measurement.

The short proof extends naturally to measurements whose parts carry different weights, and even to a reversed version of the inequality. As a payoff, the binary case yields a new gentle measurement lemma, where matrix ordering replaces closeness in trace norm. Gentle measurements matter because they extract information while barely disturbing a quantum state.
arxiv-2510-19711:
Sejal Babel and three co-authors describe the spectrum of an ergodic invariant measure by watching its generic points, the typical orbits that statistical theorems describe. They define regular Wiener-Wintner generic points, extending an earlier characterization of generic points for measures with discrete spectrum. The paper also studies what happens when sequences of generic points converge in the Besicovitch pseudometric.

Spectra turn out to behave well under such limits: the collections of points generic for discrete-spectrum, totally ergodic, mixing, or zero-entropy measures are all closed sets. The same closure holds for the corresponding measures under a related metric. As an application, the methods give a new proof that the Mirsky measure, built from sets of B-free numbers, has rational discrete spectrum.
arxiv-2510-19811:
Johnny Tian-Zheng Wei and nine co-authors release Hubble, a family of open-source language models built specifically to study memorization. Standard models are trained on a large English corpus, while perturbed versions get controlled insertions of sensitive text, such as book passages, biographies, and test sets, at known points in training. The core release spans one- and eight-billion-parameter models trained on up to five hundred billion tokens.

The experiments show memorization risk depends on how frequent the sensitive data is relative to corpus size, and that inserted material can be forgotten if exposure stops. The authors draw two practical lessons: dilute sensitive data in larger corpora, and place it early in training. The suite doubles as a testbed for membership inference and unlearning research.
arxiv-2510-19911:
Yoo Jung Kim and twenty co-authors show, on the sky, an imaging method that beats the diffraction limit of a single telescope. Their instrument is a photonic lantern feeding a spectrometer on the Subaru Telescope's SCExAO system. It sorts incoming light into spatial modes. That keeps phase information that plain intensity imaging throws away. Air turbulence is the main obstacle. A calibration strategy, using focal-plane images recorded at the same time, handles it.

Pointed at the classical Be star beta Canis Minoris, the system found spectral-differential spatial signals. It rebuilt images of the star's hydrogen-emitting disk. In about ten minutes it located the disk's photocenter to fifty microarcseconds. It also measured the disk's near-far side asymmetry for the first time. The result opens a route to high-resolution spectroscopy without interferometers.
arxiv-2510-20211:
Zhenning Yang and six co-authors present NSync, a system that automatically reconciles cloud Infrastructure-as-Code programs with changes made outside them. Tools like Terraform treat a configuration file as the source of truth and reshape real infrastructure to match it. Changes made through consoles or other tools are invisible to that file, causing drift that later operations may undo or trip over.

NSync works from cloud API traces, since every infrastructure change ends in API calls at the lowest layer. An agentic design uses language models to infer intent from noisy API sequences, synthesize targeted configuration updates with specialized tools, and learn from a growing base of past reconciliations. A new evaluation pipeline for injecting drift supports their testing.
arxiv-2510-20311:
Donghoon Ha and Jeong San Kim ask if best tests of quantum state chains can split by step. The tests use max-confidence rules, where the aim is to name a state with top trust. Their answer is yes, in full. The best test of a whole chain is just the best test at each step, done one by one.

The top trust for a chain comes from the top trust at each state in it. No joint test can beat that split form. The pair also give a full if-and-only-if test for best state tests under max-confidence rules. That test rounds out the proof and guides real use.
arxiv-2510-20411:
Suchir Salhan and seven co-authors build ContingentChat, a teacher-student plan to lift talk flow in a BabyLM model trained on 100 million words. Good talk flow means replies that are prompt, on point, and apt in light of the last turn. Child and carer chats show this trait at its best. A new post-train set pairs the small model with teacher demos at its own level.

Post the train step, the small model makes replies with more sound form and more links across turns. Tests with flex teacher decode plans add just small gains past that step. The team finds clear help from aimed post-train work. Full talk flow stays a hard mark for such small models.
arxiv-2510-20611:
Mirza Raquib and seven co-authors build PSO-XAI, a breast cancer find frame that pairs swarm search for trait picks with clear AI marks. Past finds shift in truth, cost much, and risk a wrong call. Machine learning can aid, but picks of traits drive both score and trust. Their swarm search cuts the trait set first, then a broad set of models makes the calls.

The frame faces 29 models in all: plain, group, net, chance, and near-case kinds. Cross-checks run through all tests, and clear marks come with each call. Scores top near 99 in 100 on all marks, with less bulk in the data. The team holds clear marks as a must for clinic trust.
arxiv-2510-20711:
Peter Milonni works alone on a small but classic question, how the energy of a simple oscillator shifts when it sits inside warm blackbody radiation. His route is direct, based on the total energy of the field and oscillator taken together as a function of how the medium bends light.

At high heat, Milonni finds the energy shift falls and the free energy shift rises, each growing with the square of the heat level. The result matches a well known finding from the mid nineteen eighties by Ford, Lewis, and O'Connell. Short notes like this one matter because they give a clean check on results that rest on far heavier methods.
arxiv-2510-21011:
Ilona van der Linden leads six co-authors on an audit of race and gender in personas that language models generate for forty one United States occupations. As generative tools increasingly portray workers, skewed portrayals can entrench stereotypes at scale.

Over one and a half million personas from four major models are compared with Bureau of Labor Statistics data. Models compress each occupation toward one dominant demographic profile, showing far less variation than the real workforce. Shifts and exaggerations relative to reality are measured per model and occupation, giving deployers concrete evidence of representational bias in generated professional imagery and text.
arxiv-2510-21111:
Weijie Zhou leads seven co-authors on active visual reasoning for multimodal models in physical environments, where views are partial and occluded rather than static and complete. People solve such problems by moving, examining, and handling objects in a loop of perception and action.

The Active Visual Reasoning task formalizes that loop for models, demanding careful information gathering through interaction before answering questions. A system named PhysVLM-AVR is built for the setting. Benchmarking active exploration matters because real robots and assistants rarely enjoy the tidy full views that standard vision tests provide.
arxiv-2510-21211:
Mithilesh K. Parit and five co-authors use scattered light to study a cloud of erbium atoms as it shifts between two quantum states. In one state the atoms form a Bose-Einstein condensate, and in the other they gather into droplets, driven by magnetic forces between the atoms.

When the cloud scatters light in a shared, amplified way called superradiance, the strength of that scattering changes in a non-steady pattern across the shift. The team also used the scattering to remove atoms quickly, then tracked how the cloud expanded to tell the two states apart, backed by calculations using a Gaussian trial form. They followed how the crossover point moves as the direction of the magnetic field changes.
arxiv-2510-21611:
Vishnu Varma, Bernhard Mueller, and Raphael Hirschi fake the churning inside a massive star just before it explodes, so that supernova simulations can start from a realistic three-dimensional state. Full convection simulations of the star's final hours exist but cost far too much to run for every exploding-star study that needs one.

Their recipe expands a synthetic velocity field in vector spherical harmonics, dialed to match the typical sizes and speeds of real convective flow in each churning zone. The fake flow obeys physical constraints: it barely compresses, carries no net rotation, and has no radial swirl component. A public Python implementation lets the supernova community generate such starting states cheaply and test how lopsided beginnings shape the explosion that follows.
arxiv-2510-22011:
Fraisse Sacré Takouchouang and Ho Tuong Vinh build a system that recognizes sign language gestures automatically, aiming to widen access for deaf communities to services such as healthcare and education. Their study, written in French, pairs two kinds of neural network with a vision tool that tracks hand landmarks.

A convolutional network reads the shape of each frame while a memory-equipped network follows how the gesture unfolds over time. The landmark extractor supplies clean keypoints instead of raw video. Built with common open tools and a live interface, the system translated gestures in real time with average accuracy around ninety-two percent. Distinct signs such as greetings and thanks scored very well, while visually similar signs were sometimes confused, a limit the authors flag for future work.
arxiv-2510-22211:
Jiazheng Zhu leads a sixteen-author team taking the ultraviolet measure of Ansky. Ansky is a galaxy whose X-ray outbursts repeat on a schedule. Such quasi-periodic eruptions are rare. They are increasingly tied to stars torn apart by black holes. Yet Ansky's slow fade looked more like an active galactic nucleus. Its restless behavior muddied the family tree.

A fresh ultraviolet spectrum tips the scales. It is strikingly featureless. None of the broad emission lines of an active nucleus appear. Its steep continuum slope matches tidal disruption events better. Against other featureless disruptions, Ansky is far dimmer. It also evolves far more slowly. That hints at a distinct subclass. An off-center intermediate-mass black hole looks unlikely as the cause. Ansky stands as evidence that these eruptions have more than one origin.
arxiv-2510-22611:
A special class of rings in abstract algebra is examined by Peter Danchev, Mina Doostalizadeh, Mehrdad Esfandiar, and Omid Hasanzadeh in a 2025 paper. In these rings, every unit, meaning an element with a multiplicative inverse, can be written as one plus an element from a radical like set.

The class extends two earlier ring classes while keeping its own special properties. Danchev and co-authors add results linking these rings to Dedekind-finite, semi-potent, and Boolean rings, and give several characterizations. They also study how the property survives common ring constructions and when group rings have it, clarifying how units interact with radical like parts.
arxiv-2510-22711:
Telling which variable causes another is hard when hidden factors affect both at once. Wei Chen, with six co-authors, tackles causal direction in 2025 for linear, non Gaussian systems where any number of latent confounders, meaning unobserved common causes, may be present.

Their method builds a higher order cumulant matrix, a summary of joint statistical patterns, in a specific way. Surprisingly, causal asymmetry shows up directly in where that matrix loses rank. The authors prove the direction can be identified, and their procedure needs no iterative search. Experiments confirm the method works and matches the theory as sample sizes grow, relaxing assumptions older methods required.
arxiv-2510-22811:
Many agents learning together must share what they learn. Jingyuan Liu, Hao Qiu, Lin Yang, and Mengfan Xu study that setting in 2025. Each agent faces a multi armed bandit problem. A bandit is a repeated choice among uncertain rewards. Agents talk over random communication graphs.

The graphs change at each time step. Edges appear by chance under an Erdos-Renyi model. The graph need not stay connected. Rewards for one arm can differ by agent. Their algorithm mixes arm elimination with random gossip. Gossip spreads estimates through chance contacts. The regret bound grows only with log time. Regret means loss versus the best global arm.
arxiv-2510-22911:
Counterfactual explanations show the smallest change that flips a decision. Daniel Sin and Milad Toutounchian present a geometric method in 2025. It aims at personalized treatment plan settings. Their method works in high dimensional spaces. It uses four steps, from model fitting to boundary search.

The method is called Segmented Sampling for Boundary Approximation. Binary search finds many discrete boundary points. The closest feasible point becomes the explanation. Immutable traits can be held fixed as constraints. Age and sex are examples of such traits. Across four datasets, distances fell versus current methods. Runtime also improved by orders of magnitude. Categorical features are handled as well.
arxiv-2510-23811:
Mehdi Nategh and two co-authors study persistence modules indexed by multi-dimensional grids, objects used in topological data analysis to track features across several parameters at once. For modules that split into simple pieces, the barcode summarizes when features appear and vanish. It is built from Young diagrams in higher dimensions, using their extended interiors.

The main theorem gives a necessary and sufficient condition, stated purely in terms of the partitions, for two such modules to share the same rank invariant. The rank invariant records the ranks of the maps between parameter points, a coarser summary than the full barcode. In the one-dimensional case, barcode and rank invariant determine each other, so the invariant is complete. The new result carries that tidy relationship into the multi-parameter world for the decomposable case, clarifying exactly what the rank invariant can and cannot see.
arxiv-2510-23911:
Arno Uhlig and two co-authors publish a reality check on cloud scheduling, built from inside SAP's own infrastructure. The dataset covers about 1,800 hypervisors and 48,000 virtual machines over thirty days, with fine-grained time-series telemetry from real enterprise workloads, including heavy S/4HANA systems. Public cloud datasets rarely offer this mix of scale and enterprise realism.

The findings expose waste and friction. CPU contention passes forty percent in places, some virtual machines wait up to 220 seconds for a processor, and host loads are badly imbalanced, with peaks near ninety-nine percent. Over eighty percent of machines use less than seventy percent of the CPU and memory they were given. From these patterns the authors derive requirements for better placement and scheduling algorithms. The full dataset is public, inviting data-driven tests of scheduling ideas on a real large-scale cloud.
arxiv-2510-24011:
Hiroki Nakano and four co-authors study what happens to readers when AI involvement in a text is disclosed. As writing assistants spread, whether to reveal their use is a live design question. The team ran a study with 261 participants and 990 responses across six kinds of communicative acts, varying how much AI help was said to be involved.

Disclosure generally hurt. Ratings of trustworthiness, caring, competence, and likability all fell, with the sharpest drops in social and interpersonal writing. Participants' own comments blamed a loss of human sincerity, reduced author effort, and a sense that AI simply does not belong in those contexts. One factor softened the blow: readers with higher AI literacy reacted less negatively, sometimes even appreciating the use. The authors close with design advice for writing tools — transparency should be context-sensitive, so honesty about AI does not needlessly cost authors their readers' trust.
arxiv-2510-24111:
Mathias Dufresne-Piché and Siva Nadarajah give a proof sketch for a striking accuracy trait of certain high order numerical schemes. The schemes, called ESFR methods, solve flow problems on unstructured grids with good stability and flexibility. Tests had long shown error that shrinks faster than expected, a trait called superconvergence, but no formal proof existed.

The authors focus on the linear advection problem with an upwind flux and trace the error in wave spread and decay. They show the trait comes from the scheme's ability to build very accurate rational approximations of the exponential function. This links the numerical result to known theory for such approximations and explains the observed extra accuracy.
arxiv-2510-24211:
Junhyuk So and three co-authors propose Speculative Coupled Decoding, a method to speed up autoregressive image generation without losing quality. Such models build an image token by token, often taking thousands of steps for one sample, which slows practical use. Earlier speculative methods gave limited speedup, hurt quality, or needed a trained draft model.

Their framework extends Speculative Jacobi Decoding and needs no training, while guaranteeing lossless results. By coupling the speculative steps in a new way, it generates several tokens in one forward pass more effectively. The authors aim for a practical accelerator that other visual generation systems can adopt directly.
arxiv-2510-24411:
Qiushi Sun and thirteen co-authors introduce OS-Sentinel, a safety framework for mobile GUI agents that operate phones through vision language models. Such agents can automate digital tasks but may also perform unsafe operations, from system compromise to privacy leakage. Detecting those risks across the vast space of mobile actions is a formidable, underexplored challenge.

To ground the work, the team built MobileRisk-Live, a dynamic sandbox with a benchmark of realistic trajectories annotated in fine detail. OS-Sentinel applies hybrid validation within realistic workflows to catch unsafe steps. The paper establishes a foundation for mobile agent safety research and a way to measure it.
arxiv-2510-24811:
Disha Sheshanarayana and Tanishka Magar make long model thought chains leaner with a check first frame called ProofSketch. Step by step thought helps chat models solve hard asks, but long chains cost time, compute, and tokens. Their frame mixes a closed form check step with a short draft of the proof path.

A rank based check grades each draft, and the draft grows or shrinks to fit the ask. That loop trims waste while it guards the right path. In tests, ProofSketch cut token use while right rates rose at the same time. The pair pitch it as a path to thought that is both cheap and checked.
arxiv-2510-24911:
Alessandro Santini, Stefano Barison, and Filippo Vicentini mix classic and quantum steps to map the tones of a molecule's acts. Such tone maps, or spectra, come from how a system replies over time when it is poked. Full classic runs stall at long times, while pure quantum runs face hard state setup.

Their plan sets a poked ground state on a classic machine, then runs short quantum steps from states drawn off it. Those runs span a small space where long time acts can then be run the classic way. On test molecules, the maps matched exact math well, with thin circuits and few samples. Long time scales past pure classic reach came in view.
arxiv-2510-25411:
Sana Hafeez, Ghulam E Mustafa Abro, and Hifza Mustafa model quantum threats. Their 2025 paper secures drone corridors in 6G networks. Unmanned aerial corridors need integrated sensing and contacts. They also improve situational awareness for operators. Yet those surfaces present new security vulnerabilities.

Quantum computing raises harvest-now-decrypt-later attack risks. Quantum-enhanced spoofing also threatens these systems. Their Quantum-Resilient Threat Modelling approach addresses both. It integrates classic, quantum-ready, and quantum-aided adversaries. Post-quantum cryptography supplies countermeasures in their design. ML-KEM handles key establishment for secure links. Falcon gives authentication within control signalling. Scene watermarking strengthens security sensing through coded surfaces. Their utility metric jointly optimizes secrecy and throughput. Monte Carlo tests used urban canyon channel models. Spoof finding approached near certainty at low false alarms.
arxiv-2510-25511: Giovanni Bazzoni and Giorgia Petracci finish a sorting task in pure geometry. Their 2025 paper covers seven-part nilpotent Lie groups. Each group has a left-fixed, purely coclosed G2 form on it. Past work sorted the groups that split into parts. It also sorted the groups that do not split, up to step four. This paper sorts the rest: the non-split groups at steps five and six.
arxiv-2510-25611:
Thomas E Cecil and Patrick J Ryan present an updated differential geometry paper. Their 2025 version updates a 1979 conference paper. Original exposition appears together with new notes. Those notes reference progress since the original version. The main result concerns compact isoparametric hypersurfaces. Such surfaces sit inside a sphere in Euclidean space.

Every such hypersurface is tight, they prove. Tightness means height functions have minimal critical points. Morse inequalities set that minimum number required. Since the hypersurface lies in the sphere, tautness follows. Spherical distance functions also have minimal critical points. A second result covers focal submanifolds of hypersurfaces. Those focal submanifolds must also be taut in sphere. Proofs rest on Munzner fundamental structural work. That work describes families of isoparametric hypersurfaces. Updated notes connect old results to modern progress. Readers gain both classic proof and current context. Tight embeddings remain central in global differential geometry.
arxiv-2510-26211:
Yuwei Ou and Yunying Wang settle the stability of a symmetric planetary configuration for elliptical orbits. In the planar n body problem, a regular n gon central configuration generates an elliptic relative equilibrium, a solution where the polygon keeps its shape while each body follows a Kepler ellipse. Moeckel had shown spectral instability for the circular case, at zero eccentricity, for all n of at least three, but the elliptical range stayed open.

Ou and Wang prove spectral instability for every eccentricity from zero up to one and every n of at least three. They introduce a related beta system tied to the Lagrange solution and a method that tests hyperbolicity at finitely many points to map large hyperbolic regions. For three, four, and five bodies, the instability is hyperbolic throughout.
arxiv-2510-26311:
Ruilin Tong, Haodong Lu, Yuhang Liu, and Dong Gong improve data free continual learning by synthesizing old data from the model itself. Continual learning trains a model on a sequence of tasks without forgetting earlier ones, but storing old data for replay is often barred by privacy or security. Model inversion generates synthetic inputs from a trained model, yet generating from compressed output labels alone causes drift from real data, and full model inversion is expensive.

Their per layer model inversion optimizes one layer at a time. The idea comes from faster convergence in single layer problems. It provides a strong starting point for full inversion and cuts iterations sharply. Layer specific modeling and alignment then reduce the drift between synthetic and real data, which matters most for large pretrained models.
arxiv-2510-26411:
Riccardo Renzulli, Colas Lepoutre, Enrico Cassano, and Marco Grangetto open up a medical AI model to see what it has learned. Their tool, MedSAE, probes MedCLIP, a model trained on chest X-rays and doctors' reports. Raw features inside such models mix many ideas, which makes them hard to trust in a clinic.

Renzulli and his three co-authors train sparse autoencoders, small networks that force each active unit to stand for one clear idea, on MedCLIP's inner space. They grade the result with correlation checks, entropy measures, and automatic naming by the MedGemma model. On the CheXpert data set, the new units were cleaner and easier to name than the raw features. Code is public, and the team frames the work as a step toward medical AI that doctors can inspect.
arxiv-2510-26511:
Ziqian Liu, with five co-authors, models the swing voters who can decide a presidential election. Standard opinion models put voters on one line, where backing one party means opposing the other. That view misses neutrals and leaners, the swing groups that often settle close races.

Liu and the team build a two-dimensional model with five voter groups, and they add an antagonism effect: the push each camp uses to stir dislike of the other side. Mixing open-mindedness, stubbornness, and campaign pressure, they trace how swing voters emerge and shift. Surprisingly, extreme antagonism can backfire: when both parties push hard, the one that polarises more can drive swing voters away and hand the win to the weaker rival. Checks on retweet networks from the 2020 United States election fit the model's claims.
arxiv-2510-27311:
Lorenzo Giordani, Gerhard Roehrle, and Johannes Schmitt extend a line of algebra work in this 2025 paper. They study reflection arrangements, sets of mirror planes fixed by a group of symmetries. Around the mirrors lies a space with holes where planes were removed. They ask which traits of that space stay fixed under the group.

Earlier work settled the case for mirrors over the complex numbers. This paper takes up mirrors over the quaternions, a four-part number system used for rotations. For one broad family, the counts of fixed traits match the complex case in a clean way. One new family of counts appears, from a special group type. They also describe bases, the building-block sets, for the fixed part.
arxiv-2510-27411:
Helcio Felippe, Alec Kirkley, and Federico Battiston build a fair way to compare group networks in this 2025 paper. A hypergraph links groups, not just pairs: one link can join a whole team. Comparing such networks is key for clustering and spotting odd ones out. Older tools only handle pair links and can credit fake matches.

Their yardstick comes from information theory and rests on mutual information, the overlap in what two descriptions reveal. It counts true shared structure while discounting matches that arise by chance. The yardstick comes in layers, from coarse to fine, within and across group sizes. Tests on synthetic networks check that the scores behave. On real group networks, the method surfaces patterns that pair-based tools miss.
arxiv-2510-27511:
Chunyin Chen, Sizhe Yan, and Biao Wu present a chaotic quantum system whose entanglement refuses to grow with system size. Entanglement entropy usually follows a volume law in excited states of chaotic many-body systems, serving as a chaos diagnostic. Their Floquet-driven system with Rydberg-like blockade is fully chaotic by level statistics and local thermalization, yet every Floquet eigenstate obeys a strict area law.

Entanglement across any cut stays bounded by a small constant independent of size. The anomaly traces to Hilbert space structure imposed by the blockades, which restricts the Schmidt rank across bipartitions. A duality maps constrained Hamiltonians to single-particle quantum walks on median graphs, yielding a general construction for systems with predetermined entanglement bounds. Entanglement alone, they conclude, cannot diagnose many-body chaos.
arxiv-2511-00011:
Alexander Okupnik, Johannes Schneider, and Kyriakos Flouris build an two-way system where an artificial partner dances with a person by copying and creatively lifting their motion. Motion capture data drives a diffusion model whose traits are pulled in the denoising process. Language models support verbal contact but lack body, and dance is offered as a primal bodily complement.

The system in part copies an new motion sequence and partly invents, creating an artificial other on stage or screen. Human-computer contact readers get a creative test bed for bodily AI. The work asks how machine partners can respond to bodies, not just words.
arxiv-2511-00411:
Zenghao Niu, Weicheng Xie, Siyang Song, Zitong Yu, Feng Liu, and Linlin Shen study adversarial examples, inputs crafted to fool neural networks, and how well attacks transfer between different models. Transfer faces a dilemma: push hard on one model and the attack overfits it, or wander widely for generality and the attack weakens. Their method, gradient-guided sampling, tries to hold both ends at once.

Built on a momentum-based attack, the method samples randomly at inner steps but steers the sampling along the previous step's gradient direction, with random step sizes. The result lands adversarial examples in regions that are both flat, which aids transfer, and high in loss, which keeps potency. Broad tests across network architectures and multimodal language models beat leading transfer attacks.
arxiv-2511-00611:
Zhihan Zhu, Yanhao Zhang, and Yong Xia introduce a new sparse transform framework for compressed sensing, the art of recovering signals from far fewer measurements than tradition demands. Classical sparse transforms generalize well but ignore what is known about the specific signal at hand. Their POST framework, short for prior-to-posterior sparse transform, fuses the two virtues: any existing transform's generality plus reference knowledge's specificity.

Inside the framework they derive an explicit transform, called HOT, that adapts to real and complex signals alike. Theory confirms its sparse representation power under single and multiple references, even when the reference knowledge is weak. Experiments across audio sensing, 5G channel estimation, and image compression show consistent gains for several recovery algorithms, at negligible extra cost. Prior knowledge, used this way, is nearly free accuracy.
arxiv-2511-00711:
Nardeep Kumar and Arun Kanwar present TRISKELION-1, one model that tries to describe, predict, and generate at once. Most models pick one job: rebuild data, sort it into classes, or sample new examples. TRISKELION-1 joins all three aims in a single encoder-decoder design, trained with variational objectives, as its authors describe it.

Tests on MNIST, the classic handwritten digit set, show the three jobs can live in one model without breaking each other. Reconstruction, classification, and sampling all stay stable side by side. The authors call the design a blueprint for broader systems that link clear interpretation, accuracy, and creativity. It is a proof of concept on a classic test bed, and it invites trials on harder tasks.
arxiv-2511-01011:
Maciej Malicki builds a logic on an unusual foundation. A co-valuation is, roughly, a minimal finite cover, and in his system co-valuations play the role that ordinary valuations of variables play in classical first order logic.

He shows the basic machinery of model theory can be rebuilt in this setting, including ultraproducts, compactness, and omitting types. A recent duality between certain countable posets and well behaved compact spaces makes those spaces the counterparts of countable universes. Although no topology appears at the start, the logic fits compact topological objects naturally: connectedness and covering dimension are easy to express, atomicity can be analyzed. The framework cooperates with Fraisse style constructions.
arxiv-2511-01211:
Chaofeng Wu reframes what makes an economics paper novel. Rather than a single attribute, novelty becomes a paper's position in an evolving intellectual landscape. That position splits into two independent dimensions. Spatial novelty is how distinct the paper is from its neighbors. Temporal novelty is how strongly it engages a moving research frontier.

Large language models supply semantic isolation metrics that locate each paper against the full text literature. Applied to a large corpus of economics articles, the two dimensions predict different futures: temporal novelty mainly predicts citation counts, while spatial novelty predicts disruptive impact. Combining them yields a scheme of four semantic neighborhood archetypes, each with a distinct impact profile that can be foreseen.
arxiv-2511-01411:
Reza Karimzadeh and colleagues explain vision models with contours instead of masks. The usual explanation tools shade dense pixel masks showing what a classifier used, but those masks come out fragmented and overfitted, needing cleanup before a person can read them.

Their method, Extremal Contours, needs no training. A star convex region, described compactly by a truncated Fourier series, is optimized against an extremal preserve and delete objective using the classifier's own gradients. The result is guaranteed to be one simply connected mask with orders of magnitude fewer free parameters and stable updates. On ImageNet classifiers it matched the fidelity of dense masks with better run to run consistency, and explicit area control yields importance contour maps. A multi contour extension localizes several objects at once.
arxiv-2511-01511:
Hannah Schunker and Asha Lakshmi K review Joy's law, a pattern noticed in sunspot groups: their tilt away from an east-west line grows with latitude. Explaining that tilt matters. In leading theories of the solar dynamo, the tilt is the step that converts the Sun's toroidal magnetic field back into a poloidal one. Observed tilts also help flip the sign of the Sun's global magnetic dipole.
