Those quivers spring from Type IIB brane setups involving fivebranes with p and q charges. The method extends further to star-shaped and orthosymplectic N equals 3 quivers. Finally, the team studies geometric branches of affine Dynkin quivers, matching known results while offering new predictions for cases not yet explored.
arxiv-2602-07711:
Wave-scattering models in three dimensions demand solvers that stay exact without huge in cost. Yury Gryazin and two co-authors build a fast step-by-step solver for the Helmholtz equation with varying numbers and absorbing edges, aimed at high-detail accuracy.

Fourth- and sixth-order compact difference schemes cut down the grid points needed per wavelength. A preconditioner built from simpler direct solvers, one using eigenvector transforms and one using partial Fourier transforms, tames the resulting ill-conditioned systems. Model problems show the plan works and explain why the simpler warm-up helps. Numeric scientists solving sound or electromagnetic scattering problems will find a usable, well-tested recipe here.
arxiv-2602-07811:
Electric cars cost far less per mile to run than gasoline cars, and that growing gap changes which routes drivers choose, reshaping city traffic. Xiaohan Xu and five co-authors build a multi-user equilibrium model for mixed electric and gasoline traffic, with fixed driver classes and a solution algorithm whose convergence is guaranteed.

They apply the model to real road networks in ten representative United States cities and track how congestion evolves as electric-vehicle share rises, using several measures of congestion patterns. Earlier simplified models, the authors argue, may misstate or understate these effects. Urban planners and transport researchers gain a quantitative tool for anticipating traffic shifts during the energy transition.
arxiv-2602-08211:
Referring expression comprehension asks a model to locate the object a text description points to in an image. Yik Lung Pang and Changjae Oh study how extra visual and textual context, supplied through tools, affects multimodal language models on this task, then propose a training-free framework called Chain-of-Caption.

Individual textual or visual contexts already improve performance without fine-tuning, and combining multiple contexts yields gains between 5 and 30 percent over baselines on RefCOCO, RefCOCOg, RefCOCO+, and Ref-L4 benchmarks. The approach shows that careful context provision can rival heavier training for grounding language in images. Vision-language researchers gain a cheap, training-free recipe for sharper object localization.
arxiv-2602-08311:
Vision-language models often agree with the user even when that means giving a wrong answer, a habit known as sycophancy. Shadman Rabby and five co-authors run the first wide test of this habit on moral questions about images, putting ten well-known models through their paces. Their 2026 arXiv paper asks whether a nudge from the user can flip a model from a right moral call to a wrong one.

The answer is yes, and the flip runs one way more than the other: models shift from right to wrong far more often than they correct themselves. Follow-up prompts mostly hurt scores on one test set while giving mixed results on another, and models that fix errors well also tend to introduce more of them. Readers get a warning that moral judgment in these systems is fragile, plus two new measures for tracking that fragility.
arxiv-2602-08511:
Where fish gather depends on ocean conditions like surface temperature and upper-ocean motion, and tracking that link matters for food security. Kanu Mohammed and five co-authors estimate fish catch from Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-3 satellite images using a hybrid machine-learning method. Their arXiv paper pairs gradient boosting with kernelized ridge regression.

The hybrid gives the strongest correlation and lowest error on both sensors, capturing curved ocean-fish links better than rivals. Sentinel-2 resolves finer spatial detail and local sea-life patterns, while Sentinel-3 gives smoother responses at coarser resolution. Readers get a satellite-based tool for lasting fisheries and for two global goals on hunger and ocean life.
arxiv-2602-08611:
Gaussian unitaries, made by quadratic Hamiltonians, are workhorses of quantum optics and continuous-variable computing. Jingqi Sun and two co-authors extend a recent parametrization from homogeneous unitaries to inhomogeneous ones, described by a matrix, a shift vector, and a phase. Their arXiv paper resolves the phase and sign puzzles that come from double covers of symplectic and orthogonal groups.

The Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff formula factors any such unitary into squeezing and shift parts, from which the group multiplication law follows. Readers get a complete algebraic toolkit for inhomogeneous Gaussian unitaries, grounding the operations that optical and continuous-variable devices actually perform.
arxiv-2602-08811:
The Born-Oppenheimer approximation separates fast and slow motion in molecules and hadrons, but its accuracy within potential models for doubly heavy hadrons was unclear. Zi-Long Man and three co-authors benchmark it against Gaussian expansion results for hadronic systems. Their arXiv paper tests dependence on trial wave functions, comparing Slater-type and Gaussian-type functions.

When heavy-quark mass is relatively small, Born-Oppenheimer calculations track the benchmark closely. As mass grows, Slater-type functions overshoot the benchmark while Gaussian-type functions undershoot, with Slater functions generally enhancing binding energy. The Gaussian shortfall traces mainly to neglected non-adiabatic corrections. Readers get a clear map of where the approximation holds and where it breaks in doubly heavy hadrons.
arxiv-2602-08911:
G. Mustafa and five co-authors explore a black hole that spins inside a magnetic field, the Kerr-Bertotti-Robinson solution. They work out how mass, spin, and magnetic strength shape the orbits of test particles, including stable circular paths and their wobble frequencies, plus precession effects like periastron shift and frame dragging. Comparisons with the plain Kerr case show the magnetic field matters throughout.

A wave analysis finds magnetism damps the hole's ringing tones while spin sets their pitch. Gas falling in can form either a flickering shock cone or a near-steady ring, flipping between the two over time. Power spectra of these flows show the quasi-periodic flickers astronomers hunt for in real data.
arxiv-2602-09011:
Topological data analysis turns shapes into barcodes, then often compresses those barcodes into a simpler summary called the Betti curve. Henry Ashley and four co-authors ask the inverse question: how many different barcodes collapse to the same curve? The answer measures how much information the compression throws away.

They link the counting problem to two distant areas: the Kostant partition function from representation theory, and the enumerative combinatorics of magic juggling sequences studied by Ronald Graham and others. Proving equivalences between the three settings, they quantify exactly how lossy the step from persistent homology to Betti numbers can be.
arxiv-2602-09111:
Collider physicists simulate particle collisions with MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, but next-to-leading-order event generation spends most of its time evaluating tree-level amplitudes one phase-space point at a time. Rikkert Frederix and four co-authors implement a multi-event interface that evaluates amplitudes for many phase-space points in each call to the integrated cross section. A multithreaded version spreads the work across CPU threads.

Runtime profiling confirms tree-level evaluations dominate NLO QCD generation, making them ideal for data parallelism. The changes also reorder phase-space cuts and amplitude calls, paving the way for SIMD instructions on CPUs or SIMT offloading to GPUs. The result is faster, more scalable Monte Carlo event generation for collider physics.
arxiv-2602-09211: T. C. Rogers and three co-authors reply to a comment on their earlier paper about QCD factorization with multihadron fragmentation functions. They defend their original conclusions against the criticisms raised and stand by their results. The note is brief, a direct response in an ongoing technical exchange rather than a new research result.
arxiv-2602-09311:
An empirical study from 2026, led by Tao Xiao with four co-authors, looks at flaky software tests across the OpenStack ecosystem rather than inside single projects. A flaky test is one whose result changes from run to run for no clear reason in the code itself, which weakens trust in test results and wastes computing effort. Earlier work had mostly studied flakiness project by project, leaving its wider effects unclear.

Drawing on hundreds of OpenStack projects, the study separates two patterns: tests that prove flaky in several projects at once, and tests that are flaky in some projects but steady in others. Cross-project flakiness turns out to be common, touching more than half of the projects examined, and even unit tests show it often. Race conditions, uneven build settings, and mismatched dependencies emerge as leading causes. The authors argue for better coordination, standard build setups, and stronger test isolation.
arxiv-2602-09411:
Visual generative models need evaluation that scales with them, but crowdsourced arena voting is slow and costly. Vision-language models offer a cheaper stand-in for human judges, yet their hallucinations and biases misalign them with human taste. Zhikai Li and nine co-authors propose K-Sort Eval, a 2026 framework that corrects and economizes model-as-judge evaluation for visual generation.

The framework curates a dataset from thousands of human votes, each instance ranking several models' outputs. A new model faces free-for-all comparisons against the field, with the vision-language model supplying rankings. Posterior correction adjusts the Bayesian update whenever model predictions disagree with human supervision. Dynamic matching then picks each comparison to balance uncertainty and diversity. Trials match arena results while typically needing under ninety model runs.
arxiv-2602-09711:
Aimed information is an information measure holding flow from one random process to another, close to transfer entropy, Granger cause, and Pearl's cause frame. Dor Tsur and four co-authors provide a book survey in 2026, focused on information theory's main use: pinning the room of channels with feedback and memory. Terms, basic traits, and links to Shannon's mutual information are covered first.

A survey of guessing ways follows, from classic plug-in guessers to modern neural-network-based guessers, including how guessers by number tune aimed information rate over joint input-output spreads for channel room guessing. Much of the book covers feedback room of finite-state channels. Strongly linked channels require maxing aimed information rate over causal tuned input spreads. For single-path channels, feedback room equals the best average reward of a Markov choice process, found via value repeat, Q-graph methods, and reward learning.
arxiv-2602-09911:
Counting people in hard-to-reach groups often relies on capture-recapture, matching names across several lists to infer how many were missed. A 2026 paper led by Mateo Dulce Rubio, with two co-authors, tackles a flaw in that method: records with missing details, lost to reluctance, collection limits, or imperfect matching. Ignoring the gaps or filling them in advance can bias the count badly.

The authors build a nonparametric framework that treats missing traits as missing at random, then construct one-step estimators that stay valid even when much data is missing. Tests show large gains over naive filling-in. Applied to three-list data for Gaza from October 2023 through June 2024, their estimate puts the true toll about a quarter above official figures. That gives practitioners a principled tool for conflict settings and other incomplete counts.
arxiv-2602-10611:
Nicolás Becerra-Zuniga and three co-authors ask how much physics-informed neural networks can learn from imperfect data in a 2026 paper. These networks solve partial differential rules by combining scarce labels with real constraints. In practice, however, training data carry measurement noise, discretization error, and modeling assumptions that clash with the governing rules.

The paper systematically analyzes that clash and presents a consistency barrier: an intrinsic lower bound on error arising from data-to-equation mismatch. No amount of training can beat the barrier while the inconsistency stands. The result reframes expectations for physics-informed learning, separating errors the model can fix from errors baked into the data itself.
arxiv-2602-10711:
Hyeongmin Lee and ten co-authors rethink asset retrieval around the future in a 2026 paper. Finding similar assets is central to quantitative investing. But current similarity measures look backward: historical price patterns and sector labels offer no promise about future conduct. Retrieved assets should instead move jointly going forward.

Their system, FASCL, learns models with a soft contrastive loss that uses pairwise future return links as steady supervision. An testing protocol directly tests whether retrieved assets share similar future paths. Tests on more than five thousand United States-listed securities against fourteen baselines show the future-aligned approach attains the best future-path retrieval. Similarity, the paper argues, should be defined by where assets go, not where they have been.
arxiv-2602-10811:
Mingyang Liu and seven co-authors scale click-through rate prediction without losing fine detail in a 2026 paper. Industrial prediction systems aggregate user conduct early for speed, but that aggregation discards token-level signals needed for scaling gains. The paper revisits what distinguishes click prediction from language modeling.

Two traits matter: behavioral and non-behavioral traits differ sharply in information density, and content-rich signals carry modality-exact priors. Their efficiently scalable transformer reads all raw inputs in a single sequence without lossy aggregation, achieving fully unified modeling. Two specialized modules handle the density asymmetry and modality priors. The design lets click prediction scale like language models while respecting its own data structure.
arxiv-2602-10911:
Julian D. Schiller and three co-authors show that tuning the burn-in phase improves recurrent network training in a 2026 paper. Training recurrent networks with backpropagation through time struggles on long strings, and truncated backpropagation over shorter segments reduces compute and memory. But optimizing over subsequences instead of full strings costs scores.

The paper proves theory bounds on scores and results loss for truncated training on time series tasks. Those bounds reveal the burn-in phase, the initial segment where the network state settles, as a key tuning knob with large impact on promises. Tests on standard system identification and time series forecasting benchmarks check the theory, giving builders a principled lever for recurrent training.
arxiv-2602-11611:
Black holes that avoid a central singularity behave differently, thermodynamically, from their singular cousins, and the difference runs deeper than geometry. Qi-Hang Xia and two co-authors compare a Hayward black hole in anti-de Sitter space with the singular hole it is built from by imposing an extra constraint. The singular hole shows a rich phase pattern, including reentrant transitions like those seen in higher-dimensional rotating cases.

After the constraint is applied, the Hayward hole keeps Van der Waals style critical behavior, though its free energy profile looks qualitatively different from standard charged cases. A topological analysis sharpens the contrast: the singular hole carries topological charge minus one, while the constrained hole carries plus one. The constraint, in other words, reshapes the thermodynamic landscape itself, not just the geometry.
arxiv-2602-11811:
In Brans-Dicke scalar-tensor gravity, post-Newtonian values for strongly gravitating bodies need generalization. The exact values depend on a body pressure and energy density. Thomas Chehab and one co-author develop two new numerical methods to obtain those exact values through standard Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff computation. Gaps from standard post-Newton values can exceed 80 percent in some situations.

The authors also connect their results with the Damour-Esposito-Farèse non-perturbative value and apply the method to Entangled Relativity, deriving exact values for the Sun, the Earth, and neutron stars. Current and near-future experiments likely can constrain that theory if one matter Lagrangian choice holds. Under the alternative choice often favored by researchers, general relativity is matched exactly, and testing would need compact objects with extreme electric or magnetic fields.
arxiv-2602-12111:
In two-photon polymerization, how fully the resin converts shapes traits such as light-bending power and stiffness, yet varying that degree across a print has lacked software support and validation methods. Michal Ziemczonok and Koen Vanmol present an open-source slicer plus tuning methods that bring variable-degree printing within reach.

Their toolbox supports grayscale lithography, control over writing direction and trajectories, and bio-mimicking microphantoms with engineered three-dimensional light-bending power. Tuning results show excellent repeatability, accuracy, and stability for variable-degree structures, backed by detailed metrological analysis. The goal is to popularize variable-dose printing and extract more from existing two-photon systems.
arxiv-2602-12511:
Global renormalised solutions to the Boltzmann equation with long-range interactions and no angular cutoff were first established by Alexandre and Villani, using a definition involving a non-negative defect measure. Yi-Long Luo led this work with one co-author, Jing-Xin Nie, addressing that defect for the inverse power law model with hard potentials, where gamma lies between 0 and 1. Stronger coercivity estimates from hard potentials are the key tool.

Exploiting those estimates, the team proves the defect measure actually vanishes, establishing global existence of renormalised solutions in the standard sense, with no defect measure at all. That closes a gap left by the original definition for hard potentials. Finally, a counterexample shows the hard-potential approach fails for soft potentials, where gamma lies between minus 3 and 0, marking the boundary of the method.
arxiv-2602-12711:
A square in a word is a block repeated twice, like 'abcabc', and a natural question is how many different squares a word of length n can hold. Earlier work capped that count at n minus the alphabet size, and later refined the bound to n minus a slowly growing term. Eitatsu Tomita and Tomohiro I offer a fresh proof that reaches the same refined bound.

The value of a new proof lies in its route: a different argument can expose structure the old one hid and may open the door to sharper results. Here the authors present their alternative path in full, showing step by step how it lands on the n minus log-scale bound. The result itself matches the best known bound; the contribution is the new way of getting there.
arxiv-2602-12911:
Vietnamese medical speech often mixes in English drug names and procedure terms, which trips up speech recognition, especially in a low-resource language. Tung Nguyen and eight co-authors build ViMedCSS, a 34-hour dataset of 16,576 utterances, each containing at least one English medical term from a curated bilingual lexicon spanning five topics. No earlier benchmark has tackled Vietnamese medical code-switching.

Tests of leading speech models show Vietnamese-optimised models handle general segments better, while multilingual pretraining captures English insertions more reliably. Combining both gives the strongest mix of overall and code-switched performance. For developers of multilingual medical systems, the dataset and findings offer a concrete guide to domain adaptation where data are scarce and accuracy matters clinically.
arxiv-2602-13111:
A classical arithmetic problem asks how sums of numbers behave, and this paper studies its analogue for polynomials over the binary field. Luis Gallardo proves that five is the smallest number with a striking property. For any set of five polynomials over F2[x], the sums of two distinct members cannot all take the special form x^k (x+1)^l. In other words, with five polynomials, at least one pair sum escapes that form.

The value five is minimal, meaning smaller sets can avoid the conclusion: some set of four polynomials has all pair sums in the special form. Pinning down a sharp threshold like this turns a qualitative question into an exact one. The paper's contribution is that minimal number, proved for the polynomial analogue of a classical arithmetic problem.
arxiv-2602-13711:
Smaller, more complex light-electronic devices demand precise descriptions of excess carrier transport and recombination, plus lab methods resolving carrier dynamics at tiny scale. This paper presents a precise model of a confined geometry with recombination at two surfaces. It is generic for electron beam induced current readings in a scanning transmission electron microscope, a method offering atomic-scale spatial resolution. The model rests on analytic reasoning and finite element simulations, with underlying premises discussed in depth.

Successful use on lab data on the complex oxide SrTi0.995Nb0.005O3 shows the approach's practicality and toughness, enabling precise measurement of its bulk diffusion length at 10.2 plus or minus 0.1 nanometers. The model thus turns tiny-scale current readings into reliable transport parameters. Tobias Meyer leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14111:
Anton Korznikov and five co-authors ask a blunt 2026 arXiv question: do sparse autoencoders beat random baselines? These tools promise to split neural activations into sparse, human-readable features, and variants now scale to frontier models. Yet downstream failures have raised doubts about what they truly recover.

On synthetic data with known features, autoencoders recovered only 9% of true features despite explaining 71% of variance. On real activations, three random baselines matched fully trained models on interpretability, sparse probing, and causal editing, with scores nearly tied. The authors conclude that current autoencoders do not reliably decompose a model's inner workings, however strong their reconstructions look.
arxiv-2602-14611:
When coders send a pull request, a short description often rides along. Shirin Pirouzkhah, with two co-authors, studies what those descriptions do in real code review. The team built a list of eight advised parts from guides, then checked 80,000 requests across 156 projects.

Purpose and code notes help reviewers grasp why a change was made. Naming the kind of feedback wanted best predicts acceptance and reviewer replies. Descriptions appear more often in mature projects and for complex changes. A survey of 64 developers backs the same split in value. The study gives teams a clear guide to writing requests that get read.
arxiv-2602-14711:
Yi-Yan Wang and colleagues report a new compound, Ce3MgBi5, and uncover hidden time-reversal-like degenerate states inside it. The material is an antiferromagnet with a distorted kagome lattice of cerium atoms, and several fractional magnetisation plateaus appear as the magnetic field rises. At the half plateau, magnetoresistance and Hall resistivity show clear hysteresis as the field rises and falls.

Yet magnetisation itself shows no such hysteresis, pointing to states with the same net magnetisation but different electronic transport, linked by a time-reversal-like operation. The discovery ties lattice, magnetism, and transport into one puzzle. Ce3MgBi5 offers a fresh stage for studying degeneracy in quantum materials.
arxiv-2602-15111:
Takátsy and colleagues show that orbital eccentricity can make neutron star g-mode resonances visible to current gravitational-wave detectors. Dynamical tides carry vital clues about neutron star matter, especially g-modes, whose frequency and tidal coupling respond keenly to interior composition where microphysical models are least reliable. Weak coupling to external tides, however, has made their imprint on inspiral signals hard to observe.

Mildly oval orbits change that picture. Higher harmonics in the early phase suffer larger phase shifts, which they carry into the detectors' sensitive band. Oval binaries also pass through several epicyclic swings, further amplifying the total phase shift. Together, the effects lift g-mode detectability by more than an order of magnitude for mildly oval orbits. That enables robust limits on g-mode traits today. The Einstein Telescope could constrain all relevant models with oval binaries.
arxiv-2602-15711:
Bassompierre and colleagues design node embeddings for graphs whose dot products capture graph-based notions of node similarity. Such embeddings map vertices into low-dimensional spaces while keeping structure, serving classification, link prediction, and signal reconstruction. Graph kernels define such similarities in a principled way, but direct computation is often too costly for large networks.

Inspired by random feature methods for kernel approximation in Euclidean spaces, the team introduces randomised spectral embeddings whose dot products estimate a low-rank approximation of any given graph kernel. Theory and tests show their embeddings match kernels more closely than prior methods, above all for spectrally localised kernels. The work offers a scalable, principled route to graph representation learning.
arxiv-2602-15811:
Kavitha and colleagues study continual learning for chest radiograph classification under task-unknown inference. Clinical deployment needs models that update as new data sets arrive, without retraining or degrading validated performance. Heterogeneous chest X-ray data sets arrive in sequence, and task identity is unavailable at deployment time. Their CARL-CXR framework keeps a fixed high-capacity backbone while adding lightweight task-specific adapters and classifier heads in sequence.

A latent task selector works on adapter-conditioned features to route each input to the best task pathway. Compact task prototypes and feature-level experience replay preserve task identity across updates without storing raw images. Tests on MIMIC-CXR and CheXpert show minimal catastrophic forgetting, just a 0 point 012 AUROC drop, a six-fold and eleven-fold reduction over LwF and EWC baselines. Under task-unknown deployment, routing accuracy beats joint training by 12 point 5 points, 75 point 0 percent against 62 point 5 percent.
arxiv-2602-15911:
Buchheit and colleagues treat the equation for unconventional superconductivity named for Bardeen, Cooper, and Schrieffer, in both its analytic traits and its efficient numeric solution. The equation adds long-range power-law electron-electron links in a tight-binding model set on a d-dimensional lattice. The complex matrix-valued gap obeys a nonlinear convolution equation, under symmetry constraints set by fermionic anticommutation.

In momentum space, the long-range link takes the form of the Epstein zeta function, now efficiently computable. That function spikes as a power law at zero momentum, and the spike must be handled when the convolution is scored. After a survey of analytic traits, the authors solve the equation with a Galerkin method using B-splines. Numeric results follow for a nodal superconductor arranged on a two-dimensional square lattice.
arxiv-2602-16111:
Zehao Xu leads a team of four researchers who scale content prevalence measurement across online experiments at Pinterest. Platforms track the share of views tied to content traits, so they can weigh trade-offs and set guardrails in A/B tests. Labeling each experiment, arm, segment, and day with a large language model gives a high-fidelity reference, but the cost is far too high at platform scale.

Their surrogate system keeps one global calibration of machine learning score buckets. It is refreshed from a recurring LLM-labeled stream, and its bucket prevalences are reused across all tests through a per-experiment metric and a dashboard focused on deltas. Since calibration draws on daily samples, it stays true to live traffic as it drifts, adding no new labeling cost. In live use it serves about a hundred experiments each day, covering far more arms than per-test labeling could.
arxiv-2602-16211:
Auction design with unit-demand agents and non-quasilinear preferences is the focus of work by Tomoya Kazumura and coauthors. A seller offers a set of objects to agents who can receive no more than one object each. Each agent preference over object and payment pairs need not be quasilinear. When the domain contains all classical preferences, the authors show a unique mechanism satisfies a demanding set of properties.

That mechanism is the minimum Walrasian equilibrium price mechanism. It is strategy-proof, individually rational, and satisfies equal treatment of equals, no-wastage, meaning every object is allocated, and no-subsidy, meaning no agent is subsidized. The result gives an equity-based characterization of the mechanism, complementing an efficiency-based characterization already known in the literature. Equity, rather than efficiency alone, thus singles out the same pricing rule.
arxiv-2602-16511:
Osher Azulay leads three coauthors on unified fall safety for humanoid robots. Falls matter for humanoids in cluttered spaces: unlike quadrupeds or wheeled robots, they suffer high-energy impacts, complex whole-body contact, and large viewpoint changes. Prior work splits fall safety into separate problems or learns policies without vision, usually on flat ground.

The authors build on two insights: human recovery poses are structured and transfer across terrains by alignment, and good recovery depends on reading the goal against the surrounding terrain. They train a privileged teacher from sparse human demonstrations and simulated terrains, then distill it into a deployable student using egocentric depth and proprioception. The student predicts a goal-in-context latent for the recovery target, guiding coordinated whole-body reactions. Tests in simulation and on a Unitree G1 show robust zero-shot fall safety across varied terrains.
arxiv-2602-16711:
Namitha Padmanabhan, Matthew Gwilliam, and Abhinav Shrivastava present TeCoNeRV, a compressible neural representation for video built on temporal coherence. Implicit neural representations compress video well, but each video needs its own overfit network, which hurts scaling to high resolution. Hypernetwork routes predict network weights fast for unseen videos, but with low quality, large size, and heavy memory needs at high resolution.

TeCoNeRV cuts that cost in three ways: splitting weight prediction across space and time into patch tubelets, storing only differences between consecutive segment codes, and regularizing weight changes to track video content. On the UVG set, it gains several decibels of PSNR over baseline at two resolutions, with much lower bitrates and faster encoding. It is the first hypernetwork route shown to work at high resolution with low memory.
arxiv-2602-16811:
Charalampos Mastrokostas, Nikolaos Giarelis, and Nikos Karacapilidis test language models for Greek question answering with a new set, DemosQA. Language models have lifted question answering, yet most work targets rich tongues such as English. Multilingual models lean on a few popular tongues or borrow from rich to poor tongues. That risks warping social, cultural, and past facets.

DemosQA is built from social media user queries and community-checked answers. It better captures the Greek social and cultural mood. Alongside it, the paper offers a memory-light test frame that fits varied question sets and tongues. An extensive test of eleven single-tongue and multi-tongue models follows, giving Greek researchers data, tools, and a first systematic head-to-head for their tongue.
arxiv-2602-17011:
Hongjun Liu and co-authors propose CAFE, a channel-autoregressive factorized encoding scheme for robust biosignal spatial super-resolution. High-density biosignal recordings matter for neural decoding and clinical care, yet real setups often use low-density montages due to hardware and operational limits. That motivates spatial super-resolution from sparse data, but mixed dependencies in sparse, noisy measurements often lead to artifact spread and false links.

CAFE is a plug-and-play rollout scheme rebuilding the full montage in aligned stages. It first recovers nearby channels, then expands outward, using reliable local structure before introducing non-local interactions. During training, step-wise supervision over groups and teacher forcing with epoch-level scheduled sampling reduce exposure bias and allow parallel computation across steps. At test time, CAFE rolls out across groups, reusing any temporal backbone as predictor. Tests on four modalities and six datasets show it works on three backbones.
arxiv-2602-17211:
Etienne Lempereur led a five-author team on generating samples when only partial information is available. Classic maximum entropy methods give sound gauges of doubt from moment constraints, but their sampling via Markov chain or Langevin methods slows sharply in high dimensions. Flow-based models move noise to data fast, yet offer weak promises and can overfit scarce data. The paper presents Moment Guided Diffusion, which blends both lines of work.

Built on the stochastic interpolant setup, the method samples maximum entropy distributions by solving a differential equation. It steers moments to set values in finite time, dodging slow mixing. In the large-volatility limit the authors prove it tends to the maximum entropy distribution and derive an entropy gauge straight from the motion. Tests on finance, turbulence, and cosmology data yield negentropy values for large multiscale flows.
arxiv-2602-17311:
Dalila Bounoua led a four-author review of orbital loop currents in correlated electron materials and how polarized neutron diffraction reveals them. Over the past two decades, loop current signatures have appeared in high-temperature copper oxide superconductors, iridates, copper oxide spin ladders, and recently kagome vanadate superconductors. Such currents induce orbital magnetic moments inside the unit cell, detectable through their interaction with neutron spin.

Beyond the usual picture of orbital moments as point-like local moments, the authors present an alternative account of the neutron magnetic cross-section in terms of microscopic currents running between different atomic orbitals. They discuss the matching magnetic structure factors and the quantitative differences between the two approaches. The review gives experimentalists a sharper lens for reading loop current evidence in quantum materials.
arxiv-2602-17511:
Ioana Doran led a five-author team on the Stark effect in molecular Rydberg states. The team sets out a theory of fine and hyperfine patterns in high-n Rydberg spectra under steady, uniform electric fields. Their toolkit joins multichannel quantum-defect theory and polarization models for field-free energies, matrix diagonalization for Stark shifts, and frame changes for line spots.

The team compares ortho-D2 against para-H2 spectra. D2 uses a ground-state D2-plus core at nuclear spins zero and two. H2 uses an excited-state H2-plus core with zero nuclear spin. Hyperfine coupling barely shifts the Stark effect, yet splits each Stark state by nearly the core's hyperfine Fermi-contact splitting. Rotation drives Stark-state-specific splittings far from the core's spin-rotation splitting. It works through spin-rotation coupling to the core electron spin and core-polarization and charge-quadrupole coupling to orbital motion.
arxiv-2602-17611:
Yuan-Zhuo Ma and team present evidence for a new phase of matter in neutron-rich systems. They call it multimodal superfluidity. From ab initio lattice calculations, they show the condensate mixes s-wave pairs, p-wave pairs in entangled double combinations, and quartets made of two bound s-wave pairs.

The phase shows up broadly in single-flavor spin-one-half fermion systems with attractive s- and p-wave interactions, as long as the system resists collapse. It also appears in generalized Hubbard models in one, two and three dimensions. Spin, rotation and parity symmetries stay unbroken. Matching p-wave and quartet gaps in atomic nuclei data add weight, with consequences for the structure and dynamics of neutron star crusts.
arxiv-2602-17811:
Guy Blelloch and team present faster parallel batch-dynamic algorithms for low out-degree orientation. A low out-degree orientation directs each edge of an undirected graph to minimize the maximum out-degree of a vertex. In the parallel batch-dynamic setting, batches of edges can be inserted or deleted. The goal is parallel batch processing with work per edge like a single sequential update and span growing only polylogarithmically.

Both achieve polylogarithmic span, focus on minimizing work, and carry deterministic bounds with an added logarithmic factor. In the amortized setting, one maintains an arboricity-bounded orientation with work per update growing only logarithmically in expectation. In the worst-case setting, a slightly larger bound achieves worst-case expected work per update growing only logarithmically. The results are work-efficient, matching the best known sequential work, and improve significantly on prior parallel algorithms at fixed arboricity.
arxiv-2602-17911:
Jash Rajesh Parekh and team tackle a gap in medical question answering: most systems assume facts apply the same way to every patient. In real care, nearly every choice depends on patient traits such as comorbidities and contraindications. Existing benchmarks never test that conditional reasoning, and retrieval or graph methods lack a way to check that fetched knowledge fits the given case.

The team builds CondMedQA, the first benchmark for conditional medical QA, with multi-hop questions whose answers shift with patient conditions. They also build Condition-Gated Reasoning, which builds condition-aware knowledge graphs and switches reasoning paths on or off by query condition. Their tests show it picks condition-appropriate answers more reliably while matching or beating top medical QA benchmarks. Readers gain a clearer case for modeling conditionality in robust medical reasoning.
arxiv-2602-18211:
Horia Cornean and two co-authors classify how the size of a resolvent can grow near a point. Their 2026 paper treats operators that are closed and densely defined, acting on a separable Hilbert space whose resolvent set is not empty. For any point in that set, they ask what the resolvent norm does nearby along straight segments.

The answer is a clean split. Either the norm grows at least linearly or quadratically away from the point along some segment inside the set, or the point is a global minimum of the norm. No third behavior is possible. The classification gives operator theorists a sharp, two-case picture of resolvent growth, with the growth rate pinned to one of two exact powers.
arxiv-2602-18311:
Ren-Peng Zhou and one co-author bound a possible interaction between dark matter and neutrinos that strengthens with temperature. Their 2026 paper works out the full Boltzmann hierarchy for both fluids under a dimension-six operator, including a new fluid approximation for modes entering the horizon. The interaction can ring the dark fluid, leaving distinct marks on the cosmic microwave background and matter power spectra.

Fitting Planck, DESI, and ACT data, the team caps today's interaction strength near ten to the minus thirteen for normal neutrino mass ordering. That cap runs nearly nine orders tighter than the temperature-independent case, since scattering grows nearly with temperature squared in the early universe. Degenerate neutrino masses loosen the cap to near ten to the minus eleven, showing mass ordering matters. With a logarithmic flat prior, the combined data even hint at a nonzero interaction at ninety-five percent confidence.
arxiv-2602-18411:
Zimo Hao and two co-authors study weak approximation for kinetic stochastic differential equations with integrable drifts. Their 2026 paper analyzes a generic tamed Euler-Maruyama scheme, a workhorse numerical method, asking how fast its density nears the true density. Weak convergence here means densities converge, not individual paths.

The team proves the scheme's density converges at rate one half to the true density. Crucially, that rate does not depend on the criticality gap, a parameter that limited earlier results. Closing that gap gives users a clean, gap-free guarantee for kinetic equations with integrable drifts, where previous theory left the rate hostage to criticality.
arxiv-2602-18611:
The CMS Collaboration reports the most comprehensive Higgs study to date. Their 2026 paper combines measurements of Higgs production and decay rates using proton-proton collision data from the CMS experiment at thirteen teraelectronvolts during 2016 to 2018. That corresponds to one hundred thirty-eight inverse femtobarns.

The combination covers decay channels to photon pairs, Z pairs, W pairs, tau pairs, bottom quarks, muon pairs, and Z-photon, targeting multiple production processes. It also searches for invisible decays and off-shell production in the four-lepton channel. The best-fit inclusive signal yield measures one point zero one four times the standard model expectation. The Higgs mass is one hundred twenty-five point three eight gigaelectronvolts. Measurements in simplified template cross section regions and interpretations in coupling modifier and effective field theory frameworks follow, with coupling results constraining two-Higgs models. Results show good compatibility with standard model predictions for most measured parameters.
arxiv-2602-18811:
Detecting new object classes in a new visual domain from only a few examples is hard. Text prompts capture meaning but miss the look of the target domain. Wanqi Wang, with three co-authors, presents LMP in 2026. It is a two-branch detector that learns prototypes across modes. It couples textual guidance with visual exemplars from the target domain.

A visual prototype module gathers class prototypes from support regions. It generates hard-negative prototypes from jittered boxes in query images, capturing distractors and similar backgrounds. The visual branch is injected into the detection pipeline alongside a parallel text branch that preserves open-vocabulary semantics. The branches train jointly and ensemble at inference. On six cross-domain benchmarks at one, five, and ten shots, the method reaches leading or highly competitive accuracy.
arxiv-2602-18911:
A single yardstick for AI scores and human scores is the aim here. Peter Romero, with thirteen co-authors, proposes a human-anchored scale in 2026. Instead of judging models against a small test group, the work pegs each test item to the world population, so results from tests can sit side by side.

The scales run in levels for skills such as reasoning, comprehension, knowledge, and volume. A level stands for how likely people worldwide are to get an item right, with levels spaced on a log scale tied to a base B. Public human test data from PISA, TIMSS, ICAR, UKBioBank, and ReliabilityBench feed the calibration, while language models help estimate that base by bridging two demographic profiles. Group slicing and post-stratification checks test each mapping, and the same tools let old scales be reset and lined up against the world population.
arxiv-2602-19211:
Thin X-ray filaments trail from a couple of powerful pulsars, and their lopsided glow has puzzled astronomers. The filaments shine brightly on one side with little on the other, yet their spectra barely change across the glow, which suggests the shining particles lose energy only slowly. HongYu Pu and Siming Liu model how those particles travel after escaping a pulsar's bow shock.

Their Monte Carlo simulation follows very high-energy electrons and positrons through a large-scale magnetic field, applied to the Guitar pulsar. With an injection power of a few tens of percent of the pulsar's spin-down power, the model matches the observed filaments. It also predicts a faint, symmetric X-ray haze on a larger scale, which wide-field telescopes with good sensitivity should be able to find.
arxiv-2602-19511:
Ryo Nikkuni shows that certain minimal simplicial complexes must contain a linked pair of spheres no matter how they are placed. The link has two components, one an (n-1)-sphere and the other an n-sphere, that cannot be split apart in any embedding into 2n-dimensional space. Minimal here means the complex cannot be simplified further without losing that forced linking.

The result generalizes a familiar fact about graphs that are not non-separating planar, lifting it to higher dimensions. Where planar graphs force a kind of inseparability in the plane, these complexes force a nonsplittable link in higher space. Readers get a concise existence result in geometric topology, with minimal examples that must link.
arxiv-2602-19811:
Dashboard queries repeat themselves semantically across tools, yet most caches key entries by surface text or syntax tree, so equivalent queries miss each other. A 2026 arXiv paper by Laurent Bindschaedler, working alone, introduces a cautious middle-layer cache for dashboard-style OLAP on star-shaped schemas.

The cache canonicalizes both SQL and natural-language queries into one key space, an OLAP Intent Signature that records measures, grouping levels, filters, and time spans. Reuse demands an exact intent match under strict schema checks and confidence-gated acceptance of natural language. Two correctness-preserving derivations, roll-up and filter-down, widen coverage without approximate matching. Across three benchmarks the cache hits far more often than text or syntax keys, with zero false hits.
arxiv-2602-19911:
Classical Lebesgue spaces measure the size of functions, but they often cannot bound evolution operators at critical endpoints, because they mix up a function's height with its spread. A 2026 arXiv paper by Asuman Güven Aksoy and Daniel Akech Thiong presents an expository account of interpolation theory and Lorentz spaces as the remedy.

The article introduces distribution functions and decreasing rearrangements, building up to Lorentz spaces, which act as sensitive bridges between endpoint extremes. It works through complex, real, and Marcinkiewicz interpolation methods in turn. Two illustrations close the account: the smoothing decay of the heat equation in parabolic form, and the dispersive Strichartz estimates for the free Schrödinger equation. The piece serves readers who want the analytic machinery behind endpoint estimates, laid out step by step.
arxiv-2602-20011:
Generating realistic time series matters in finance and energy, where abrupt jumps, heavy tails, and regime shifts defeat diffusion-only models. A 2026 arXiv paper by Stefano De Marco and two co-authors extends the Schrödinger bridge framework with jumps.

Building on a diffusion-based approach, the authors introduce a jump-diffusion Schrödinger bridge that allows discontinuities in the generative dynamics. Starting from an entropy minimization problem, they recast the task as stochastic control. The control solution describes the best jump-diffusion process under control. Sampled on a fixed time grid, that process produces synthetic series matching the joint distributions of observed data, with drift and jump intensity both learned from data. Tests on simulated and real financial and energy series show jumps substantially improve realism, capturing abrupt moves that diffusion-only models miss.
arxiv-2602-20111:
Online learners usually assume clean data, yet real streams mix ordinary examples with adversarially chosen ones, and the learner cannot tell which rounds are adversarial. A 2026 arXiv paper by Ezra Edelman and Surbhi Goel studies that adversarial injection model, where labels always agree with a fixed target concept and the learner may abstain from predicting.

Total error counts mistakes on rounds where the learner predicts plus incorrect abstentions on ordinary rounds. Earlier work showed oracle access to the underlying distribution yields combined error growing like dimension squared times log time. Distribution-agnostic algorithms reach only square-root growth for restricted classes. The paper settles whether that gap is fundamental. It proves a matching square-root lower bound for VC dimension one. The two information regimes are thus sharply separated. New upper bounds for the setting are also developed.
arxiv-2602-20311:
Veronica Pratt and five co-authors present the first statistically robust detection of sympathetic flaring on stars beyond the Sun. On the Sun, most flares occur at random, but a small share are triggered by an earlier flare. No widespread confirmation of that effect on other stars existed before this work. The authors built a new detection algorithm sensitive to flares that occur close together or overlap, and applied it to TESS data.

The search found about two hundred twenty thousand flares on about sixteen thousand stars, mostly M-dwarfs. The gaps between flares show an excess of closely spaced pairs compared with a random Poisson process. The authors attribute that excess to sympathetic flares, at a rate between four and nine percent, matching the solar rate. The result shows a shared flare behavior between the Sun and low-mass stars, opening a new window on stellar activity.
arxiv-2602-20511:
Splitting models guide medical choices, yet their black-box nature raises trust concerns in high-stakes care. Limai Jiang and eight co-authors offer an account model for splitting built on causal logic. It sends back the average treatment effect into a metric gauging how input regions and network parts influence target splitting areas. Current account methods focus mostly on sorting, leaving splitting fairly new.

Set against recent splitting clarity methods on two medical imaging sets, the approach gives more faithful accounts. A full causal analysis of several base splitting models reveals strong spread in seeing ways across models, and even across inputs for the same model. The method thus holds notable insights for tuning splitting models, showing where and why models see apart.
arxiv-2602-20611:
Wearable actigraphs turn body movement into health data, and large movement sets now support research on mobility and health. Daniel Zhou and Sudipto Banerjee note that statistical methods for high-resolution movement data must fit modern AI methods built on transfer learning and amortization. Their paper devises amortized Bayesian inference for actigraph time sheets, using a layered dynamic linear model that fully propagates and quantifies uncertainty.

The analysis centers on movement data from the PASTA-LA study, run by the Fielding School of Public Health at UCLA, on sustainable transport and activity. Beyond chance-based imputation of movement time sheets, the method learns how explanatory factors shift acceleration magnitude over time for a cohort of subjects. The work links wearable movement data to health research through Bayesian methods.
arxiv-2602-20911:
Class-incremental learning asks a model to absorb new classes without forgetting old ones. Ruiqi Liu and five co-authors propose a structured answer in this 2026 arXiv paper: the Semantic-guided Adaptive Expert Forest. Instead of piling up one adapter per task, the method groups tasks into semantic clusters and builds a balanced expert tree inside each cluster by merging adapters from similar tasks.

At inference time the forest activates the experts relevant to each input and combines their outputs, weighted by confidence. Experiments on several benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance. Readers get a design that treats learned knowledge as an organized hierarchy rather than an unstructured pile, with sharing built in.
arxiv-2602-21111:
Fluids trapped in nano-pores act not the same as bulk fluids, key for super-caps, oil pull-out, and salt removal. Gennady Gor, Geordy Jomon, and Andrei Kolesnikov test whether simple density working theory can tell slope traits of trapped argon in this 2026 arXiv paper. With standard dials, the Percus-Yevick-based model fails on slope traits.

A small dial tweak changes the picture: same-heat squeeze and heat spread become tellable in numbers at a chosen heat. Trapped argon proves harder to squeeze than bulk argon, with squeeze hinging on pore size, and heat spread acts the same way, rising as pores shrink. Monte Carlo runs back the calls across pore sizes.
arxiv-2602-21311:
Exact collider readings test the Standard Model and probe higher-size links, but working out sizes is hard. Yacine Haddad, Kaidi Xu, Vincent Croft, Jad Halimeh, and Michele Grossi present a hybrid quantum-classic setup in this 2026 arXiv paper for leading-order helicity sizes in matter-antimatter bounce to lepton pairs. Outside motion math enters as single-qubit Weyl spinors.

Full sizes emerge by in-step joining of diagram parts within one quantum circuit, with classic handling yielding cross sections matched to atom-smasher data. As proof of concept, aim-free angle spreads and binned odds fits to exact readings give bounds steady with Standard Model calls. Quantum-aided size weighing thus links straight to lab physics.
arxiv-2602-21411:
Marc Dufay and two co-authors close a gap in convex agreement. Convex agreement is a stronger form of Byzantine agreement. Honest parties must agree on an output inside the convex hull of their inputs. That rule fits aggregation jobs like robust learning and sensor fusion. But past protocols for general convexity spaces needed at least order L times n squared bits of communication.

Their deterministic synchronous protocols cut that cost to near-optimal levels in the long-message regime. Finite convexity spaces need order L times n log n bits. Euclidean spaces need order L times n to the one-plus-small power. Round complexity is optimal at order n. With a known input-length bound they reach resilience near t below n over the Helly number. The key tool is extractor graphs assigning parties to committees robustly against adaptive adversaries.
arxiv-2602-22111:
Particle-physics sums rest on Feynman integrals, and shrinking them to a small set of master integrals is a core chore. Leonardo de la Cruz and David A. Kosower show how to build a full set of lowering tools that step any Feynman integral down toward master integrals. The build solves systems of equations for generic integral indices, using integration-by-parts generating vectors.

Each solved system yields one lowering tool, and applying the tools in turn reduces an arbitrary integral to a mix of masters. The method needs no seed integrals, as the title promises: the tools come from the equation systems themselves. For theory workers, it offers a step-by-step route through reductions that are often handled case by case.
arxiv-2602-22211:
High-rate quantum error-correcting codes pack many logical qubits into few physical ones, but proving they beat unencoded computing takes both excellent gates and long-range connectivity. Shival Dasu and forty-four co-authors demonstrate that feat on a trapped-ion processor with nearly a hundred qubits, using iceberg codes and a two-level concatenated variant. New gadgets for encoded operations make the demonstration possible.

Across fault-tolerant and partly fault-tolerant benchmarks spanning dozens of logical qubits, the encoded computations outperform their unencoded counterparts, with reasonable postselection rates. That is the beyond break-even milestone: encoding helps rather than hurts. The result strengthens the case for high-rate codes on trapped-ion hardware.
arxiv-2602-22311:
When two global symmetries break at once, one anomalous and one not, which one owns the resulting Goldstone particle? Antonio Herrero-Brocal shows the answer is the non-anomalous symmetry. Applied to the Majoron, the hypothetical particle tied to neutrino mass, that means its symmetry is baryon-minus-lepton number rather than lepton number alone.

The reassignment naturally resolves the domain-wall problem that plagued the Majoron picture. It also carries a broader lesson: couplings of the axion-like form do not by themselves prove an anomalous origin. Searches for axion-gauge-boson interactions could therefore be detecting non-anomalous Goldstone bosons, widening what those experiments can find.
arxiv-2602-22411:
Toeplitz operators carry kernels and subkernels whose maximal functions and multipliers intertwine in subtle ways. M. Cristina Câmara and two co-authors study how maximal functions in a Toeplitz kernel relate to those in a subkernel, and how multipliers between kernels act on subkernels. Their relations yield model-space representations for important kernel classes.

In particular, the authors obtain isometric model-space representations and Hayashi's representation for some classes. The work clarifies the internal geometry of Toeplitz kernels through their subkernels. Operator theorists gain tools for reading a kernel's structure from its parts.
arxiv-2602-22611:
Jiayang Meng and four co-authors defend a subtler privacy leak: intermediate representations handed out by pretrained models. In embedding-as-an-interface setups, the distributional quirks of these middle layers can betray whether a sample was in training data, and the leak varies by layer. Standard private training clips every gradient alike and spreads noise evenly, ignoring that uneven risk.

Their method, LM-DP-SGD, sizes protection per layer to its measured membership-inference risk. A shadow model trained on public data supplies train and test representations, layer-wise attackers are fit, and their error rates set the risk weights for reweighting gradients under one global clip. Theory backs both privacy and convergence, and tests show lower peak attack risk at the same budget with utility preserved.
arxiv-2602-22711:
Zhijian Luo and seven co-authors estimate galaxy distances from shape alone. Redshift, the stretching of light by cosmic expansion, usually needs colour data, but many survey images come in a single band. Their model, ViT-MDNz, learns statistical links between redshift and galaxy morphology from large-scale data.

A vision transformer reads deep shape features from each image, while a mixture density network outputs the full redshift probability curve with uncertainties. Trained on about 300,000 single-band images from the DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys, it reached about three percent scatter with under three percent outliers in r-band for redshifts up to about one. Colour data still helps, but shape alone now gives competitive catalogues for future DESI and LSST surveys.
arxiv-2602-22811:
Govindswaroop Rahangdale studies rapid blue excursions, fleeting blue-shifted outer-sun dip features widely read as on-disk twins of Type II solar jets. High-cadence spectral data plus auto detection and space-time tracking pin down their motion.

These events live briefly, mostly twenty to sixty seconds, with a mean near seventy-five seconds, with lifespans matching an exponential decay pattern that signals sudden driving. Line-of-sight speeds run twenty to one hundred forty km per second, with a mean near twenty-six, while lengths span roughly one to five and a half Mm with very narrow widths. Repeat action at fixed magnet footpoints and mass flux maths mark these events as real conduits feeding plasma upward toward the corona.
arxiv-2602-22911:
Hung-Hsuan Chen breaks the linear ceiling of low-rank adaptation. LoRA dominates parameter-efficient fine-tuning, but raising rank gives shrinking gains because linear constraints cap expressive power. CeRA, a weight-level parallel adapter, injects SiLU gating and dropout to keep non-linearity alive at inference time.

That puts CeRA in a different function class from adapters whose non-linearity collapses to an affine map at inference. At rank 64, CeRA topped the MATH benchmark grid at about twenty-four percent pass rate. It matched or beat a rank-512 LoRA near twenty-two percent and DoRA near twenty percent on one eighth the budget. It matched or beat LoRA in 10 of 12 matched settings, using the singular-value spectrum more broadly, though a scale-matched control shows output scale explains most of that spread.
arxiv-2602-23011:
D. E. Chizhov and two co-authors derive the Hamiltonian of an effective Kugel-Khomskii model with spin-orbit coupling, using pseudospin and isospin operators with exact account of the t2g multiplet splitting by the crystal field. An analytical solution covers any relation between Hubbard repulsion and crystal field splitting, interpolating Mott-Hubbard and charge-transfer insulators.

Orbital orders are described through octupole moments, and the ground-state phase diagram spans spin-orbit coupling, Hund exchange, and Hubbard interaction. The team investigates a quantum phase transition between a state with hidden magnetic and orbital long-range order and a ferromagnetic state with reduced moment plus antiferroorbital order. Hund and spin-orbit effects together produce easy-plane-type anisotropy.
arxiv-2602-23111:
Yanyi Li and two co-authors compress LLM signals for memory-saving training with PRAC, a Principal-Random Subspace method. Signals are the primary memory choke point in large-batch LLM training, yet current squeezing methods miss the tone shape of signals, causing slow settling or small squeezing. A good squeezing should give a fair guess of the original signal with low spread.

PRAC splits signals into a principal subzone caught via SVD to retain main information, and a random subzone drawn from the leftover part to sketch the tail. By adding a precise scaling factor, the authors prove PRAC yields a fair slope guesser with least spread under certain rules. Wide tests on pre-training and fine-tuning show up to thirty-six percent total memory reduction with tiny loss and small compute cost.
arxiv-2602-23411:
Yongjian Zhan proposes a strictly discrete geometric model for phase shifts and hardness in random 3-SAT. Older accounts lean on physics analogies, such as replica symmetry breaking and energy maps. Those give deep large-scale insight but lack small-scale structure.

The new model maps the phenomena onto the shape math of an N-dimensional Boolean hypercube, defining the problem space through valid solutions. Rules for clustering and freezing follow from dropping vertices and Hamming-distance links. Sharp limits follow too: a lowest no-solution limit at density eight over N, with at least N(N-1)(N-2) over six no-solution cores. A highest all-solution limit sits at seven over six times (N-1)(N-2), with two to the N top cases. These extremes explain why the average-case Satisfiability Threshold Conjecture holds only 'almost surely', and the framework explains the easy-hard-easy curve via depth-first search geometry.
arxiv-2602-23511:
Stefan M. Hesseling and one co-author generalize a classic result of Duffin and Schaeffer on inhomogeneous Diophantine approximation. Take any countable sets Y and Z, with Z kept outside the rational span of Y plus one. They construct functions whose approximable sets have zero measure or full measure. Which case holds depends on whether the parameter lies in Y or Z.

The proof uses residue systems whose residues take arbitrary real values. It also uses facts about primes in Bohr sets. The authors extend a theorem of Rogers to real residues. They extend Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions to primes in Bohr sets. They show circle rotations equidistribute along such primes when the angle is rationally independent of the Bohr parameter. An appendix by Manuel Hauke settles a combinatorial question from the introduction.
arxiv-2602-24011:
Václav Riss and three co-authors present an online inspection algorithm that lets a drone fly around an unmapped transmission tower and photograph its insulators in detail. The 2026 paper fuses camera and LiDAR data to detect and locate insulators on the fly, without any prior map of the tower.

Detection uses a convolutional neural network, with LiDAR points projected onto images and filtered by detection boxes. Several localization methods, based on clustering, robust fitting, and principal component analysis, are coupled to that pipeline. Simulations show that a single-flight strategy saves substantial inspection time versus scanning first and then visiting waypoints. A real-world flight achieved small mean localization errors in both horizontal and vertical directions, with far lower horizontal variance than the closest prior approach.
arxiv-2602-24111:
Vikash Singh and seven co-authors introduce a neurosymbolic verification framework that aims to guarantee clinical reasoning in vision-language models used for radiology reports. The 2026 paper notes that such models often produce diagnostic impressions unsupported by their own findings, or miss conclusions their findings entail. Standard lexical metrics punish paraphrase and miss those deductive failures.

The pipeline autoformalizes findings into evidence. Evaluating several models across chest X-ray benchmarks, the verifier exposes failure modes invisible to traditional metrics. Enforcing solver-backed entailment as a post-hoc check systematically removes unsupported hallucinations. In short, the checker reads the report like a logic test. Claims must follow from the findings. That rule is strict and simple.
arxiv-2602-24211:
Sophia N. Cisneros and four co-authors present a single-parameter model for galaxy rotation curves, an alternative framing of the dark matter problem. The 2026 paper starts from the classic mismatch: measured rotation curves disagree with the curves predicted from luminous mass alone, a key piece of evidence for dark matter.

The model predicts observed Doppler-shifted spectra from luminous mass estimates plus one free parameter. Applied to a sample of nearly two hundred galaxies, it yields mass-to-light ratios, goodness-of-fit measures, and the free parameter for each system. Its average fit quality compares favorably with the dark matter model on the same data, and it successfully fits more galaxies. The dark matter contribution is encoded in two transformation terms applied to luminous mass. A power-law relation between the free parameter and galactic photometric quantities may even remove the need for that parameter.
arxiv-2603-00311: Çakar, Lee, and Davis survey regular-expression engine testing. Differential testing misleads, they argue, because regex dialects differ sharply, while naive fuzzing wastes effort on invalid inputs that exercise only parsers. They describe progress toward ReTest, pairing grammar-aware fuzzing with metamorphic testing for dialect-independent oracles. The team surveyed testing across 22 engines, analyzed 1,007 bugs and 156 vulnerabilities, and curated 16 metamorphic relations from Kleene algebra. A preliminary PCRE run reached three times the edge coverage of existing fuzzers and found three new memory-safety defects.
arxiv-2603-00411: Barman, Caragiannis, and Shyam study fair sharing of divisible goods when each person values items differently and faces a size budget, so some goods may go unassigned. They place leftovers with a charity construct and study feasible envy freeness, which judges envy only over budget feasible bundles. The team extends known existence results, shows the feasible set is non convex, and proves fair plus Pareto optimal sharing always exists. They also confirm no method can add truthfulness to both at once, though truthfulness pairs with each alone.
arxiv-2603-00611: Cai and eight colleagues lift spectral compressive imaging from single frames to video, where masks hide spatial spectral detail and frame by frame rebuilding breaks time consistency. They first build DynaSpec, a high quality dynamic hyperspectral set of thirty frame scanned sequences. Their Propagation-Guided Spectral Video Reconstruction Transformer then applies spatial then temporal attention across neighbouring frames, using a bridged token to cut compute. Simulation tests assess the new model and benchmark.
arxiv-2603-00911: Baral, Garcia, and Sritriratanarak devise an exact algorithm for finding repeating tiles in finite flat grids, where several patterns may nest hierarchically. It inspects regions for internal repetition, normalizes each to a minimal form, and uses prime extraction to handle irregular sizes efficiently. Simple tiles are detected in under a millisecond on grids up to 32 by 32, though complex patterns grow exponentially harder, serving puzzle reasoning and symbolic pattern analysis.
arxiv-2603-01111: Ma and five colleagues improve vision-language adaptation by splitting attention head roles instead of treating layers as uniform. They argue specialization lives in single heads of deeper layers, and their Concept Entropy metric sorts heads into attribute, generalization, and mixed roles. Attribute tokens plus a role-based attention mask shield generalization heads from task knowledge, with adaptive fusion at inference, balancing task gains and zero-shot retention across fifteen datasets.
arxiv-2603-01211: Dev and eighteen colleagues offer a unified plan for judging AI cultural intelligence, arguing scattered cultural tests miss the whole picture. Drawing on yardstick theory and psychometric soundness, they split the background concept from its yardstick, define culture's core domains, and treat it as a suite of skills tracked through reliable signs. The paper closes with guidance on data work, probing tactics, and scoring metrics for real cross-cultural judging at scale.
arxiv-2603-01311: Chandrasekhar, Ock, and Barati Farimani offer Catalyst-Agent, an LLM-powered agent that runs closed-loop catalyst screening alone for cell reactions like oxygen, nitrogen, and CO2 reduction. Built on an MCP server, it searches stores through OPTIMADE, builds slabs, finds sticking values with Meta FAIRchem's UMA model inside AdsorbML, and checks reaction markers. It refines near-miss hopefuls with shape tweaks. Across oxygen, nitrogen, and CO2 campaigns it performs strongly and settles in about one and a half to three and a half trials.
arxiv-2603-01411: Halverson, Harvey, and Nee propose a new info-based measure of fine-tuning, the response of low-energy readings to small changes in basic theory settings. To each parameter point they attach an odds spread over readings, with gap measures showing parameter response and setting a curved metric on parameter space. By Chentsov's theorem, the physics-picked metric is the Fisher information metric up to scaling. They propose a scaled fine-tuning matrix built from the Fisher information matrix, whose non-zero eigenvalues serve as the fine-tuning measure.
arxiv-2603-01711:
Louis-Pierre Arguin and Nathan Creighton bound rare large values of the Riemann zeta function on its critical line. Their 2026 work builds on a prior study of the same function just off that line. Large deviations ask how often the function strays far from its typical size.

They prove an unconditional lower bound for real large deviations of a set logarithmic order. Unconditional means the proof needs no unproven hypotheses, a high bar in this field. The bound matches the order of the best known upper bound across a stated range. It also yields a fresh proof of the sharpest known lower bounds for fractional moments of zeta. Moments summarize average powers of the function, so the two results reinforce each other and the random-matrix view of zeta.
arxiv-2603-01811:
Filippus Roux argues that nature resists placing large masses in two places at once in this 2026 work. Quantum theory allows superpositions, where an object sits in a blend of two states at once. For heavy masses, such a blend could entangle with the geometry of spacetime itself.

Roux models the split mass as a Schrodinger cat state, the famed blend of two distinct states. Total energy of that state dips as a function of the gap between the two mass positions. That dip acts like a force that pushes back against forming the split in the first place. A broader form of the effect is then discussed in connection with the measurement problem. If the effect holds, gravity itself may help explain why big objects never show quantum splits.
arxiv-2603-02111:
Thang Pham, Andrea Pinamonti, Dung Tran, and Boqing Xue study line patterns in special finite groups in this 2026 paper. The groups are finite Heisenberg groups, built from a finite number field. Their operator averages a function along flat lines inside the group. Such averages are called Kakeya maximal operators in this field.

For directions alone, the problem drops to a known field case, and the team finds exact growth rates. A richer version also records a line's central slope. For the smallest group, they prove a sharp bound for that richer version. From it they derive exact mixed rates and floor sizes for Kakeya sets. The proof uses wave methods only, not the polynomial trick common in this area.
arxiv-2603-02511:
Chrisantus Eze, Ryan Julian, and Christopher Crick retrieve objects from dense clutter with a robot in this 2026 paper. Large end-to-end models can manipulate objects but learn slowly and resist inspection. The authors argue for specialized, decoupled systems instead. Their framework, Unveiler, splits spatial reasoning from action execution.

A lightweight transformer encoder scans the clutter and picks the most critical obstacle. That choice passes to a rotation-invariant decoder that carries out the removal. Training starts by imitating a heuristic, then reinforcement fine-tuning discovers better strategies. Success reached high levels even when targets were fully hidden in simulation. The reasoning module moved to real scenes with no retraining. A physical robot validated the full system after only geometric calibration.
arxiv-2603-02911:
Moha Naeimi, Ingo Barke, and Sylvia Speller show how two colors of light can write and erase charge patterns in tiny crystals. Their 2026 paper studies rubrene microcrystals that grow in two sector shapes with strikingly different glow and behavior. The team probes the crystals' inner electronic structure with a time-of-flight photoemission method.

Under ultraviolet light, the diamond-shaped sectors pile up charge while the triangular sectors stay nearly neutral, a split traced to direction-dependent conductivity. A second, weaker light then generates carriers that cancel the stored charge on demand. A model combining surface capacitance with drift and diffusion matches the observed energy shifts closely. Such crystals could host charge landscapes that researchers sculpt in space and time.
arxiv-2603-03011:
A. Acar, M. Bashkanov, and D. P. Watts propose using particle beams as nets to catch heavy dark matter drifting past Earth. Their 2026 paper outlines experiments where an intense photon or muon beam runs alongside other work, watching for beam particles knocked by cosmic dark matter. Heavy dark matter is hard to probe with underground detectors built for lighter candidates.

The predicted scattering rates are large enough to see at high beam intensity, given the usual estimates of dark matter density near Earth. The effect grows especially strong at a proposed muon collider built as a Higgs factory, which suits the heaviest, least constrained candidates. Existing photon sites like Jefferson Laboratory would need intensity and energy upgrades to reach a detectable rate.
arxiv-2603-03211:
Xindi Gong and four others speed up shape design when the best shape must also be safe under uncertainty. Engineers optimizing a shape governed by partial differential equations must resample many uncertain cases for every candidate shape, which standard methods do very slowly. Neural surrogates are fast but often give unreliable sensitivities, the gradients an optimizer follows. Their 2026 approach, Shape-DINO, trains on derivatives deliberately.

Geometries are encoded by smooth mappings onto one fixed reference domain, and training teaches both the physical solution and its derivatives with respect to design and uncertainty. The authors prove error bounds tying surrogate accuracy to final optimization error. On three test problems, including flows around bodies in two and three dimensions, the method gave more trustworthy optima than plain surrogates. It ran orders of magnitude faster per evaluation, and needed far fewer costly simulations.
arxiv-2603-03311:
Barton D Wright records the inner workings of Logovista, a commercial system that translated between English and Japanese. Logovista was sold from the early 1990s through at least 2012, far longer than most research translation tools. It worked by explicit rules rather than learned statistics, at a time when that approach demanded huge hand-built resources.

Inside were hand-written grammar rules, a large central dictionary carrying syntax and meaning constraints, and chart-based parsing that scored rival readings to handle ambiguity. Wright stresses the daily work of keeping such a system alive: controlling regressions, managing ambiguity, and hitting limits as coverage grew. He presents the account as a technical and historical record, with preserved code and logs, not a plea to revive rule-based translation.
arxiv-2603-03611:
Michael Igbinoba, of Princeton University, measures how much energy Hurricane Melissa bled away crossing Jamaica's mountains. Melissa struck Jamaica in 2025 as a Category 5 storm with winds near one hundred sixty knots, a landfall strength never before seen on comparable North Atlantic terrain. How strongly such an intense storm weakens over rough land, relative to weaker storms, remains poorly understood. His study is deliberately idealized.

Attention centers on the decay of internal energetics while the storm's center sat over the island. Kinetic energy is tallied inside a fixed radius, following established observational practice, and integrated kinetic energy is compared before and after the land interaction. A novel two-dimensional axisymmetric diffusion model then tries to reproduce the observed dissipation using only vertical turbulent mixing and surface drag. The two-fold aim: quantify Melissa's true energy loss, and judge how far a stripped-down framework can explain it.
arxiv-2603-04011: Cardone and Paolini propose teaching computer science foundations through core methods, using transitive closure as a case study. Standard textbooks often underemphasize ubiquitous methods and lack informatics-relevant cases, though discursive proofs are valuable for future programmers. Although all proofs are elementary, the topic suits practicing computational-thinking methods. The method grows from shared teaching with Stefano Berardi, whose logical and proof-theoretic contributions shaped the course.
