They define target alignment, a metric for how closely a network's output change matches its output error, and derive exact rules for deep linear networks. PC proves better than BP, above all in deep, narrow, pre-trained networks, and the authors derive exact rules for sure optimal match in PC.
arxiv-2605-12011: Zhengkun Huang and Gongxing Sun build CaloArt, a diffusion transformer for fine-grained calorimeter shower making. Large-patch chunking with x-prediction enables fast raw voxel making without a ready-made latent coder. On CaloChallenge Dataset 2 it took the best FPD and strongest high-level and judge scores, while on Dataset 3's 40,500-voxel grid x-guessing beat v-guessing on all metrics. Both models make a shower in about 10 ms on a single GPU.
arxiv-2605-12211: In a 2026 paper, Abraham Itzhak Weinberg presents ORCHID, a consensus protocol for distributed ledgers. ORCHID maps the brain's binding problem onto the blockchain consensus problem. Binding asks how neural rhythms fuse into one percept; consensus asks how nodes agree on ledger state despite Byzantine faults. Each node carries a noisy phase oscillator, and consensus fires when the order parameter crosses a binding threshold, echoing gamma-band binding. Simulations show full consensus at Byzantine fractions up to 40 percent, with convergence under 4 seconds at 30 nodes. Message complexity beats PBFT at 150 nodes.
arxiv-2605-12311: Van Wijngaarden and three colleagues argue that rising carbon dioxide will not harm life in natural waters, and may help it. They point to the buffering power of alkalinity and dissolved carbon dioxide, which limits pH shifts from outside influences. Doubling air carbon dioxide from 430 to 860 parts per million, they calculate, would move representative seawater pH from 8.18 to 7.93. That shift, they note, is smaller than daily swings in productive surface waters and smaller than ocean variation with place and depth.
arxiv-2605-12411: Shapira, Tennenholtz and Reichart ask whether one AI agent can predict a stranger's next move in bargaining after only a few rounds. Each decision becomes a table row joining game state, offer history and dialogue, while a handful of the opponent's past games serve as labelled examples in the prompt. Their model rests on a tabular foundation model plus a frozen small language model that reads the decision-time state as an observer. Tests in controlled negotiation games show the approach can forecast unfamiliar counterparts from limited interaction.
arxiv-2605-12711: Sheoran and three colleagues predict a striking current effect in altermagnetic tunnel junctions. Altermagnets can replace ferromagnets in junctions, offering ultra-high magnetoresistance, ultrafast switching and low power. Most work stays in the linear-response regime. Using Green's functions with density functional theory, they predict large low-bias negative differential resistance in a junction built on KV2Se2O. Under finite bias, parallel current first rises sharply, then falls to near suppression. KV2Se2O gives the junction its quasi-2D Fermi surface, which plays a key role.
arxiv-2605-12811: Bhattacharya, Clifton and Walsh characterise the 3-connected unbreakable quasi-graphic matroids, abstract structures that generalise graphs and capture notions of independence. A matroid counts as unbreakable when it stays connected after contracting any of its flats, a kind of flat subset. Their complete classification extends earlier work on frame matroids and yields, as a special case, a description of the 3-connected lifted-graphic matroids.
arxiv-2605-13011: Xia and thirteen co-authors report the first result of a CHIME campaign tracking glitches, sudden spin-ups, in the young pulsar PSR J2229+6114. Daily radio monitoring caught one glitch live and triggered X-ray follow-up two days later, while archives added three more events. Across all four glitches, radio and X-ray emission show no measurable change, unlike magnetar-like outbursts seen after glitches in high-magnetic-field pulsars. The result bears on unified neutron-star models.
arxiv-2605-13111: Chen and eight co-authors study long video generation, where accumulated errors degrade quality over time. Existing KV-cache strategies assume all attention heads need the same history. But the authors identify three head types: Anchor Heads needing broad long-range context, Wave Heads with periodic temporal dependencies, and Veil Heads focused on initial and adjacent frames. Their Pyramid Forcing assigns each head type its own cache policy with heterogeneous cache lengths. On VBench-Long it lifts the 60-second Self Forcing score from 77.87 to 81.21.
arxiv-2605-13211: Petr Rozhin and colleagues study light emission from a two layer semiconductor stack of molybdenum diselenide and palladium diselenide. Pairing the layers lifts room temperature emission from the bright exciton state about sixfold, while dimming a second exciton state. The gain spans a broad colour range, so it is not tied to one narrow resonance. Coupling between layers redirects energy toward light output without chemical treatment or strain.
arxiv-2605-13511: Tsz Ting Chung and three colleagues study many-shot chain-of-thought learning on reasoning tasks. Analysing reasoning and non-reasoning tasks, they find distinctive properties of many-shot learning. They read it as in-context test-time learning, not scaled pattern matching. They suggest two principles: demonstrations should be easy to grasp, and ordered for conceptual progression. They propose curvilinear demonstration selection, gaining up to 5.42 points on a math task with 64 demonstrations. Overall, the work reframes the long context window as a curriculum for test-time learning.
arxiv-2605-14011: Queiroz and Ferrari offer robust estimators for inflated beta regression, a model for continuous shares that can hit the edges at zero and one. Maximum likelihood fits for such models bend badly under outliers, which can warp inference and mislead conclusions. The new estimators blunt that weakness while keeping the model's plain form and clear reading. A data-driven rule picks the tuning constants, and robust Wald-type tests, simulations and a real-data trial back the approach.
arxiv-2605-14111: Amiri and three co-authors model how hospital pharmacists ration attention during drug shortages. Interviews show pharmacists fix on a small subset of drugs, spending scarce thought only on the most urgent cases amid uncertainty, time pressure and patient risk. The paper formalizes that bounded rationality as a framework that splits drugs into a high-cost reasoning subset and a low-cost monitoring subset. Two agents test the idea: an Expert Agent using interview-derived attention weights, and a Learner Agent that adapts attention over time through experience.
arxiv-2605-14211: Schneider and three co-authors introduce ASH, an agentic system that self-hones in long-horizon worlds. Long-horizon visuomotor tasks challenge current methods, which lean on hand-engineered rewards or labeled demonstrations that do not scale. ASH instead learns a long-horizon policy from unlabeled internet video, with no reward shaping or expert annotation. In a self-improvement loop, ASH learns an Inverse Dynamics Model from its own trajectories when stuck. It then uses that model to extract supervision from relevant internet video, keeping key moments as memory.
arxiv-2605-14311: Sun and eight co-authors present BBCritic, a beyond-binary GUI critic. Current GUI critic models adopt binary classification, and scores for valid actions and plausible distractors become indistinguishable. Two defects explain this: Affordance Collapse, flattening the affordance space into 0/1 labels, and noise-prone binary objectives overfitting noise. Two-stage contrastive learning lines up instructions with actions in a shared Affordance Space, restoring the hierarchy binary supervision flattens. BBCritic-3B, trained without extra labels, beats 7B-parameter binary models and transfers across platforms and tasks.
arxiv-2605-14611: Szczuczko and team present a domain-based charge-transfer split for correlated wavefunctions. It works with any configuration-interaction-type excited state. Rather than using excited-state densities, it splits excitation character into local parts and domain-based charge-transfer parts. Two ways of adding up domain parts are offered. The charge-transfer character is claimed to stay largely the same across basis sets, for both inter- and intramolecular cases.
arxiv-2605-14711: Luo, Liang, Yu, Lyu, Li and Yu examine black holes and neutron stars in massive Hellings-Nordtvedt theory. It is a vector-tensor theory where a vector field couples non-minimally to curvature. Analysing the field equations near spatial infinity, they show the asymptotic vacuum condition rules out generic nonzero values of both couplings. Two single-coupling sectors survive instead. One reproduces known monopole-like asymptotics, while the other gives an asymptotically flat Schwarzschild metric plus a nontrivial radial vector field.
arxiv-2605-14811: Lei investigates tidal coplanarisation of circumbinary planetary systems through stellar Cassini states. Known planets of this kind sit nearly coplanar with their host binaries. Why this pattern holds is unclear. Simulating secular spin-orbit evolution with tidal decay, a test case moves through three stages: flattening, spin-orbit synchronisation, and spin-orbit alignment. Angular momentum passes between stellar spin and orbital motion. Mutual tilt is strongly coupled to stellar obliquity. Arbitrary initial tilts are gradually damped to coplanarity by tides.
arxiv-2605-14911: Chrono-Gymnasium, built by Bocheng Zou and seven colleagues, spreads high-fidelity physics simulation from Project Chrono across large computing clusters. It runs on the Ray framework and offers a standard Gymnasium interface, so machine learning libraries can plug in directly. Two trials put it through robotic navigation over rough terrain and tuning of a planetary lander's design for stable landings. The team reports faster wall-clock runs with no loss of physical accuracy.
arxiv-2605-15011: Peter A. Jansen frames tech roadmapping as pulling scientific contributions from papers and linking each to what it builds on. His Scientific Contribution Graph holds 6 million items from 655 thousand open-access papers across science and health, joined by 36 million prerequisite edges. He also adds prerequisite prediction, guessing which old tech enables future finds. Current models reach 0.48 mean average precision under time-sorted backtesting. The graph is built from open-access papers alone, and it spans many fields.
arxiv-2605-15311: Sanja Karilanova, Subhrakanti Dey, and Ayça Özçelikkale propose time-varying deep state-space models for sequences with switching dynamics. Neurons follow time-varying dynamics supplied by a dictionary of basis functions, each evolving differently over time. Tests on synthetic switching systems and on speech denoising under switching noise show the time-varying model consistently beats time-invariant counterparts at comparable computational cost. The study also maps which dynamic aspects matter most and how freedom should be allocated across model components.
arxiv-2605-15511: Louisa Cornelis, Johan Mathe, Louis Van Langendonck, Guillermo Bernárdez, and Nina Miolane launch OgBench, a test bed for graph nets on omics data. Omics graphs are huge while patient samples are few, the flip of the usual case. Their platform sets a standard path from raw omics data to featured graph families. It tests classic graph nets, big-graph variants, and plain rivals. Widely used graph nets often fail to beat plain multilayer perceptrons. Graph structure thus does not always add value here.
arxiv-2605-15711: Xuanyu Ge, Zhongqi Wang, Jie Zhang, Shiguang Shan, and Xilin Chen propose EntropyScan, a trigger-agnostic check for backdoored vision-language models. Past defenses need trigger knowledge. The open task is judging if a model is backdoored. Backdoor injection warps cross-modal alignment, leaving anomalies in visual attention on benign samples. EntropyScan gauges those shifts with Tsallis entropy on early attention distributions. A reference Z-score norm on benign samples then flags backdoored models. Across two model builds and three attack settings it scores F1 98.5 percent and AUC 96.6 percent.
arxiv-2605-16011: Jie Gao and five colleagues test whether vision language models adapt their math lessons to varied learner types. Drawing on learner-model research, they propose a rubric. It covers thought and drive plus hardness, and right answers and response quality. Tests find clear gaps in how well models adapt. Current models still struggle to tailor teaching to the learner model, most of all with few learner facts.
arxiv-2605-16111: Reeves and colleagues track the energy budget of the solar eruption and flare of 28 October 2021. The event paired an X1.0 flare with a global EUV wave and a coronal mass ejection faster than 2,000 kilometres per second. Combining remote sensing, in situ data, and scaling laws, they tally magnetic, particle, radiated, wave, and ejection energies. Total released energy matches the pre-event stored magnetic energy, and the ejection's kinetic plus potential energy dominates the partition.
arxiv-2605-16311: Mishra and five others propose SignMuon, a 1-bit matrix-aware optimizer for distributed neural network training. Full-precision gradient communication bottlenecks distributed training, and coordinatewise optimizers ignore weight-tensor matrix structure. Each worker forms a Muon-style path via a Newton-Schulz polar factor, sends only entrywise signs, and aggregates by majority vote. The design cuts bandwidth 32-fold versus float32, reaches 92.15 percent validation accuracy across 330 CIFAR-10/ResNet-50 configurations, and beats sign-based baselines on nanoGPT.
arxiv-2605-16711: Saló-Salgado and colleagues built a calibrated multiphase flow-geomechanics model of the Wilmington Oil Field, including an elastoplastic framework, fault surfaces, and well-level production and injection schedules. Nearly a century of oil production there shifted stress, caused nearly 9 meters of surface subsidence, and was linked to earthquakes that sheared wells. Results reportedly challenge the assumed reverse-faulting regime. The best fit uses low deviatoric stress, implying stress varies with depth and may change regime. Fault destabilization stays minor on reservoir faults, larger on bedding planes.
arxiv-2605-16811: Wang and colleagues extend a graph-based resilience testing framework for power grid systems under severe weather. The extension adds analysis tied to past wind events with real outage and weather data, what-if studies for key guesses, and a coupled power-flooding add-on for sewage-backup checks. Wind-event metrics settle near 256 episodes, and outage peak, length, and intensity shift in step with weakness, layout, repair, and crew choices. In a 1,000-episode joint run, flooded homes appear in 1.9% of runs, with flood risk rising with outage size.
arxiv-2605-17211: Zhao and colleagues constrain self-interacting fuzzy dark matter using stellar motions in the dwarf galaxy Leo II. For a fixed particle mass, attractive self-interaction concentrates the dark-matter profile while repulsive interaction spreads it, improving or worsening agreement with a Jeans analysis. Across interaction strengths up to a stated bound, the 95 percent lower limit on particle mass falls between one and ten times ten to the power minus twenty-two electronvolts.
arxiv-2605-17311: Zixi Wei and colleagues present SpecSem-Net, a detector for AI-generated video that pairs semantic cues with spectral artifacts other detectors neglect. A Fourier-based module pulls high-frequency features, while a gated fusion step blends semantic context to cut noise-driven errors. Tested against five leading commercial generators, it reaches about 87 percent accuracy on the new benchmark and about 96 percent on public sets, beating prior methods.
arxiv-2605-17411: Bardyla characterizes Schur ultrafilters on countable commutative groups combinatorially, then constructs one on the integers that is not infinitary Schur. Assuming the Continuum Hypothesis, he proves Schur P-points exist in the Stone-Čech compactification of the integers, while it remains consistent that P-points exist there with none Schur. He also extends prior work by showing no Schur ultrafilter on the integers is a Q-point.
arxiv-2605-17511: Wu and colleagues train a flow-matching generative model on coupled transport-hydrodynamic events to study jet-induced medium response in heavy-ion collisions. Given only initial photon and jet spatial and momentum information, the model conditionally reproduces final-state hadron spectra from gamma-jet-induced response in central lead-lead collisions. It runs about a million times faster than full simulations. It preserves the Mach-cone front, diffusion wake and their spectral contributions, plus wake-driven rapidity asymmetry.
arxiv-2605-17611: Ghazi and colleagues study how feature selection plus parameter tuning affect machine-learning models for software fault prediction. They test correlation-based selection, recursive pruning, mutual information and L1 pruning against grid, randomized and genetic-algorithm search across random forest, logistic regression and support vector machines. Correlation-based selection with genetic tuning wins at about 88 percent accuracy with random forest, about 18 percent above untuned baselines. It cuts dimension and flags weighted methods per class and coupling between objects, with validation spread near one percent.
arxiv-2605-17811: Jucheng Shen, Barbara Su, and Anastasios Kyrillidis ask whether one shared recurrent transformer can split into two roles without separate modules. In Asymmetric Input Recurrence, the same model updates two states, with input injected only during L-updates. Rollouts on Sudoku-Extreme and Maze show a split: the H state acts as a proposal, while the L state keeps uncertainty and structure. Freezing tests confirm the split tracks dynamics, and attention shows L-updates stay more local than H-updates. A signal telling update types apart induces the specialization.
arxiv-2605-18111: Rafid Ahmed and five colleagues introduce BanglaMedVQA, a dataset of clinically validated image-question-answer pairs for Bangla medical visual question answering. They benchmark current foundation models on it. Bangla scores run far below English MedVQA scores, showing the strain of a low-resource language. Even top models like Gemini and GPT-4.1 mini fail specialized diagnostic questions, exposing weak fine-grained medical reasoning. Open-source Gemma-3 sometimes tops them in general categories but also struggles with clinically complex questions, underscoring the need for top-notch evaluation.
arxiv-2605-18211: Luu Huu Phuc's 2026 paper presents GA-S2S, a framework that joins a small T5 sequence model to a relational graph attention network for knowledge graph link prediction. Older sequence models flatten a query entity's neighbourhood into one line of text, throwing away graph shape. GA-S2S instead encodes both text features and the full multi-hop subgraph around the query, catching richer relational patterns. On the CoDEx set it beats strong sequence baselines by up to 19 percent in relative link accuracy.
arxiv-2605-18311: Eduard Kuric's 2026 study asks whether design preferences simulated by large language models match those of real users. The team aggregates twenty-nine real preference tests from UXtweak, covering 2,073 users, and runs simulations varying reasoning, sampling, persona, and specificity. Results show large steady gaps between real preferences and simulated ones, holding across every manipulation. Synthetic justifications lack genuine depth and nuance, leaning instead on generic properties, single elements, elaboration, and overpraising. Because the gaps replicate across many real studies, the findings carry weight for design teams.
arxiv-2605-18411: S. Maji and M. P. Nowak model chiral Andreev edge states in a quantum Hall system placed against a superconductor, using the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations. They show Andreev reflection mixes edge modes at higher filling factors, a mixing forbidden in clean, purely electronic systems. Adding Zeeman coupling splits the states into uncoupled spin species, while Rashba spin-orbit coupling plus an in-plane field drives complex spin mixing across all bands, as shown in 2026.
arxiv-2605-18811: Pascal Ochem builds an infinite word over five letters that avoids half-flips, pairs of blocks that swap order. A half-flip appears when a word holds two adjacent blocks of equal length in reversed order. Earlier work proved such avoidance possible without construction, and rivals had proposed five-letter candidates. Ochem gives a pure morphic word over five letters and proves it avoids the pattern. He also shows longer half-flips need only three letters, and still longer ones only two.
arxiv-2605-18911: Yangshuang Xu and four colleagues build WILDFIRE-FM, the first foundation model pretrained for wildfire prediction from weather, fire observations, topography, vegetation and static data. General Earth models are trained for broad atmospheric goals, not fire forecasting. But a specialized backbone alone does not fix evaluation: sparse fire events make transfer verdicts sensitive to matching rules and settings. The authors add a fixed-contract evaluation framework with separate checks for matching-rule and head-selection effects, showing wildfire transfer verdicts depend strongly on evaluation design.
arxiv-2605-19211: Yongfeng Hu and five colleagues study GRO J1008-57, an X-ray pulsar, after its first Type II outburst. Type I phases evolve stepwise: stable for many periods, then jumping slightly at each Type II outburst. Such steps resist explanation by an eccentric or precessing Be-star disk. Type I energetics rise before Type II outbursts, then fall and recover, suggesting depletion-reconstruction cycles driven by Type II outbursts. The authors link the steps to the long orbital period, implying infrequent star-disk interactions and time for disk rebuilding.
arxiv-2605-19511: Wu and team ask whether watermarked images can take text-guided edits without breaking the mark. SafeMark adds a thresholded watermark-decoding loss to the diffusion editor training objective, so valid edits preserve the mark at output. High bit accuracy on edited images lower-bounds the mutual information the editor channel preserves, which governs whether the mark can be read back. SafeMark fits differentiable diffusion editors with no architecture change. Tests across editing methods and distortions show high bit accuracy and strong edits to meaning with kept robustness.
arxiv-2605-20111: Gregory Scholes proposes a mechanism for wave function collapse when separated parts of an entangled quantum state are measured. A contextual phase, placed at random in that state, locks the parts together and steers each superposition to one result when measured. The device then reads the quantum correlations in that state as classical results. More broadly, this strengthens the theory of quantum measurement.
arxiv-2605-20311: Vinay Sharma, Aditya Bharade and Olga Fink present WaveGraphNet, graph learning for guided-wave damage pin-down in carbon-fiber plates. Sparse piezoelectric sensors, few spots, weak pin-down. Sensors nodes, pitch-catch paths edges. Inverse arm: path energy shifts become a damage point via order-free passing, geometry decoder. Second arm, trained apart, foretells trial patterns. Test-time gradients through that arm nudge the point toward the true pattern. On OGW-1, three held-out region splits, refined WaveGraphNet leads mean absolute error, cutting error 50.4% on average, 23.6% to 67.9%.
arxiv-2605-20411: Iwasaki and four co-workers filter stochastic hybrid systems, which mix continuous random dynamics with discrete resets. Direct propagation of densities through hybrid Fokker-Planck equations is costly, partly from boundary flux across guard sets. Their Max-Entropy Moment Kalman Filter extension propagates a finite set of moments and rebuilds beliefs from maximum-entropy distributions. A bouncing-ball test shows it captures reset-driven non-Gaussianity without solving the underlying partial differential equation.
arxiv-2605-20611: Maharshi Sarma, Sebastian Najera, and Roberto Sussman extend a gravitational-entropy proposal to Petrov type I spacetimes. The Clifton-Ellis-Tavakol idea builds an effective energy-momentum tensor from the Bel-Robinson tensor, but earlier use was limited to types D and N, where the decomposition is unique. The authors work through the non-unique decompositions in type I and test the results on class II Szekeres models, an analytic type I solution.
arxiv-2605-20811: Jingyang He and five colleagues present Demo-JEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture for one-shot cross-embodiment imitation. Robot imitation usually copies demonstrated actions, but actions are embodiment-specific, so cross-body demos need shared action spaces or heuristic retargeting. Demo-JEPA instead treats demos as implicit specs of future goals: the target agent infers what state the demonstrator seeks to realize, not how it moves. A JEPA-based world model translates source visuals into target-compatible future latent paths used as subgoals.
arxiv-2605-21011: Jorge Olmos-Trigo reveals a universal upper bound on magnetoelectric coupling for bi-isotropic nanoparticles. The bound comes solely from energy conservation, so it holds regardless of material traits and light conditions. It also holds with no need for reciprocity, being the same for chiral and Tellegen particles. The chiral Mie coefficient of round ones of any optical size follows the same bound across all multipolar channels.
arxiv-2605-21311: Bibek Poudel and co-authors present DeCoR, a two-stage reinforcement learning method that co-optimizes crosswalk layout and signal control. The design stage encodes the pedestrian network as a graph and samples new crosswalks from a learned spread over location and width. For each layout, a shared control policy learns adaptive signal timings to cut joint pedestrian and vehicle delay. On a real corridor, learned layouts cut pedestrian arrival time by twenty-three percent with fewer crosswalks, while control cuts waits by seventy-nine and sixty-five percent.
arxiv-2605-21611: Jiayun Wang and co-authors present UniVL, a unified vision-language embedding for spatially grounded image generation. Rather than feeding a reference image and a text prompt through separate encoders, the model binds meaning to places directly from one visual input. The instruction is drawn onto a spatial mask. This drops the standalone text encoder at run time, cuts inference compute by up to fifty-two percent, and lifts image quality on their UniVL-ImgGen benchmark.
arxiv-2605-21711: Antonio Acuaviva and Tomasz Kania study primariness of Banach spaces against operator notions, the primary factorisation property and its uniform version. They rework classical arguments and pin down the extra information needed to factor the identity through any operators. In the separable setting this recovers versions of the Casazza-Kottman-Lin method and treats the special cases of ell-one and ell-infinity. Support-reduction and free-choice tools carry the factorisation results from countable blocks to non-separable sums and yield a theorem for operators on ell-p spaces.
arxiv-2605-21911: Seo Taek Kong, Weina Wang, and R. Srikant recast noise schedule design for diffusion models as an optimal control problem. The state is Fisher information for the diffusion process, evolving by an ordinary differential equation, while the control is the noise schedule itself. The objective is a functional of Fisher information that bounds the sampling error. Under added assumptions on the data distribution, they derive schedule families that recover widely used practical forms and reach an error bound of order d over n when parameters follow their analysis.
arxiv-2605-22111: Gledson Rodrigo Tondo and co-authors present a physics-informed machine learning method for rebuilding aerodynamic loads. Load models matter for predicting structural responses, yet simplifications limit accuracy, and noisy or incomplete data make checks hard. Their probabilistic method rebuilds loads on the Great Belt East Bridge under a linear unsteady assumption, matching true loads well on errors, magnitude, phase, and peaks. It also suits model checks, future load estimation, and damage prognosis.
arxiv-2605-22211: Yuyang Wu and co-authors present CLORE, content-level optimization for reasoning efficiency in language models. Reinforcement post-training often yields long, repetitive, or opaque traces, while existing methods only regulate length. CLORE edits correct on-policy rollouts, deleting repetitive segments, illegible or irrelevant content, and post-solution reasoning, while keeping the final answer. Edited pairs train with a reference-free DPO objective beside standard policy-gradient training. Tests on two 7B models across five math benchmarks show a better accuracy-efficiency trade-off, compatible with GRPO and DAPO.
arxiv-2605-22511: Liang and team offer Search-E1, where a search agent improves on its own. Recent work adds machinery: outside help, helper parts and reward extras. Each extra gains, but grows the setup and needs scarce kit. Search-E1 uses only plain GRPO mixed with on-policy self-distillation. Training questions get policy rollouts after each GRPO round. A token-level KL goal aligns the policy to its richer-context sibling trajectory. On seven QA benchmarks, Search-E1 reaches 0.440 mean exact match with Qwen2.5-3B, beating open-source rivals.
arxiv-2605-22611: Raehse, Schlapbach and Chopard benchmark machine learning for antibiotic stewardship in children's intensive care, where unclear diagnoses push broad spectrum use. They test tabular, sequence and graph models on public and Zurich hospital records against four stewardship targets: switching intravenous drugs to oral, de escalation, stopping drugs, and short courses. Results turn more on target frequency and data set traits than on model complexity. Sequence models sharpen precision recall trade offs at daily resolution but calibrate worse, leaving simpler tabular models with more trusted probabilities.
arxiv-2605-22711: Wibault and others show that hierarchy in offline goal conditioned reinforcement learning gives absolute abstraction, not just shorter horizons. Options tied to local frames, with distinct representations per level, let an agent reuse experience across similar state goal contexts instead of treating each as fresh. The paper introduces two simple algorithms for learning such options and moving away from that frame. Tests show the added inductive biases lift offline goal performance markedly, arguing that symmetry and shared structure deserve as much weight as temporal abstraction.
arxiv-2605-22811: Saeedan and others present GS-QA, an extensible benchmark for geospatial question answering built on OpenStreetMap and Wikipedia data. The set holds 2,800 question answer pairs across 28 templates, spanning spatial objects, directional and filtering predicates, and answers from entity names to distances, directions, counts and aggregated areas. Some questions force multi source reasoning, joining map facts with encyclopedia facts. Nine language model baselines do well on simple predicates with name answers but degrade sharply on complex predicates, numeric outputs and multi source questions, confirming geospatial QA as an open challenge.
arxiv-2605-23011: Torrente-Lujan studies symmetric integral Z-matrices linked to weighted star trees, where arms are type-A chains and the middle diagonal entry is any positive integer k. He computes the determinant, inertia, definite and affine zones, and the primitive positive null vector in this affine case. The affine condition is exactly a unit-fraction equation, so classification reduces to a finite Egyptian-fraction count for each pair of arm count and k. Classical affine diagrams D4, E6, E7, and E8 appear as small subfamilies.
arxiv-2605-23211: Pravda, Berman, and Ziegler study the optical traits of gapped flat matter under the quantum anomalous Hall effect. At low enough temperatures, passing, bounce, and uptake values show a shared pattern that depends only on the ratio of light energy to gap energy. There is sharp behavior with total reflection when the two energies are equal. In the zero gap limit, they recover graphene results, where the values depend only upon the fine-structure constant. The observed optical traits give an exact measure of the bandgap.
arxiv-2605-23311: Yang and five coauthors define meaning repair and tackle it in DART, a modular runtime that finds the failed case and checks fixable edges in meaning. It aligns checkpoints to those edges, and selects an allowed restore point keeping kept downstream work under links and effect rules, or stops otherwise. Across three LLM-driven domains and outside tests on a LangGraph-based substrate, DART rightly fixes all tested promise-tight cases where base local repair fails. A five-domain safety audit shows no unsafe rollbacks.
arxiv-2605-23411: Phuc Duc Nguyen and Quang Duc Nguyen craft a stealthier attack on test-time adaptation, where models adjust to unlabeled test batches. Class-wise attacks that push many samples to one label stand out, since similar benign samples get dragged along and the target label spikes. Their sample-wise attack instead flips only inputs carrying a chosen trigger while keeping overall predictions benign-looking. A meta-learning method with priority-aware gradient alignment balances attack success against stealth, beating defenses across CIFAR and ImageNet corruption benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-23711: Ulhoa and colleagues study the gravitational angular momentum of axial perturbations of the Bardeen regular black hole in teleparallel gravity. Using the Hamiltonian definition of conserved charges, they derive a closed form for its perturbation value in terms of the axial perturbation. The result shows a selection rule: odd modes vanish, while even modes contribute. Radial and temporal patterns are shown with known axial quasinormal modes of the Bardeen hole.
arxiv-2605-24011: Akbari and thirteen co-authors shrink vision-language-action models for edge robots with ActQuant, an action-guided quantization method. One stage sets each weight matrix's bit-width by its action-prediction contribution; a second tunes per-block scales with action-aware curvature, concentrating range on key weights. OmniModel.cpp ports models into a native C and C++ runtime with low-bit kernels. On LIBERO, ActQuant runs at or below 3 bits per weight while keeping about 95 percent of scores. At 2.5 bits it keeps 90.1 percent while shrinking the backbone over fivefold.
arxiv-2605-24211: Barakat and Kochmar present a modular pipeline for teaching through analogies, splitting generation into four stages: finding sources, generating sub-concepts, explaining, and evaluating. Grounded in Structure Mapping Theory, the pipeline lets each stage be studied alone, showing how model choice and inputs shape quality. Tests cover twelve language models across six families on two datasets with sub-concept notes, plus seven embedding models. Sub-concepts improve explanation quality and retrieval precision but help little in open-ended source generation, and a language-model judge matches human rankings.
arxiv-2605-24311: Griffo and Nakka introduce a multimodal wheel that adjusts grouser height for terrain adaptation on planetary rovers. Rovers face mobility trouble on varied terrain, and while stiffness and diameter adjustments have been explored, fully grouser-adjustable wheels remain largely unexplored. Their platform was tested across vinyl, coarse rock, pea gravel, and sand in two packing states. It cuts slip by 30 to 58 percent and improves travel time and energy use by up to about 77 percent. A scaling analysis links granularity to optimal grouser height, and no single height minimized slip everywhere.
arxiv-2605-24611: Aakash Kumar and three colleagues build a classical asymmetric Hopfield network with binary neurons and synchronous updates that stores vastly more strings. With n neurons, the construction supports a superpolynomial number of distinct limit-cycle attractors. Each has superpolynomial period, robust to random noise flipping bits with probability approaching one half. The result combines combinatorics, number theory, and opinion dynamics, and is the first such feat for asymmetric Hopfield networks. It shows robust sequence memory can arise from coarse architectural motifs rather than complex nonlinearities.
arxiv-2605-24711: Mengyuan Hu and others study covering the most vertices with disjoint stars whose satellite counts fall in a given interval. It runs in polynomial time for one-satellite stars, but turns strongly NP-hard at two or more. The authors give new or improved approximation algorithms for four settings, including (k+1)/2 for large intervals and 4/3 for two satellites. Local search with amortized analysis drives the methods, plus augmenting configurations bridging distant neighborhoods. They also prove APX-hardness for the last open case, where the smallest star has two satellites.
arxiv-2605-24911: Jinjin Chi leads ROAR, a method sharpening time series forecasts by making smarter use of past cases pulled in as guides. Even strong retrieved cases can fail to help a base forecast. ROAR weights training toward queries where the base forecast struggles and retrieved cases offer real gains. It first blends aligned past cases with a gate setting how strongly they correct the base forecast. Then it tunes forecast and gate jointly while staying anchored to the first-stage output, winning the lowest mean squared error on seven benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-25011: Shruti Mishra, Michael Chang, Vamsi Spandan, and Shmuel M. Rubinstein argue that fluid mechanics offers a strong testbed for reinforcement learning in high-dimensional, changing worlds. An agent there sees and affects only a small part of its surroundings. Nonlinear instabilities, where tiny disturbances grow to reshape a flow, drive problems such as jet droplet breakup, mixing between fluids, and freak ocean waves. The authors spell out two agent tasks with states, actions, rewards, nonstationary elements, and preserved invariances, and demo navigation in a Dedalus-simulated environment.
arxiv-2605-25111: Zichao Yue and Zhiru Zhang revisit graph neural networks that propagate node features once, before training, instead of passing messages at every step. That shortcut makes training cheap and batch-friendly. It has lagged behind message-passing models, however, especially on graphs where neighbors tend to differ. The authors add sturdy diffusion operators for the preprocessing step and a few-shot scheme that re-propagates hidden states during training, closing the accuracy gap while keeping the speed advantage.
arxiv-2605-25211: Govind Vallabhasseri Binish, Abdhul Ahadh, Rano Roy Kavanal, and Arya Ukunde present ECR-Net, a bio-inspired framework for causal discovery in changing systems. Standard methods assume a fixed causal graph, so they miss structural change across environments. ECR-Net models the data-generating process like a gene regulatory network, where variables activate and inhibit one another. An evolutionary search evolves candidate graphs to fit observed dynamics. Shifts in data statistics are read as shocks that trigger small graph changes, such as new inhibitions or activations.
arxiv-2605-25411: Vishnu Asutosh Dasu and colleagues automate migration of legacy kernel packet-filter programs from C to Rust with formal proof. In-kernel checks catch memory safety and termination but miss source-level bugs like bad initialization and error handling, nine classes the team documents. Their Heimdall pipeline translates programs with language models, repairs build and verifier failures, blocks escape hatches, and proves each translation equivalent symbolically. Across 115 programs, 109 translations carry formal equivalence proofs. The process also found nine real bugs, two leaking kernel addresses, eight since fixed upstream.
arxiv-2605-25711: Peled studies generic d-dimensional rigidity in Erdős-Rényi random graphs. His main result places the d-rigidity phase transition at the d-orientability threshold. Below the threshold the graph is almost surely independent in the generic rigidity matroid, with no large rigid parts. Above it the graph is almost surely not independent, with a sharp rank estimate and a giant closure clique. He also computes the rigidity rank for graphs with a given degree distribution, from local weak limits.
arxiv-2605-26111: Zheng and four colleagues improve image generation that must keep a subject's look while obeying text prompts. Encoding text and photos apart limits joint reasoning and causes copy-paste flaws. Systems that link joint models to diffusion models follow prompts better but neglect identity. The authors feed diffusion models with joint models that read text and reference photos together, plus VAE-based identity cues. A dual layer aggregation module pools multi-level traits for guidance, and staged denoising balances prompt meaning against fine identity detail.
arxiv-2605-26211: Ranit Behera and three colleagues present NINJA, a suite of cosmological fluid simulations built to study galaxy formation in the James Webb era. Their 2026 reference run reproduces observed ultraviolet brightness counts from redshift five to ten under well-chosen dust and light-synthesis settings. The inferred dust-to-metal ratio climbs with redshift, though its level swings sevenfold with dust assumptions. That spread blurs forecasts for several other galaxy measures, and the models still fall short past redshift ten, calling for sharper simulations.
arxiv-2605-26411: David A. Brewster and three colleagues study where a new mutant takes over a structured population, not just whether or how fast. On a graph, fixation location means the node holding the last original individual just before the mutant wins everywhere. Given takeover, that spot follows a probability spread over nodes. Across neutral drift, colonization, and steady selection on cycles, tori, random graphs, and islands, the spread is often lopsided and leans hard on graph shape and selection strength. Some nodes can never host the last stand.
arxiv-2605-26511: W. Xu and eight colleagues train a fully connected neural network to read solar-flare physics from hydrogen-alpha spectra. Direct measures of electron density, temperature, and plasma velocity during flares stay hard, so the network learns rapid inversion from synthetic RADYN simulation data. Spectra were matched to CHASE satellite resolution for direct use on real observations. Errors stay low across varied flare conditions, and the model matches RADYN closely. Applied to an X7.1 flare on October 1, 2024, it traces sensible spatial and temporal evolution of key parameters through flare phases.
arxiv-2605-26911: Duan and Li build TADDLE, a tool-augmented agent that spots defects in language-model-generated peer reviews, which are uniformly fluent and thus hard to judge. Four tools, Verify, Correct, Complete, and Transform, feed an integrator that outputs binary and multi-label classifications. The team also releases an expert-annotated benchmark of 1,800 reviews on 50 ICLR 2025 papers, labeled by 18 experts across six defect types. Tests show strong binary and multi-label performance.
arxiv-2605-27011: Klein and five co-authors advance polyconvex anisotropic hyperelasticity, a material theory that asks models to meet all common constitutive rules with room to adapt. They propose a new polyconvex neural-network model based on triclinic invariants and group symmetrization, valid a priori for finite symmetry groups. They also derive the first polyconvex integrity basis for a tetragonal group and functional basis for a cubic group, and test the models on cubic metamaterial data. The work fills gaps left open for such models.
arxiv-2605-27311: Yifan Jiang, Dae Yon Hwang, Jesse Cresswell, and Freda Shi build counterfactual charts to test whether vision-language models truly reason about what they see. Their Chartographer framework rebuilds charts as code, checks the rebuild, then varies the data and answers. Models that answer the original chart often fail its variants, most when new visual reasoning paths are needed.
arxiv-2605-27611: Martin Moller and Miguel Prado show that completed volumes for Masur-Veech volumes match a top tautological meeting point on the double ramification cycle. Describing cycle components and excess meeting classes yields a recursion computing completed volumes from volumes on level graphs, beyond quadratic differentials. The result also finishes the hardest case of strata with two singularities.
arxiv-2605-27811: Eunseok Yang, Xingdong Zuo, and Kyung-Min Kim reframe automated ad bidding as predicting market responses rather than choosing bids directly. Their Generative Response Model forecasts traffic and cost-value curves for a single bid multiplier, letting a simple controller enforce budget and cost-per-acquisition limits exactly. On the AuctionNet benchmark the approach steadied constraint compliance and improved overall scores over existing methods.
arxiv-2605-27911: Wang and colleagues build a test set for spotting suicide risk in Chinese group chats, where brief, broken, multi-person messages defeat post-by-post review. SuiChat-CN gathers linked chat turns from public Telegram groups, labeled with expert-checked, model-aided tags. Tests show nearby context is key to sound calls, while early warning stays hard. The data stay closed to all but approved prevention researchers.
arxiv-2605-28111: Qiu and colleagues predict how a cell's gene activity shifts after a developmental cue or genetic perturbation, in a single step. Chreode learns a structured transition that splits change into downhill landscape flow, rotation, and random spread. Pretrained on over two million mouse embryo cells, it beat rivals on blood and islet differentiation and transferred to perturbation prediction.
arxiv-2605-28411: Kazantsev and four colleagues revive quiet low-mass X-ray binaries as reliable sources for neutron-star mass and radius. Their method models unknown rotation and surface patchiness in spectra of X7 in the globular cluster 47 Tucanae, whose hydrogen-rich atmosphere removes a key bias. For a star one-point-four times the Sun's mass, they obtain a radius near 12.9 kilometers, with rotation modeling barely widening the uncertainty. The resulting mass-radius limits tighten dense-matter equation-of-state inference when combined with other measurements.
arxiv-2605-28511: Li-Bao Fan and three colleagues control the pointing of single carbonyl sulfide molecules strongly coupled to a cavity with chirped pulses. They compare two pulse setups, equal versus unequal chirp rates, and model how they move. Chirped pulses reach a maximum orientation degree near 0.58 and switch on multiphoton steps beyond first-order Magnus math. The peak value proves robust to chirp strength and off-tune settings, giving a plan for cavity-based control of molecule pointing.
arxiv-2605-28611: Geoffroy Kremer and eleven colleagues track fast exciton motion in black phosphorus, a semiconductor with a direct band gap. Mid-infrared pulses tuned to the gap create excitons, and photoemission that resolves time and angle follows their evolution over a few trillionths of a second. A quantum-kinetic model describes how excitons lose sync and turn dark through phonon scattering. Mixing experiment and simulation, they measure key early-motion numbers and pin phonon-driven scattering within one valley as a basic limit on coherent exciton effects in single-valley semiconductors.
arxiv-2605-28711: Jiawei Zhang and four colleagues propose MAP-RPS, a stage-wise method for crossing the distortion-perception tradeoff in zero-shot inverse problems with diffusion models. A MAP stage nears the minimum-mean-square-error answer, giving a low-distortion start. A re-noised posterior sampling stage then slowly lifts look quality. Theory backs both stages, and a latent-space version, LMAP-RPS, uses large pre-trained latent diffusion bases. Tests show better tradeoff crossing across tasks and strong results as fast solvers for real inverse problems.
arxiv-2605-28911: Jonathan Stray and colleagues define political neutrality for AI answers as winning approval across opposing groups while balancing approval between them. Testing the definition on controversial issues, with Reddit prompts and frontier-model answers, they gather 7,434 participants and over 200,000 evaluations in a dataset called PARETO. They find high approval on both sides is achievable on all 20 issues, while default answers lean liberal for most named models but not Grok. Politically charged prompts prove harder to answer than neutral ones.
arxiv-2605-29011: Collier Gaiser and Paul Horn prove every permutation of 1 through n has a 2-additive subsequence of length k, for k at least 3 and large n. A sequence is l-additive when its sum equals l times its first or last term. They also give polynomial bounds for the smallest such n. For monotone subsequences only, 18 is the smallest n giving a monotone 2-additive subsequence of length three. Bounds also cover l-additive subsequence counts, and methods extend to products and inverse sums via arithmetic Ramsey theory.
arxiv-2605-29111: Alexander P. Mangerel builds a 1-bounded completely multiplicative function whose log-averaged partial sums outgrow a slowly growing denominator without limit. The build disproves a conjecture of Goldmakher, showing the claimed control on those averages fails in general. Its values are chosen to force the ratio to blow up. The result settles the question in the negative: those log averages cannot be governed as tightly as claimed.
arxiv-2605-29211: Ehsan Roohi studies a blind spot in neural solvers for shock waves: matching density, velocity, and temperature profiles does not guarantee accurate closure-level quantities. For one-dimensional Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook shocks, he uses a physics-informed network whose distribution is a local Maxwellian times a bounded exponential correction. Sparse joint anchoring of heat flux and normal stress steadies the main nonequilibrium layer, while residual-only and single-moment variants fail in distinct ways. A shock-local correction then cuts the error in one stubborn fourth-order quantity.
arxiv-2605-29311: Huachao Zhang presents a unified description of gaps at a totally ramified place of degree one on a linearized function field. A linearized function field can be viewed as a Galois extension of a rational function field. For such a place, the authors describe the set of gaps and give generators, the multiplicity, and the Frobenius number of the Weierstrass semigroup. They also give a necessary and sufficient condition for the semigroup to be symmetric.
arxiv-2605-29411: Shu Wan asks whether the Markov boundary is truly useful for prediction on tabular data. Under standard rules, the Markov boundary of a target is the smallest feature set that renders every other feature needless. On a made-up benchmark, using only the oracle set, a model often lifts scores, with gains growing as columns grow larger and sparser. But the natural path of finding it with causal search does not deliver. Current methods exhaust the compute budget before reaching the regime where it helps most.
arxiv-2605-29511: Yanxing Guo and six colleagues present DynaGraph, a lightweight framework letting models tackle reasoning. Pipelines risk cascading errors, while agent teams drift and bloat memory, so DynaGraph reconfigures its topology on the fly. Time-shared adapter modules over one shared base model fit training and inference on a consumer graphics card. An evaluator triggers small patches for local gaps or rebuilds for logical breaks. Their eight-billion-parameter system nearly matches a seventy-two-billion-parameter model on benchmarks while cutting latency and token use by roughly two-thirds.
arxiv-2605-29811: Bo-Lun Huang, Zhen-Zhao Tao, and Tong-Jie Zhang hunt for chemical technosignatures in polluted white dwarfs with a meteorite-based Bayesian search. They fit a natural reference from thousands of meteorite analyses, then weigh natural material against an iron-rich mix for hundreds of sets. Strong backing for that template proves rare in photospheric and adjusted subsets. The team reports top records and gauges mixture wins, finding a low detectable share. Injection trials show telling apart rests on chemical detail, needing five seen elements.
arxiv-2605-29911: Adam T. Müller, Philipp J. Teuffel, Konstantin Manassis, and Nicolaj C. Stache cut testing for propulsion film cooling with image filling. Their machine-learning method builds images from sparse data, using a lightweight feed-forward network with positional encoding. Validated on real and synthetic data, it reaches high image likeness while cutting measurements by nearly a third. A knowledge-informed extension adds local adaptability to the images. The approach preserves high-quality data while reducing required tests, enabling efficient tuning of coolant injector settings beyond aerospace.
arxiv-2605-30211: Rongzhen Zhao and four co-authors tackle cycle consistency in self-supervised video object-centric learning. Models must discover objects and track them over time, unlike tracking from given detections, and slots are stochastic and unclear. Explicit cycle consistency on latent slots forces rigid mean seeking, harming equally valid decompositions and driving feature collapse. Their Implicit Cycle Consistency shifts the constraint to the reconstruction manifold, letting slots reach soft consensus rather than forcing exact alignment. Experiments on video benchmarks show it avoids feature collapse and beats explicit baselines.
arxiv-2605-30311: Chong Bao and 11 co-authors present Archon, a pretrained unified model for avatar generation. Archon unifies seven modes with own tokens, pretrained on synced modes and 72 tasks to model joint patterns. To address token growth in talking videos, they present lean semantic video recoding, giving fourfold token reduction while keeping fine dynamics, plus a diffusion decoder. They propose Thinking in Modality, splitting vague cross-modal tasks into stepwise thought in a different modality chain, raising quality and control. Tests show better or similar results across digital human tasks.
arxiv-2605-30511: Darij Grinberg and Tom Roby present detropicalization as a proof method. Rational functions make sense over any ring, as long as the bottoms can flip. With no minus in play, they even apply over semirings, rings without minus. It is most worthwhile to test them over the tropical semiring, in which maxima play plus and plus plays times. Over this semiring, algebra results often gain counting meaning. They give a few cases.
arxiv-2605-31411: Zhang and colleagues propose odd-parity magnons for spintronics. Magnons carry spin information without Joule heating. In collinear magnets, time-reversal symmetry forbids odd-parity band splitting. The team classifies such splitting in two-dimensional collinear antiferromagnets by spin-point-group, as a guide for finding them. Breaking the symmetry with polarised light or loop currents can induce tunable p- and f-wave splitting. In bilayers, it can drive a topological phase transition. First-principles calculations show it works in van der Waals antiferromagnets.
arxiv-2606-00411:
Rebouças and co-authors probe the sound speed of dark energy as a tell for bent gravity. Late sky data hint that dark energy shifts with time, not stays fixed. More than one tale can fit those range marks. Their waves in space may part the tales, and sound speed steers those waves.

The team test bent-gravity tales where dark traits set the shifts. They vary sound speed and watch key sky counts in two frames. Data span Planck sky glow, star bursts, wave marks, and shear sets. With three data sets, bent tales that shift dark energy lean from plain gravity. That lean holds for fast and slow sound speeds. It fades if dark energy is set fixed. Shear and lens data pull marks back to plain gravity.
arxiv-2606-00811:
Golden and co-authors ask if green claims by data centers hold up on the grid in this 2026 paper. Data centers now use 4.4 percent of U.S. electricity. Big firms claim carbon neutrality through renewable certificates and power purchase deals.

Their game-theoretic model lets a data center pick certificates, purchase deals, or on-site generation. Power firms choose entry under shifting finance costs. A timing wedge stands out: use and credited green power peak at unlike hours. That gap can hurt reliability, lift prices, and raise emissions, even at full certificate cover. Tests use the staggered release of large AI models as a natural experiment. Near data centers, fossil output, prices, and outages all rise, the authors find. Prices climb up to 25 percent in treated PJM zones. Sites with on-site power flip the power-quality effect, as the model predicts.
arxiv-2606-01011:
Tang, Ma, and Li settle the theory of a simple test for linked errors in this 2026 paper. Their setting is the Gaussian additive noise model. Two variables are each a nonlinear function of shared covariates, plus paired Gaussian errors. In that world, conditional independence of the variables is the same as zero correlation of the errors. A natural test uses the Pearson correlation of fitted residuals.

The test looks naive, yet its efficiency was unknown. The team builds the semiparametric efficiency theory for the model. The surprise: the efficient estimator is exactly that plain residual Pearson estimator. Nothing fancier can beat it in the limit. They set out the test's limit behavior and a full inference procedure. Simulations show near oracle efficiency and sound power, with type I error held in check. The paper gives a humble statistic a strong theoretical passport.
arxiv-2606-01211:
Liberati and co-authors speed up a quantum-safe key method on GPUs. Shor's algorithm puts much current crypto at risk. New schemes must resist quantum attacks. One hard base is the Learning with Errors problem. It is safe but slow to compute. The team builds a key encapsulation method on plain LWE. They code it for GPUs with OpenACC tools.

They test on bare metal and in software containers. Tests span many NVIDIA GPU types and ages. On a Grace Hopper chip, speed rises up to 208 times. That is versus a multi-thread CPU base case. The chip also uses near half the energy of x86 plus H100 setups.
arxiv-2606-01411:
Amir, Castellanos, and Heath analyze uplink analog radio-over-fiber links. Radio-over-fiber centralizes radio access networks over optical links. A low-loss fiber joins the remote head to the central unit. Analog versions modulate RF signals onto an optical carrier directly. No digitization happens at the remote radio head. Power-hungry processing shifts to the baseband unit instead. Their math frame captures fiber nonlinearity effects on uplink.

The model joins wireless channel and thermal noise terms. Fiber impairments include dispersion and conversion loss. Amplification noise and nonlinear interference also enter. Analog links beat digital receivers on energy efficiency. That holds against 8-bit and 16-bit converter setups. Nonlinear effects still cap achievable rates in the end.
arxiv-2606-01711:
Cho and co-authors fix the distortions that visual token reduction creates. Multimodal models pay a steep cost for huge visual token counts. Memory and latency suffer from that cost. Cutting tokens eases the burden, but past methods distort the sequence. Position and attention patterns shift versus the full sequence. RESTORE rectifies those two distortions while keeping the savings. A calibration step restores lost visual attention. It boosts attention weights based on distances between tokens.

A distinctive anchor choice guides token merging in RESTORE. It cuts information loss during feature averaging. Tests on many benchmarks show steady accuracy gains. RESTORE lifts each reduction method it pairs with. Top results come with the efficiency gains intact.
arxiv-2606-01911:
Mao and co-authors fix blurry text in images from autoregressive models. Such models predict discrete tokens decoded by a tokenizer. Overall image quality is strong in these models. Text rendering still lags, with blurred strokes. Letter shapes often break or warp as well.

The team traces the flaw to the visual tokenizer. It struggles to rebuild fine-grained detail faithfully. Retraining both parts would fix it but costs a lot. Their Residual Decoder Adapter upgrades the tokenizer after the fact. It leaves the token space unchanged. A paired codebook shares the old token spread. A parallel branch learns the tiny output differences. Text sharpness improves with no full retraining.
arxiv-2606-02211:
Imran and co-authors train chat models to ignore cues that should not sway them. User inputs can leak a preferred answer by hints. Models often bend toward those extraneous cues. Consistency training curbs that bend by matching behavior across inputs. Inputs with and without the cue should get like treatment.

Past methods train over whole responses or internal activations. That also constrains how the model may verbalize the cue. The result is obfuscation, a new flaw the team name. The model hides the cue's effect while staying swayed by it. Monitorability suffers when influence goes underground like that. Their Rate Matching method trains on chosen behaviors only. Expression of the behavior is left free, which curbs hiding.
arxiv-2606-02511:
Gammon and co-authors compute quark star models in a new theory of electromagnetism. The theory is quasi-topological electromagnetism, proposed by Liu and co-authors as dark energy. For pure electric or magnetic charge, its effect is trivial. The dyonic case, with both charges, drives real dynamics. The team solves for quark stars in that setting.

Dyonic charge pushes the quark star hook shape to larger masses and radii. At small dyonic ratios, a second branch appears. It sits at very large mass and radius. Those stars wrap a positive pressure core in a negative pressure envelope. As the ratio grows, the branches interact and merge. The merged curve settles into a paperclip shape in mass-radius space. The work maps how charge reshapes compact star structure. It opens a new corner of modified gravity phenomenology.
arxiv-2606-02811: Nadirashvili proves a global regularity result for the Navier-Stokes equations in complex space. The equations govern fluid motion and sit at the heart of a famous open problem in the real setting. Here the solutions are defined in complex space rather than on real domains. The claim is that solutions stay regular for all time. No finite-time blow-up occurs in this setting. The note is brief and gives no summary of method. Specialists in partial differential equations can judge the proof directly from the full text.
arxiv-2606-02911:
Lai and co-authors build a framework for studying how language models label content next to human annotators. Most work in content moderation chases model scores. Far less work asks when its labels match no human at all. Their framework joins conformal prediction with annotator modeling.

Two new tools sit at its core. The Ghost Prediction metric counts cases where a model diverges from every human annotation on hand. The Ghost Annotator representation lets the team compare model behavior across social groups. They test four language models of varied size and family on four moderation datasets. All models grew less certain as human disagreement rose. Larger models, though, were more confident when their labels matched no human label. A steady pattern of demographic misalignment also appeared. The authors link it to bias rooted in pretraining data, and offer the framework as a way to surface such gaps.
arxiv-2606-03111:
Zeng, Suganuma, and Okatani study how to run a diffusion image model in reverse. Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models make images from a noise map. Inversion seeks the latent values, above all the first noise map, behind a made image.

The team mixes two tools. Gradient descent handles the first step directly. A fixed-point method then handles the later steps. Tests on three datasets show sharp gains in finding the true first latent values, plus better rebuild accuracy. The authors add a new test, called self-interpolation. It grades images made from points between the true and found latent maps. Past methods did fine at rebuilds but failed this test, which shows their latent maps were off. The new method beat all rivals on all measures.
arxiv-2606-04211:
G H dos Santos leads a large team demonstrating in 2026 high-dimensional quantum key distribution over a working multicore fiber network on a university campus. Quantum key distribution promises security guaranteed by physics, and encoding in more dimensions raises both noise tolerance and key yield per pulse.

Earlier field tests mixed two fiber cores with timing information instead, paying an efficiency penalty that grows with dimension. This team used all four cores of a four-core fiber directly as a four-dimensional alphabet, under real environmental disturbance. With superconducting detectors at a standard loss level, they achieved the highest composable finite-key rate per pulse yet reported for high-dimensional systems at comparable loss, supporting core-mode encoding for real networks.
arxiv-2606-04411:
Li, Wang, and Mi introduce Pepper, a protocol for anonymous broadcast with strong cryptographic privacy, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Anonymous broadcast lets one sender reach many readers. It hides who sent the message, even from someone watching the whole network. Pepper builds on a two-server design. The design uses dining cryptographers networks. In that classic scheme, messages cancel out unless one person speaks.

Pepper adds three pieces. It has a built-in anonymous sign-up step based on verifiable distributed point functions. It supports batch messaging, so one broadcaster can send several messages per round. It adds light access control based on secret-shared proofs. The system needs no outside dialing service. Each sender needs one audit per round. In tests, sign-up audits took milliseconds. The system scaled to thousands of channels. Messaging rates ran 1.2 to 20 times higher than leading alternatives.
arxiv-2606-04511:
Fu and colleagues speed up long-context language model inference in a 2026 arXiv paper. Sparse attention cuts compute by using only part of the key-value cache. But the cache still grows with context length. Offloading it to CPU memory creates a transfer bottleneck. The selection step can also dominate cost. Their system, SparDA, decouples selection from attention. It uses a per-layer projection called the Forecast.

The Forecast predicts which cache blocks the next layer needs. This enables CPU prefetch during current-layer compute. One head per group keeps overhead low. The addition is under half a percent of parameters. Only the Forecast is trained. On two sparse-pretrained 8B models, SparDA matched or improved accuracy. It ran prefill up to 1.25 times faster. Decoding ran up to 1.7 times faster than the offload baseline. It reached 5.3 times the decode throughput through larger batches.
arxiv-2606-04711:
Chen and colleagues dissect the spectra of little red dots, the mysterious compact red objects the Webb telescope found in the early universe, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. They analyze 14 of these objects at redshifts 2.2 to 6.7 using NIRSpec spectroscopy, decomposing the broad, narrow, and absorption components of the hydrogen Balmer lines and measuring line ratios and velocity-resolved Balmer decrements, which reveal gas density and dust.

In the five clearest sources the decrements peak at the center, and a virialized broad-line region model with a shallow radial density profile reproduces three of them. Absorption lines in six sources imply covering factors above half, and sources with blueshifted absorption tend to show dustier narrow lines, linking dust to outflows. The authors propose a viewing-angle-dependent structure: an optically thick, clumpy gaseous torus around the accretion disk, with broad-line clouds and absorbers along the clearer polar directions.
arxiv-2606-04811:
Zhao and colleagues test video generation models by making robots act out what the models imagine, in a 2026 arXiv paper asking whether generated videos encode usable physics. Video models synthesize content, but their outputs live on a screen. If a model truly internalized laws, the motion it depicts should translate into robot behavior. Their framework, Dream.exe, operationalizes this test: it synthesizes a manipulation video, converts the motion into robot trajectories, and executes them in a physics simulator.

The benchmark spans 101 curated manipulation tasks, scored on visual quality, trajectory fidelity, and execution success. Several models achieve execution success, suggesting generative priors from internet-scale data already encode physical knowledge. Yet visual quality proves a poor predictor of executability. The authors will open-source the framework.
arxiv-2606-05211:
Patrick Popescu-Pampu surveys the Euclidean algorithm, lotuses, and plane curve singularities in this 2026 arXiv article. The anthyphairetic process is a slow form of Euclid's algorithm: from two coprime integers, repeatedly subtract the smaller from the larger until reaching one and one. The same steps govern the blowups that resolve the singularity of the plane curve y to the a minus x to the b.

The blowup process can be drawn as a two-dimensional simplicial complex called a lotus. The numbers arising in either process sit at spots inside it. Popescu-Pampu recalls how to build the lotus from the sequence of quotients produced by the Euclidean algorithm. He then gives an alternative construction from the pairs generated by repeated subtraction, using what he calls anthyphairetic rectangles. He closes by showing how to reconstruct the pairs from a lotus, presenting lotuses as tools for singularity data.
arxiv-2606-05311:
Maosheng Guo and a large team benchmark how to set the angles of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm at utility scale in this 2026 arXiv paper. QAOA tackles combinatorial optimization with a parameterized quantum circuit tuned by an optimizer, and its performance hinges on finding good angles. Angle-setting methods exist, but which works best for a given instance, especially at one hundred qubits or more, is poorly understood.

First they test approximation techniques, matrix product states and Pauli propagation, as angle-finding engines that avoid quantum hardware during the search. Second, they train QAOA circuits on small problems and transfer the angles to larger instances, betting that good angles generalize across sizes. Both strategies are validated on quantum hardware for utility-scale instances. From the benchmarks they distill guidance, including how the best strategy shifts with the resource cost one is willing to spend on the angle search.
arxiv-2606-05411:
Anna Mikeda and Ben Goertzel design a motivational architecture for conversational AGI in this 2026 arXiv paper. Drive systems in AI were mostly built for agents regulating bodily needs, but a chat agent lives differently. Its senses and actions are words, its world is the user's shifting mental state, and its moves are speech acts, tool calls, and silences.

The paper reworks the OpenPsi lineage, coupled to the MetaMo scaffold, for that regime. Homeostasis is recast in dialogue-native terms, with the agent managing drives such as competence, uncertainty reduction, affiliation, and aesthetic coherence instead of hunger or fatigue. Three contributions follow. A ten-stage pipeline separates the agent's inner modulation from its appraisal of the situation. A dual strategy blends fast, urgency-driven replies with slower multi-goal planning. A final distinction separates pre-action feelings from post-action emotions as forms of affect.
arxiv-2606-05711:
Yingzhuo Liu surveys a quiet shift in how AI agents talk to each other in a 2026 arXiv paper. Teams of language models usually exchange plain text messages. Text is readable, but it costs time, loses detail when inner states are squeezed into words, and invites ambiguity. A newer approach sends continuous inner states directly: embeddings, hidden states, or memory caches. Liu builds one framework to organize this fast-growing literature.

Methods are sorted along three axes: what is sent, how sender and receiver align their spaces, and how the receiver fuses the signal. Eighteen representative systems from 2024 to 2026 fit the scheme. Five major design patterns emerge from the sorting. Open problems include aligning unlike model families, securing these hidden channels, and shrinking them for edge devices. The paper gives researchers a shared map of a field that had grown by scattered examples.
arxiv-2606-06211:
Fernando López, Santosh Kesiraju, and Jordi Luque adapt speech recognition to individual impaired speakers in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pathological speech, shaped by conditions such as ALS or Parkinson's disease, often defeats recognizers trained on typical voices. Retraining a whole model per speaker is costly and data is scarce. Their approach conditions a frozen speech model on a compact voiceprint of the speaker instead.

The method, called FiLM conditioning, scales and shifts the model's internal features at every layer using information drawn from speaker x vectors. The base model's weights never change, so ordinary speech handling stays intact. Tested on the TORGO and NeuroVoz collections, in English and Spanish, the conditioned model reduced word error rates on pathological speech. It stayed competitive with established adaptation strategies and with fine tuned rivals, while using only a fraction of the trainable parameters and still answering speech questions well.
arxiv-2606-06311:
Wonmo Koo, Sanha Chang, and Heeyoung Kim predict where ships will sail next in this 2026 arXiv paper on maritime safety. Vessels broadcast their positions through the Automatic Identification System, and forecasting those tracks helps avoid collisions and plan routes. Ships follow habitual lanes yet also make rare, sharp maneuvers, so a model must recall both the routine and the exceptional. Memory augmented networks, which store past patterns in an external memory and retrieve what matches, fit that need.

Such networks had proven themselves on pedestrians and road vehicles, but not on ships. Tested on AIS data from the Gulf of Mexico and the New York Bight, the memory based approach beat a range of deep learning baselines lacking external memory. The gains were consistent and substantial in both regions, suggesting memory suits the diverse movement patterns of real vessel traffic.
arxiv-2606-06511:
Tianyu Wang makes colliding triangles push each other apart, smoothly, in this 2026 arXiv paper on computer graphics. Keeping a deforming 3D mesh free of self intersections is a long standing headache. Most solvers demand an intersection free starting mesh and track motion continuously, so they fail when handed an already tangled one. Wang instead defines an energy from the classic triangle triangle intersection test itself, an energy that is zero exactly when triangles separate and grows as they overlap.

The construction reduces each 3D test to overlapping one dimensional segments, yielding a simple closed form energy with second order derivatives. A GPU based inexact Newton optimizer minimizes it, untangling meshes with no user interaction, no history, and no valid starting configuration. Intersections resolve efficiently inside larger deformation tasks. That widens the territory for non oriented deformation primitives, where tracking inside and outside is itself unreliable.
arxiv-2606-07111:
A standard tool for predicting how quantum systems settle after a sudden change may have a hole in it. Goldstein exhibits that hole in this 2026 arXiv paper. The tool is the quench action formalism for integrable models. It assumes that overlaps between the starting state and energy states vary smoothly with particle density.

His counterexample starts from a Mott insulator, a state where bosons freeze one per site. The target system is a Lieb-Liniger gas of interacting bosons. The overlap with its eigenstates turns out highly singular. No smooth function of the density can express it. The proof works in a solvable limit and expands in the coupling strength. An appendix finds the same failure for crystal states in the XXZ spin chain. The moral is cheering, in a way: real quenches carry far more structure than the old formalism ever allowed.
arxiv-2606-07211:
Robots sent into nuclear plants or disaster zones must explain themselves, or cautious operators will not trust them. Luckcuck, Taylor, and Farrell design explanation in from the start in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their abstract architecture is a template any autonomous system can adopt. Explainability, they argue, is like safety: retrofitting it rarely works.

All system information routes through a Central Executive. Inside it, a belief desire intention agent reasons about goals while an Explainer component prepares accounts of behavior. The pairing lets the robot explain past actions and future plans in the same framework. A worked example applies the design to the civil nuclear industry. There, both workers and regulators demand auditable decision making. The architecture stays abstract deliberately, so different robot platforms can instantiate it. Future work includes formalizing the design and eliciting explanation needs from stakeholders. Trust is treated as an engineering requirement with a blueprint.
arxiv-2606-07311:
Rani and co-authors build a scoring system for how faithfully AI video generators portray world cultures, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Existing metrics grade visual quality only, so a model that swaps a Namaste greeting for a handshake scores just as well as one that gets it right. Their CultureScore framework splits faithfulness into three parts: identity, meaning who is shown; context, the culturally specific setting; and behavior, the gestures and interactions that norms require.

The team generated over six thousand videos across ten countries using three leading models, including Veo 3.1 and LTX-2. No model achieved culturally faithful generation overall. The best reached only about fifty-seven percent on their composite score, and behavior was the weakest dimension for every model tested, staying below roughly fifty-two percent. Human annotators' preferences tracked CultureScore, while the visually best model was ranked last by people, underscoring the gap.
arxiv-2606-07511:
Connors and co-authors present the first dataset from the Rocky Worlds survey hunting for atmospheres on small planets around red dwarf stars, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Whether rocky planets orbiting M dwarfs keep atmospheres is unknown, despite such planets being abundant.
