The target, GJ 3929 b, is a warm Earth-sized planet receiving 17 times Earth's sunlight, with a mass near 1.75 Earths. The James Webb Space Telescope watched 4 of its eclipses at 15 micrometers, probing day-night heat redistribution and carbon dioxide absorption.

Combining all 4 observations, including 2 unpublished, gave an eclipse depth near 118 parts per million and a dayside temperature around 640 kelvin. The dataset remains consistent with a bare rock, though it leaves more room for thin atmospheres than the first 2 suggested. Only thick carbon dioxide atmospheres without thermal inversion are ruled out. The paper documents analysis lessons, showing one detrending method is sturdier against aperture choices than the standard approach.
arxiv-2606-07711:
Hao Yang and colleagues tackle a portability problem for AI agents in this 2026 arXiv paper: memory written by one language model often serves another badly. Users switch models between tasks, and agents route steps to different models for cost reasons. Memory systems built around a single model therefore strand useful experience whenever the model changes.

Their system, Rosetta Memory, adapts memory from both sides with two trained operators, one shaping how experiences are stored and one shaping how they are presented when read. A training curriculum deliberately favours whichever models currently gain least, so the operators generalise broadly. A reward based on the gap over naive memory keeps credit with the memory rather than the model. On three multi-hop question benchmarks, including HotpotQA and MuSiQue, the system beat the baselines and stayed robust when an unseen model replaced the original one.
arxiv-2606-08011:
Boxuan Lyu and co-authors train a model to rewrite sentences so that another model translates them better, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Rewriting a source text before machine translation can raise quality, smoothing awkward phrasing into something the translator handles well. But prompt-based rewriting can backfire, especially with smaller models of about four billion parameters: uncontrolled rewrites drift from the original meaning and quality drops.

The flaw, they argue, is that prompts never optimise the thing that matters, the downstream translation. Their approach uses reinforcement learning with translation itself as the reward: a rewrite earns credit only when the resulting translation improves. The title's loop runs both ways, rewrite to translate, translate to reward. Tying training directly to translation outcomes aims to keep the gains of preprocessing without the degradation naive prompting causes.
arxiv-2606-08511:
Jie Ma and colleagues make multimodal language models faster by letting them look less, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models face an inference bottleneck from the quadratic cost of self-attention over long visual token sequences. Images become hundreds of tokens, and every layer attends across all of them. The authors identify an inefficiency they call visual attention saturation. Visual tokens rapidly establish their spatial structure in early layers. Visual-to-visual attention in deeper layers is thus redundant, while the feed-forward networks there remain essential.

Their method, Visual-Skip, is a training-free scheme that decouples spatial interaction from semantic evolution. Rather than discarding tokens, it imposes block-wise sparsity by bypassing the saturated visual self-attention modules in deeper layers. The skipping can adapt to the task, since different tasks demand distinct reasoning depths. The approach requires no retraining.
arxiv-2606-08711:
Tribel and Bontempi benchmark neural networks that repair the errors of cheap wave simulators, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Numerical dispersion, where simulated waves travel at slightly wrong speeds, is an artifact of finite difference solvers. Learning-based correction has been studied only for a restricted family of designs and only for the elastic wave equation. The authors build a deep finite difference framework on 2D anisotropic acoustic wave spread.

Their testbed covers twenty-seven thousand velocity fields, the material structures through which waves propagate. Twelve correction designs, from linear regression to Fourier neural operators, are benchmarked under one protocol. Differences thus reflect architecture rather than evaluation luck. The paper supplies the shared evidence base the young subfield lacked until now in this area of work.
arxiv-2606-08811:
Hoseini, Quix, and Decker offer a framework for comparing how organizations structure their data systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A data architecture is the design deciding how data is stored, integrated, governed, and served for analysis. Candidates have multiplied, with overlapping names. The authors define DATER, a set of requirement dimensions, and use it to examine six architectures. The list runs from the data warehouse and data lake to the lakehouse, fabric, and mesh, plus a semantic data lake.

Each is traced from its roots and scored against the same dimensions, exposing where rivals genuinely differ and where they rebrand shared ideas. The central conclusion is that no single architecture satisfies every technical need. The right choice depends on context, and hybrid designs are common. Lakehouses and fabrics, for instance, deliberately blend the strengths of lakes and warehouses. The study aims to help readers pick architectures instead of following fashion.
arxiv-2606-09011:
Grace and Datar use electric fields to mimic the crowded environments that make weak acids release protons, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hydrogen fluoride and hydrogen chloride are a contrast: HF is a weak acid, HCl a strong one. The authors computed potential energy surfaces, maps of a molecule's energy as its bond stretches, for both under static electric fields. Such fields mimic those from hydrogen-bond networks.

Both bonds softened and destabilized as the field grew, but at very different thresholds. HCl's ground-state surface became dissociative, meaning the molecule falls apart at any bond length, near 450 megavolts per centimeter. HF held together until nearly 700 megavolts per centimeter. The difference tracks HCl's polarizability, its electrons shifting more easily, and its weaker bond localization. Dipole moments confirmed HCl's stronger electronic response. The results connect a property to the macroscopic gap in acid strength.
arxiv-2606-09311:
Sergi Masip and colleagues give world models a sense of direction over long horizons without demanding a picture of the goal, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures learn latent dynamics and plan by optimizing action sequences with sampling methods like the Cross-Entropy Method. Flat planning collapses on long tasks: rollouts are expensive, errors compound, and a goal image is usually required. FF-JEPA adds a second, action-free model beside the standard forward model.

That latent planner predicts the next subgoal from the current state, chopping one long trajectory into a chain of short, tractable optimization problems. The forward model then only has to reach the next subgoal, not the distant end. On PushT, preliminary results show FF-JEPA succeeding at long-horizon tasks from random starts where the flat LeWorldModel baseline fails. The planners train on unlabeled demonstrations, pointing toward goal-free robot learning that scales.
arxiv-2606-09411:
Charles Westphal and his colleagues show that language models hiding secrets in innocent-looking text can dodge the detectors built to catch them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A fine-tuned model can encode a prompt-borne secret into fluent output, a steganographic trick that leaks data without any visible trace.

The authors adversarially fine-tuned steganographic trojans into five open models, including Qwen and Llama variants. The trojans still recovered their secrets with exact-match rates between fifty-eight and seventy-nine percent. Both linear and nonlinear probes failed to extract them, and general ability dropped by only a few percent. An information-theoretic analysis explains the evasion: the payload hides in interactions that low-order probes cannot see. The fix is a recontextualisation dataset that restricts those hiding places, and on it, probe detectability returned for all five trojans.
arxiv-2606-09511:
Sandeep Gupta and Roberto Passerone build a screening system that keeps poisoned images out of foundation model training data in this 2026 arXiv paper. Modern visual models curate their own vast datasets with self-supervised methods, scraping unvetted external sources at billion scale. That openness invites data poisoning, where attackers slip in corrupted examples that later distort the trained model's behaviour.

Their Poisoned Data Detector runs before training begins. It combines the pretrained ImageBind model, which embeds images and text in a shared space, with classical classifiers such as random forests, support vector machines, and nearest-neighbour methods. The team evaluated the detectors on one hundred seventy-six thousand images from three datasets, under three different adversarial attacks, in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings. The support vector machine version performed best overall, including on real-face collections it had not been tuned for.
arxiv-2606-10011:
Rastinejad and colleagues present a multi-wavelength campaign on the first supernova of its kind caught at the moment its shock broke out, in a 2026 arXiv paper on astronomy. In March 2026 the Einstein Probe found its nearest fast X-ray transient, matching expectations for shock breakout emission, the first flash as a supernova shock exits the star. The counterpart, SN 2026gzf, is a broad-lined Type Ic supernova, and the first with a definitive X-ray breakout detection.

Radio follow-up over roughly six to fifty-five days ruled out an on-axis jet above a stated energy threshold for plausible surrounding densities. Fitting its light curve with five physical models, the team finds combined emission from circumstellar interaction and radioactive nickel decay fits best. Rate estimates suggest most such supernovae produce fainter breakout signals than this event, since otherwise the Einstein Probe would detect several to sixteen per year.
arxiv-2606-10211:
Leary and his team build tooling for checking whether AI-generated software tests deserve trust, in a 2026 arXiv paper on software engineering. Such tests must be mapped to the code they target, placed into real projects, built, run, measured against the baseline suite, and repaired when needed. In practice that checking is split across build systems, runners, coverage tools, mutation tools, and scripts.

Their open-source prototype, TestMap, runs evidence-backed test creation for C# and .NET codebases. It supports codebase analysis, source-test mapping, base execution, code metric capture, test smell detection, and coverage checks within one pipeline. The framing treats generated tests as both code artifacts and checking artifacts: they must themselves be validated before serving as evidence about the system under test. TestMap aims to make model and plan comparisons solid rather than anecdotal, as teams adopt model-assisted testing in real codebases.
arxiv-2606-10311:
Rocha and his team study how software developers move from knowing about accessibility to building it, in a 2026 arXiv paper on software engineering and inclusion. In company settings, accessibility is usually treated as a compliance rule rather than a chance to innovate, and builders struggle to design truly accessible products. The study reviews fourteen project proposals for LLM-based access tools and focus group discussions with nine people at a Brazilian technology company.

Inclusive innovation emerged most when efforts were led by people with disabilities themselves, rather than designed on their behalf. The authors argue that if organizations adopt similar shared ways, accessibility can evolve from an afterthought into a driving force for tech quality and cultural change. The work connects LLM-assisted development with disability-led innovation, hinting the new tooling wave is a chance to rethink who leads access work inside companies.
arxiv-2606-10411:
Jarolim and his team reconstruct the magnetic field above a solar filament using data from two heights, in a 2026 arXiv paper on solar physics. Solar eruptions release magnetic energy stored in the lower atmosphere. Whether that energy sits in a ready-made flux rope, a twisted bundle of field lines, or a sheared arcade that forms a rope only during eruption is hard to determine. Their data-driven method combines photospheric and chromospheric vector magnetograms in one multi-height fit, handling variable formation heights and the one hundred eighty degree flip in measured direction.

Tests against radiative magnetohydrodynamic models show photosphere-only models can misread the pre-eruptive setup, while chromospheric constraints recover the three-dimensional structure far better. Applied to Swedish Solar Telescope data on an active region filament, the method reconstructs a field matching a pre-eruptive flux-rope setup.
arxiv-2606-10611:
Lehuger and Henon-Just apply reinforcement learning to industrial cutting layouts in this 2026 arXiv paper. The two-dimensional irregular nesting problem asks how to pack irregular polygon parts into the smallest possible area, as when cutting printed circuit boards. Traditional solvers search with hand-built heuristics and are blind to shape geometry, relying on guided brute force. The authors pair a learning policy with a Polygons Transformer, an encoder that reads continuous polygon outlines and lets parts attend to one another. That lets the agent learn geometric intuition from data.

Trained with a combinatorial optimisation reinforcement learning framework, the agent reaches area utilisation competitive with Sparrow, the leading handcrafted solver, matching it on the four-polygon tier with no human-engineered rules. The eight-polygon tier exposes scalability bottlenecks, which the authors flag honestly. They release a training dataset from complex geographic contours and a benchmark for the task.
arxiv-2606-10711:
Pattison and colleagues argue the coming agentic web needs new rules, not just new protocols, in this 2026 arXiv paper. AI agents are now capable enough to search, negotiate, and transact for users online. Yet platforms block or degrade agent access, and the law draws no line between malicious bots and agents acting with a user's delegated authority. The missing piece, they argue, is normative infrastructure: accepted laws, norms, and practices governing agentic access, built through a society-wide conversation.

They defend three principles. A delegation principle: users should ordinarily be entitled to use authorised agents. Two-way transparency: agents disclose their principals and purpose; platforms disclose how they treat agents. And proportional restriction: platforms justify curbs only by concrete or expected harms. The paper maps legal and administrative pathways, from regulatory decisions to legislation, that could enact these principles and support an open economy of agent-advocates.
arxiv-2606-10811:
Malde argues that underwater acoustics needs its own deep learning, not borrowed vision models, in this 2026 arXiv paper on marine science. Echo sounders are a window into the ocean, producing echograms that experts read to find and classify fish and targets. Over the last decade, deep learning has been applied to this data: tiling echograms for classifiers, segmenting with U-Net architectures, detecting schools with object detectors. The results have been rather modest, Malde notes, beside deep learning's transformation of images and text.

His diagnosis is twofold: acoustic data has properties image methods fit poorly, so advances need methods designed for the physics of sound data. And the field lacks the infrastructure breakthroughs feed on: data formats, and, even more, high-quality data sets with established performance goals. Until those shortcomings are remedied, method development stalls. The paper is a position piece: a research agenda for interpretation of ocean observations.
arxiv-2606-10911:
Vojtěch Staněk and colleagues audit the datasets behind deepfake speech detection in this 2026 arXiv paper. Claims about detector fairness and robustness rest on these collections, so the team compiles 39 of them and checks access, documentation, demographic and language coverage, scale, and the genuine-speech sources underneath.

Two problems stand out. Most datasets carry no demographic labels at all, and only a few mark gender or language, so fairness checks by subgroup are mostly impossible. The datasets also recycle the same genuine-speech corpora, so a detector tested across collections may be retested on near-identical voices, inflating claims about how well it generalizes.
arxiv-2606-11011:
Andrews and four co-authors work in partition theory in a 2026 arXiv paper, counting ways a whole number can split into sums of smaller parts. They study two signed partition functions, counting rules attaching plus or minus weights to each split, where parts above one are governed by the smallest even part and the count of ones. Earlier work left two conjectures about these functions unproved.

The team settles both conjectures. The first gives one function's generating function, a compact formula encoding every count at once, as a rational term plus a false theta series with periodic signs. The second shows the companion function's coefficients take only the values minus one, zero, one, and two. Their engine is a master identity linking both generating functions through an extra variable tracking non-compulsory parts. Setting it to minus one, with a Rogers-Fine evaluation, yields both results.
arxiv-2606-11111:
Mashood and Nabeel present a longitudinal study of malicious internet domains in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such domains deliver phishing, malware, and fraud, while attackers register new ones constantly. They collected about 1.52 million domains flagged by at least five VirusTotal scanning engines. All were first seen between January and May 2026, and enriched with registration and passive DNS records.

They split the set into compromised domains, legitimate hijacked sites, and attacker-created domains, the latter about 89.3 percent of the total. Across eight dimensions of analysis, patterns emerge. Most attacker-created domains are short-lived and used within weeks of registration. A few registrars and top-level domains account for most abuse. Cloudflare infrastructure is heavily exploited for domain fronting. Bulk registrations of thousands of domains from one registrar in a single day are widespread. WhatsApp and Google are among the most impersonated brands. The annotated dataset is shared publicly for further research.
arxiv-2606-11411:
Romadanov, Musikhin, Mun, Nam, and Raitses study how background gas distorts plasma measurements in a 2026 arXiv paper. Charge-exchange collisions affect measurements of plasma plumes in vacuum facilities, especially when background pressure makes the mean free path comparable to the plume size. They investigate that regime in a gridded ion source's 400 electron-volt argon plume.

Fast-ion and low-energy fluxes were measured with a retarding potential analyzer and planar probes; fast-neutral flux came from a thermal probe's deposited-power measurements. Low-energy ion flux grows with pressure and distance. After isolating fast ions, their attenuation fits a semi-empirical quasi-two-dimensional model including charge exchange and plume divergence better than a one-dimensional law. The model misses fast-neutral flux both ways: low at small distances, high at large distances and pressure. Background pressure affects both plume and diagnostic response, so complementary diagnostics are required.
arxiv-2606-11511:
Ramírez-González and Machado study a branching particle system with one very long-lived type in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. The system is a critical multitype Bellman-Harris process: particles move by stable processes and reproduce under a critical offspring law. The lifetime distribution of type one has infinite mean, with a regularly varying tail, while other types have lighter polynomial tails.

Under a space-lifetime condition linking the tail exponents, the motion dimension, and the branching law's stability index, plus a local increment condition on the heavy lifetime, the authors prove convergence. The system converges to a Poisson random measure concentrated on the infinite-mean type. In other words, at large times only the long-lived type survives in the limit, and its spatial distribution becomes Poisson. The result extends theory for heavy-tailed branching systems.
arxiv-2606-11711:
Alexander Ryabchenko, Idan Attias and Daniel M Roy study online learning with late feedback and limited memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. In online convex optimisation, a learner predicts, then learns the cost of earlier rounds after a delay. Standard theory assumes every pending round can be tracked until feedback lands. Real systems have finite capacity, and feedback from untracked rounds is lost forever.

The authors impose a hard cap on tracked pending rounds. Their semi-clairvoyant model lets the learner watch delays expire rather than knowing them in advance. A scheduler randomises which rounds to track and weights observations by importance, reducing the problem to a weighted variant they solve with adapted algorithms. The resulting regret bounds, measuring loss against the best fixed choice in hindsight, are the first for this setting. Capacity growing only logarithmically with time recovers standard delayed rates, and performance degrades gracefully below that.
arxiv-2606-11911:
Juliette Murris, Bernadette Stolz and Karsten Borgwardt give topological data a statistical toolkit in this 2026 arXiv paper. Topological data analysis summarises the shape of data in persistence diagrams, records of when loops and cavities appear. These diagrams do not live in a vector space, so standard statistics and machine learning apply awkwardly. Their method, STRAND, treats each topological feature's persistence as a survival time, borrowing the mathematics of survival analysis.

The resulting persistence survival function becomes the single central object. From it they derive a non-parametric two-sample test with calibrated false-positive rates and high power from few diagrams. They also derive readable effect sizes and a stable feature vector for downstream learning. Validation covers synthetic shapes with controlled topology, fourteen graph and point cloud benchmarks, and functional brain connectivity data. The authors claim STRAND first unifies hypothesis testing and vectorisation for persistence diagrams in one representation.
arxiv-2606-12111:
Emma McGinness and three colleagues model a thousand-year-old supernova remnant in this 2026 arXiv paper. SN 1006, the wreck of a star seen to explode in the year one thousand six, shines from radio waves to gamma rays. Its bright polar caps, aligned with the ambient magnetic field, make it a natural laboratory for how shock waves accelerate cosmic rays.

The team built a self-consistent multi-zone kinetic model including shock modification by the accelerated particles themselves, magnetic field amplification and particle drift. It reproduces the remnant's observed spectrum and spatial structure, except the radio profile, which they argue needs full three-dimensional fluid effects. Where the shock runs parallel to the magnetic field, acceleration is strikingly efficient, around twenty percent, while perpendicular regions manage under one percent, matching kinetic simulations. Electrons, not protons, produce most of the gamma rays, making SN 1006 a leptonic source, except in the northwest.
arxiv-2606-12411:
Jung and co-authors give chatbots a notebook of revisable thread summaries instead of a growing transcript, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Long conversations force models to re-read everything each turn, wasting compute and burying old facts. Truncation loses information; one-shot summaries cannot be corrected and errors compound. Their C-DIC system treats a conversation as interleaved threads, each with a compressed state stored in one compact dialogue memory.

Each turn runs a loop: retrieve the relevant thread states, revise them with new information, and write them back. Training uses truncated backpropagation through time, adapted so the model learns cross-turn dependencies without unrolling the whole history. On long-form dialogue benchmarks the method beats static compressors on quality and efficiency. Perplexity and latency stay stable across hundreds of turns. In one test, after 196 intervening turns, C-DIC recalls how many dinner parties the user mentioned, where baselines fail.
arxiv-2606-12611:
Silva and co-authors race nine automated machine-learning tools at catching network intruders, and find most stumble over rare attacks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Intrusion detection on the NSL-KDD benchmark is heavily imbalanced: some attack types are vanishingly rare. Many studies cheat by collapsing the task to two classes or deleting the rare ones. This evaluation keeps all five classes, including the scarce R2L and U2R attacks, under one reproducible protocol.

Frameworks with ensemble learning and imbalance-aware tuning do best. PyCaret leads with a macro-F1 of sixty-six percent, helped by stacking and automated tuning; AutoGluon follows at fifty-five. Tools without native balancing support, including LazyPredict, TPOT, and FLAML, degrade badly on the minority classes. High headline accuracy can coexist with blindness to rare attacks, so accuracy-driven tuning alone fails here. The authors offer the study as a standard benchmark.
arxiv-2606-12911:
Nguyen and colleagues present PiDA, a phonetically informed data augmentation method that makes Vietnamese speech translation robust to recognition errors, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In cascaded speech translation, recognition slips spread into the translation. The team sorts recognition errors for Vietnamese, sorting substitution errors by phonetic cause and gauging their impact with linear mixed-effects models.

They confirm that most substitution errors arise from phonetic confusions, words misheard as similar-sounding alternatives, rather than random noise. These errors degrade translation quality: on the FLEURS Vietnamese-English benchmark the mismatch costs between 6.79 and 10.64 BLEU points. PiDA therefore trains the translation model on synthetic text with the same flaws, substituting words with sound-alike alternatives drawn from phonetic word embeddings. Fine-tuning on the PiDA-augmented data lifts translation of erroneous outputs by up to 2.04 BLEU points over standard fine-tuning.
arxiv-2606-13111:
Dalerci and colleagues present MÖVE, a holistic benchmark for testing large language models in the German public sector, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Model selection for public administration is ad hoc, and existing benchmarks are English-centric, United-States-centric in content, and focused on task performance. MÖVE tests 39 models across 2 dimensions using 10 German-language data sets, including gold- and silver-standard data sets the authors built to reflect public-sector domains.

Performance criteria cover summarisation, question answering, and topic extraction. Governance criteria assess hallucination leanings, energy consumption, provider transparency, and alignment with German constitutional values and knowledge of positions held by German political parties. The scoring mixes classical metrics, embedding-based methods, and language-model-as-judge methods. The headline result is that no single model wins across all criteria: top models differ between tasks, and model size alone is a poor predictor of quality.
arxiv-2606-13211:
Alshahrani and Behzad build a cross-modality framework on hallucination in medical imaging AI, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hallucination here means clinically plausible yet wrong outputs: fabricated anatomical structures, missed findings, incorrect laterality, and invented values in generated reports, with effects on biopsy decisions, staging, and treatment planning. The narrative review draws on peer-reviewed studies, benchmark data sets, and FDA guidance from 2023 to 2026 across CT, MRI, PET and SPECT, ultrasound, and digital pathology.

The review's most striking numeric finding runs against intuition: general-purpose foundation models beat medical-specialised models on hallucination-specific benchmarks, with a median hallucination-free rate of 76.6 percent against 51.3 percent. Narrow domain fine-tuning can thus introduce overfitting-induced confabulation. Physics-informed design constraints, chain-of-thought prompting, shown to cut hallucination by up to 86.4 percent, and human-in-the-loop safeguards each target a distinct failure mode and work best when used together.
arxiv-2606-13311:
Kim, Jeon, and Kim address anomaly detection where context matters in this 2026 arXiv paper. A ship's movement may be normal in calm weather yet suspicious in a storm, so detectors judge behaviour relative to context. Rare contexts, though, appear so seldom that models grow unstable there and raise excessive false alarms. The authors propose RGFiLM, a module that scales and shifts internal features according to context. A rarity score, computed from how often each context occurs, gates that adjustment.

Under rare contexts the gate acts decisively, while under common contexts it stays conservative. The team tests the module on maritime trajectory data, combining ship tracking sequences with weather records in a scenario built around environment-driven detours. Placed inside a sequential anomaly scoring pipeline, the method steadies decisions exactly where frequency bias previously caused trouble. The design targets safety-critical settings where the rarest situations often carry the highest stakes.
arxiv-2606-13611:
Arnab Pradhan, Rufino, and Watson study the early universe through string theory's thermal scalar in this 2026 arXiv paper. Winding strings, which wrap around a compact dimension, produce a mode called the thermal scalar. It becomes massless at the Hagedorn temperature, the limit where string behaviour changes radically. The authors couple this mode to the string-frame gravi-dilaton action, obtaining a framework for winding-mode dynamics near that transition and its role in cosmology. Below that temperature, the phase space contains configurations balancing the scalar against dilaton evolution.

Those configurations are boundary states rather than attractors, so the universe does not settle into them. When the scalar's mass depends on the scale factor, winding-mode back-reaction opposes expansion and can reverse it. Above it, the scalar turns tachyonic and generates negative energy density, enabling branch changes between solutions. They conclude these transitions give no graceful exit to standard cosmology.
arxiv-2606-13711:
Hossein Nasiri and colleagues simulate how Wi-Fi networks interfere in the 6 gigahertz band in this 2026 arXiv paper. The United States opened that band to unlicensed use under four power regimes, from standard power down to very low power, to protect incumbent services. The mixed power levels also create coexistence problems among Wi-Fi networks, a topic prior work had not examined. The authors build a simulation testbed for Wi-Fi 6E networks to study self-coexistence under mixed regimes, and document the method.

They evaluate scenarios in which low-power indoor and standard-power access points operate in overlapping spaces. The analysis shows how a high-power neighbour can degrade a low-power network's performance even when both follow the rules. Regulators set the regimes to protect incumbents; this work asks whether the regimes protect Wi-Fi from itself. The testbed gives researchers an instrument for the band.
arxiv-2606-13811:
Feris and co-authors teach a large language model to read quantum operators directly, not just their names as text. A quantum operator is the matrix describing how a quantum state changes. Language models normally cannot take in such number grids. Their 2026 arXiv paper maps these operators, written as Pauli transfer matrices, into the hidden space where the model stores word meanings. A small encoder sits before the model to do this mapping.

The team tests the idea on circuit synthesis. That task means finding a short gate sequence that performs a given operation. They use four-qubit operators in the Clifford plus T gate set. The model matches leading specialized methods. Its scores keep rising as training data grows, with no sign of leveling off. It also accepts plain language limits on gates, including limits never seen in training. That points toward models reasoning about quantum hardware directly.
arxiv-2606-14111:
Venturin and Clementi teach a coarse-grained protein model the laws of heat so it stays valid across temperatures. Coarse-graining lumps atoms into beads for speed; machine-learned versions are accurate but usually trained at one temperature, so they cannot predict heat uptake. Their 2026 arXiv paper splits the coarse-grained potential of mean force into energetic and entropic parts. The network design enforces the exact thermodynamic relation between them, guaranteeing sound behavior at new heat settings by construction.

Testing used Chignolin, a small folding protein, with two hundred fifty microseconds of atomistic simulation across five temperatures from three hundred to four hundred kelvin. The model reproduced the heat dependence of the full-atom free energy surfaces, correcting heat-unaware baselines. A cheap post-hoc correction recovered the full-atom heat capacity without retraining. The authors present a physically grounded path toward transferable coarse-grained work on biomolecular systems.
arxiv-2606-14211:
Zhu finds that language model agents cannot judge their own work even after seeing results, and fixes it with a bonus costing nothing. Agents observe environment feedback yet mis-assess their outputs afterward, even on questions answered correctly; standard reinforcement learning barely helps, due to a credit-assignment mismatch. His 2026 arXiv paper proposes RefGRPO, adding a free calibration bonus for reflections matching the actual outcome.

No reward model, judge, or annotation is needed; a dynamic schedule balances the bonus coefficient. On text-to-SQL across five benchmarks, underconfidence, flagging correct work as wrong, fell from forty-four point four percent to seven point seven percent. Task accuracy rose from seventy-five point one to seventy-six point five percent. Calibrated reflection turns the agent into its own verifier, enabling self-improvement with reflections as pseudo-rewards, and selective prediction: commit only to rollouts flagged correct.
arxiv-2606-14311:
Carenza, Gonnella, Levis, and Negro shear a fluid of tiny spinning particles and find that spin itself acts like a thinner. Dense chiral fluids, whose self-spinning constituents generate transverse forces, model systems from starfish embryos to magnetic colloid monolayers. Their 2026 arXiv paper simulates a two-dimensional Lennard-Jones model with transverse interactions, across solid and liquid regimes, under shear.

In the solid regime, spinning fluidizes the system, weakening hexatic order, the six-fold bond pattern of near-crystals. In the liquid regime, viscosity follows the Green-Kubo relation if temperature is replaced by a chirality-dependent effective temperature. Beyond linear response, flow curves collapse onto one curve when plotted against the ratio of shear rate to spinning rate: thinning-by-spinning. At large forcing, handedness matters: when transverse interactions oppose the shear, stresses relax through string-like flow channels.
arxiv-2606-14411:
Mirowski and a large team introduce Fabula in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer support for fiction writers. Fabula is an interactive app that works from detailed narrative plans, breaking stories into scenes and beats that writers can regenerate or revise at either the plan level or the script level.

The team built and tested the tool with working writers through design interviews and writing sessions involving forty-two experts, plus larger internal and external trials. They probed whether a model-based auto-evaluator tuned to expert taste improves stories, whether writers want the plan visible beside the script, and how well narratology assumptions fit other storytelling traditions. Critical feedback turned Fabula into a probe for discussing feedback tools and interactive storytelling more broadly.
arxiv-2606-14511:
Ceccarello and co-authors study how test workloads are built for vector similarity search in a 2026 arXiv paper. Similarity search finds the stored vectors closest to a query and underpins databases and deep learning systems. Benchmarks compare search algorithms, yet the hardness of the query sets used is rarely controlled, so results can mislead.

The team first evaluates several hardness measures against the actual effort an index spends answering each query. They then propose two workload generators, HephAnn and HephGrad, that synthesize queries meeting a user-specified hardness target. Both hit the target hardness in tests. HephGrad ran faster, while HephAnn made fewer assumptions about the hardness measure. Such controlled workloads let researchers probe how search algorithms behave as queries grow harder, rather than at one accidental difficulty level.
arxiv-2606-14611:
Gupta, Marathe, and Vullikanti study how to block drug flows on networks that are only partly known in a 2026 arXiv paper. Interdiction means placing surveillance or blocks on network nodes and edges to minimize illicit flow from source to destination. In counter-narcotics work the trafficking network itself is uncertain, since data are scarce and partial by nature.

The authors first generate an ensemble of plausible networks consistent with a limited real-world dataset, mixing simulation with mathematical programming. They then formulate the robust interdiction problem and solve it with integer linear programming. Even modest budgets cut flows significantly, but the best strategy varied sharply across scenarios. Their robust strategy performed near-optimally on every near-real realization while staying stable under structural uncertainty, giving policymakers a principled basis for spending interdiction budgets.
arxiv-2606-14711:
Dahshan, Mamun, and Debnath coordinate small language models at the network edge in a 2026 arXiv paper. Large models live in the cloud, incurring bandwidth, latency, and privacy costs, while small models run locally but are weaker and less robust. Their layer, SWARM-LLM, routes each query between local answering, collaboration among peer small models, or summoning a cloud foundation model, guided by lightweight uncertainty and safety signals.

The prototype runs three heterogeneous small models on commodity hardware with a seventy-billion-parameter cloud model on call. On a controlled workload of easy, hard, and safety-oriented queries, SWARM-LLM substantially improved hard-question performance over an edge-only deployment while sending only about a quarter of queries to the cloud. The authors frame the design as a practical trade-off among accuracy, latency, cost, and privacy for edge deployments.
arxiv-2606-14811:
Khanal presents a system for drawing building wireframes from 3D point clouds in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is an entry to the S23DR 2026 Challenge. A wireframe is the set of edges outlining a building's shape. The input is a point cloud built from many photos. Older methods first find corners, then link them. This system skips that step.

The model, WireframeDETR, predicts the full edge set at once. It borrows the DETR set-prediction design from image work. Three tweaks help it train. Contrastive denoising steadies early matching. A multi-scale encoder blends layer outputs with learned weights. Loss weighting shifts focus to the decoder layers that gain most. On the public test set the system scored an HSS of about zero point five eight. Its F1 score was about zero point six six.
arxiv-2606-14911:
Guo and Xia design antenna subarrays for imaging moving targets with radar in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is Part II of a two-part study. Synthetic aperture radar builds images from a moving platform. A moving target's image shifts and blurs unless its motion and height are jointly recovered. Their method uses planar arrays and a multidimensional Chinese remainder theorem to resolve the ambiguity.

This part analyzes a common-scaling two-subarray design. Both subarrays share one scaling factor, so ambiguity resolution runs on a single integer frequency vector. The unambiguous range matches the general framework of Part I. But the conditions for robust recovery grow weaker, and the error bounds grow tighter. A conventional separated scheme cannot realize this design under the same platform limits. Recovery quality also depends on array geometry, not just antenna count. Non-separable layouts can do better.
arxiv-2606-15111:
Chaurasiya and coauthors compare two kinds of reconnection events in the Sun's lower atmosphere in a 2026 study. Ellerman bombs flare in active regions, while quiet-Sun versions appear in calmer areas. Both are thought to mark magnetic reconnection, the snapping and rejoining of field lines. The team uses coordinated observations from three instruments.

Data come from the Swedish Solar Telescope, the IRIS spectrograph, and the Solar Dynamics Observatory. K-means clustering picks out the events, and spectral inversions with the STiC code estimate their temperatures. Active-region bombs often sit between opposite magnetic polarities and heat the lower chromosphere strongly. Quiet-Sun bombs lack polarity signatures and show no clear temperature rise, possibly a resolution limit. Some active-region events reach transition-region temperatures and flicker with periods near six to seven minutes. Footpoints of spicules, solar jets, sometimes coincide with the events, hinting reconnection helps launch them.
arxiv-2606-15411:
Alipour and coauthor design a distributed algorithm for the minimum dominating set problem in a 2026 theoretical computer science paper. A dominating set is a group of network nodes such that every node is in the group or next to one. In the distributed setting each node computes by exchanging short messages with neighbors in synchronous rounds. The authors target graphs of bounded arboricity, networks sparse enough to split into few forests, where earlier algorithms traded rounds against accuracy.

Their deterministic algorithm finishes in the provably optimal number of rounds while sending only a single bit per round. Its approximation quality improves on the previous best method that also avoided knowing the sparsity parameter in advance, and the algorithm is simpler. The one concession is that nodes must know the maximum degree beforehand. Tight round and message bounds matter for huge networks, where communication, not computation, is the scarce resource.
arxiv-2606-15611:
Mao and colleagues present MuDuo in 2026, a semi-supervised framework for segmenting organs in paired PET and CT scans, where expert labels are scarce. PET shows metabolic activity with blurred boundaries, while CT gives crisp structure, so the two modalities complement each other. MuDuo sets two foundation models to teach each other and a small student: SAM-Med3D for the CT side and SegAnyPET for the PET side.

Through mutual distillation, the generalist knowledge of both teachers flows into one lightweight student network, with no manual prompts needed. Unlabeled scans supply most of the training signal. On the AutoPET benchmark the student reaches state-of-the-art accuracy using only five labeled cases. It also posts a much lower boundary error than the comparable SemiSAM-plus baseline. Clinics could build reliable segmentation for radiotherapy planning from a handful of annotated scans.
arxiv-2606-15811:
Tan and colleagues present FuseChain in 2026, a runtime defence that reconstructs software supply-chain attacks from scattered evidence. Such attacks unfold in stages across sources: package traces, process events, network telemetry, and alerts each capture fragments at different granularities. Analysing the sources separately misses low-frequency evidence and the temporal context that gives it meaning.

FuseChain aligns all telemetry on one event-time axis as a temporal heterogeneous provenance graph, learning anomaly-centred representations from benign-prefix data. A key design lesson emerges: jointly optimising anomaly detection and stage prediction fails under sparse, imbalanced telemetry. Decoupling them works. A lightweight decoder on a frozen anomaly backbone lifts deployable stage reconstruction recall from about 0.37 to about 0.88 across seven attack scenarios. Adaptive retrieval further raises observable-stage recall from about 0.52 to about 0.66 without touching the detector. Fusing evidence first and interpreting stages second is the deployable pattern.
arxiv-2606-15911:
Wei and colleagues present Interactor in 2026, a framework that generates ad descriptions for sponsored search through draft-and-revise cycles, optimised with agentic reinforcement learning. Ad descriptions, unlike titles, have room to fold in world knowledge and detailed selling points matched to a searcher's intent. The generation model acts as a policy interacting with an environment of generative reward models.

Those reward models grade each draft on several axes, including knowledge capacity and faithfulness to the landing page, returning binary signals plus reasoning feedback. The policy then refines the description over multiple turns, rather than settling for a one-shot output. On industrial datasets, Interactor outperforms prior approaches at producing knowledge-rich, faithful descriptions. It has run online in a leading search ads system since May 2026, contributing to both revenue and user experience. The design treats ad copy as an iterated negotiation with critics, not a single generation.
arxiv-2606-16011:
Nikeghbal and colleagues measure in 2026 whether language models stick with a correct answer under a counterargument. Accuracy benchmarks cannot see this stability dimension. Their protocol lets a model answer a multiple-choice question, then challenges a correct answer with an argument for a wrong option, recording any flip. The design isolates argument content from social pressure, varying length, self-attribution, and source model.

Across seven frontier models and fifty-seven MMLU subjects, flip rates range from about eighteen to ninety-seven percent, differences invisible to accuracy. Telling a model the argument is its own consistently raises flips, by about seven points on average, up to nineteen. Pooling arguments across models and picking the best per question beats any single source. A challenge set, MaxFlip, amplifies flips by up to twenty-four points. Which model is challenged matters more than which model argues, and STEM answers hold firmer than humanities ones.
arxiv-2606-16111:
Li and colleagues align tool-using language agents in 2026 on two goals at once: solving tasks well and wasting fewer tool calls. Alignment methods usually maximize task accuracy alone. Tool-use efficiency, though, decides whether an agent is practical to deploy. The authors treat the pair as a multi-objective problem where neither goal should silently dominate.

Their framework, ParetoPO, works in two stages. First, hypervolume-guided dynamic weighting explores trade-offs along the Pareto frontier, the set of policies no rival beats on both goals. Second, Pareto ranking replaces the weighted signal, promoting nondominated trajectories through dominance-aware credit assignment. This gives fine-grained, action-level learning across the conflicting objectives. On mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question answering, ParetoPO finds policies with better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs than static and heuristic baselines in the reported tests.
arxiv-2606-16211:
Tan and colleagues build a benchmark and a reasoning system in 2026 for medical questions whose evidence is scattered across sources. Biomedical answers often need knowledge graphs, literature documents, and web resources together. Existing benchmarks focus on exam knowledge, reading comprehension, or short inference chains. Source-conditioned graph work stays underexplored, the authors argue.

Their benchmark, BioMedHop, holds 10,045 instances across knowledge-graph, document, web, and hybrid evidence settings. Task types cover shared-neighbor matching, intersection reasoning, path-based work, and counting, in multiple answer formats. Their system, BioWeave, retrieves graph paths and gathers document and web clues into one unified evidence graph, then verifies answers through entity-level alignment and pruning. Extensive experiments show BioWeave outperforms existing baselines, with stronger reasoning and more faithful evidence support in the reported results.
arxiv-2606-16311:
Duguet and co-authors settle in 2026 when games with integer choices can have equilibria with rational values. The games are mixed-integer linear-quadratic generalized Nash equilibrium problems: each player optimizes a quadratic objective, with integer and continuous choices, under constraints that may involve rivals' strategies. With rational input data, one might hope for rational equilibria. The authors split the class into four subclasses, by whether objectives carry player-quadratic terms and whether constraints depend on rivals.

Only one subclass passes: player-linear games with no player-quadratic terms and no rival-dependent constraints admit rational equilibria, whenever equilibria exist at all. Each of the other three classes contains games whose only equilibria are irrational. The consequences are computational. The good subclass gains a finite-time algorithm for computing an equilibrium. For the others, no such general algorithm can exist, pushing research toward approximation schemes.
arxiv-2606-16511:
Zhou warns in 2026 that fashionable tail-aware metrics for language model evaluation can manufacture findings from noise, and supplies a protocol to catch them. Recent work urges moving from mean scores to tail measures, including the extreme-value tail index. Zhou asks whether that tail-shape number adds real information beyond the mean and a standard tail-magnitude statistic. The answer, under discipline, is no.

The contribution is a pre-registered five-gate protocol: any positive tail-shape claim must pass admissibility, goodness-of-fit, threshold-stability, and effect-size gates. Applied to a standard toxicity evaluation with two structurally different scorer families, the gates catch three distinct false positives a naive analysis would have published: finite-sample variance, bounded-support contamination, and threshold-fishing. The headline claim is rejected on both scorers. Tail shape fails to separate four instruction-tuned models beyond what mean and tail magnitude already say.
arxiv-2606-16811:
Kato and colleagues scale language model reasoning from very few labels in a 2026 machine learning paper. Training models to reason step by step usually needs many checked answers to judge which reasoning traces are sound. Human labeling at that scale is slow and costly.

Their semi-supervised framework turns verification into a data factory. A lightweight classifier, trained on only a few labeled samples, grades whether an intermediate reasoning trace is valid. An entropy-based confidence filter then discards shaky traces, and the surviving high-confidence ones fine-tune the model. Tests cover verifiable math problems and visual question answering with program generation. The method matches the accuracy of training with ten to fifteen times more labeled data. Ablations show both the classifier and the entropy filter are essential: naive self-labeling gains little, and filtering stops performance from saturating early.
arxiv-2606-17811:
Andriushchenko and colleagues present UMB, a shared file format for the models used in probabilistic model checking, in a 2026 extended paper. Tools in this field check systems that behave with chance, yet they had no good way to swap low-level models with each other. Each tool used its own text format, which slowed work and made files huge.

UMB stores these models in a compact binary form built on one clear math base and a small set of bit-level parts. Top tools in the field have already adopted it, and a Python library lets users read, build, and check models with ease. The format is built to grow, with plans for stored policies and property files, and cross-tool checks run on an ongoing basis.
arxiv-2606-18111: This paper learns fair Pareto-optimal policies in multi-objective reinforcement learning. The policies balance competing objectives without sacrificing fairness across groups. Pareto optimality means no objective can improve without hurting another. The work brings equity into the mathematics of trade-offs.
arxiv-2606-18511:
Khan and Cheng explore whether mixed reality could stitch together the paper and digital halves of interface design work, in a 2026 human-computer interaction paper. Designers sketch and brainstorm on paper, then rebuild ideas in digital tools for precision and sharing, and the repeated translation between the two worlds wastes effort.

The authors first interviewed nineteen professional designers about how they actually move between paper artifacts and digital ones. They then ran nine study sessions built around a conceptual mixed reality probe that combined paper and digital prototyping, inviting participants to brainstorm what such a tool should do. Designers valued the prospect of continuous hybrid workflows, less manual reconstruction, spatially anchored workspaces, and real-time collaboration across media, and they imagined AI assistance and richer dynamic content. From the sessions the authors derive four design dimensions meant to guide future mixed reality tools for design practice.
arxiv-2606-18811:
Jang and the team diagnose why swapping stronger pretrained encoders into learned sparse retrieval can make training collapse, in a 2026 information retrieval paper. Sparse retrievers such as SPLADE build their representations from the encoder's masked-language-model head. So a natural expectation is that backbones should beat the BERT version. Instead, under standard training recipes, some degrade badly or fail outright.

The culprit is scale. Backbones whose MLM-head outputs have large norms amplify sparse activations. They distort the unnormalized dot-product matching scores, and destabilize contrastive training. The fix is a zero-cost initialization-time correction. It rescales the MLM-head projection by a constant factor before training, changing neither architecture nor objective. With it, backbones such as ModernBERT and Ettin turned from unstable runs into competitive retrievers. That held across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. In several settings they matched or surpassed the BERT baseline.
arxiv-2606-18911:
Chatzittofi and the team extend nucleation theory, the physics of how a phase is born inside a metastable one, to nonequilibrium systems whose order parameter is not conserved. The work is a 2026 statistical physics paper. Nucleation theory weighs a gain against a surface cost, to find the barrier a droplet must cross. The nonequilibrium version existed for conserved fields, as in phase separation. That leaves out cases from magnetic order to population dynamics.

The catch in the nonconserved case is that the droplet's profile during noise-driven growth differs from its profile during relaxation, which alters the nucleation barrier. The authors show the barrier can be worked on by setting the reaction coordinate, the droplet radius, so those deviations are removed. They derive results for models from population dynamics and active matter, covering systems where the new phase spreads by conversion, not transport. They find agreement with sim runs.
arxiv-2606-19211:
Rombach and colleagues report thermal tests of a robotic fiber module for Stage-5 telescopes in 2026. Thermal stability is essential for fiber positioners, since temperature shifts can change how parts behave and spoil accuracy. The module packs six units at a small pitch for dense fiber placement in new instruments. The team set out to qualify it across the full range of expected operating temperatures at observatories.

Units were tested at set points from well below freezing to warm room conditions. At each point, the team measured placement repeatability, hard-stop consistency, backlash, and non-linearity. Across the whole range, behavior stayed stable with no measurable degradation in any metric. No mechanical or electrical damage appeared either. The results confirm the small-pitch design has the thermal resilience needed for Stage-5 telescope instruments.
arxiv-2606-19411:
Xu recasts determinantal point process MAP inference as a continuous problem in 2026, aiming at scalable diversity-aware data selection. Selecting a small, diverse, high-quality subset from a huge pool recurs across machine learning. Determinantal point processes give a principled notion of diversity for that task. Their MAP objective, though, is NP-hard, and greedy or sampling algorithms scale at high cost with pool size.

The recasting works over the Stiefel manifold. Its first-order conditions form a nonlinear eigenvalue problem with eigenvector dependency of a new form. That problem admits a self-consistent field iteration with a local contraction guarantee tied to the spectral gap. The resulting solver needs only matrix-vector products with the kernel. Variety thus drives an eigenvector-dependent operator rather than a brute-force search. This kind of relaxation could bring principled selection to the data-centric scale, replacing greedy shortcuts.
arxiv-2606-19811:
Yifan Wang, Jeonghun Lee, and Sunčica Čanić couple fluid flow to a spongy elastic solid with a provably sound scheme in 2026. Fluid-poroelastic interaction pairs Stokes flow with Biot poroelasticity across a shared interface. Explicit interface treatment is fast but often unstable in partitioned solvers.

BDF2 time stepping pairs with second-order extrapolation of interface data. A Robin reformulation of the coupling keeps the split stable. Fluid and solid subproblems then solve independently, in parallel, each step. Energy identities and trace estimates yield a closed stability bound under a parabolic time-step condition. Projection-based analysis delivers matching error estimates for all four fields. Total error behaves like the spatial term plus the squared time step, as designed. Manufactured-solution tests confirm second-order time accuracy, and a moving-domain example shows wider promise.
arxiv-2606-20111:
F. Moradi Jangal, H. R. Moshfegh, and K. Azizi model hybrid stars, dense stellar remnants whose cores may mix ordinary nuclear matter with hyperons and free quarks. Their 2026 paper works inside a relativistic mean-field framework, a standard way to compute how strongly interacting matter behaves at extreme density. Its coupling constants, the numbers fixing interaction strengths, come from QCD sum rules rather than free fitting.

The team first checks bulk nuclear matter and the single-particle potentials of nucleons and hyperons. They then build the equation of state under beta equilibrium, using a sigma-omega-rho model for hadrons and both MIT bag and Nambu-Jona-Lasinio models for quarks. Phase transitions are handled by Gibbs and Maxwell constructions. From the resulting equations of state they compute mass-radius curves, particle fractions, and tidal deformability, predictions testable against multimessenger observations of real mergers.
arxiv-2606-20311:
Evelyn Fiore, George Nasr, and Cooper Stone extend a classic dice puzzle: relabeling dice without changing the odds of any sum. Their 2026 paper continues work using cyclotomic polynomials for dice relabeling, building on the famous Sicherman dice, the one alternative labeling of two ordinary dice preserving every sum's frequency. The new question restricts the dice: pairs where each die has a different perfect-square number of sides, such as four and nine. Which relabelings preserve the sum distribution then?

Generating functions encode the labels and sum frequencies, and factoring them with cyclotomic polynomials reveals the possible labelings. The authors classify what happens for square-sided pairs and offer conjectures for future work. The problem is recreational in origin, going back to Sicherman and Martin Gardner, but the machinery is real algebra. Square-sided dice are a natural next case because their generating functions factor in constrained ways.
arxiv-2606-20411:
Hsiao-Ru Pan and Bernhard Schölkopf make Direct Advantage Estimation cheaper and usable when the agent cannot see the full state. Their 2026 paper tackles two limits of DAE, a method known for sample-efficient deep reinforcement learning. DAE assumed full observability, and modeling transition probabilities cost too much for high-dimensional observations.

The theory extends to partially observable domains with minimal changes. Discrete latent dynamics models then approximate the transition probabilities at far lower cost. On the Arcade Learning Environment, DAE scales well as the function approximator grows, and it keeps its sample-efficiency edge. Bringing DAE to realistic, partially observed settings widens where its efficiency gains can be used.
arxiv-2606-20711:
Mingde Xu and nine colleagues present Video2Code in 2026, a method that turns user interface videos into interactive webpages. A video shows both how a page looks and how actions change its state. Direct use of video models is not enough. Sparse sampling can miss short action boundaries. State, action, and next state links then break, so the generated code cannot reproduce behavior.

Video2Code treats the task as recovering executable state transitions. It first scans the video coarsely to find action-critical regions. A temporal clipping tool then revisits those regions at higher resolution. Only then does it generate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. Training uses action-aligned video and code supervision. By spending its visual budget where actions happen, the method aims to build pages that work, not just pages that look right in a still screenshot.
arxiv-2606-21311:
Ali Banjafar and Guido Falk von Rudorff address bloated molecular representations in 2026, the long numeric fingerprints that machine learning models use to predict chemical properties. Standard fingerprints are built to serve every property at once, so most entries are dead weight for any single task. Their method selects and reweights features for one target property, using cheap semi-empirical data rather than costly accurate labels to guide the choice.

Across four properties, three representations, and two datasets, the median representation shrank by 72 percent with no loss of accuracy. Tuned for accuracy instead, dipole moment models reached the same quality with only 19 percent of the training data. The selection also reveals which features matter for each property, yielding compact, data-efficient models and a clearer physical reading of the fingerprints.
arxiv-2606-21611:
Lucas Fagan, Michele Tarquini, and seven colleagues diagnose why reinforcement learning stalls on hard mathematics in 2026, using the Andrews-Curtis conjecture as the test bed. The conjecture asks whether any balanced presentation of the trivial group can be simplified to nothing by allowed moves. The landscape, they find, has two humps: instances are either trivially solvable or effectively impossible, with almost nothing in the learnable middle.

Two attacks follow. New data generation populates the difficulty gap, and algorithmic upgrades add supermoves and Transformer-based architectures. Performance jumps over prior baselines. The team also publishes the first large public benchmarks of their kind: AC-19, with 125,192 presentations of graded difficulty, and AC-1M, over 1.1 million hard ones. For RL research, the lesson travels: when rewards are sparse, the curriculum may be the algorithm.
arxiv-2606-21711:
Alex Friedlan and Hae-Young Kee show in 2026 that symmetry can force exotic superconductivity in kagome metals. A pair-density wave, where Cooper pairs carry finite momentum and the condensate ripples in space, is a long-sought phase. Studying the extended t-J model on the kagome lattice, they trace the pairing landscape to the symmetry-enforced sublattice structure of the electronic wavefunctions.

At a sublattice-pure van Hove singularity, a pair-density wave emerges inevitably. Near a second, mirror-flipped singularity type, chiral, uniform, and nematic states compete instead. When further-neighbor hopping brings the two singularity types close, frustration in the interband channel stabilizes a chiral interband superconductor. The overlooked mirror-flipped singularity thus becomes a distinct route to unconventional pairing, rooted in correlations and mirror symmetry rather than fine-tuning.
arxiv-2606-21811:
Gandhi and colleagues propose, in 2026, that large code agents work better when a small critic model steers them instead of solving tasks alone. Training a full agent end to end is expensive, and it tends to leave strategy-level reasoning underdeveloped Earlier critics only scored finished attempts.

Their critic gives feedback during the run, commenting on the partial trajectory every few steps while the agent itself stays frozen. Trained on trajectories from one 32-billion-parameter model, the critic transferred to two unseen agents and raised their scores by about three to four points on SWE-bench Verified. Adding the target agent's own trajectories pushed gains higher still, at a small fraction of a strong teacher's cost. On one large agent, critic guidance both raised accuracy from 20.8 percent to 25.2 percent of tasks solved and cut the cost per task by more than half.
arxiv-2606-22111:
Ebeling and Holovko revisit, in 2026, the statistical theory of strong electrolytes and high-temperature plasmas built by pioneers Günter Kelbg and Ihor Yukhnovskii. Both systems consist of charged particles whose interactions follow Coulomb's law, and the older methods were designed to make series expansions for them converge. The authors extend those methods using an exponential interaction model.

They show the two classes of system are structurally very similar. Their physics is governed mainly by terms of the fourth and sixth powers of the charge. At higher densities they predict a structural transition to oscillating correlations between particles. Thermodynamic functions cross smoothly from a square-root rise to a slower rise respecting the Onsager bound. Charge and mass asymmetries are also studied, with applications to multiply charged ions and helium plasmas above one hundred thousand kelvin.
arxiv-2606-22211:
Lee and colleagues report, in 2026, a field study of how the r/LocalLLaMA community adopts and adapts open foundation models. Research on AI openness usually asks which parts or release practices make a system count as open. Less is known about what openness means to the people running and adapting these models under real constraints.

Through close reading of community discussions, the authors find members understand openness in practical terms. It means reliability, local control, privacy, and adapting models under limits on compute, licensing, and usability. Motives for adopting open models include autonomy, tinkering, and resistance to platform shake-ups. Deterrents include steep learning curves and performance gaps against closed systems. Shared datasets, test frameworks, and inference tools sustain the ecosystem. The authors draw lessons for how producers could support downstream usability and tooling.
arxiv-2606-22511:
Yuanhao Ding and five colleagues propose a decoding method for language models in this 2026 paper. In open-ended generation, models fall into a likelihood trap, producing repetitive and dull text that drifts away from human writing. Popular fixes cut off the unreliable tail of the word distribution, but fixed repetition penalties ignore how the score scale changes step to step.

Their method, Variance-Calibrated Modulation, reshapes the score spread before any truncation and needs no training. One mechanism, a contextual searchlight based on pointwise mutual information, suppresses global stopwords while lifting words the context actually evokes. The second, adaptive self-debiasing, scales penalties by how spread out the model's scores are in real time, keeping them fair at every step. Across open-ended writing, factual questions, and math problems, the method reduced the likelihood trap. It added negligible computing cost and improved diversity, coherence, and, at higher temperatures, reasoning accuracy.
arxiv-2606-22811:
Jinchuan Tian and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon University, LY Corporation, and NVIDIA Research present a speech synthesis system steered by plain language in this 2026 paper. Conventional text-to-speech tools demand rigid inputs: a transcript plus fixed slots for speaker, emotion, and style. Real user requests rarely arrive in that tidy form.

Their system, Bagpiper-TTS, first reasons over a natural language request to derive a rich caption, a detailed blueprint covering both the words to speak and nuanced delivery metadata. That caption then guides the actual synthesis. One model thereby covers many jobs beyond standard narration, including multi-talker dialogue, speaking a user's intent, role-play voices, and even singing. On the Seed-TTS-Eval benchmark the system reached a word error rate under two percent. It also matched dedicated models in both automated judge scores and human listening evaluations across its applications.
arxiv-2606-23011:
Linqi Wang and colleagues help groups of agents agree on a Nash equilibrium without a central boss in a 2026 control paper. A Nash equilibrium is an outcome where no agent gains by changing its own choice alone. Here the agents' dynamics are unknown linear systems, outside disturbances push them around, and no agent sees everyone's decisions. Each agent must steer from partial information while respecting shared equality constraints. The team builds one framework covering all of those difficulties at once.

Wang and colleagues recast the search as a cooperative output regulation problem. Their design combines an equilibrium model, a distributed communication protocol, and an internal model that cancels disturbances. Controllers come straight from noisy input and state data by solving semidefinite programs, with formal guarantees of stability and convergence. Simulations on drone networks and a rotorcraft formation confirm the method works and stays robust.
arxiv-2606-23211:
Angela Monti, Fasma Diele, and Carmela Marangi check whether splitting methods preserve Turing patterns in a 2026 numerical analysis paper. Reaction-diffusion systems of two species can form Turing patterns, spots or stripes born from instability. Simulators often split each step into a diffusion part and a reaction part. The authors build matrix-oriented splitting schemes for two-dimensional domains, with the Gierer-Meinhardt activator-inhibitor model as the test case. Diffusion gets either an implicit Euler treatment or an exact one, while several local maps handle the reaction step.

Monti and colleagues derive the fully discrete stability conditions, known as Jury conditions, for the split schemes. The first condition carries the true continuous Turing mechanism, while the second captures purely numerical effects. They exhibit two opposite failures: one scheme invents a spurious pattern where none should grow, and another suppresses a genuine pattern.
arxiv-2606-23411:
Danyal Maheshwari, Julia Pelzer, and Miriam Schulte predict groundwater heat plumes with a quantum neural network in a 2026 paper. Geothermal heat pumps warm the groundwater beneath cities like Munich. Planners need to forecast those heat plumes. Full simulations are high-dimensional, far beyond current quantum hardware. The team compresses simulation output into a compact set of representative parameters as training targets. Their quantum convolutional network then learns to predict those parameters as a surrogate model. The design has quantum convolution and pooling layers plus a fully connected quantum readout.

Maheshwari and colleagues evaluate the network on an ideal simulator and a noisy simulator. They also run it on IBM's 127-qubit Kyiv processor, with and without advanced error mitigation. Performance is benchmarked by mean squared error on training and test sets.
arxiv-2606-23611:
Nicolicioiu, Ghotra, Moss, and Courville clean noisy image text datasets by letting the model being trained do its own filtering, in a 2026 paper on machine learning data curation. Vision language models such as CLIP learn from huge collections of image and caption pairs scraped from the web. Those collections carry many mismatched or junk pairs, and manual cleaning is impossible at that scale. Standard fixes lean on heuristics or a pretrained model, which imports that model's biases.

The proposed method, Self Filtering, alternates two steps. First a CLIP model trains on the current dataset. Then the model scores pairs and selects a fresh mixture, favoring likely clean pairs while keeping diverse samples from the whole pool. Training on data filtered this way improves downstream performance, with no extra data and no pretrained filter involved.
arxiv-2606-23811:
Balasubramanya, Niebler, and Shapiro settle which Coxeter groups can avoid a certain strong form of action on curved spaces, in a 2026 paper on group theory. A group has Property NL, no loxodromics, if no element of it ever acts as a loxodromic element, one that steadily stretches some hyperbolic space along an axis. Coxeter groups are symmetry groups defined by relations read off a labeled graph. Earlier work on the property handled right angled groups and triangle groups.

The authors prove a complete characterization for all finitely generated Coxeter groups. Such a group has Property NL exactly when it is a direct product of spherical Coxeter groups, which are finite, and affine ones, with one infinite dihedral exception excluded. Since a group's building blocks can be read from its graph, the property can be decided from the graph too.
arxiv-2606-23911:
Rokon and colleagues replace click based training data for Walmart's product search with labels from a cascade of language models, in a 2026 paper on information retrieval. Clicks are the usual training source for dense retrieval, but they carry position bias and vanish for rare queries, while human labeling at this scale is unaffordable. Disagreement among three production retrieval systems, the team shows, is itself a structured signal. Easy positives are items all systems find. Hard positives are ones only keyword search finds. Hard negatives fool exactly one system.

A three model cascade grades the mined pairs, matching human annotators about eighty nine percent of the time. A three stage curriculum trains the model on over two hundred forty million examples by difficulty. Offline, ranking quality rises about five percent over the click trained baseline, most on rare queries. A two week live test confirmed gains in ad spend and clicks.
arxiv-2606-24211:
Cao and colleagues dissect how a revived black hole pushes back on the galaxy that hosts it. The post-merger galaxy 4C+29.30 carries a rejuvenated active galactic nucleus, with radio structures on many scales. That makes it a natural lab for feedback, the ways a black hole's output reshapes its galaxy. Their 2026 analysis combines optical spectroscopy from SDSS MaNGA and CFHT SITELLE with radio imaging from VLASS.

Mapping ionised gas across the galaxy reveals a galaxy-scale biconical outflow. Its axis sits noticeably off the radio jet's direction. Broad line widths and Seyfert-like ionisation mark the outflow as mostly a radiatively driven wind, from a black hole feeding at a healthy fraction of its limit. The northern radio lobe tells a second story. Localised gas acceleration and turbulence betray jet-driven shocks ploughing into interstellar gas. Cao's team concludes both channels operate at once, misaligned yet coexisting.
arxiv-2606-24411:
Fedotov, Fears, and Han show that in biology's races, a mixed field beats a uniform one with the same average speed. Many signalling processes depend on the fastest few searchers among a large redundant population: one sperm among millions, a few motor proteins, a handful of calcium ions. First passage time theory describes such races for identical searchers, but real populations are heterogeneous, and the 2026 paper asks what that changes.

Averaging over a heterogeneous population of memoryless random walkers produces ensemble self-reinforcement, an effect with no homogeneous analogue. The distributions of the first passage time and its minimum shift drastically relative to a uniform ensemble with identical mean rates. Most strikingly, the typical and minimum first passage times shrink by an order of magnitude under heterogeneity. Exact analytical predictions back the claim. Fedotov's team concludes heterogeneity is a tunable parameter biology can exploit, not noise to be averaged away.
arxiv-2606-24811:
Lei Wang builds a fuller way to read the spins of hyperon pairs produced in particle collisions. Spin correlations measured after hadronisation show how quantum information survives confinement. Experiments usually report one scalar number for a lambda and anti lambda pair. Wang's framework is process independent and uses the weak decay angles of the pair. Those angles can fix the whole two spin tensor, not just its scalar trace.

Applied to a short range correlation measured by the STAR experiment, the framework exposes a hidden freedom. Many density matrices share the published scalar value. Some completions are separable, while others violate the positive partial transpose test for entanglement. A string breaking benchmark turns the trace into a sharp, falsifiable pattern of component signs. Feed down from heavier particles must be handled as a tensor effect, Wang argues, not a blanket dilution.
arxiv-2606-24911:
François Pachet gives sequence generators a dial that can attract or repel chosen patterns. Variable order Markov models generate symbolic sequences, like melodies, while preserving local style. Over long runs they fall into tunnels of repeated suffixes and near periodic passages. Earlier work compiled regular constraints into automata and sampled exactly with belief propagation. Pachet shows the same machinery works softly, in both directions. A weighted automaton scores how active a family of target patterns is in a candidate continuation.

Belief propagation then samples from a distribution tilted by that score. With negative coupling, target patterns grow costly and get avoided.
