They advise that trials be considered first for all patients.
europmc-pmc7553211:
Boersma, Black and Ward estimate chronic condition prevalence among US adults in 2018. Data came from the National Health Interview Survey. Ten diagnosed conditions were counted for each adult.

More than half of adults had at least one condition. That share was 51.8% of the adult population. A total of 27.2% had multiple chronic conditions. Rates were highest among women in the survey. They were also highest in adults aged 65 or older. Non-Hispanic white adults and rural residents ranked high too. The sample held 25,417 adults in total. The results help track chronic disease burden over time.
europmc-pmc7581511:
Swanson and co-authors present an ISAPP consensus statement defining synbiotics. A panel met in May 2019 to update the term. Experts in nutrition, physiology and microbiology took part.

A synbiotic is a mix of live microbes and substrates. The substrates are used by host microbes selectively. The mix must confer a health benefit on the host. A complementary synbiotic pairs a probiotic with a prebiotic. A synergistic synbiotic uses a substrate picked for its partner microbes. The panel set out evidence levels for claims. Safety, targets and stakeholder effects are also covered. The statement aims to keep innovation open in this field.
europmc-pmc7654011:
Wu and co-authors use genetics to test whether bowel disease causes bone loss. They apply Mendelian randomization, a method that uses gene variants as natural tests. The bowel diseases are ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease. The outcome is bone mineral density at several body sites.

The team drew on public genome-wide study data and used several checks for bias. They report that genes linked to ulcerative colitis cause lower total body and forearm density. Genes linked to Crohn's disease affect density at the femoral neck. The results split by disease and by site, which past survey studies had blurred.
europmc-pmc7656711:
Zhang and co-authors report a new cell therapy built from stem cells. The team made macrophages from induced pluripotent stem cells. They gave these cells a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. The aim is a ready supply of cancer-fighting cells.

The CAR cells acted only when they met the target antigen on cancer cells. They released signaling proteins, shifted to an attack state, and ate more tumor cells. They also fought cancer in living tests. The authors say the platform could yield an unlimited source of such cells, unlike cells taken from each patient.
europmc-pmc7665311:
Turoňová and co-authors study the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2 in its natural setting. The spike lets the virus enter host cells and is a prime target for antibodies. About 20 to 40 spikes stud the surface of each virus particle. Past work used lab-made spike, not spike on real virus.

Using imaging of intact virus, the team found the spike stalk bends at three hinges. Sugar chains shield these hinges well. This flex may let many spikes grip a flat host cell surface at once. The results ground vaccine and drug design in how the spike truly sits and moves.
europmc-pmc7758411:
Jin and co-authors review how COVID-19 activates and damages the lining of blood vessels. Endothelial cells line all vessels and carry high levels of the viral entry protein ACE2. They govern inflammation and clotting at the vessel wall. Evidence ties their dysfunction to severe disease.

When these cells switch on, the vessel barrier leaks and clots form more readily. Inflammation at the wall grows, and white blood cells slip into tissue. Lung vessel damage is a hallmark of the acute respiratory failure that kills patients. The authors set out the cell and molecular steps in this process. They end with treatments that aim to protect the vessel lining.
europmc-pmc7806511:
Meredith and co-authors report fast use of virus sequencing to trace COVID-19 spread inside a hospital. The burden of hospital-linked SARS-CoV-2 infection was unclear. The team set up rapid genome sequencing during care. Genetic data were combined with clinical details.

Sequencing results came back fast enough to act on. Staff could judge whether cases on a ward were truly linked. Linked cases point to spread within the hospital. Unlinked cases suggest separate introductions from outside. That split guides infection control steps. The authors present rapid sequencing as a practical surveillance tool. It can run as a standing part of hospital safety work.
europmc-pmc7808711:
The CDC COVID-19 Response Team, with the Food and Drug Administration, reports allergic reactions after the first Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine doses. The report covers the United States from December 14 to 23, 2020. The vaccine had gained emergency use approval on December 11.

Cases include anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction. By January 3, 2021, the country had logged 20,346,372 COVID-19 cases. Deaths stood at 349,246. Against that backdrop, reaction reports were tracked closely. The document sets out what was seen in the first days of rollout. It gives clinicians guidance on spotting and treating such reactions. All 20 people with follow-up information had recovered or been discharged home.
europmc-pmc7857411:
Ng and co-authors test whether past cold coronavirus infections leave useful immunity to SARS-CoV-2. Seasonal coronaviruses infect most people in childhood. Memory from them might soften the new virus. The team checked people never infected with SARS-CoV-2.

The cohort held 350 uninfected people. A small share carried antibodies that reacted to SARS-CoV-2. Those antibodies came from seasonal virus exposure. Some could even block the new virus weakly in tests. Children and teens showed such cross-reactivity more often. The authors weigh what this means for disease spread. Old immunity may bend, but not stop, the pandemic's course.
europmc-pmc8026611:
Tang and co-authors review ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of cell death, and its stakes for health. Ferroptosis was first described in 2012 as non-apoptotic and driven by lipid peroxidation. It starts when oxidants overwhelm antioxidant defenses. Redox-active enzymes sit on both sides of that balance. Regulation reaches from epigenetic marks down to protein modification.

The review lays out two routes into ferroptosis. One depends on transporters, the other on enzymes inside the cell. The transcription factor NFE2L2 anchors the defense against it. Selective autophagy, by contrast, can push cells toward ferroptotic death. The authors then trace what goes wrong in disease. Cancer, neurodegeneration, tissue injury, inflammation, and infection all feature. The synthesis links a young death pathway to wide clinical terrain.
europmc-pmc8027411:
Wei and co-authors identify RAB31 as the marker and driver of an ESCRT-independent exosome pathway. Exosomes form as small vesicles inside multivesicular endosomes, then leave the cell. The ESCRT machinery was long thought essential for making them. Yet vesicles still formed without it, hinting at another route. The team tracked what that route requires.

The authors report that active RAB31, switched on by EGFR phosphorylation, starts the process. It engages flotillin proteins in lipid raft patches of membrane. That drives EGFR into endosomes to form the inner vesicles, no ESCRT needed. RAB31 then recruits TBC1D2B to switch off RAB7. That move stops the endosomes from fusing with lysosomes. Cargo escapes destruction and ships out as exosomes instead.
europmc-pmc8075011:
Shmueli asks which beliefs predict the intent to take a COVID-19 vaccine. The study joined two classic models of health behavior. An online survey reached Israeli adults from May 24 to June 24, 2020. It asked about risk, benefit, social pressure, and confidence. Of 398 eligible respondents, 80% said they would take the vaccine.

A unified model drawing on both theories predicted intent well. It explained 78% of the variance in answers. Men, the more educated, and past flu shot takers showed higher intent. Perceived benefit of the vaccine was the strongest single push. Perceived severity of the infection and cues to act also raised intent. Social norms and self-efficacy mattered on the planned behavior side. Half the sample had skipped the last flu shot. Even so, two-thirds of those skippers planned to take the COVID shot.
europmc-pmc8106311:
Tremblay and Ainslie count how many people live at high altitude, country by country. Old global guesses swung wildly, and national figures did not exist. The pair layered LandScan population grids over global terrain data. They tallied residents in 500-meter elevation bands for every country. Thin air, cold, and strong sun shape life up high. Knowing who lives there shapes health research.

Their count comes to 500.3 million people living at 1,500 meters or higher worldwide today. Of those, 81.6 million live at 2,500 meters or more, and 14.4 million live at 3,500 meters or more in the final tallies. Ethiopia holds the largest high population at the lower two bands. China leads at the highest band counted. Bolivia has the greatest share of its people up high. Most altitude science still studies visiting lowlanders. Half a billion permanent residents argue for a shift.
europmc-pmc8106911:
Hockenberry and Wilke present BACPHLIP, a tool that predicts a bacteriophage's lifestyle from its genome. Phages split into two camps by habit. Temperate phages hide inside host cells in a latent phase. Virulent ones copy themselves at once and burst the cell. Knowing the camp matters for ecology and for therapy. Guessing it from sequence alone was unreliable.

The tool scans a genome for a set of conserved protein domains. A random forest classifier reads that pattern and calls the lifestyle. Training used 634 phage genomes with known habits. On a separate test set of 423 phages, the calls hit 98% accuracy in the authors' hands. Older tools managed only 79% on the same test. The code is free on GitHub for anyone to use. Users can even retrain the model themselves. Fast, open lifestyle calls help sort the phage flood.
europmc-pmc8123811:
Vogt and co-authors lay out how the body moves, stores, and rations iron. Most body iron rides in red blood cells as hemoglobin. Worn-out red cells are recycled by macrophages in spleen, liver, and marrow. Food iron enters gut cells through the transporter DMT1. Ferroportin then hands it to the blood, where transferrin carries it. The liver stores the surplus locked in ferritin.

One hormone runs the whole rationing system. When iron loads rise, liver cells release hepcidin. Hepcidin binds ferroportin and drags it inside for destruction. Less iron then escapes into the blood from any cell. The review follows each player at cell and system level. Receptors, transporters, and stores each get their mechanism. Too much iron burns tissue; too little starves blood. The hepcidin dial keeps the balance fine. Its faults explain inherited and acquired iron diseases.
europmc-pmc8271111:
Andreatta and Carmona present UCell, an R package for scoring gene signatures in single-cell data. Researchers often need to grade each cell against a gene set. Many scoring tools slow down or wobble on large, mixed datasets.

UCell scores rest on the Mann-Whitney U statistic. They stay stable as dataset size and mix change. Computation takes minutes, even on modest machines. The package plugs straight into Seurat objects. Any single-cell data matrix can be scored. Code and documents sit on GitHub for free use. The tool suits the huge atlases now common in the field.
europmc-pmc8284311:
Jones and co-authors show that the antibody LY-CoV555 protects primates from SARS-CoV-2. The antibody targets the viral spike protein. Neutralising antibodies can treat infection or guard people before vaccines reach them.

In lab tests, LY-CoV555 neutralised the virus. In nonhuman primates, it protected the airways against infection. The study spans antibody design through animal proof. Teams from drug and academic labs shared the work. Such antibodies offered a stopgap early in the pandemic. The data supported moving the antibody toward human use. Airway protection was the key sign they sought.
europmc-pmc8319411:
Qiu and co-authors show that soil erosion cuts microbial diversity and soil function. Erosion drives land degradation worldwide. Its effect on soil microbes and their many jobs stayed unclear.

The team studied two sites with unlike soil texture and climate. Eroded plots held fewer microbial taxa than intact plots. Their microbe networks were simpler, with fewer links. Dominant groups such as Proteobacteria and Bacteroidetes shrank. Other groups gained ground instead. Soil lost part of its multifunctionality with the microbes. Restoration plans must rebuild the living soil, not just the surface.
europmc-pmc8361711:
Donoso-Quezada, Ayala-Mar, and González-Valdez review lipids in exosome biology and cell talk. Exosomes are tiny vesicles cells release to signal each other. Their mix tracks with diseases such as cancer and diabetes.

Lipids form a core part of exosome makeup. They shape how vesicles form, release, and find targets. They also steer uptake by receiving cells. The review covers those functions in order. It then surveys the tools that read exosome lipids. Uses in diagnosis and therapy close the picture. Membrane chemistry turns out to carry much of the message.
europmc-pmc8370411:
Williams and co-authors test the role of CD4 T cells in a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. The protein alpha-synuclein builds up in this disease and stirs the immune system. T cells enter the brain, but their exact effect was unclear.

Mice with extra alpha-synuclein in the midbrain showed more MHCII protein on brain immune cells. Interferon-gamma producing CD4 and CD8 T cells also moved in. Mice that lacked CD4 were protected from the loss of dopamine nerve cells. Blocking T cells with genetic changes or the drug fingolimod cut the immune response. The authors suggest that aiming at these T cell responses could slow the disease.
europmc-pmc8539411:
Burgess and co-authors review the science of wound healing in diabetes. Diabetes is a growing chronic disease marked by long high blood sugar. Poor wound healing hits about a quarter of patients, per the authors. It often ends in lower limb amputation, at high human and money cost.

High sugar helps germ films grow on wounds and makes them hard to treat. The review covers weak vessel growth, nerve damage, and a stalled inflammatory response. Barrier breaks and mixed infections add to the burden. Current and future treatments are matched to each fault. The authors urge plans that strike many causes at once.
europmc-pmc8728211:
Del Toro and co-authors report on IntAct, a database of molecular interactions between proteins and other molecules. The data are curated from published work and direct deposits. Twelve global partners of an international consortium share the curation work. As of August 2021, the database held more than one million binary interactions.

IntAct aims for fine detail in each record. That detail helps users judge what an experiment really showed. Recent work focused on key curation areas and fresh progress there. A rebuilt website presents the data in a friendlier, fuller way. The authors describe the new site and the curation model behind it.
europmc-pmc9139611:
Grochans and co-authors review the epidemiology of glioblastoma multiforme, an aggressive brain tumor. It accounts for 14.5% of all central nervous system tumors and 48.6% of malignant ones. Median survival is only about 15 months. The review asks who gets this tumor and what may raise the risk.

Data show it is the highest-grade primary brain tumor and is more common in men. Risk of glioma rises with age, and survival stays low despite medical gains. Proof on possible risk factors is murky in several areas. Those areas include stimulants, some drugs, cell phone use, and heavy metals. Readers get a clear summary of spread, pattern, and open risk questions.
europmc-pmc9238111:
Salari and co-authors pool worldwide studies on how often older adults fall. Falls are among the most common and serious problems of old age. Injuries can be fatal or can cut the ability to manage daily life. The team searched major databases with no time limit up to August 2020.

They included 104 studies with a total sample of 36,740,590 people. The pooled prevalence of falls in older adults was 26.5%. Oceania had the highest rate at 34.4%, followed by the Americas at 27.9%. Rates fell as sample size and study year rose. The authors urge policymakers and care providers to plan prevention programs. Such steps could cut a common cause of harm in later life.
europmc-pmc9276711:
Caliendo and co-authors trace how highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 crossed the Atlantic in 2021. In December 2021 the virus was found in poultry and a free-living gull in St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador. It was the first such report in the Americas since June 2015. The team used family-tree analysis plus wild bird migration data.

The Canadian viruses matched most closely those in northwestern Europe in spring 2021. Likely routes ran via Iceland, Greenland and the Arctic, or open-sea pelagic paths. Wild birds, not trade, appear to have carried the virus. The finding raises concern about further spread across the Americas. The lineage already threatens poultry, wildlife, and human health on other continents.
europmc-pmc9470311:
Chagas and co-authors examine flavonols and flavones as anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antibacterial compounds. Plant compounds have served as medicines for centuries. Flavonoids are plant chemicals with a wide range of such effects. Diet supplies many of them through fruit and vegetables.

The review profiles key flavonols such as quercetin and kaempferol. It also profiles flavones such as luteolin and apigenin. Food sources and structural traits are set out for each. The authors then trace how these compounds act. They calm inflammation and blunt oxidative damage. They also act on bacterial metabolism. Pairing them with antibiotics may help against resistant strains. Cell targets that back these effects get a full account. The work frames diet compounds as aids in infectious and inflammatory disease.
europmc-pmc9671811:
Xu, Xie, and Al-Aly chart long-term neurologic outcomes after COVID-19 in a Veterans Affairs cohort study. Brain effects of the acute illness were well mapped already. A full one-year account of later brain harms had not been done. The team built the count from national health records.

The COVID cohort held 154,068 people with the infection. Two control sets held more than five million people each for contrast. At 12 months, risks ran high across a wide harm list. Stroke, memory faults, and peripheral nerve disorders all rose. Migraine, seizures, and movement disorders also rose in the data. Mental health and sensory harms joined the pattern as well. The hazard ratio for any neurologic aftereffect was 1.42 overall. Risk stayed up even in people never sent to hospital. The authors urge care plans that expect lasting brain effects.
europmc-pmc9729111:
Aragam and co-authors hunt and sort risk variants and genes for coronary artery disease at huge scale. Their genome-wide study drew 181,522 cases among over a million people. Finding risk spots has run ahead of grasping how they act. The team set out to close that gap with deep follow-up.

The scan found 241 signals, including 30 new risk sites. A cross-ancestry blend with a Japanese study added 38 more. Fine mapping narrowed many spots to a few likely variants. Clustering hints pointed to early growth pathways. Cell cycle and vessel cell movement paths also stood out. Eight sorting methods together named 220 candidate genes. Most top picks won support from three or more methods. Lab tests backed one gene tied to vessel cell motion. The authors offer the map for experiments on disease roots.
europmc-pmc9961011:
More and co-authors review silver nanoparticles as killers of drug-resistant bacteria. The review covers how the particles are made from elemental silver. It then details how they attack multidrug-resistant and biofilm-forming pathogens. Studies show they cause oxidative stress and membrane damage in bacteria.

Protein dysfunction and DNA damage also drive bacterial death. The particles can block cell adhesion and so prevent biofilm formation. Benefits in medicine face limits from harm to humans and the environment. Ongoing clinical trials are briefly noted. Other uses include diagnostics and wound healing support. The authors discuss functionalized particles as a path to safer use. The review weighs a potent tool against its real risks.
europmc-pmc9977911:
Calabresi and co-authors revisit alpha-synuclein in Parkinson's disease and related disorders. The protein's key role in Parkinson's was found twenty-five years before this review. Abnormal forms trigger slow, selective nerve cell death. Harm runs through mitochondrial faults, lysosome failure, and calcium imbalance.

The same protein drives dementia with Lewy bodies and multiple system atrophy. Pure autonomic failure and REM sleep behavior disorder also link to it. Early synaptic changes arise before overt nerve loss. Inflammation appears early in models and in patients. That timing hints at a link between inflammation and synaptic failure. The authors stress early mechanisms as routes to biomarkers. They also frame them as targets for disease-modifying therapy.
evans-wentz-fairy-faith-1911:
W. Y. Evans-Wentz walked the Celt lands to ask folk what they held on fays. The Fairy-Faith in Celtic Countries came out in 1911. He went through Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Cornwall, Brittany, and Man. Old men and women told him what their kin had seen and feared.

First-hand tales fill the book: troops of fays, hid folk, and stolen babes. Evans-Wentz then weighs what the tales may mean for the mind and soul. He treats the faith with care, not with scorn. The book is the base work for all grave study of fay lore.
examen-des-principes-des-alchymistes-sur:
Pousse's Examen des principes des alchymistes examines alchemists' claims about the philosopher's stone. François Pousse wrote the work in French. Its Paris title page is dated M. DCCXI, or 1711. It was sold by Daniel Jollet and Barthélemy Girin, with royal approval and privilege.

A dedicatory epistle to Jean Paul Bignon, Abbé de Saint-Quentin, fronts the book. Bignon led the royal academies of sciences and medals. Pousse jokes that his book will rob alchemy's believers of promised happiness. Kings would trade sceptres for shepherd staffs under its critique, he writes. The epistle frames the work as a bold, ironic attack. The body then tests alchemical principles piece by piece.
florio-italian-1611:
John Florio published Queen Anna's New World of Words in 1611, a greatly expanded Italian-English dictionary. Florio taught languages at the court of James the First and had already issued a smaller word book in 1598. The new volume, dedicated to Queen Anne, carried some 46,000 Italian words explained in English.

Entries give rich clusters of English equivalents, along with proverbs and phrases from Italian writers. Florio also translated Montaigne's essays, and his word-hoard fed the English of his age; scholars still debate his links with Shakespeare's circle. The dictionary was the first full bridge between Renaissance Italy and Jacobean England. Students of both languages still consult it for words that later books dropped.
fouque-undine-1811:
Friedrich de la Motte Fouque, a German officer and writer, wrote this tale of a water spirit in 1811. F. E. Bunnett turned it into English, in the full text of nineteen parts. The tale grew from old lore of the undine, the maid of the waters.

Undine is raised by a fisherman, weds a knight, and by that bond wins a human soul. Joy turns to grief as the knight fails her, and the waters call her back at last. The short tale fixed the form of the water spirit in the books of Europe.
froude-history-england-vol-11:
After the Armada comes triumph in the eleventh volume of Froude's History, from 1865. Spain lies humbled at sea, and England stands exalted among the powers. Elizabeth sits at the very zenith of her glory as queen.

Froude savors the victory toward which his long narrative has built. Sea dogs raid, courtiers scheme, and the queen holds her state with cool mastery. He writes the moment when England became a great power in earnest. The volume glows with national pride, and its flowing style shows why Froude ranked as the most dramatic English historian of the Victorian age.
frus-1861-d11:
On 16 July 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Baron von Gerolt, Prussia's minister in Washington. Gerolt was Prussia's minister in Washington. The letter is document 11 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A letter to a foreign envoy in Washington worked the home end of diplomacy. Seward used such talks to press the Union's view of the war on each court through its own man. This exchange with Prussia's envoy sits just before the first great battle at Bull Run. Prussia's weight in Germany made its envoy a man worth the Secretary's direct time.
frus-1861-d111:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Anson Burlingame on 13 April 1861. Burlingame was named the American minister to China that spring. The letter is document 111 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The China post lay half a world away, yet it drew a letter the day after Fort Sumter fell. Seward had to keep every post filled, near or far, as war began. His note to Burlingame shows the wide reach of the service in that first week. Burlingame became a famed envoy in China and died in its service years later.
frus-1861-d211:
Mr. Wood was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 5 September 1861. It stands as Document 211 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d311:
Word from Mr. Harris reached Washington on 9 July 1861, in a letter to William H. Seward. It stands as Document 311 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d11:
Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London was the reader in mind when William H. Seward wrote on 31 January 1862. It stands as Document 11 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the winter of the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d111:
Orders from Washington reached Charles Francis Adams in a State Department letter dated 28 July 1862. It stands as Document 111 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d211:
Writing on 6 March 1862, Lord Lyons addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward in a note printed as Document 211 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Lyons served as Britain's minister in Washington through most of the Civil War.

March opened the war's great spring campaigns, and within days the ironclads Monitor and Virginia would fight at Hampton Roads. A battle with loud echoes in naval capitals. British officials followed American events with care. Notes like this one, formal and to the point, carried the legation's business while the war widened around it. Stuart had served at the legation for years before he took charge of it.
frus-1862-d311:
Two Seward dispatches to Paris are dated 19 September 1862, and the first is Document 311 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Both went to William L. Dayton, the American minister to France.

Seward wrote two days after Antietam, with the battle's scale known but its meaning still argued over. For Paris, the key fact was that Lee's invasion had been stopped. Seward's paired letters that day carried Washington's account to the French capital. There, the truce plan's fate depended heavily on how the Maryland campaign was read. Paris and London consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d411:
On 21 October 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Gustav Koerner, the American minister in Madrid. The dispatch is Document 411 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

By October 1862 the fighting at Antietam had slowed talk of foreign intervention, and Lincoln had announced his emancipation plan. Koerner's work in Spain shifted toward keeping that gain: holding Madrid to neutrality and watching Cuba, where Spanish rule sat close to Confederate shores. Seward's instruction belongs to the autumn effort to turn a military reprieve into lasting diplomatic safety for the Union.
frus-1862-d511:
August 1862 opened at The Hague desk with this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to James Shepherd Pike, dated 4 August. It is Document 511 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

August was the month of the second call for troops and of rising talk in London and Paris about stepping between the combatants. Seward's orders stiffened his ministers against any hint that the Union would accept mediation. Pike, in a small and friendly capital, had the easier version of that task, but the line had to be identical everywhere. The dispatch shows the Department keeping its whole European front in step as the war entered its most dangerous diplomatic season.
frus-1862-d611:
George G. Fogg, the American minister in Switzerland, received this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 10 March 1862. It is Document 611 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, opening the Swiss file.

Switzerland was a small republic whose example Americans liked to cite and whose neutrality was absolute. Fogg, a New Hampshire editor and abolitionist, held the post at Berne. Orders to such a mission dealt with the standing courtesies and the war's presentation in a friendly, watchful little state. The dispatch begins one of the volume's shortest files. It is a reminder of the Department's reach. That care extended to every flag under which an American minister served, however quiet the post.
frus-1862-d711:
From Washington on 6 October 1862 came this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Andrew B. Dickinson. Dickinson was the American minister in Nicaragua. The letter is document 711 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, answering Dickinson's September reports.

Seward's answers gave envoys their marching orders and told them how Washington read their news. For Nicaragua, the transit route and the republic's steadiness sat at the heart of the brief. This letter is one turn in that exchange. It shows the State Department keeping its grip on a distant post whose ground mattered far more than its size.
frus-1863p1-d11:
William H. Seward sent this second letter of 8 December 1862 to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 11 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, right after its twin. The two letters split the day's London business between them.

A secretary's mail often came in such pairs: one letter for the record of a talk, one for fresh orders. Seward's sheets to Adams kept the legation in step with a government whose war news changed by the week. Read beside document 10, this one shows the grain of that work — brief, plain notes that added up to a policy.
frus-1863p1-d111:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward a second time on 6 March 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 111 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a same-day letter often held the overflow: a talk in full, a set of facts, a press view. Adams's pair of 6 March fits that mold. This letter is its second half, sent as the ship fights in Britain's yards grew warm. With its twin, it shows the London brief at full stretch in the first week of spring.
frus-1863p1-d211:
Washington's orders to London on 5 June 1862 came in this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 211 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Seward's orders set the line Adams had to press on the British government. They told him what to demand, what to soften, and when to wait. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d311:
Mr. Stuart, an officer of the British legation in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 November 1862. His note is document 311 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863.

Small cases fill this part of the volume: a vessel, a cargo, a British subject under arrest. Together they show how a war at sea kept landing on diplomats' desks. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d411:
The American answer to London on 6 March 1863 took the form of this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 411 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

For historians, this exchange shows Anglo-American tension being managed day by day. It is the paper record of a war that never happened between the two countries. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d511:
A letter of 14 May 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 511 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports.
frus-1863p1-d611:
Document 611 in the volume is a letter of 13 August 1863 from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The day-to-day work was unglamorous: answering complaints, passing on claims, and keeping track of ships, prisoners, and papers. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1911:
Argentina honors its own past in the 1911 volume. Sarmiento's birth centennial fills one file. American residents present a statue of Washington in another. Austria-Hungary extradites two brothers as an act of comity. Military fugitives face military courts in a related file. Brazil joins Argentina and America in one correspondence. They address the Peru-Ecuador boundary dispute together.

Mexico's revolution supplies the mid-volume violence. A mob attacked the consulate at Ciudad Porfirio Diaz. The attack of November 10, 1911 drew an instant official apology. Demonstrations, pacific and violent, followed for months. Such reports fill the Mexican file. Belgium merges its Kongo consular service with its own. The volume records a hemisphere arming and arguing. Ceremony cannot hide the strain.
frus-1919Parisv11:
The American delegation's own house fills Volume XI. Its commissioners meet from January 31, 1919 onward. Technical advisers join their sessions in the record. A steering committee keeps its own minutes too. The rest covers the delegation's staff and machinery. Hundreds of papers track who served and how. A mid-volume letter weighs the Danzig question. Germany's delegation raises hard points of treaty reading. Fair clarification, the writer urges, should come early.

The letter shows the delegation still working in autumn. Its questions outlasted the signing ceremony. The volume is the conference seen from one office. Schedules, quarrels, and errands fill its pages. History here wears a name tag and a desk.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d11: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on June 20, 1943, two days after the president's paired letters to London and Moscow. His message is Document 11 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The summer correspondence between the two men ran at a pace that matched the war itself. What this note carried, the catalog does not say. It survives in the Foreign Relations series as one link in the long exchange behind the autumn summits.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d111: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on November 10, 1943, his last letter to China's leader in this series before the journey. It is Document 111 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Cairo Conference opened twelve days later. The record supplies the date and the names and leaves the subject to the text. The letter is part of the Foreign Relations series' account of how the Cairo meeting was arranged.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d211:
Ambassador Averell Harriman sent President Roosevelt a secret cable from Moscow on 11 November 1943, numbered SD 1. He warns that a thorny subject is almost sure to come up at the coming conference: Soviet pressure on Sweden to help in the war. Molotov had raised the point more than once since the Moscow conference ended.

Harriman reports a talk with Sweden's minister in Moscow. Finland, the minister said, would quit the war quickly if sure Soviet troops would not occupy her afterward, and Sweden could feed Finland for six months once German shipments stopped. But he doubted Sweden could move either Moscow or Helsinki in time, and he noted the Swedish king hoped to spare his people the suffering of joining the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d311:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote a most-secret memorandum at Cairo on 25 November 1943 attacking the American plan for a supreme commander over the war against Germany. He sets out, point by point, why the appointment would not cure the troubles seen since the Salerno landing.

The real divergences, Churchill argues, are political as much as military. Only governments and the Combined Chiefs can settle them. A supreme commander would thus be squeezed into a narrow strip of work, or else supplant the chiefs entirely. No single officer, he doubts, could decide across so vast a range. His own rule is that command in each theater should go to the ally with the largest forces there: the Mediterranean British, Overlord American. A merged command, by force counts, would fall to a Briton, an outcome he calls invidious and refuses to impose.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d411:
The agreed text of the Tehran communiqué, is dated 4 December 1943. It is the version Churchill and Stalin accepted. It is printed with its handwritten deletions, and with Harriman's note in the corner of the single sheet. An editorial headnote explains how this copy differs from both the third draft and the text finally released.

The text is headed Declaration of the Three Powers. It is timed for release at eight in the evening, Moscow time, on 6 December. It declares the three nations' determination to work together in war and in the peace that follows. Complete agreement was reached on the scope and timing of operations from the east, west, and south. The leaders claim the supreme responsibility of making a peace. The peace must command the good will of the overwhelming mass of the world's peoples. They close as friends in fact, in spirit, and in purpose.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d511:
Charles E. Bohlen, first secretary at the American embassy in Moscow, wrote this memorandum dated December 1, 1943, the final day of the Tehran Conference. Bohlen spoke Russian and served as President Roosevelt's interpreter with Stalin, taking notes at talks where no other American record was made. The State Department printed his memorandum in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Bohlen's papers are prized because he sat between the leaders, hearing both languages at moments that shaped the postwar world. A memorandum from the last day of Tehran carries the closeness of that seat. For readers, it offers the conference through the eyes of the man who made its conversations possible.
frus-1944-quebec-d11:
Two weeks after the Normandy landings, Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on June 20, 1944. The beachhead was secure but the breakout had not yet come. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

With the invasion ashore, the leaders' agenda shifted: reinforcing France, finishing in Italy, and looking toward the autumn meeting that became the Second Quebec Conference. Churchill's June letters worked that transition. For readers, this message shows the alliance moving from the question of whether the invasion would succeed to the harder politics of what its success would mean for Europe's future.
frus-1944-quebec-d111:
Trade barriers are the subject of this short note from Harry Hopkins to President Roosevelt, dated September 8, 1944. Hopkins, the president's closest aide, wrote just before Roosevelt left for the Quebec Conference with Winston Churchill. He worried Churchill saw freer trade as Secretary Hull's pet project, not the president's own policy.

Hopkins urged Roosevelt to correct that idea in person at Quebec. Making clear the president himself backed lower trade barriers would strengthen America's hand in later bargaining with Britain, he argued. The note is brief, but it shows how personal diplomacy was prepared. Even a prime minister's assumptions were worth fixing before the talks began.
frus-1944-quebec-d211:
A verbatim transcript of the Quebec press conference survives in the Roosevelt Papers, the editors note, and a substantively complete text is printed in Rosenman's edition of the president's papers. Roosevelt first reviewed the Second Quebec Conference in very general terms. He expressed hope for Germany's surrender and discussed joint action against Japan and Pacific logistics.

He stated specifically that questions of command in the Pacific war had not been discussed. Instead he described the existing division of responsibility among Mountbatten, MacArthur, and Nimitz. Churchill then commented on the conference results and on British and Canadian participation against Japan, and Mackenzie King made brief closing remarks. The conference communiqué was released to the press the same day, September 16.
frus-1945-50-intel-d11:
Arnold Miles of the Budget Bureau staff wrote to Stone, the bureau's assistant director for administrative management, on 19 September 1945. The paper moved inside the bureau on the eve of a landmark order. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Budget Bureau staff work decided much of what presidents finally signed, since the bureau drafted the orders themselves. Miles wrote one day before Executive Order 9621 ended the OSS. Readers should read his paper as part of the penumbra around that order. In such memos, officials weighed where the OSS's people, files, and duties should land. Small staff papers like this one are where big decisions take their final shape.
frus-1945-50-intel-d111:
Ladd of the FBI wrote to Hoover on 14 May 1946. Ladd's memoranda kept the director informed on the bureau's intelligence fronts, the central group among them. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By May the CIG under its new leaders was reaching toward the Latin American field the FBI regarded as its own. Ladd's paper belongs to the bureau's watch on that reach. Readers following the FBI thread can see its method again: steady reporting, claims restated, and a director who answered encroachment with paper of his own. The border war between the bureau and the group, fought in memoranda, is one of the volume's most instructive threads.
frus-1945-50-intel-d211:
A memorandum dated 17 April 1947 links two senior offices. The sender was the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy). The reader was Acting Secretary of State Acheson. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 211, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

A short memo could set a meeting, kill a plan, or start one. This one played its part in that daily traffic. That plainness lets a reader see how an issue moved from a working office up to the men who decided it. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d311:
A memorandum dated 7 September 1949 links two senior offices. The sender was Robert P. Joyce of the Policy Planning Staff. The reader was the Counselor of the Department of State (Kennan). Readers meet it as document 311 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. By then the Dulles Report was months old, and the argument had moved to putting its advice into practice.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d411: A short paper dated 19 January 1950 carries only the heading Memorandum for the Record, with no writer and no reader named. It is document 411 in the Foreign Relations volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Papers of this kind set down what was said or decided at a meeting. The file would then hold it, even when no order followed from it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d11: On 19 October 1944 Stalin sent Roosevelt another message, the third Soviet letter in this opening run of papers. It stands as document 11 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering the Malta and Yalta conferences. The full text appears as the Office of the Historian published it, in sequence with the replies it answered and prompted in return.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d111:
Ambassador John Winant wrote to the President from London on 10 January 1945 about three papers awaiting approval. His personal and secret message, number 2047, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. All three concern how the allies would control Germany.

The control machinery agreement, Winant reports, already has State Department and Joint Chiefs approval. The zones protocol waits only on allied agreement for American control of Bremen and Bremerhaven, the ports feeding the American zone. Britain has approved both papers, and the Russians, he hears, are looking on them with favor. Winant hopes the surrender instrument and both agreements can be settled by 14 January, one year after the European Advisory Commission began.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d211:
H. Freeman Matthews briefed the Secretary on France's German claims on 19 January 1945. His secret memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, was written for Stettinius's Sunday talk with the President. The Rhineland and a French zone head the agenda.

The five French proposals, Matthews recalls, already have the President's approval in principle, from signing the surrender to a share of Berlin. Paris has also formally told the three allies, in a note of 13 January, that it wishes to join the coming three-power conference. London, he judges, will answer with favor. If Moscow grows sure that Washington will oppose an invitation, the picture changes. The paper goes on to weigh the play of the three capitals.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d311:
British chiefs of staff put their case on Asia in writing at Malta on January 31, 1945. Their memorandum covers the split of resources between the India-Burma and China theaters. London granted the scale of American pledges to China, both political and military. It asked Washington to grant the weight of Britain's stake in Burma in return.

The British argued that the ground had shifted since an earlier American reservation was accepted without debate. British land forces in Burma now leaned heavily on air transport for their safety. China, meanwhile, faced a far more urgent crisis than a year before. The paper is a frank bid for a fairer share.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d411:
An invitation with blanks stands at the center of this American proposal of February 9, 1945. The United States, speaking for itself and for Britain, the Soviet Union, China, and France, invites the government of a named state to send representatives. The conference of the United Nations would meet on April 25, 1945, or soon after. The city is left blank in the draft.

Its task: prepare a charter for a general international organization to keep peace and security. The sponsors suggest the conference build on the Dumbarton Oaks proposals, made public the past October. The blank spaces show history caught mid-decision — San Francisco not yet named, the date already fixed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d511:
Dictated at San Francisco on June 3, 1945, this memorandum by Hiss rebuilds a Yalta moment from his own longhand notes. It covers the plenary session of February 6, 1945, at Livadia Palace. Roosevelt asked Stettinius to explain the American proposal on the voting formula. Stettinius, he noted, had been at Dumbarton Oaks; none of the three delegation heads had.

The President felt strongly, Hiss records, that people would insist on something insuring peace — not for all time, but say for fifty years. Stettinius then read the American statement on voting in the Council. The memo, dictated four months later, shows the record of Yalta still being assembled at the founding conference itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d11:
Relations with Russia are the number one problem affecting the future of the world. Harriman made that case at the White House on May 15, 1945, in Grew's memorandum of the conference. The President, Grew, Harriman, and Bohlen took part. The State Department, Grew said, held it vital that the Big Three meeting come as soon as possible, not be postponed until July.

Harriman argued that the two countries were getting farther and farther apart at the present moment. Beyond the general picture stood specific questions, such as treating Germany on a tripartite basis. The memorandum shows the Moscow embassy pressing Washington for speed, with the alliance drifting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d111:
The British Chiefs of Staff accepted the American line on small staffs in a memorandum dated June 30, 1945. The paper, C.C.S. 880/6, is document 111 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It reports London's answer to the U.S. memorandum of June 28, which had argued against big military staffs at Terminal.

The British agree that large staffs will not be required. Each of their chiefs will bring his personal staff plus four or five staff officers. The secretariat will take only enough people to run the conference's normal paperwork and administration. The brief memo closed the question of military manpower for Potsdam and matched the lean approach both sides wanted for a summit meant to be short.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d211:
Ambassador Kirk passed on Field Marshal Alexander's news about Yugoslavia in a telegram from Caserta on July 12, 1945. The message is document 211 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Alexander had learned the British government's intentions while in London.

The British expected to discuss the Tito-Šubašić agreement at the coming Big Three meeting, Alexander said. Churchill would make it quite clear that his government was not satisfied with how the accord had been carried out so far. Britain would hold Tito to strict account for putting it into effect. The agreement was meant to unite Tito's movement with the royal government and open the way to free elections, and London judged Tito to be stalling.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d311:
Budapest reported a Soviet move on July 13, 1945, in Schoenfeld's cable to the Acting Secretary of State. General Key had received a note from Marshal Voroshilov, dated July 11, setting out Moscow's decision on new procedure for Hungary's Allied Control Commission. A first translation was already in hand.

The new procedure seemed to follow, in the main, lines Washington had suggested in May, with details added by the American mission. Yet Schoenfeld found much ambiguity in Voroshilov's wording. Key meant to take the unclear points up with the Marshal directly. The cable holds a rare note of cautious hope from Hungary.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d411:
Moscow's own formula arrived in Winant's top secret cable from London of July 11, 1945. The Soviet delegation to the European Advisory Commission that night communicated new wording for the disputed final paragraph of the report on the French zone agreement. The formula had been sent from Moscow after Gousev's return there.

The Soviet text recommends that the question of fixing the boundaries of the French area in greater Berlin go to the Control Council. It states that the French area, since the Soviet area of the city suffered the greatest destruction, will be formed from the American and British areas. The formula also went to the British and French delegations, for a meeting on July 12.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d511:
Eastern Poland's boundary is fixed in a briefing book paper dated July 3, 1945. Its recommendation restates the Crimea settlement. The United States, in the Big Three agreement of February 11, 1945, approved the Curzon Line. With Extension A, that line forms the boundary between Poland and the Soviet Union. Deviations of five to eight kilometers in Poland's favor are to be allowed in some regions.

The basic data trace the land between the Riga and Curzon lines. It includes pre-1914 Austrian and Russian territory. Eastern Galicia was renounced by Austria in the Treaty of St. Germain in 1919, and awarded to Poland in 1923. The former Russian territory came to Poland by the Treaty of Riga of 1921. In September 1939 the Soviet Union occupied both parts.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d611:
The United States Chiefs of Staff replied to the British on sharing war facts with Russia, July 8, 1945. Their top secret memo is document 611 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It answers the British proposal printed as document 609.

The U.S. chiefs say the matter is not a fit one for a joint Allied agreement. Each side, in effect, may set its own rule for what it tells Moscow. They add one firm pledge of their own. They will not pass to the Russians any facts on British forces or plans without prior British consent. Nor will they pass on facts that came from a British source. The Combined Chiefs took up the paper at Potsdam on July 19, where the British pressed their case again.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1011:
Collado drafted this agreement on the German fleet and merchant marine at Babelsberg on July 29, 1945. The fleet would be split equally at once among the Soviet Union, Britain, and the United States. Most German submarines would be destroyed. A few would be kept for tests and training, under a mixed commission's eye.

The merchant marine would also be split in equal thirds in the end. Until Japan falls, though, every German merchant ship stays at work in the war, run by the joint shipping boards. Final division would come six months after Japan's defeat. Officers of the three powers could inspect vessels wherever they are held.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1111:
Alexander Kirk, the American ambassador in Italy, cabled the Acting Secretary of State on 17 July 1945. That was the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. Kirk reported from Rome, where he watched a beaten country try to build a new order after the fall of Mussolini.

Italy was a live question at the summit. Its peace treaty, its borders, and the shape of its new state all waited on the talks. Kirk's dispatch fed the view from Rome into the bargaining in Germany. Cables like his kept the men at the table supplied with facts from the ground, not just claims from other teams.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1211:
The Soviet team tabled this proposal on 30 July 1945, with three days of the conference left. By that stage, fresh papers were rarely opening bids. They were endgame moves, put forward when the deal's shape was set and each side hunted last gains.

Moscow's late papers deserve close reading for that reason. A demand repeated at the end marks a point the Soviet side prized. A demand dropped marks the price of the deal. This proposal stands in the record as one such move. It gains meaning from its neighbors, the replies and drafts that surround it in the volume.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1311:
Harrison wrote to Stimson on 23 July 1945, one of two committee-channel papers of that date in the volume. The acting chairman's notes came thick as the summit and the atomic file both neared their peaks. Each carried Washington's end of the secret to the war secretary in Germany.

The exchange between these two men is the policy spine of the bomb's story at Potsdam. Tests, targets, warnings, and timing all passed along it. This message is a link in that spine. It shows the committee's work feeding the summit at the moment the final choices about the weapon were being formed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1411:
The sixth Caffery cable to Secretary Byrnes dated 6 August 1945 closes the day's run from Paris. Six cables to the secretary in one day is a remarkable count in any foreign service. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A run's last cable often carries the day's summing-up or its sharpest ask. Whether this one does, readers can judge by setting it at the end of the sequence where the editors placed it. The whole cluster marks the high point of French pressure in the volume. A freed ally, shut out of the summit, demanding its place in the peace by sheer weight of well-aimed paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-11:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 18, 1945, record the U.S. military team's morning session at Potsdam. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers. Three items stand out in the part printed here.

First, the chiefs reviewed and amended a memo to the President on the surrender formula for Japan. They approved it as amended during the discussion. Second, Admiral Leahy reported a talk with the President on staff relations with allied nations. Truman thought it undesirable to raise a military alliance with Britain just then. Allied relations, he held, were not settled enough to warrant a permanent link between commands. Third, Admiral King and General Marshall each proposed changes to the draft memo on French and Dutch participation in the Japan war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-111:
Dated July 25, 1945, this rapporteur's report carried a Potsdam working group's results to a higher level of the conference. Subcommittees did the detailed labor at Potsdam. Their rapporteurs then had to state, in short compass, what had been agreed and what had not. The report entered the record printed in the second Potsdam volume.

Inside is the state of a negotiation at one point in time. Settled lines appear beside open brackets and rival drafts. For leaders scanning many files, such a report was the quick way to see where work stood. It shows the conference's layered method: detail below, decision above.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d711:
Document 711 is a proposal tabled by the United States delegation on July 17, 1945, the opening day of the Potsdam Conference. Delegations opened by putting written proposals on the table. Each one marked out ground its side wanted the talks to cover. The text was printed at the head of this run in the second Potsdam volume.

An opening-day proposal shows intent before bargaining began. Readers can set its lines beside the final protocol and see what survived. That gap between ask and outcome is where the conference happened. The document also shows the American team's method: arrive with texts ready, and force the talk onto paper early.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d811:
Melbourne wrote from Rumania on July 23, 1945, in document 811. The acting representative in Bucharest reported to the Acting Secretary of State. Two Rumanian letters in two days mark an active file. This one joined the second Potsdam volume beside its fellows.

Frequent reports from one post trace a situation in motion. Melbourne could correct and extend his own record. Readers follow Bucharest's politics almost day by day. The document shows the value of a resident observer over a visiting one. He knew the players, and his letters carry that knowledge to the summit's readers then and now.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d911: American staff drafted this undated memorandum, filed with the July 22, 1945 papers, as an alternative reply to the Soviet stand on war booty. It quotes the Soviet definition of war trophies. Under that idea, the paper argues, any occupying power could strip its own zone and call the goods booty. Overall reparations planning for Germany then becomes meaningless. The United States would accept the position. It would remove plants and goods from its own zone, for itself or for others, and expects the other powers to do the same.
frus-1946v11:
The American Republics close the 1946 set in Volume XI. Regional papers come first, on a planned peace and security meeting and the Bogotá conference groundwork. Arms aid policy, the end of the Proclaimed List, and coffee and wheat questions follow.

Argentina takes the longest country run, built around the State Department's Blue Book and the arms question. Bolivia's violent revolution and recognition problem come next. Brazil fills the later pages, with base disposal, debt, and coffee talks. Embassy reports show wartime controls coming off and old trade ties being rebuilt.
frus-1952-54Guat-d11: An editorial note in the Guatemala volume traces the coup plan to its start. In early July 1952, Nicaraguan President Somoza pitched an overthrow of Arbenz to Colonel Neil Mara, an aide to President Truman. Mara's report persuaded Truman, who at once authorized CIA action. The State Department was not informed. The note cites two published histories for the tale. It also warns that little paper on the start of the operation was found.
frus-1955-57v11:
The United Nations and general world matters fill Volume XI of the 1955–1957 set. Broad UN policy leads, in a hundred papers. Membership bids and the China seat fight take the longest run that follows.

Law of the sea and Antarctic policy sit in the middle blocks. Outer space study closes the volume, with the Geophysical Year beside it. The papers catch the moment when rockets and new states both changed the agenda. Delegation cables show old fights over seats sharing days with the first talk of orbits. Space files rest on the Geophysical Year plans.
frus-1958-60v11:
Lebanon and Jordan fill Volume XI of the 1958–1960 set, built around the 1958 crisis. Lebanon's slide into civil war leads. The Eisenhower Doctrine frames the first files, and joint war plans follow.

United States forces land in Lebanon in July, and British troops enter Jordan. The Iraq revolt drives the rush in these pages. The Murphy mission and a UN emergency session fill the middle. Withdrawal and the Chehab government close the crisis. Later files run to 1960, on aid levels and King Hussein's visit. Aid talks with both kingdoms fill the final block.
frus-1961-1963-cuban-missile-crisis-vol-:
Volume eleven of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1961 to 1963 is devoted to the Cuban Missile Crisis and its aftermath. The Office of the Historian compiled it from declassified records. For thirteen days in October 1962, the world stood at the edge of nuclear war.

The documents follow the Executive Committee's secret debates as Kennedy weighed invasion, air strikes, and blockade. The naval quarantine, the downed U-2, and the near accidents at sea all stand in the record. Behind the public standoff runs the secret deal: Soviet missiles out of Cuba, American missiles quietly out of Turkey. The volume is the crisis in its makers' own words.
frus-1964-68v11:
Volume XI of the 1964-1968 series is devoted to arms control and disarmament. Its 302 documents follow U.S. work on test limits, missile defense, and talks with the Soviet Union. The papers trace the long push for a treaty to stop the spread of nuclear weapons. They also cover talks in Geneva and private exchanges with Moscow. Soviet envoys such as Dobrynin appear in records of key talks.

Much of the volume turns on the question of missile defense. U.S. officials weighed the cost of such systems and their effect on the arms race. The records mix memos, cables, and talk notes. They show a policy built step by step, often in secret.
frus-1969-76v11:
Volume XI of Foreign Relations of the United States, 1969-1976, is devoted to the South Asia crisis of 1971. Its 335 documents run in one sequence. They follow the Pakistani army's crackdown in East Pakistan and the refugee flood into India. They cover U.S. ties with Pakistan and the tilt toward it. The volume ends with the war between India and Pakistan and the birth of Bangladesh.

The records include backchannel messages and talks with leaders of both states. They show Washington pressing for a political deal while aiding refugees. Secret contacts with Bengali figures appear in the later papers. The volume is the full U.S. record of the crisis.
frus-1981-88v11:
Volume XI of the 1981-1988 series is devoted to START I, the talks on strategic arms. Four chapters divide the span by period, from July 1981 to January 1989. An appendix closes the volume. The papers follow the U.S. effort to move past SALT toward deep cuts. Counting rules for bombers and cruise missiles fill many pages. Instructions to the Geneva team weigh how to carry INF's checking rules into START.

The middle chapters cover the Reykjavik shock and the recovery after it. The last chapter ends with the talks still open as Reagan left office. The treaty itself would be signed in 1991, under Bush. The volume is the full negotiating record.
gao-gaoreports-b-295911:
Public Facility Consortium I, LLC, and JDL Castle Corporation are the protesters in GAO files B-295911 and B-295911.2, dated May 4, 2005. The General Services Administration had leased a building to be built for the Social Security Administration in Roanoke, Virginia. The award went to Damon Harwood Company. The protesters said the winner's site failed zoning law. GAO denied the protests. Proof of zoning compliance goes to a firm's ability to perform, a matter of responsibility, not to whether its offer is acceptable.

The general zoning term in the solicitation was no special, definitive test of fitness. The contracting officer's fitness finding stood on a full record.
gao-gaoreports-b-298011:
American Printing House for the Blind protested Library of Congress awards in GAO decision B-298011, dated May 15, 2006. The work was books on tape. Three firms won deals. A cap set 500 titles per bidder. One winner would also do tape copy work for 1,000 more titles as a sub. The firm said that broke the cap.

GAO denied the protest. Sub work on one step of more titles is not an award of those titles. The cap binds deals held, not sub steps done for peers. A claim that bids were not made in a free way was also cut. That point goes to fitness, which the buyer weighs, not GAO.
gao-gaoreports-b-298411:
Advanced Systems Development, Inc. protested a Defense Department award to KENROB Information Technology Solutions, Inc. Washington Headquarters Services ran the buy. The contract covered information technology services, hardware, and software for Pentagon-area work. GAO ruled in B-298411 and B-298411.2 on September 19, 2006.

The firm said the agency ran flawed price discussions. GAO agreed. The agency fixed an error in the awardee's price but hid that fix in talks. It then warned the awardee on a false price point. The awardee cut its price and won on that gap. GAO also found gaps in the price review. It sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-309911:
FitNet Purchasing Alliance saw its protest thrown out; the GAO decision is B-309911, dated November 2, 2007. The Army ran a reverse auction for 50 wardrobe lockers. The lockers were bound for Fort Bragg, North Carolina. The buy ran through the Federal Supply Schedule. FitNet said the buy had to be set aside for small firms.

GAO dismissed the protest. FitNet holds no supply schedule deal of its own. That gap means it is not a party with a stake to press the claim. Standing rules gate who may fight a buy's terms. A firm that could not win the work cannot force a set-aside fight.
gao-gaoreports-b-310611:
Merlin International, Inc. lost its protest. GAO decided B-310611 on January 2, 2008. The Army sought code software to lock data on mobile gear. The order went to MTM Technologies, Inc. on a sole-source path. Merlin said the winner's gear would not run on the set systems. It said it was shut out of a chance to bid.

GAO denied the protest. The winner's blanket deal held the proof the call asked for. That proof was a pledge that the gear fits the set systems. A pledge of that kind met the call's terms. No fresh test was owed to a firm that sought to break in late.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-211:
Endangered Species, GAO-05-211 of April 6, 2005, asks if scarce rescue funds go to the species that need them most. More than 1,260 species sit on the federal list of those at risk. Since 1973, few have died out, but only 9 have healed enough to leave the list. The Fish and Wildlife Service spent $127 million on named species from fiscal year 2000 through 2003.

Rules tell the service to rank species and fund by rank. GAO tests if the cash flow matched the ranks. It lists the other forces that sway each pick. Funds track top ranks in the main, it finds.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-611:
Guarding weapons-grade nuclear material at five Energy Department sites is the subject of GAO-05-611, dated July 15, 2005. The guards generally met current readiness rules on shooting skill, fitness, gear, and training. Two weak spots stood out. No rule sets how often each officer must join mock-attack drills, and sites do not track who takes part. Radios also failed the men: 66 of 105 officers interviewed said their sets were not always dependable.

A tougher attack model, set in October 2004, must be met by October 2008. GAO says that will take fast, joined-up action. Plans point to an elite guard force modeled on Special Forces, plus new security technology.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-711:
Democracy aid in the Middle East is reviewed in GAO report GAO-05-711 (August 8, 2005). The partnership initiative, launched in December 2002, funds political, economic, and school reform plus women's advancement. It had committed about 45 percent of its $129 million for fiscal 2002-2003 itself, with partners committing the rest. Reviews of older aid steered it toward gaps, like backing women candidates.

Watch over live projects lags the strategy. Roles between the State Department and the aid agency blurred, and project files are incomplete. A July 2005 framework splits the duties. GAO adds recommendations on tracking results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1011:
Danger pay and combat tax relief get a management check in GAO-06-1011, issued September 28, 2006. Troops in set danger areas earn extra pay. They can also exclude income from federal tax. A trip that spans two months can draw two full months of benefits. GAO ran the review under its own authority. It judged how danger areas are reviewed and how travel to them is controlled.

Headings carry the findings. Management of danger pay could gain from added oversight. No department-wide policy watches cross-month travel to the designated areas. That gap sits at the heart of the double-month issue. The department does track the pay and tax data and reports some of it to Congress. The report carries recommendations and one matter for Congress to weigh.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-11:
How well the Department of Health and Human Services manages its technology spending is graded in GAO-06-11, a report from October 2005. HHS runs over 300 programs and planned to spend over $5 billion on IT in fiscal year 2006. GAO measured the department against its own investment management framework. The framework tracks how mature an agency's selection and oversight practices are.

HHS had built 63 percent of the base practices for handling projects one by one. For managing its full portfolio, the share was only 30 percent. Its top board did not regularly review component agency projects. Close to 90 percent of discretionary spending lacked proper executive review. The department also skipped ongoing portfolio checks and reviews after projects launched. Improvement efforts existed but were not tied into one clear plan. GAO warned that weak control puts a multibillion-dollar budget at risk.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-111:
Army National Guard equipment shortages are documented in GAO-06-111, a report GAO issued on October 4, 2005. Guard forces then made up over 30 percent of U.S. ground forces in Iraq. Much Guard gear stayed overseas for follow-on units. GAO asked whether the Guard had the gear it needs for current missions.

Deploying units got gear first, but the transfers hollowed out units at home. By July 2005 the Guard had shifted more than 101,000 items from nondeployed units. Inventories of over 220 high-demand items, such as radios and night vision gear, ran dry. The Army could account for only about 45 percent of items left overseas. Over 64,000 items worth more than $1.2 billion had been left since 2003. GAO urged a funded plan to replace lost stocks and equip the modular force.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-211:
The Global Information Grid, the Pentagon's planned data network, is the subject of GAO-06-211, dated January 30, 2006. The Defense Department expects to spend about $34 billion through 2011 on the grid's core. It would give troops data on demand, in real time. Leaders call it the base of information superiority and network-centric warfare. GAO judged the management setup and whether the department's three big decision processes fit a joint project.

No single office is truly in charge, GAO found. The chief information officer leads on paper but holds less sway than the services. Each service can fund or skip the joint systems the grid needs. The processes for setting needs, splitting funds, and buying systems all favor single-service projects. They link poorly with each other as well. GAO warned the department may never know if the grid stays on cost or pays off.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-311:
Radiation detectors handed to foreign borders meet hard reality in GAO-06-311, a report dated March 14, 2006. The atomic energy agency counted 662 confirmed trafficking cases in nuclear material from 1993 to 2004. Three U.S. agencies supply detection gear and training to border guards abroad. GAO measured how far that aid has spread and what it costs. It catalogued the problems the programs face. It also checked how the three agencies coordinate their efforts.

Corruption, upkeep, and coordination all hamper the work, GAO found. Bribes can wave a suspect load through a working gate. GAO urged the energy and state departments to act on five fronts. Long-term cost plans should price in anti-corruption steps. Basic portal monitors need upgrades, and handheld units need care everywhere. A shared master list of U.S. gear would end blind spots. The report treats smuggling defense as a chain no stronger than its weakest post.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-511:
Surplus federal land can pass to towns and nonprofits for public use. Issued June 21, 2006, report GAO-06-511 reviews public benefit conveyances. The General Services Administration runs the program. It has given the Defense Department authority for properties closed under base realignment. Sponsoring agencies check that grantees use land as agreed. GAO counted conveyances from fiscal years 2000 through 2004.

GAO recorded the number, types, and locations of the properties. It assessed efforts to ensure agreed use. It also named challenges facing agencies and grantees. Most conveyances were used as intended, GAO found. Chances exist to enhance federal oversight, it added. Readers get program scope and gaps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-811:
Cyber security research across the government is mapped in GAO-06-811. GAO released it on September 29, 2006. Better security tools are needed to build safer networked systems for agencies and firms. The National Strategy to Secure Cyberspace sets federal research priorities in this field. GAO identified which federal bodies fund and perform cyber security research. GAO also judged how well their work is coordinated and shared.
