GAO found numerous federal entities active in cyber security research and development. Oversight and coordination among them had improved, GAO said. Limitations remained, though, in tracking the full federal effort. Agencies used varied methods to move research results into practice. GAO urged tighter coordination so scarce research funds are not spent twice on the same problems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-911:
Small travel firms and claimed savings in a federal travel system are checked in GAO report GAO-06-911, dated September 15, 2006. In November 2003 the General Services Administration gave three 10-year deals for e-Government Travel Service. The shared system was meant to cut cost and lift service.

The agency had projected about $473 million in savings from fiscal years 2002 to 2013. GAO weighed whether small travel agencies got a fair path into the program. It also tested how sound the savings claim was. GAO urged steps so agency process would not block small firms, and asked for tracked savings reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-11:
Study aid relief for troops on active duty is checked in GAO report GAO-07-11, dated November 1, 2006. The HEROES Act was passed to aid service members called to duty mid-study, or while paying back student loans. It lets lenders and schools give relief that fits that service.

GAO asked how the Education Department has put the act in place. It reviewed what the nine largest federal loan lenders do for borrowers in uniform. It polled a sample of schools on their aid for such students, and visited four campuses. More facts, GAO said, could show how far the relief in fact reaches those it was meant for.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-211:
Seabasing would let U.S. forces stage from ships when no friendly port or airfield is near. GAO warned against rushing it in GAO-07-211, issued January 26, 2007. The services are each building pieces of the idea. Some pieces could cost billions of dollars. GAO asked whether the Pentagon manages the effort jointly. It also asked whether a joint testing plan exists. Costs of the options were a third question.

No one was steering the joint effort as a whole, GAO found. The department had written a joint concept paper. But each service kept its own concept and projects. No dedicated team ran the work day to day. There was also no joint plan for experiments to test the idea. War games and trials ran in scattered fashion. Without a shared approach, GAO said, the services risk building gear that does not work together.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-411:
Emergency alerts reach the public through the Emergency Alert System, and GAO-07-411, issued March 30, 2007, tests how well that system works. Broadcasters carry the alerts, guided by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) and the Federal Emergency Management Agency. GAO reviewed how well the media meet federal duties. It also weighed the flaws users see and the push for one joined-up alert system.

The system's reach is broad, but its backbone is shaky. No full national test had been run. In a partial test in January 2007, three main relay stations failed to pass the message along. Staff training also varied. GAO found that plans to fuse warning systems were young and would take years. For now, the public has little proof the national alert would work when needed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-611:
Who watches the board that runs the federal retirement plan is the question in GAO-07-611, dated June 21, 2007. The Thrift Savings Plan held about $210 billion for 3.7 million members as of February 2007. The Federal Retirement Thrift Investment Board runs it. Doubts about oversight of that board drove the study.

GAO laid out the oversight web Congress built in law. It compared the board's legal duties with those of private plan sponsors. It set the plan's investment rules beside private practice. It also checked the board's duty to teach members about saving. One gap stood out: the Labor Department audits the plan, but it has no formal channel to send Congress concerns that fall outside an audit. GAO repeated past advice to create one. Contact between the board, Labor, and Congress has also been rare and reactive.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-711:
Weapons and gear sent to Iraqi security forces are tracked in GAO-07-711, dated July 31, 2007. Since 2003, the United States has given about $19.2 billion to build those forces. The Defense Department sought $2 billion more. A joint command in Iraq ran the training and supply work. GAO checked the property records for U.S.-funded gear. It asked whether the department could prove the gear reached Iraqi hands.

No rule set clearly said which property rules bound the program. Congress funded it outside the usual aid channels, which gave wide freedom. For 18 months, no central log tracked gear handed out. GAO found a gap of at least 190,000 weapons between two sets of records. Staff shortages helped cause the lapse. GAO told the Defense chief to set clear rules for the program. It also told him to back them with staff, supply networks, and sound systems. The department agreed with both points.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-11:
The personnel agency's own workforce is studied in GAO report GAO-08-11, dated October 31, 2007. The Office of Personnel Management runs human resources for the federal workforce. GAO judged how well the agency staffs and grows its own people. This report is the third in a series on that question.

GAO compared staff survey results from 2004 and 2006. Views of leadership rose sharply, with honesty scores up 8 percentage points. Results on performance culture were mixed. Talent management stayed a concern, as training satisfaction fell 5 points. GAO also checked whether the agency has plans to secure the skilled staff its mission needs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-211:
Tax agency computer security is faulted in GAO report GAO-08-211, issued January 8, 2008. The Internal Revenue Service leans on computers to collect about $2.7 trillion in fiscal year 2007. Weak controls put taxpayer data at risk of misuse or loss. The review grew out of GAO's audit of the agency's books.

GAO found that the agency had fixed or eased only 29 of 98 past security flaws. New flaws joined the old ones. Together they form a material weakness in internal controls. GAO set out seven actions to build a true agencywide security program. Training, testing, and contractor oversight all feature.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-311:
Enhanced National Guard readiness for civil support missions is the subject of GAO report GAO-08-311, dated April 16, 2008. Heavy use of Guard forces overseas had raised doubts about their ability to aid civil authorities after a catastrophic incident. GAO assessed the current funding approach and three alternatives, including one in the 2008 National Defense Authorization Act.

GAO found that no comprehensive planning had been done to identify the Guard's needs for large multistate missions, because planning duties were unclear. Most Guard capability was funded through defense appropriations for warfighting missions. GAO set out seven guiding principles for judging funding options and found that no approach met all of them. GAO recommended that the Department of Defense report to Congress on steps to include the principles in carrying out the 2008 act, and the department generally agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-511:
Unmanned aircraft systems are studied in GAO report GAO-08-511, issued May 15, 2008. Federal users fly them for border patrol and science work, and towns eye them for police and fire tasks. Each flight still needs a case-by-case safety review by the Federal Aviation Administration.

These aircraft cannot yet see and avoid other traffic, a basic safety duty. They also lack security protection, and no standing rules govern them, so approvals stay case-by-case. A flood of requests could swamp the agency's staff. GAO suggested Congress create a single coordinating body inside the agency. It also urged the agency to issue its program plan and study its flight data, and the Department of Homeland Security to weigh the security risks of routine access. Both departments agreed with their parts.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-02-1911:
James George Frazer published Volume 2 of the third edition of The Golden Bough in 1911, subtitled The Magic Art and the Evolution of Kings, Part 2. Frazer, a Cambridge scholar, built his vast study of magic and religion from reports across the world. The third edition ran to twelve volumes.

Part 2 of The Magic Art presses on with charms, rites, and the rise of sacred kings. Frazer argued that magic came before religion in human thought, and that kings began as magicians. His examples range from rain makers to tree spirits on every continent. The volume shows his method at full scale: one custom matched against hundreds of kin worldwide.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-03-1911:
Volume 3 of Frazer's Golden Bough, third edition, appeared in 1911, under the title Taboo and the Perils of the Soul. James George Frazer gathered customs from peoples worldwide to show how taboo worked. Taboo, a word from Polynesia, named things and persons set apart as dangerous and holy.

Chapters cover taboos on kings, strangers, food, words, and the dead, and beliefs about the soul leaving the body in sleep or shadow. Frazer argued that taboo guarded early societies where law did not yet reach. His mass of examples, drawn from travelers and missionaries, made the volume a storehouse for later students of religion, even those who rejected his theories.
golden-bough-3rd-ed-vol-04-1911:
Volume 4 of the third edition of The Golden Bough appeared in 1911, titled The Dying God. James George Frazer's theme was the god who dies and returns, a figure he found in rites across the ancient world. The priest of Nemi, slain by his successor, stood behind the whole work.

Frazer traced dying gods through grain rites, sacred kings, and seasonal festivals in many lands. He held that such rites acted out the death and revival of plant life each year. Critics later doubted his single pattern, but the evidence he gathered stayed valuable. The volume is central to his claim that myth and ritual grow from the same root.
govdocs-archive_org-TheSpotlightVolume27:
The Spotlight was a populist weekly newspaper published in Washington, and this file holds a single issue: volume 27, number 11, dated March 12, 2001. Single issues are kept as issued, so the paper can be read exactly as its subscribers saw it.

Inside are the paper's news stories, commentary, and notes from its own distinct perspective, which favored economic nationalism and deep suspicion of global institutions. The Spotlight spoke to readers who distrusted the mainstream press, and it kept a loyal following for decades. As a record, the issue shows what that audience was reading in the spring of 2001.
heindel-rosicrucian-mysteries-1911:
Max Heindel put out The Rosicrucian Mysteries in 1911. The book is a plain first step into the scheme of the Rosicrucian Fellowship. Heindel had set up that group in the United States not long past. He calls the book a first exposition, made for new hands.

Seven worlds stack up in his scheme, from dense flesh to pure spirit. Man has more than one body in his count, and death is a shift, not an end. Steps of growth lead the soul to full sight of hid things. The book is the gate text of Heindel's whole school.
hill-new-evidences-psychical-research-19:
J. Arthur Hill adds fresh proof to the pile in New Evidences in Psychical Research, his book of 1911. Hill was a keen hand in the chief band for such study. He prints his own tests. Sittings with seers sit by tales that checked out true. Some talks seemed to come from the dead through more than one voice in far towns.

His tone is calm, fair, and shorn of wild zeal. He asks fans to weigh, not to swoon. The book is a fair flag of the field in its prime age. It shows its care at work.
history-of-egypt-from-330-b-c-to-the-pre:
S Rappoport's eleventh volume covers Roman, Christian, and Arabic Egypt. The head notes list its span in one sweep. Augustus remodels the government, and a new calendar is set up. Jews and Greeks clash at Alexandria, and Strabo visits the land.

The rise of Christianity brings the Arian controversy and Athanasius. Monasticism grows, Alexandria declines, and the Arab invasion follows. Arab dynasties close the volume's long arc. A frontispiece shows the great dam at Aswan, a sign of the new age. Readers get a thousand years of Egypt's faiths and rulers in one full volume.
history-of-friedrich-ii-of-prussia-volum:
Thomas Carlyle opens volume eleven of his Frederick the Great with a death and a sudden change of reign. Book eleven, Friedrich Takes the Reins in Hand, covers June to December 1740. King Friedrich Wilhelm died on the last day of May, and his son, author of the Anti-Machiavel, took the throne amid hopeful rumors. Europe expected a gentle philosopher-king who might halve the army.

Carlyle shows instead a young ruler keeping his father's soldiers, closing the gates of Berlin while officials swore loyalty, then acting fast. Reports from ambassadors and newspapers fill out the picture of Europe guessing wrong. By year's end the reign of reason was turning toward war.
hobhouse-liberalism-1911:
L. T. Hobhouse set out the new liberalism in Liberalism, a compact book of 1911. Older liberal thought had stressed freedom from state meddling above all. Hobhouse argues that real freedom needs food, schooling, and fair terms of work. The state, used with care, becomes a tool of liberty rather than its foe.

He traces liberal ideas from early toleration to his own social program. Each stage widens the circle of who counts as fully free. The book became the classic statement of social liberalism's case for state action. British reform in his century ran on lines he helped draw. It remains a clear, brief classic.
husserl-philosophie-als-strenge-wissensc:
Edmund Husserl published his essay Philosophy as Rigorous Science in the journal Logos in 1911, and the German text is given here. Husserl taught at Göttingen and had founded phenomenology, a method that studies how things appear to the mind. The essay served as a public call to rebuild philosophy on firm ground.

Two foes draw his fire: the view that thought is just brain work for science to explain, and the view that truth shifts with each age. Both, he argued, end in doubt about all knowledge. His fix was a strict method that sets aside rash claims and studies experience itself. The piece set the course for much of later European thought.
ibn-arabi-tarjuman-1911:
Ibn Arabi was the great Sufi sage of Spain and the East. His Tarjuman al-Ashwaq, the Interpreter of Desires, holds his love poems. R. A. Nicholson turned them into English in 1911, with the Arab text at hand. A young woman of Mecca first woke the poems in him.

On their face, the odes praise her grace in rich, warm lines. Ibn Arabi then adds his own notes to bare the hid sense. Each grace, he says, points to God and the soul's love for Him. The book is a core text of Sufi thought on love.
ibsen-a-dolls-house-sharp-1911:
Henrik Ibsen wrote A Doll's House in Norwegian, and R. Farquharson Sharp made this Dent version in 1911. The play detonated modern drama when its last scene first stunned audiences in Copenhagen and beyond. Nora's door slam at the end was heard, as the phrase goes, round the world.

Nora Helmer seems a gay, childish wife in a snug and prosperous bourgeois home. A secret loan and a forged name rise to threaten her husband's new bank post. Torvald's rage at the scandal shows Nora she has lived as a doll, not a person. She walks out on husband and children to find herself, in a shocking close. The play still sparks debate on marriage, duty, and a woman's right to selfhood.
ibsen-collected-works-archer-vol-11:
Archer's eleventh and final Ibsen volume gathers the last plays: Little Eyolf, John Gabriel Borkman, and When We Dead Awaken, in 1908 translations. Guilt, age, and the unlived life haunt all three. An old man facing death wrote these spectral dramas, and they read like reckonings.

A drowned child accuses his parents in Little Eyolf; a ruined banker paces his room in Borkman, dreaming of lost empire. When We Dead Awaken lets a sculptor and his model count what their art cost their lives. The volume completes the English edition that defined Ibsen abroad. It also closes the career of the father of modern theater on a note of strange, cold beauty.
international-weekly-miscellany-of-liter:
Women and literature in France heads the International Weekly Miscellany for August 12, 1850. That was volume one, number seven, at New York. A Paris letter argues that French women reign as queens and govern as ministers. Painters' studios hold as many women as men, the letter claims.

Verse inside recalls a wild, unworldly youth given to his own eager thoughts. The speaker weighs trivial pleasures against books and nature at that early age. Essays and tales from European papers fill the rest. The number shows the weekly's habit of translating continental gossip for American readers.
james-memories-studies-1911:
Memories and Studies, published in 1911, is a posthumous gathering of James's essays, memorial pieces, and addresses. It shows the philosopher among his dead: teachers, friends, and fellow workers remembered with unusual tenderness.

The volume includes his memorial of Louis Agassiz, his Harvard teacher, and his celebrated address on Emerson. Other pieces take up the moral equivalent of war's themes, the energies of men, and the will to believe's echoes. James writes of persons as he wrote of ideas, with sympathy and precision. The book is the most personal of his volumes, a portrait of a mind through its attachments.
james-more-ghost-stories-1911:
More lore and more curses fill M. R. James's next set of ghost tales, from 1911. Its best known tale sends a curse by runes on a scrap of paper. A proud man who spurned a scholar's work finds dread dogging each step he takes.

James keeps his dry wit and slow build. Old halls, inns, and church tombs hide each threat. Facts pile up till doubt fails. The set shows his craft at full strength. It fixed his name as the chief of the form. A lost maze, a cursed inn, and a school tale with a grim well fill the set. Each shows James at ease with pace, lore, and shock.
james-some-problems-philosophy-1911:
Some Problems of Philosophy, published in 1911 after James's death, is the unfinished introduction to philosophy he was writing at the end. It is subtitled a beginning of an introduction. The book breaks off mid-course, brought to print by his son's care.

James takes up substance, design, free will, and the quarrel between monism and pluralism. He tests each against his pragmatic method: what difference would the answer make in experience? The writing has his late clarity and charm. Though a fragment, it serves as the best short doorway into his thought. Readers meet the philosopher mid-argument, still working.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-11:
Side by side, the Huron and Quebec missions run through Volume 11, from 1898. Thwaites sets the later 1630s on two fronts of one shared enterprise. While Brébeuf builds among the Hurons, the St. Lawrence colony takes shape below.

Letters from bark chapels sit beside reports from the river towns. Both tell of scarce food, hard travel, and slow gains in faith. The writers count each baptism and mourn each early death. Year by year and letter by letter, the record keeps its march. It shows French America's bold age from two ends at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ab-fifteenth-da:
The Fifteenth Day of Ab was a popular festival in Judea in the time of the Second Temple. It fell near the fifteenth day of August. The Mishnah says the maidens of Jerusalem, rich and poor alike, dressed in white that day. They went out to dance in the vineyards and to be chosen as partners for life.

The Talmud gives many reasons for the day, and the oldest one named is the great wood-offering. On that day priests and people brought wood for the altar for the whole year. Josephus calls it the Feast of Xylophory, or wood-bearing. The entry ends by treating it as an old midsummer festival whose first reason was forgotten.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abd-ul-hamid-ii:
Abd-ul-Hamid II was the thirty-fourth Ottoman sultan, born on September 22, 1842. He succeeded his brother Murad V on August 31, 1876. Turkish Jews, the entry says, saw his reign as the start and surety of their good state in the empire. He was the first Turkish ruler to grant them full equality before the law.

On taking the throne he ordered set salaries for the chief rabbis, making them state officials. Each Passover he sent 8,000 francs to the chief rabbi of Constantinople for the Jewish poor. In 1881 he voided town elections in Crete from which Jews had been barred. After a fire left six thousand Jewish families homeless in 1882, he did all he could to aid them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abin-ben-adda-3:
Abin ben Adda was a Babylonian amora of the fourth century, a disciple of Rab Judah ben Ezekiel. He was an older peer of Raba ben Joseph. The entry is clear that he was no first-hand thinker. His service to both the Halakah and the Haggadah lay in memory. He stored up and passed on the rulings and remarks of the great men before him, above all those of R. Isaac.

One long chain of his, in Berakot, works out God's nearness step by step. From one verse of the Psalms he draws the Presence in the synagogue, and with ten men at prayer. From the same verse he draws it with three men in judgment. Other verses then carry the Presence to two men at study, and even to one man alone with the Torah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-academies-in-pa:
Academies in Palestine traces schools of Jewish learning in the land itself. A tale told by Hoshayah speaks of 480 synagogues in Jerusalem. Each had a school for Bible study and one for oral law. Above them stood a kind of high academy of scribes. Its grown pupils were called disciples of the wise. The houses of Hillel and Shammai held their famed debates there.

When Jerusalem fell, Johanan ben Zakkai set up a new home for the law at Jabneh. That school took the place of the Great Sanhedrin. It drew the men who had lived through the fall. It raised a new set of teachers after the Bar Kokba war. Later parts follow learning at Tiberias. There the Masorite line of Ben Asher brought the work to a high point. Tiberias then faded as a seat of study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adler-cyrus-811:
Cyrus Adler was a book man of the Smithsonian Institution. He founded the American Jewish Historical Society. He was born at Van Buren, Arkansas, on September 13, 1863. He studied at the University of Pennsylvania and at Johns Hopkins. He took his doctor's degree in 1887. He taught Semitic tongues at Johns Hopkins. From 1887 he also worked for the National Museum in Washington.

He spent fifteen months in the East as an agent for the Chicago World's Fair. His work stocked its Oriental shows. He helped run the United States shows at three fairs. The Historical Society grew from an appeal he sent out early in 1892. He served as its clerk, then as its head from 1898. He edited the "American Jewish Year Book" from 1899. With Allan Ramsay he put out a book of folk tales heard in Constantinople.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agrigentum-see-: Agrigentum is a town on the south coast of Sicily. It held a large Jewish flock as early as Pope Gregory the Great, who ruled 590-601. No word survives of the flock's start or its full past. In the fifteenth century it still ranked among the island's chief flocks. Two men of the town wrote on Cabala. David of Agrigentum wrote a mystic note on a prayer. Joseph ibn Shraga wrote wide Cabala notes. In 1492 all Jews were cast out of the island, and the flock's tale ends.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aibu-ibu-1011:
Aibu, also read Ibu, is a name borne by four amoraim in this entry. Three of them belonged to the family of Abba Arika, called Rab, in Babylonia. The first was Rab's own father. He was Rab's elder half-brother Hiyya's kin by blood and by marriage both. He traced descent from the royal house of David, and studied under Eleazar b. Zadok.

The second Aibu was a son of Rab. He lacked his father's gift for study, the entry says plainly. Rab advised him to take up worldly work instead, and gave him rules of conduct for it. He became a farmer. The third Aibu was a grandson of Rab. He was so little known as an authority that copyists sometimes wrote Abbahu's name in place of his. A fourth Aibu is left to the entry that follows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-al-rabi-ibn-abu:
Al-Rabi ibn Abu al-Hukaik was a Jewish poet of the Banu al-Nadhir in Medina. He flourished shortly before the Hegira, in 622. His family held the fort Al-Kammus, near Khaibar. Like most Jews of Medina, he took part in the feuds of its two Arab tribes. He was present at the battle of Bu'ath in 617.

Al-Rabi was a poet of note in his day. He once matched verses with the famed Arabic poet Al Nabighah. Nabighah would recite one half-line, and Al-Rabi had to cap it in the same meter and rime. Other poems bear his name on weak authority. His brother Sallam and his three sons were among Mohammed's bitterest foes. The entry also rejects a claim that Al-Rabi was a Muslim: Arabic sources, it says, are clear on his Jewish birth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alemeth-1111: Alemeth is a name found in the genealogy of Benjamin in Chronicles. The first Alemeth was a son of Jehoadah. In a later chapter of the same book he is called the son of Jarah. A second mention of the name is not explained here at all. The entry sends the reader to the article on Almon for that one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-algazi-hayyim-1: Hayyim Algazi was a rabbi in Constantinople in the seventeenth century. He studied under Joseph di Trani. He wrote notes on a civil law part of an older code. That older code was by Jeroham ben Meshullam. Hayyim's notes came out in Constantinople in 1668. They bear a Hebrew title that means the paths of justice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ararat-1711:
Ararat is a district in eastern Armenia, between lakes Van and Urmia and the river Araxes. The Bible name matches the Assyrian Urartu. Assyrian kings Asshurnazir-pal and Shalmaneser II invaded and partly conquered that land, the entry says.

Cuneiform writing reached Urartu by the ninth century B.C., and many stone inscriptions have been found there. A strong native line of kings rose about the middle of that century. Assyria revived under Tiglath-pileser III about 740 B.C. and attacked for a generation. Urartu won its freedom again, until Scythians overran it near the end of the seventh century. The Bible names Ararat four times, once as the refuge of Sennacherib's killers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aronson-rudolph:
Rudolph Aronson, composer and theatrical manager, was born in New York on April 8, 1856. After New York high school he trained at the Vienna Conservatory and then at the Paris Conservatoire, where he studied the French composers closely. His taste ran to light, lyrical music rather than the classics. Back in America he first won notice directing fashionable concerts in Madison Square Garden.

Their success let him build a concert hall at Forty-first Street and Broadway, opened on May 27, 1880, where he introduced the roof garden as a summer feature. With new capital he opened the Casino on October 22, 1882, a Moorish-style theater devoted to light opera, called here the first lasting home of light opera in America. He also wrote over 150 dances, marches, and orchestral pieces.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ash-ariya-1911:
Ashariya was a Muslim theological school founded at the start of the tenth century by Abu el-Hasan al-Ash'ari. Its aim was twofold. It fought the doctrines of the Rationalists, the Motazilites. At the same time it softened the hard, unbending line of the Orthodox party. Three questions drove the quarrel: whether the Koran existed before creation, whether human acts are fixed beforehand, and how God's attributes are to be understood.

On the Koran, the school took a middle path. The book as handed down was created, it held, but its principles existed before the world. The entry notes that rabbis held a like view of the Torah. On human acts, the Ash'ariya sided in the main with the Orthodox, who read the Koran literally, yet sought room for justice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-asiel-2011: Three men share the name Asiel in this entry. The first stands only in the genealogy of Simeon, in First Chronicles chapter 4. The second was one of the five skilled writers who wrote out the law for Ezra, in Second Esdras chapter 14. The third was an ancestor of Tobit, in the first chapter of the book of Tobit, where the older version reads the name as Asael. Nothing further is stated about any of the three.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lyon-robert-102:
Robert Lyon, an American journalist, is the subject of an entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in London on January 15, 1810, he tried business there first. In 1844 he emigrated to the United States. A manufacturing venture failed, and he turned to publishing. He died in New York City on March 10, 1858.

The article remembers him for one paper above all. On October 26, 1849, he launched The Asmonean, the first American Jewish weekly of its kind. He ran it until his death, while also editing the New York Mercantile Journal. Writers such as Isaac M. Wise contributed to the paper regularly. The Asmonean never won more than local fame, the entry admits. Still, the piece preserves the start of the American Jewish press and the editor who began it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-makai-emil-1031:
Emil Makai, a Hungarian poet, receives a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Mako on November 17, 1871, he was the son of Rabbi A. E. Fischer. He studied at the Rabbinical Seminary in Budapest. There he stood out early for his poetical talent. He died at Budapest on August 6, 1901.

The article praises his gift for carrying Hebrew poetry into Hungarian. He rendered medieval poets such as Gabirol, Ha-Levi, Moses ibn Ezra, and Al-Harizi. Immanuel of Rome also found a voice through him. His own works include Absalom, a biblical drama, and a collection drawn from the Hebrew poets in 1891. The Song of Songs followed in 1892, beside volumes of his own lyrics. The brief entry preserves a poet who died at twenty-nine, having spent his short life as a bridge between two literatures.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marhab-ibn-al-h:
Marhab ibn al-Harith, a Jewish warrior of Arabia, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was killed during Mohammed's invasion of Khaibar about 628. Of Himyarite descent, he won fame for bravery in defending one of Khaibar's forts. The sources picture a giant of a fighter.

The article lingers on his last combat. Marhab wore two cuirasses, a double turban and helmet, with a sword at each side and a three-pointed lance. Following Arab custom, he sent out a poem challenging any of Mohammed's heroes to single combat. One account gives the answering fight to Ali, Mohammed's cousin. Ibn Hisham instead names Mohammed ibn Maslamah, avenging his brother. In that telling the two men fought around a tree until its branches were cut away. Marhab dropped his sword, and his foe struck the fatal blow. The entry weighs both versions of a famous duel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mem-10611:
Mem is the thirteenth letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and M. Seligsohn describe it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name means "water." Its early shape is said to have looked like waves. Like some Hebrew letters, it has two forms, one for the start and middle of a word and a final form for the end. In post-Biblical reckoning its value is forty.

The second half of the article is grammar. As a labial, mem swaps with the other labials. This happens across the Semitic tongues. At times it swaps with the liquids too. In word building it works as a prefix. It marks place, time, instrument, or agent. It builds the participles of most Hebrew verb stems. It builds a large class of nouns too. One short paragraph carries the whole entry, cross-referred to the article on the alphabet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meshullam-ben-i:
Meshullam ben Isaac, called in full Salem ben Joseph, was an Italian poet of the Hebrew printing houses. Richard Gottheil and Isaac Broydé enter him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Mantua and Venice around the turn of the seventeenth century. Like his father before him, he worked as a corrector in the Hebrew presses of those cities. He graced the trade by supplying the books he corrected with laudatory poems of his own, printed at their heads.

Three liturgical poems of his are named. One is a kinah, an elegy on the great fire at Mantua in 1610, which dates his activity. One treats the Exodus from Egypt. One is a selihah built as a fourfold alphabetical acrostic. The entry rests on Steinschneider's catalogue and Zunz's history of the liturgical poets. It preserves a working poet of the press room rather than the academy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-modona-leonello:
Leonello Modona was an Italian Orientalist born at Cento in 1841. Isidore Singer and Vittore Castiglione give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was educated at Florence's Istituto degli Studi Superiori. His working life joined two trades. He compiled library catalogues. He also wrote studies that range across classics, folklore, and Jewish letters.

His titles show the range. L'Uomo e la Natura treats man and nature. Another study covers the historical Sappho and the myth of Sappho and Phaon. A third reads the Christian legend of the fall of the angels against two British Museum tablets. For Jewish readers he wrote on Sara Copia Sullam, the Venetian poetess. He also wrote on an edition of the prayer-book. The entry rests on De Gubernatis's biographical dictionary alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moreno-morenu-1:
Moreno, or Morenu, began as a proper name, by Moses ibn Ḥabib's account. Spanish-Portuguese Jews adopted it as a family name, as the Jewish Encyclopedia records in 1906. It travels in company with Paz, Shalom, and Henriquez. Families of the name appear in the seventeenth century at Bayonne, London, Amsterdam, and Hamburg. Others still live in Turkey.

The entry's notices are brief lives. David Shalom Moreno of Bayonne was celebrated for wisdom and Talmudic learning. Gabriel Moreno belonged to Amsterdam's Academia de los Floridos. Jacob Isaac Morenu was an Amsterdam physician who died in 1667. His tombstone was carved with a count's coronet for arms. A surname entry doubles as a map of the western Sephardic diaspora.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-mesharshe:
Moses Kahana ben Jacob, called Mesharsheya, was gaon of Sura from 832 to 843. Wilhelm Bacher and Max Schloessinger wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He was the son of an earlier gaon, Jacob ha-Kohen ben Mordecai. Tradition also makes him a student of the Cabala who used amulets and charms.

His fame rests on two surviving responsa. One treats questions of inheritance and was drawn on by Alfasi and other later authorities. In the other he allowed a Torah scroll to be written on untanned skin when no tanner could prepare parchment. He was the only gaon to allow it, and many Babylonian communities acted on his ruling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-muller-gabriel-:
Gabriel Müller was a dayyan, a rabbinical judge, at Mattersdorf in Hungary, born at Nadas in 1836. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He learned much of his Torah in his father Hayyim's yeshiva. In 1860 he was appointed dayyan of the community of Mattersdorf.

His books are working tools for rabbis. Birkat ha-Mizwot sets out the laws of the benedictions, and Shi'ure Mizwot treats the weights and measures of the Talmud. His Ozar Agadot gathers haggadic passages from the Talmud in four parts, issued over twenty-five years. A late work, Ma'gele Zedek, turns to ethical reflection.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naphtali-ben-da: Naphtali ben David was a German Hebrew author who lived at Amsterdam in the early eighteenth century. Solomon Schechter and A. S. Waldstein give him a short Jewish Encyclopedia notice. He came of the family of Moses Isserles, was a distinguished Talmudic scholar, and won great fame as a cabalist. His one book, Ben Dawid, printed in 1729, criticizes Lonzano's cabalistic Omer Man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-necromancy-1141:
Necromancy is divination by aid of the dead. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Persians, Greeks, and Romans all practiced the dark art. Israel may have borrowed it from Persia. The Bible bans it again and again in strong terms.

Three kinds of workers are named in the sources. The ob spoke as if from joints and arms. The yidde'oni used a bone held in his mouth. At Endor, Samuel rose as an old man in a mantle. Only the witch saw him; Saul heard just the voice. Saul had banned such workers, yet he sought one out. The art lived on into Talmudic times regardless.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-novogrudok-1161:
Novogrudok is a Russian town in the Minsk government. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews first appear there in a deed of 1484. King Casimir leased its customs to four Troki Jews. Royal tax farming shaped its early Jewish life.

In 1529 its Jews shared a special military tax. A royal edict of 1563 fixed their quarter. They were to settle below the castle there. Building on Podlyaskaya street was barred to them. Slow removal brought a fine of 1,600 ducats. Stephen Bathori renewed their charter in 1576. The Orientalist Albert Harkavy was born in Novogrudok. Of 13,656 souls in 1897, 8,137 were Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-onias-honi-ha-m:
Onias, called Honi the Circle-Drawer, was a teacher and wonder worker. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the first century before Christ. Some tales make him kin to Moses himself. He was an Essene, a man of strict faith.

Honi was held in high regard for his pure life. When he entered the school house, all grew clear. He gave plain replies to hard points of law. Yet no rule of his has come down to us. His fame rests on his wonders, the piece says. In a dry year, men begged him to pray for rain. He drew a circle and stood in its midst. Rain came at once at his word of prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ottinger-joseph:
Joseph Öttinger was an Austrian doctor from Tarnow, in Galicia. Isidore Singer and A. Beck wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on May 7, in 1818. He died at Cracow on October 2, 1895. He read at the University of Cracow in youth.

Joseph took his first degree in the year 1843. He took a surgeon's degree in the year 1850. In 1851 he took charge of talks at the school. Those talks were on the past of cures and their law. The right to teach was kept from him for years. His love of Poland stood in the way, men said. In 1867 he won that right at long last. He was chief doctor at the Jewish hospital of Cracow.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-parhon-solomon-:
Solomon ben Abraham ibn Parhon was a Spanish word scholar. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the twelve hundreds in Spain. He was born at Kal'ah, a town in Aragon land. Two great Spanish scholars were among his teachers.

Those teachers were Judah ha-Levi and Abraham ibn Ezra. Solomon tells of talks held with Judah ha-Levi in person. He tells of their stays in North Africa in past days. One work of his has lived to our own time. That one work is his word book, or lexicon, in full. In it he stands as a true pupil of Ibn Ezra. He spread the Hebrew word lore of Spain to new lands. At Salerno he found folk who knew none of that lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pentateuch-1201:
The Pentateuch is the five books of Moses. Emil G. Hirsch and Joseph Jacobs wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name is Greek for the five scrolls of the Law. In Hebrew its name means the five fifths of the Law.

The five books run from Genesis to Deuteronomy. Tradition gave their writing to Moses himself. Only the last eight verses, on his death, were excepted. Later readers spotted clashes inside the text. Ibn Ezra hinted at doubts in the Middle Ages. Spinoza later gave the work to Ezra instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phillips-george:
George Lyon Phillips was a leading politician in Jamaica. He was born in 1811 and died at Kingston in 1886. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He ranked among the island's most trusted men.

Phillips held the chief magistracy of the privy council. He filled other high executive posts on the island too. His hour of trial came in the Saturnalia of Blood. That was a season of panic and harsh rule. His calm and gentle manner steadied the councils. The colony owed much of its safety to him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-plotke-julius-1: Julius Plotke was a Frankfort lawyer and communal trustee. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Borek in 1857 and died in 1903. He practiced first at Bockenheim, then in Frankfort itself. He sat on the board of the Frankfort congregation. He served as trustee for several great relief bodies. His pamphlets described the Jews of Russia and Rumania.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-psalms-of-solom:
The Psalms of Solomon are songs that stand outside the Bible. Crawford Howell Toy wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The work is not in the Greek Bible of old. So it forms no part of the Apocrypha either. It comes down to us in Greek alone. Versions made from that Greek exist as well.

The work was most likely written in Hebrew first. It is a Palestinian work, and Hebrew was its natural tongue. Its Greek is rough and at times hard to grasp. Many dark spots come from Greek misuse of Hebrew words. That fact points back to a Hebrew source. The article weighs the songs' age, place, and faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabinovitz-samu:
Samuel Jacob Rabinovitz was a Russian rabbi and author, born in 1857. Herman Rosenthal and Benzion Eisenstadt wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Chelm in the Kovno government. In 1887 he became rabbi at Jevije. That same year he was called to Alexoty instead. His pen was as busy as his pulpit in those years.

Rabinovitz wrote many pieces for the paper Ha-Meliz. They were later made into a book at Warsaw. The book came out in 1900 on faith and nation. In 1897 he sat as a delegate at Basel. That was the first Zionist Congress of Theodor Herzl. In 1900 he became rabbi of Sopotkin.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-revai-mor-12711:
Mór Révai was a Hungarian publisher and deputy born at Eperies in 1860. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at the universities of Budapest and Leipzig. In 1880 he joined his father's publishing house.

The article says that firm was Révai Brothers, founded in 1869. Révai gave great service to popular education in Hungary. He edited a fiction magazine from 1880 to 1885. He helped issue a grand work on the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. He introduced book canvassing into Hungary, they say. His lexicon drive won twenty thousand subscribers. His hundred volume Jókai edition won a Paris grand prize. In 1901 the Szék district sent him to Parliament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-romaner-benjami:
Benjamin Zeeb Wolf Romaner was a rabbi and preacher. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He worked in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He served as darshan, or preacher, at Semigrod.

The article says he later preached at Dessau. In his old age he lived at Metz. His book is called Ir Binyamin. It treats the haggadot of both Talmudim in two parts. Part one appeared at Frankfort on the Oder in 1698. Part two appeared at Fürth in 1722. Four bibliographies support the short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rothschild-mena:
Menahem Mendel Rothschild was a German rabbi born in Frankfort-on-the-Main about 1650. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Peter Wiernik wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a grandson of Isaac, the Rothschild family's forebear.

Menahem preached for several years at Prague, in Bohemia. In 1686 he became chief rabbi of Bamberg, serving Bayreuth and Baiersdorf as well. He stayed at Bamberg until 1718, then moved briefly to Hesse. His last post was the old community of Worms, held until his death in 1731. Like many rabbis then, he was a man of considerable wealth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-jaco: Samuel ben Jacob of Troyes was a French Talmudist of the first half of the thirteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. Peiginsky wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He was a descendant of Rashi. In his youth he addressed a circular letter, probably cabalistic in nature, to Asher ben David in Provence. Asher later alludes to it in his own cabalistic work on the thirteen attributes of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarug-saruk-isr:
Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Israel Sarug. He was a cabalist of the sixteenth century, also called Ashkenazi. Sarug was a pupil of Isaac Luria, the great mystic of Safed. When Luria died, Sarug spread his master's system. He won followers for it in many parts of Italy.

His leading Italian disciple was Menahem Azariah da Fano. Sarug persuaded him to spend large sums buying Luria's manuscripts. Aaron Berechiah of Modena also joined his circle. Sarug lectured in Germany and in Amsterdam as well. Abraham de Herrera was among his Amsterdam pupils. His writings include a cabalistic essay printed in 1629. Another work teaches an ascetic way of life. He also commented on three of Luria's Sabbath hymns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schottlander-ju:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on a second Julius Schottländer. He was a German gynecologist, a doctor for women's diseases. Schottländer was born at St. Petersburg on April 12, 1860. He studied medicine at Munich and Heidelberg. He took his doctorate in 1887. He then assisted Kehr at Halberstadt and Martin at Berlin.

In 1893 Schottländer settled at Heidelberg as a physician. He became a privat-docent in gynecology at the university there. In 1897 he was appointed assistant professor. He has written several essays for the medical journals. His book Eierstocktuberculose, on tuberculosis of the ovary, appeared at Jena in 1896. The entry rests on Pagel's lexicon of physicians. The shared name with the Breslau merchant is a coincidence of the catalog.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-semiatitsch-ged:
Gedaliah Semiatitsch was a Lithuanian Talmudist who lived in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. In 1700 he joined a Hasidic party that sailed for Palestine under Judah Hasid. That journey became the subject of his best known book.

His work, printed at Berlin in 1716, tells the full story of the pilgrimage. It covers the party's adventures and the death of Judah Hasid. It also describes Jerusalem, its ruins, and holy burial places across the land. The entry preserves the memory of a traveler whose book outlived him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-she-heheyanu-13:
She-heheyanu is the blessing that thanks God for keeping Jews alive to reach a season. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Its words praise God who sustained us and brought us to this time. People first said it on meeting a loved one after long parting.

The blessing also fits good news and first uses of new things. A new house, garment, utensil, or book called for it. Trivial goods did not, unless the buyer was poor and glad. In modern use it marks first fruits of each season. It is also said after Kiddush on festival first nights. The entry traces a thank-you prayer from reunions to holidays.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-showbread-13611:
Showbread, better called presence-bread, was twelve cakes set before God in the sanctuary. Joseph Jacobs and Emil G. Hirsch wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the offering. Each cake held two-tenths of an ephah of fine flour. The cakes stood in two rows on a pure table.

There they stayed exposed to view for a full week. Each Sabbath fresh cakes replaced the old ones. Priests then ate the old bread in a holy place. Cups of frankincense rested on the rows of cakes. That incense served as a memorial offered on the altar. Kohathite priests had charge of baking and arranging the bread. Their method was kept as a family secret, later writers said. The entry explains a quiet weekly rite at the Temple's heart.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-ha-pakol: Simeon ha-Pakoli was a tanna of the second generation, a contemporary of Gamaliel the Second at Jabneh. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He arranged the eighteen benedictions of the daily prayer, the Shemoneh Esreh. He set them in the sequence handed down ever since. His name Pakoli likely came from his trade. Rashi explains that he dealt in flax and wool. Nothing further is known about his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-smolensk-13811:
Smolensk was the capital of the government of Smolensk in Russia. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It stands on the Dnieper, 250 miles from Moscow. Jews lived there as early as 1489. A letter of that year names Jewish customs collectors there.

The city changed hands again and again over time. Russians, Poles, and Lithuanians held it in turn. Its Jewish people suffered greatly from those changes. In 1654 Russia annexed Smolensk for good. By 1899 Jews numbered 4,567 of 56,389 people. Their numbers had fallen since 1896 under residence laws. The town then had two synagogues and five hadarim.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-steindorff-geor:
Georg Steindorff was a German Egyptologist born at Dessau on November 12, 1861. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. Steindorff studied Oriental languages at Leipsic and Berlin. In 1893 he succeeded his teacher Georg Ebers as professor of Egyptology at Leipsic. He later embraced Christianity.

Steindorff served as associate editor of a leading journal on Egyptian language and antiquities. His books include a Coptic grammar first printed in 1894. He also wrote on burial finds from the Middle Kingdom in Berlin museums. Other works cover Egyptian art and the glory days of the pharaohs. He edited Baedeker's guide to Egypt as well. The entry maps the output of a busy scholar of ancient Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sumptuary-laws-:
Sumptuary laws limit what people may spend on food and clothing. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Mishnah records such limits from times of war. Hard times led sages to ban costly wedding customs. The rules aimed to cut display in dark days.

During Vespasian's war, grooms lost their crowns and wedding drums. Titus's war banned the crowns of brides as well. In the last war brides could not ride in curtained litters. Teachers debated crowns of salt, myrtle, or plain reeds. One bride's crown pictured a golden city wall. Modesty later brought the litter back into use. The entry shows law trimming luxury after national disaster. It ties private spending to public mourning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tally-14211:
A tally was a wooden stick that recorded a debt. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. Notches along its edge marked the sum due. The stick was then split lengthwise in two. Each half kept part of every notch.

The debtor took one half and the creditor the other. In medieval times this was the standard receipt. Jews and others used tallies for loans. Some survive at Westminster from before the Expulsion. When a debt was claimed, the halves were joined. Any mismatch in the notches exposed fraud at once. The exchequer's stored half settled disputes as decisive. Britain's exchequer used tallies for general receipts too. The entry explains a receipt that could not be forged easily.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-templer-bernhar:
Bernhard Templer was an Austrian theologian born at Brzesko, Galicia, in 1865. Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Templer studied at the University and Bet ha-Midrash of Vienna. He also studied at the Berlin Hochschule for Jewish learning.

Templer began writing for Hebrew periodicals at age fifteen. Two years later he published a book on hard Talmudic passages. Other books treated Bible passages and medieval Jewish views of the soul. His 1895 work covered immortality, messianic belief, and the world to come. It drew on Jewish philosophers of the Middle Ages. The entry is short, but it maps a young scholar's early career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-titles-of-honor:
Titles of honor marked birth, rank, learning, and piety in Jewish life. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In the Bible, adon, or lord, named a master of property. Guests of honor and benefactors received the word too. Abraham was called lord and mighty prince.

A people's leader bore the title melek, or king. Dukes, called aluf, ruled clans under a tribal head. The king's second was the mishneh. Joseph held that rank under Pharaoh in Egypt. Moses earned the titles man of God and servant of the Lord. Other prophets shared those same honors. First-born sons held the title bekor, with its rights. Priests and Levites carried titles by descent.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trier-herman-14:
Herman Trier was a Danish educator, writer, and politician of Copenhagen. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born in 1845, he studied law briefly at the university. In 1864 he turned to pedagogics, his life's field. In that field he won international fame.

From 1876 he published studies of cultural and historical figures. His first pedagogics book argued it was a true science. With P. Voss he ran a youth periodical from 1879. He also wrote on medieval Copenhagen's history. Voters sent him to the Danish Folkething in 1884. In 1898 he joined Copenhagen's board of aldermen. The entry catches a reformer mid-career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-visontai-soma-1:
Soma Visontai was a Hungarian lawyer and member of parliament. He was born at Gyöngyös on November 9, 1854. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Budapest and became an attorney in 1882. As a student he wrote papers on political economy.

Visontai won fame as a courtroom speaker in 1890. He defended a Serbian newspaper editor in a political murder trial. The defense succeeded, and grateful voters sent him to parliament. Since 1899 he has represented his native town. He is an expert on criminal law. He also helped draft large parts of Hungary's criminal code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wiesbaden-14911:
Wiesbaden is a German town, capital of former Nassau. Gotthard Deutsch and Moritz Silberstein wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A local history claims Jews lived there in the thirteen hundreds. No documents support that early claim. No record shows persecution in Nassau either. Neither the Armleder riots nor the Black Death struck there.

A Judengasse, or Jews' street, proves their early presence. During the Thirty Years' War, Jewish families found shelter there. Clergy pressed for their removal afterward. Many citizens and officials protected them instead. Friendly feeling toward Jews grew in the town. One citizen in 1700 even adopted Jewish rites. The entry follows the community into modern times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-woolf-sidney-15:
Sidney Woolf (1844-1892) was an English lawyer famed for cases on failed firms. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London, he schooled at a private school and University College. He first worked with his brother in a law firm.

He then read law and joined the bar in 1873. He pled trade and crime cases at first. In time he led the bar in cases of failed firms. In 1890 he was made queen's counsel at last. His first law book treats bad food sold in shops. Later books treat pay for loss and firm wind-ups. He gave time to Jewish schools and synagogue work too. He sat on the board of the Anglo-Jewish Association.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yizhaki-abraham:
Abraham Yizhaki was a Turkish Talmud scholar at Salonica in the late 1500s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served as a judge in that town's court. He served under Rabbi Solomon ha-Levi in that role.

His name stands third on a court writ of 1597. It stands second on a writ of the next year. He wrote a work with the name Ahot Ketannah. That work is quoted in two books of later men. It was bound at the end of a book by Jacob Hagiz. Some lists give that work to the wrong man by slip. The work has four parts on the laws of one writ. That writ is the bill that frees a wife who is a minor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zedekiah-ben-be:
Zedekiah ben Benjamin was an Italian Talmud man and hymn scribe. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Rome in the thirteenth century of this era. He died at a date past the year 1280.

He was the elder cousin of Zedekiah ben Abraham Anaw. That man quotes him oft in his great rite book. He was a pupil of Meir ben Moses at Rome. He went to Germany to sit with a top tosafist there. That man was Abigdor ben Elijah ha-Kohen of that land. He kept in touch with that teacher in late years. One peer calls him a mate in a note of that book. Some hold he was a pupil of Abraham Abulafia as well. His own hymns of pardon live on in one draft set.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zweifel-paul-15:
Paul Zweifel was a German gynecologist who taught at Erlangen and then at Leipsic. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Höngg, near Zurich, on June 30, 1848, he took his medical degree at Zurich in 1871. That same year he won the right to lecture at Strasburg.

Erlangen made Zweifel professor of gynecology in 1876, and Leipsic called him in 1887. He held the title of Geheimer Medizinal-Rat, a senior medical honor. He wrote over one hundred papers for medical journals. His books include a textbook of operative obstetrics, often reprinted, and studies of digestion in newborns and of rickets, its causes and cure.
journal-of-discourses-vol-11:
Volume Eleven, from 1865, greets the Civil War's end from Utah's pulpits. Young reads the slaughter as the nation's chastisement, long foretold. The prophet who warned of judgment now watches it fulfilled.

Vindication brings no triumph in the sermons' sober, watching tone. Speakers turn the Saints toward building, gathering, and the years ahead. The republic counts its dead while the mountain kingdom endures intact. Old prophecies get reread in light of smoking battlefields back east. The discourses close one age of warning and open one of patient work. Grief for the nation mixes oddly with pride in Zion's peace.
justice-pg2911:
Justice is John Galsworthy's play, first produced at the Duke of York's Theatre on February 21, 1910. Its people include two solicitors named How, their managing clerk Cokeson, and junior clerk William Falder. A judge, advocates, a prison governor, chaplain, doctor, and warders fill the cast. Ruth Honeywill, a woman tied to Falder's fate, stands among them.

The acts move from the solicitors' office in July to the assizes in October. Act three enters a prison in December: the governor's office, a corridor, and a cell. Two years later the last act returns to the office in March. Galsworthy's design is plain: one small crime, then the slow machinery of law and prison working on a man.
keith-ancient-types-of-man-1911:
Arthur Keith, a Scots doctor and sage of man's rise, wrote this plain survey of fossil man in 1911. It was made for the lay reader, with clear plates and a brisk pace. Keith was then one of the best known names in the field in Britain.

He walks from the Neanderthal and Piltdown finds to the frames of Gibraltar and Java. His famed rebuild of the Gibraltar skull shows his hand at the craft of the time. The book taught a whole age the tale of fossil man as its chief men then told it.
king-john-pg1511:
This edition of Shakespeare's King John prints the full cast and scene plan. King John heads the English list, with Queen Elinor and Prince Henry. Young Arthur, Duke of Bretagne, stands as the rival claimant. Philip Faulconbridge, the Bastard, and Hubert de Burgh hold key parts.

France fields King Philip the Second, his son Lewis, and the Austrian duke. The contents move from Northampton to the French camp before Angiers. St. Edmundsbury, a battlefield, and Swinstead Abbey's orchard close the plan. Peter of Pomfret, a prophet, appears in the cast, true to the chronicles. The edition's apparatus shows the play's shape plainly: two kings, one boy's claim, and a bastard who holds England together.
lagrange-mecanique-analytique-1811:
Joseph-Louis Lagrange builds mechanics without a single diagram in Mecanique analytique, Volume One, in the 1811 edition. The whole of dynamics flows from one deep principle in his hands. Lagrange boasts in his preface that no figures will be found in the work, only algebra of the purest and most general kind.

Statics and dynamics gain a unity no earlier writer had reached. His methods still anchor how physicists treat motion and force today. The prose in French is calm, spare, and quietly proud throughout. Many call it the most elegant physics book ever written, a cathedral of reason raised on the work of Newton and his heirs.
lai-graelent-mason-1911:
Graelent is an anonymous Breton lai about a knight and his fairy mistress. Tales like it were told at medieval courts across France and Britain. Eugene Mason translated this one into English in 1911, alongside other lais of the same kind.

The fairy lady gives Graelent love and wealth, but she sets one hard rule. He must never speak of her to anyone. At court he breaks his word, and she vanishes. To win her back he must chase her through fountain and forest, past a white stag, in a pursuit that tests whether love can survive a broken promise.
lai-lespine-mason-1911:
L'Espine is an anonymous Breton lai, a short medieval tale of knights and fairy folk. No author is known for it. Eugene Mason translated the French text into English in 1911, when he gathered several of these old tales into one volume.

A young knight rides out to a thorn tree at night, drawn by a challenge and a strange summons. There he crosses into the land of the fairy king. Mortal rules stop working in that place, and wonder turns quickly to danger. The tale is brief and eerie, told in the spare way of the old Breton storytellers.
lawrence-white-peacock-1911:
D. H. Lawrence was a young schoolteacher in the Midlands when he wrote The White Peacock. His first novel, it was published in 1911 after years of drafting. Lawrence set it in the countryside around his home town of Eastwood in Nottinghamshire.

Two sisters, Lettie and Meg, move through courtships that go wrong in different ways. Around them, the gamekeeper Annable preaches a rough gospel of the body against polite society. Farming life, poaching, and the pit villages fill the background with rich detail. The novel is uneven and lush, but Lawrence's eye for nature and class tension is already fully alive.
life-on-the-mississippi-part-11:
Part Eleven opens with Chapter 51, called Reminiscences. Twain leaves for St. Louis aboard the City of Baton Rouge. He regrets talking with only two dozen steamboatmen, not a hundred. Social life in town had pleasantly swallowed his research time.

From the pilot-house bench he watches the boat straighten up. A cub takes the wheel as Captain Bixby steps in. The cub allows too much water between boat and ships. Twain feels nervous, remembering his own cub days exactly. Black smoke piled from the chimneys in the old-fashioned way. The cub presently closed up on the rank of steamships ahead.
london-south-sea-tales-1911:
Jack London cruised the South Pacific on his yacht Snark in 1907 and 1908, gathering material until illness forced him home. South Sea Tales, published in 1911, holds the fiction that came out of the Solomon Islands and Hawaii. It is his Pacific work at its most brutal and most humane.

The stories confront white traders, missionaries, and planters exploiting island peoples, and islanders answering in kind. One tale visits Molokai's leper colony, where London finds courage and dignity among the outcast sick. Another follows a pearl diver and a hurricane. London neither romanticizes the islands nor excuses the whites. The sea, the heat, and sudden violence rule these pages, told in his hardest prose.
mansfield-german-pension-1911:
Katherine Mansfield published this first book in 1911, when she was twenty-two and newly arrived in London from New Zealand. The sketches grew from her stay at a Bavarian spa, taking the waters among German guests she observed with a cold eye.

She skewers the pension's residents: their appetites, vanities, sentimentality, and casual cruelties. The pieces are short, sharp, and funny, with dialogue that pricks like pins. Mansfield later thought the book crude and tried to suppress it. Even so, the voice is already unmistakable: the outsider girl watching, and missing nothing. Her great stories were five years away.
marie-de-france-bisclavret-mason-1911:
Bisclavret, the Were-Wolf, is Marie de France's great medieval werewolf tale in Mason's 1911 translation. A Breton nobleman vanishes three days each week without explanation. His wife presses him until he confesses his secret.

He turns wolf each week and must hide his clothes to return human. The wife betrays him to a lover, who steals the clothing. Trapped as a wolf, Bisclavret lives gently at the king's court. The king's hound and the wolf's own behavior reveal the truth at last. Treachery, loyalty, and the beast within drive the lai. Marie treats her werewolf with surprising sympathy throughout the tale.
marie-de-france-chaitivel-mason-1911:
Chaitivel, the Dolorous Knight, is Marie de France's lai of love's cost in Mason's translation. Four accomplished knights all love one lady in Brittany. She cannot choose among them and keeps all four hopeful.

A tournament turns festive rivalry into real disaster for the suitors. Three knights die, and the fourth is maimed for life. The survivor proposes the lai be named for his sorrow. The lady instead argues it should bear her own grief's name. Marie leaves readers to judge whose loss runs deeper here. The debate over the title becomes the poem's true subject. Mason's 1911 translation closes Marie's set with this thoughtful, melancholy piece.
marie-de-france-chevrefoil-mason-1911:
Marie de France wrote short verse tales called lais in the twelfth century, and Chevrefoil is her smallest one. Its subject is Tristan and Iseult, the famous doomed lovers of medieval romance. Eugene Mason turned the poem into English prose in 1911.

Banished from court, Tristan cuts a message for Iseult into a hazel branch left beside her road. The sign works like the honeysuckle wound round the hazel tree. Neither plant can live once the two are pulled apart. In just a few pages the tale says all it needs about love that cannot be parted, even by exile or death.
marie-de-france-deus-amanz-mason-1911:
Deus Amanz, the Two Lovers, is Marie de France's bleakest lai in Mason's 1911 translation. A king in Normandy sets a brutal condition for his daughter's marriage. Any suitor must carry her up a steep mountain without resting.

A young lover accepts the test and obtains a strength potion beforehand. Pride makes him refuse the drink when the climb grows hard. He reaches the top carrying her, then dies of the effort. The lady dies of grief beside him on the summit. Love's cruel arithmetic governs the short, sad tale. Mason's translation preserves Marie's restraint, which makes the ending hurt more.
marie-de-france-eliduc-mason-1911:
Eliduc is one of the lais of Marie de France, the twelfth-century poet who wrote short verse tales of love and magic. Eugene Mason translated it into English in 1911. Its knight hero is torn between his wife at home and a new love across the sea.

Eliduc's second love falls into a deathlike sleep, and grief seems certain to win. Then a weasel wakes its dead mate by laying a red flower on it. Eliduc uses the same flower, and the shock of grace that follows changes every life in the tale. All three end by taking holy orders.
marie-de-france-equitan-mason-1911:
Marie de France's Equitan, translated by Eugene Mason in 1911, is a lai of adultery punished. King Equitan of the Bretons falls in love with his seneschal's wife. The seneschal is his loyal right-hand man and closest companion.

The lovers plot to kill the husband in a boiling bath. Equitan himself is forced into the scalding water instead and dies. The wife follows him into the same bath in the tale's grim justice. Marie draws the moral that evil planned for others falls on the planner. Mason's translation keeps the sting of her irony. The short lai shows Marie at her most crisp and unforgiving.
marie-de-france-fresne-mason-1911:
Fresne, the Ash Tree, is among Marie de France's tenderest lais in Mason's 1911 translation. A lady slanders a neighbor for bearing twins, then bears twins herself. Fearing the same charge, she abandons one baby at an ash tree.

A porter finds the child, and nuns raise her behind convent walls. The girl, called Fresne for the ash, grows into a lord's beloved. Her twin sister's wedding finally reveals the truth of her birth. A brocade cloth and a ring serve as the recognition tokens. Hidden birth and love recognized close Marie's delicate tale. Mason's English keeps its gentle, forgiving tone throughout.
marie-de-france-guigemar-mason-1911:
Eugene Mason translated Marie de France's Guigemar into English in 1911. Marie wrote her lais, short Breton tales in verse, in the twelfth century. Guigemar stands first among the twelve lais she composed.

A hunting accident wounds the knight Guigemar in the thigh. A magical ship with no crew carries him to a foreign shore. There a lady, locked away by her jealous husband, heals and loves him. A knotted shirt and a belt serve as tokens of their fidelity. Separation and recognition close the tale in Marie's delicate manner. Mason's translation introduces the twelfth century's great woman poet to English readers gently.
marie-de-france-lanval-mason-1911:
Lanval is Marie de France's most Arthurian lai, in Eugene Mason's 1911 translation. Sir Lanval, a poor foreign knight, receives little favor at Arthur's court. A fairy mistress chooses him in secret and enriches him.

She forbids him ever to speak of her love to anyone. Queen Guinevere then propositions Lanval and, when refused, accuses him falsely. Forced to defend himself, he breaks his vow and names his mistress. The fairy lady rides into court and vindicates him before all. Love on trial frames the tale's bright, strange climax. Mason's version keeps Marie's sparkle in this favorite among her lais.
marie-de-france-laustic-mason-1911:
Laustic, the Nightingale, shows Marie de France in miniature in Mason's 1911 translation. Two knights live as neighbors, and one loves the other's wife. The lovers can only talk through adjoining windows at night.

They claim their meetings are for listening to the nightingale sing. The jealous husband traps and kills the bird in revenge. He hurls its small body at his wife, staining her dress with blood. She sends the dead nightingale to her lover as a final message. He keeps it cased in a jeweled vessel forever afterward. Love, spite, and a dead bird fill Marie's shortest perfect tale.
marie-de-france-milun-mason-1911:
Milun is Marie de France's lai of patience rewarded, in Mason's 1911 translation. The famous knight Milun loves a lady he cannot marry openly. Their son is sent away to be raised by his aunt.

For twenty years a swan carries secret letters between the lovers. The swan flies the messages hidden under its feathers, year after year. The grown son becomes a champion and unknowingly faces his father in combat. Recognition comes through Milun's ring before either man is harmed. Father, mother, and son finally unite after the long separation. The swan post never fails in Marie's most patient love story.
marie-de-france-yonec-mason-1911:
Yonec is a lai by Marie de France, the twelfth-century writer of short verse tales about love and the strange. Eugene Mason made this English version in 1911. Its heroine is a young wife locked in a tower by an old, jealous husband.

A knight reaches her window in the shape of a hawk, and the two become lovers in secret. The husband sets a trap, and the hawk-knight dies of his wounds. Their son, Yonec, grows up hearing the hidden story. When he learns the truth, he takes up his father's sword and settles the debt in blood.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-11: Bourrienne's eleventh volume bears etext number 3561 at Gutenberg. Its head note joins the title to the year 1812. December 2002 is listed as the release date for the file. Inside the sample, though, a reader finds the license text and nothing else. The secretary's own words do not begin within the portion held here. So this note names the volume and its file facts, and claims no more than that.
my-novel-volume-11:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's eleventh book weighs hate as a force in civil life. Kind men call all wickedness a kind of madness, he notes. Yet clever rogues share much with the insane, he argues. Randal Leslie is his case: cunning, restless, and suspicious.

Randal thinks the whole world plots against his rise. His schemes grow wire-drawn to hide their own ugliness. Pride in his own wit blinds him to his shame. Lytton defends the portrait as true to refining minds gone wrong. The volume digs into ambition's dark engine, as the long tale moves toward its reckoning of hearts.
nansen-northern-mists-vol1-1911:
In Northern Mists, from 1911, Nansen turned historian of the Arctic quest itself. Volume One runs from the Greek sailor Pytheas to the Norse voyages. The great polar explorer traces how the North was slowly found, imagined, and mapped.

Nansen sifts sagas, maps, and travelers' tales, testing each claim of early discovery. Vinland, the Irish monks, and the Greenland settlements all get his keen, skeptical eye. He writes as a sailor who knows ice and fog from his own decks. The volume remains a classic survey of early northern exploration, learned and readable at once. Old maps are reprinted so readers can test his claims for themselves.
nansen-northern-mists-vol2-1911:
Volume Two of Nansen's In Northern Mists, also 1911, carries the history of Arctic discovery from the late Middle Ages toward Cabot. Nansen the explorer reads the old records like a man checking a chart. Myths slowly give way to coasts that can be sailed.

He treats Marco Polo's northern hints, the fabled islands on portolan maps, and the search for a sea road to Asia. The volume weighs what the Norse truly found against what later ages claimed for them. Nansen's verdicts are careful and sometimes sharp. The two volumes together survey a thousand years of northern dreaming and discovery.
nasa-tm-19680021153-research-achievement:
Instrumentation research for ground testing fills volume 11 of Marshall's Research Achievements Review, a 1968 memorandum, TM X-53743. Ground tests of rocket hardware are only as good as the instruments that measure them. Albert E. Schuler introduces the volume, which gathers new measurement tools built at the center in Huntsville, Alabama.

Alvin M. Payne describes gear for measuring the density of hydrogen slush, a partly frozen fuel, using radiation based densitometers. Harlan S. Harman then presents pressure sensors built for environmental extremes. His designs include a high temperature transducer with fast response. Together the pieces show how Marshall sharpened the measurements behind its test stands.
nasa-tm-19720010301-low-gravity-venting-:
Thomas L Labus, John C Aydelott, and Raymond F Lacovic of the Lewis Research Center reported these venting tests in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2479. They vented saturated Refrigerant 11 from a small cylindrical tank in low gravity. The Lewis five second zero gravity facility gave brief weightless runs. In orbit, liquid does not settle, so venting a tank can expel liquid instead of gas. Their tank was fifteen centimeters across.

The team studied three gravity levels, from full weightlessness to stronger pulls. The liquid clung to the tank walls with a near zero contact angle. Observers watched the liquid and vapor behavior during each venting run. The results guide the design of spacecraft tank vents. Refrigerant stood in for harder to handle propellants.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-11:
Volume eleven of Schaff's Nicene Fathers, first series, holds Chrysostom's homilies on the Acts of the Apostles and on the Epistle to the Romans. The volume dates from 1886. Chrysostom preached the Acts series near the end of his time in Constantinople.

The Acts homilies follow the apostles from Jerusalem outward, with Chrysostom marveling at their boldness and shaming his own softer age. The Romans homilies then work through Paul's hardest letter, untangling faith, law, and grace for lay hearers. His praise of Paul runs through both series like a refrain. The volume pairs the church's first story with its first theology, preached by its greatest preacher.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-11:
Volume eleven of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890, joins Sulpitius Severus, Vincent of Lerins, and John Cassian. The three are the voices of early western monasticism. Schaff and Wace edited the series.

Sulpitius wrote the life of Martin of Tours, the soldier-saint whose cloak, shared with a beggar, became legend. Vincent's Commonitory gives the famous rule for telling old faith from new error: what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all. Cassian's conferences then carry the wisdom of Egypt's desert monks to the West, on prayer, purity, and grace. The volume shaped how western monks lived and prayed for centuries.
nietzsche-twilight-idols-ludovici-1911:
Friedrich Nietzsche published Twilight of the Idols in 1889, a short summary of his mature thought. The English text here is Anthony M. Ludovici's translation of 1911. Nietzsche said he wrote it as a rest between larger works. Its subtitle calls it how to philosophize with a hammer.

Short sections strike at Socrates, German culture, morality, and metaphysics in turn. Famous maxims open the book, including what does not kill me makes me stronger. Nietzsche tests old idols by tapping them for hollow sounds. The style is fast, funny, and cutting. It is one of the best short entries into his thought.
onions-widdershins-1911:
