Oliver Onions filled Widdershins, his set of tales from 1911, with ghosts that gnaw at the mind. Its most famed tale lures a painter to a flat where a fair voice calls. The flat holds him. Art, love, and dread blur till he can't break free.

Onions writes with care and a slow, sure hand. Fear grows from mood and small signs, not shocks. The set is a high mark of ghost tales from its age. Its lead tale is oft called the best house tale. Onions had a deft hand for folk who drift and dream. His ghosts prey on that drift, which makes the scares feel close and sad.
openalex-w1747388711:
Daniel Furtado Ferreira described this statistics software in 2011. His review appeared in a Brazilian agricultural science journal. Sisvar is a computer system for statistical analysis. It was first released in 1996, he reports. Work on it began in 1994 in Pascal language.

Three goals drove the project from the start. It served a statistics course at Lavras university first. It aimed to be a truly Brazilian free software tool. It also aimed to give researchers fast, trusted analysis. All initial goals were achieved, Ferreira reports. Users praise its accuracy, simplicity, and interactive design.
openalex-w1975654711:
Tom Wingfield, Carlton Evans, and co-authors ran this cohort study. It appeared in PLoS Medicine in the year 2014. Tuberculosis care is free in Peru, they note. Hidden costs still hit patients and their households hard. Such extreme costs are called catastrophic, yet poorly defined.

The team studied TB-affected households in Peru prospectively. They defined catastrophic costs and measured their weight. They compared that weight with drug-resistant disease. Both can drive adverse treatment outcomes for patients. Clear cost definitions help design support for poor households. The work links TB control to poverty protection.
openalex-w2059292511:
Avi Raveh, Phillip Delekta, Craig Dobry and colleagues searched sea microbes for antiviral compounds. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Microbe products have yielded many medicines. Few had been tested against viruses. Marine bacteria offered a fresh place to look.

The team screened extracts from marine actinobacteria. A cell-based test flagged active extracts. Step-by-step separation isolated the active compound. It came from a new Streptomyces species off Papua New Guinea. The compound blocked many RNA viruses in cell tests. It worked by stalling a key energy pathway in cells. That stall starves viruses of building blocks. Related compounds showed similar antiviral effects. The work opens a route to broad antiviral drugs.
openalex-w2094457711:
Daniela Silva Canella, Renata Bertazzi Levy, Ana Paula Martins and colleagues linked ultra-processed foods with obesity in Brazil. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Factory-made food and drink sales have risen worldwide. Obesity and chronic disease rose in parallel. The team tested the link with household data.

They used a national household budget survey. It covered nearly fifty-six thousand Brazilian homes. Homes were grouped into similar strata. Ultra-processed goods supplied very different energy shares across groups. Higher availability tracked with higher average body mass. It also tracked with more overweight and obesity. Plain processed foods showed no such link. The pattern held after adjusting for other factors.

Timber cutting and oil palm planting had changed these forests faster than field surveys could track.

Using satellite images since 1990, the team mapped forest cover and logging roads across the region. They found hundreds of thousands of kilometres of roads cut through the forest. By 2009, nearly four-fifths of Sabah and Sarawak had felt high-impact logging or clearing. Brunei looked very different, with over half its land still under unlogged forest.

The team fitted models to hundreds of published lab survival experiments for both major species. Field survival data then adjusted the lab curves to real-world conditions. One species survived better in both settings, while the other tolerated a wider temperature range. Full tables split survival by age and temperature. The authors stress that local, site-specific survival estimates matter for judging outbreak risk.
openalex-w2624462411:
Julien Emile-Geay, Nicholas P. McKay, and Darrell S. Kaufman lead the PAGES2k Consortium behind this 2017 database paper in Scientific Data. The database holds six hundred ninety-two records from six hundred forty-eight locations. It covers every continent and the major ocean basins. Record lengths run from fifty to two thousand years, with a median near five hundred fifty years. Nearly half the series track modern surface temperatures closely enough to help validate them. Reconstructions built on this shared, quality-checked foundation can be reproduced by others. That helps place today's warming firmly against natural climate variability.

The ATLAS Collaboration evaluated missing transverse momentum reconstruction in this 2018 paper in the European Physical Journal C. The authors test scale, resolution, and sensitivity to running conditions with several metrics. They also lay out how errors on the measurement are derived. Good performance here underpins the credibility of ATLAS's new-physics searches. This paper is the reference for how the 2015 measurement behaved.

Following them makes results repeatable across labs. The statement also updates terms and best practices since 2014. Fields drowning in hype need such ground rules to separate signal from noise. openalex-w3020256411:

The same four clades still dominate, though most now mix across regions. One South American clade kept the strongest geographic pattern. Two clades with opposite mating types even turned up in a single Kenyan facility.
openalex-w3091700111:
Ana Pedrosa, Letícia Bitencourt, Ana Fróes, and colleagues wrote this review in Frontiers in Psychology in 2020. It surveys the emotional, behavioral, and psychological impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. The illness began as a cluster of pneumonia cases in Hubei, China, in December 2019.

They reviewed and selected the work with a critical eye. The review gathers what was known about fear, grief, isolation, and strained behavior during the crisis. It offers clinicians and policymakers a map of the pandemic's mental toll.

A small shared core of microbes appeared in fruit from everywhere.

Madame Oreille's stinginess opens volume eleven of Maupassant's Original Short Stories. In The Umbrella she guards every centime on strict principles, doles her husband barely any pocket money, and sleeps badly after any necessary expense, though the couple are comfortably off and childless. A damaged umbrella becomes the battlefield of the marriage.

Thirteen tales make up the volume, among them Belhomme's Beast, The Diary of a Madman, The Accursed Bread, Suicides, and Simon's Papa. The contents tilt darker than some earlier volumes: madness, cursed food, despair, and children at the mercy of adults. Yet the comedy of the Oreilles' umbrella feud keeps Maupassant's balance of laughter and cruelty in view from the first page.
plaw-111-347-2011:
The James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-347, signed on January 2, 2011. It amends the Public Health Service Act to aid people harmed by the September 11, 2001, attack on New York City. Title I of the act builds a health program for them.

Title I adds a World Trade Center Health Program to the health act. Its parts cover expert and steering committees, outreach, and uniform data gathering. It names Clinical Centers of Excellence and Data Centers to run the care. A second part covers the finding of responders and their health checks and treatment.
plaw-111-348-2011:
Public Law 111-348 of 2011 bears the heading Shark and Fishery Conservation Act. It amends two fishery laws to improve the conservation of sharks. The laws are the High Seas Driftnet Fishing Moratorium Protection Act and the Magnuson-Stevens Fishery Conservation and Management Act.

Title I is the Shark Conservation Act of 2010, built from those two amendments. Title II covers an international fisheries agreement and how it fits with other laws. Title III holds side items, among them small fixes to the law for the Western and Central Pacific fisheries and a part on the Pacific Whiting Act of 2006.
plaw-111-349-2011:
Public Law 111-349 of 2011 sets up a pilot program in certain federal district courts. Its aim is to grow skill in patent cases among district judges. It reaches cases under any act of Congress on patents or plant variety protection.

In each pilot court, judges who ask to hear such cases are named by the chief judge to take them. Cases are still handed out at random to all judges of the court. A judge who is not named may decline a patent case, and it is then reassigned at random to a named judge. Senior judges may also serve if an active judge is named.
plaw-111-350-2011:
Public Law 111-350 of 2011 enacts a further title of the United States Code. Title 41, called Public Contracts, gathers the general laws on government contracts into one title. Like other such acts, it is a restatement rather than a change of policy.

The act says the restatement must match the understood policy and intent of Congress in the laws it replaces. Corrections are allowed only to remove vagueness, clashes, and other flaws. Its later sections make matching changes to other laws, set cross-references, and repeal the old texts. It was approved on January 4, 2011.
plaw-111-351-2011:
The Predisaster Hazard Mitigation Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-351, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Stafford Disaster Relief Act to reauthorize the pre-disaster mitigation program of the Federal Emergency Management Agency. That program pays to cut risks before disasters strike.

Congress found the program a success that has cut deaths, injuries, and damage to property. A 2007 budget office report found it cut losses by roughly three dollars for each dollar spent. A 2005 study of FEMA hazard programs found about four dollars of benefit per dollar spent. Congress cited these savings as its reason to keep the program funded.
plaw-111-352-2011:
The GPRA Modernization Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-352, signed on January 4, 2011. GPRA is the Government Performance and Results Act, the law on how agencies plan and report their work. The act calls for reviews of program results four times a year.

Its contents cover strategic plans, performance plans, and performance reports. They set priority goals for the government as a whole and for each agency, with quarterly checks on progress. The act names a Chief Operating Officer in each agency. It also creates Performance Improvement Officers and a Performance Improvement Council to guide the work.
plaw-111-353-2011:
The FDA Food Safety Modernization Act is Public Law 111-353, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act as to the safety of the food supply. It is a broad reworking of how the Food and Drug Administration guards food.

Title I aims to stop food safety problems before they start. Its parts cover checks of records, listing of food plants, and hazard review with risk-based preventive controls. It sets performance standards and produce safety standards. It also covers defense against the deliberate spoiling of food and the gathering of fees.
plaw-111-354-2011: Public Law 111-354 is the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center Clarification Act, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends a 1978 law, Public Law 95-232, on trust land for Indian pueblos in New Mexico. The act strikes one sentence from that law, which had said the land must not count as Indian country under title 18 of the code. It then adds a bar on gaming, as defined by the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, on land held in trust under that law.
plaw-111-355-2011: Sharon Center, Ohio's post office is the Emil Bolas Post Office under Public Law 111-355. The act was approved on January 4, 2011. It covers the Postal Service site at 1332 Sharon Copley Road. Under the act, references to the site in federal laws, maps, regulations, and records mean the Emil Bolas Post Office. H.R. 4602 passed the House in September 2010 and the Senate on December 16.
plaw-111-356-2011:
The Northern Border Counternarcotics Strategy Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-356, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Office of National Drug Control Policy Reauthorization Act of 2006. The missing piece it adds is a strategy for the northern border of the United States.

Within 180 days, and every two years after, the drug policy chief must write that strategy. The chief must consult federal drug agencies and state, local, tribal, and foreign officials. The strategy goes to a long list of congressional committees, among them the judiciary, armed services, and homeland security panels of both chambers.
plaw-111-357-2011:

The act reauthorizes two million dollars a year for fiscal years 2011 through 2014 for the Interior chief to run those programs. It renames one part of the 1998 volunteer act as a National Volunteer Coordination Program. It also makes small wording fixes to the name of the refuge system law in the older act. It was signed on January 4, 2011.
plaw-111-358-2011:

Title I covers the Office of Science and Technology Policy, with parts on joint federal work in STEM schooling and advanced manufacturing research. It also covers public access to research and prize contests for new ideas. Title II turns to NASA and its role in new ideas, schooling, and the space station.
plaw-111-359-2011: Public Law 111-359, approved January 4, 2011, names a post office building in Carlstadt, New Jersey. The Postal Service site at 331 1st Street is now the Staff Sergeant Frank T. Carvill and Lance Corporal Michael A. Schwarz Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name. The bill passed the House in June 2010 and the Senate on December 16.

plaw-111-361-2011: Public Law 111-361 named the Uniontown, Pennsylvania, post office for George C. Marshall. The act was approved January 4, 2011. plaw-111-372-2011:

plaw-111-373-2011:

plaw-111-374-2011:

plaw-111-375-2011:

It also aims at earlier diagnosis, better care, and care for groups at higher risk or least likely to get help.
plaw-111-376-2011:
The Anti-Border Corruption Act of 2010 is Public Law 111-376, signed on January 4, 2011. It orders Customs and Border Protection to give polygraph tests to all applicants for law enforcement posts. It also orders the agency to start all periodic background re-checks of set law staff.

A backlog of about 10,000 background re-checks was set to grow to about 19,000 by the end of fiscal year 2010.
plaw-111-377-2011:

They cover half-time study, non-degree programs, the monthly housing stipend, and tests for licenses. They also cover the transfer of unused benefits to family members.
plaw-111-378-2011:
Public Law 111-378, signed on January 4, 2011, amends the Federal Water Pollution Control Act. It clarifies the federal duty to pay for stormwater pollution control. The change is made to section 313 of that act, on federal facilities and water rules.

Such fees may fund the full costs of a stormwater program, from gathering runoff to cutting pollutants and flow. The name given to the fee, even if called a tax, does not change that result. One limit bars paying such fees from permanent Treasury accounts.
plaw-111-379-2011: Public Law 111-379, approved January 4, 2011, names a post office building in Tyrone, Georgia. The Postal Service site at 100 Commerce Drive is now the First Lieutenant Robert Wilson Collins Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, or record uses that name from then on. The bill passed the Senate on December 16, 2010, and the House days later.
plaw-111-380-2011:
The Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act is Public Law 111-380, signed on January 4, 2011. It amends the Safe Drinking Water Act to cut the lead in pipes and plumbing. The core change is a stricter meaning of the term lead free.

Lead free now means no more than 0.2 percent lead in solder and flux. For the wet surfaces of pipes and fittings, it means a weighted average of no more than 0.25 percent lead, worked out by a set formula. The act exempts pipes used only for non-drinking uses, such as factory work and irrigation, plus items like toilets and large gate valves.
plaw-111-381-2011: Public Law 111-381, signed on January 4, 2011, grants one more tribe long lease power over its trust land. It amends the Act of August 9, 1955, with a single inserted phrase. The phrase adds lands held in trust for Ohkay Owingeh Pueblo to the list of lands that may be leased for up to 99 years. The bill passed the Senate on December 21, 2010, and the House the next day.
plaw-111-382-2011:
Public Law 111-382, signed on January 4, 2011, clarifies the power of the National Credit Union Administration to spend from its stabilization fund without borrowing from the Treasury. The fund backs insured credit unions in hard times. The act amends section 217 of the Federal Credit Union Act.

One change adds the words and any additional advances to the fund's borrowing terms. The main change rewrites the assessment power of the agency's Board. The Board may charge each insured credit union a special premium to cover fund spending, due within 60 days. In setting the charge, it must weigh the effect on credit union earnings.
plaw-111-383-2011:
The Ike Skelton National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2011 is Public Law 111-383. The act is split into three divisions. Division A holds the Department of Defense authorizations, Division B military construction, and Division C energy national security and other authorizations. Title I of Division A covers procurement, starting with the Army and the Navy and Marine Corps.
plaw-112-1-2011: Public Law 112-1 is the first public law of the 112th Congress, approved on January 31, 2011. It gives small business programs another temporary extension. The act amends the 2006 law that kept certain Small Business Administration powers in force for a set time, striking January 31, 2011 and inserting May 31, 2011. The swap covers programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958, and it takes effect on January 30, 2011.
plaw-112-10-2011:

Division A holds the Defense Department spending for 2011. Title I begins with military personnel, paying for Army pay, allowances, clothing, food, and travel. Division B carries full-year continuing appropriations for the other departments and agencies. Division C is separate subject matter: the Scholarships for Opportunity and Results Act. It stands apart from the spending titles around it.
plaw-112-11-2011: Public Law 112-11, approved on April 25, 2011, names a federal building and courthouse in Martinsburg, West Virginia. The building at 217 West King Street is to be known as the W. Craig Broadwater Federal Building and United States Courthouse. Section 2 adds the references rule: any mention of that building in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Broadwater name.
plaw-112-12-2011: Public Law 112-12 is a joint resolution of the 112th Congress, approved on April 25, 2011. Acting under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, it appoints Stephen M. Case of Virginia as a citizen regent of the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution. Case fills the vacancy left by the resignation of Phillip Frost of Florida, in the class of regents who are not members of Congress. The appointment runs for a term of six years, effective on the date of enactment.
plaw-112-13-2011: Public Law 112-13, approved on May 12, 2011, gives the Ronald Reagan Centennial Commission more time to finish its work. It amends the commission's act in two places. The due date for the commission's final report moves from April 30, 2011 to November 30, 2011. The commission's termination date moves from May 30, 2011 to December 31, 2011. Both changes are plain date swaps, with no other terms altered in the text shown.
plaw-112-14-2011: Public Law 112-14 is the PATRIOT Sunsets Extension Act of 2011, approved on May 26, 2011. It extends two sunset dates in federal surveillance law. In the USA PATRIOT Improvement and Reauthorization Act of 2005, the cutoff of May 27, 2011 becomes June 1, 2015. The same swap is made in the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004. The act's stated purpose line speaks of small business programs, but the operative text shown does only this: it keeps those expiring powers alive for four more years.
plaw-112-15-2011: Public Law 112-15, approved on May 31, 2011, names a post office in Inverness, California for a specialist. The Postal Service facility at 12781 Sir Francis Drake Boulevard is to be known as the Specialist Jake Robert Velloza Post Office. The references clause adds that any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Specialist Jake Robert Velloza Post Office.
plaw-112-16-2011: Public Law 112-16 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2011, Part II, approved on May 31, 2011. For one month only, it extends the taxes that fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund. The fuel tax and ticket tax dates move from May 31, 2011 to June 30, 2011. The trust fund's spending authority moves from June 1, 2011 to July 1, 2011. The changes take effect on June 1, 2011, and the act's purposes also include extending the airport improvement program.
plaw-112-17-2011: The Small Business Additional Temporary Extension Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-17, approved on June 1, 2011. It extends programs under the Small Business Act and the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 once more. The end date moves from May 31, 2011 to July 31, 2011, effective May 30. Section 3 also extends the end dates of two research programs. They are the Small Business Innovation Research program and the Small Business Technology Transfer program. In the sample, the change swaps 2008 for 2011 in the termination rule.
plaw-112-18-2011:
The Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2011 is Public Law 112-18, approved on June 8, 2011. It authorizes spending for the intelligence work of the United States Government, for the Community Management Account, and for the Central Intelligence Agency Retirement and Disability System.

Title I covers budget and personnel authorizations, including a classified schedule of authorizations, so the largest sums stay off the public page. Title II funds the CIA retirement system. Title III handles general intelligence community matters, such as limits on intelligence acts, staff pay rises allowed by law, details of outside personnel, and officer training. Title IV turns to parts of the community, starting with the Director of National Intelligence's office.
plaw-112-19-2011: Public Law 112-19 is a joint resolution, approved on June 24, 2011, that keeps a Smithsonian regent in place. Acting under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, Congress fills the vacancy on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution left by the end of Shirley Ann Jackson's term. The resolution reappoints Jackson, of New York, as a citizen regent for six more years. Her new term runs from May 6, 2011, in the class of regents who are not members of Congress.
plaw-112-2-2011: Public Law 112-2, approved on February 17, 2011, names a courthouse then under construction in Yuma, Arizona. The building at 98 West First Street is to be known as the John M. Roll United States Courthouse. The references clause says any mention of that courthouse in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the John M. Roll United States Courthouse.
plaw-112-20-2011: Robert P. Kogod stays on the Smithsonian's board under Public Law 112-20, a joint resolution approved on June 24, 2011. The vacancy on the Board of Regents of the Smithsonian Institution arose when Kogod's term expired. Congress, acting under section 5581 of the Revised Statutes, fills it by reappointing the incumbent, of the District of Columbia, as a citizen regent. The new term is six years, effective May 6, 2011.
plaw-112-21-2011: Public Law 112-21 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2011, Part III, approved on June 29, 2011. Like Part II before it, the act buys weeks, not years. The fuel taxes and ticket taxes that fund the Airport and Airway Trust Fund now run to July 22, 2011 instead of June 30, 2011. The trust fund's authority to spend moves from July 1, 2011 to July 23, 2011, with a matching change in a related clause. The tax changes take effect on July 1, 2011.
plaw-112-22-2011: Public Law 112-22, approved on June 29, 2011, names a post office in Rootstown, Ohio for a Marine sergeant. The Postal Service facility at 4865 Tallmadge Road is to be known as the Marine Sgt. Jeremy E. Murray Post Office. Under the references clause, any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Marine Sgt. Jeremy E. Murray Post Office.
plaw-112-23-2011: Public Law 112-23, approved on June 29, 2011, names a post office in Cary, Mississippi. The Postal Service facility at 95 Dogwood Street is to be known as the Spencer Byrd Powers, Jr. Post Office. The references clause says any mention of that facility in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Spencer Byrd Powers, Jr. Post Office.
plaw-112-24-2011:
Public Law 112-24, approved on July 26, 2011, extends the term of the sitting Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Robert S. Mueller III. Congress finds that the President asked for a two-year extension on May 12, 2011, citing the need for continuity at the Bureau amid ongoing threats and leadership changes at security agencies.

The act creates a new term of service for the office, running from on or after August 3, 2011 until September 4, 2013. The sitting director may be appointed to that term, and only that term, with the advice and consent of the Senate. Congress stresses that this is a one-time exception to the ten-year term limit, made after the killing of Osama bin Laden, and is not a precedent.
plaw-112-25-2011:
The Budget Control Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-25, approved on August 2, 2011. Congress passed it to impose budget control on the federal government, and its table of contents maps a broad bargain.

Title I sets ten-year discretionary spending caps with a sequester, meaning automatic cuts if the limits are breached, plus Senate budget enforcement rules. Title II calls for a vote on a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution. Title III sets a debt ceiling disapproval process, a way for Congress to object to raising the debt limit. Title IV creates a Joint Select Committee on Deficit Reduction, with fast-track handling for its proposals.
plaw-112-26-2011:
The Restoring GI Bill Fairness Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-26, approved on August 3, 2011. It preserves, for a time, higher tuition and fee rates at private colleges for students already enrolled in the Post-9/11 GI Bill before a 2010 improvements act changed the maximum.

For the period from August 1, 2011 to July 31, 2014, the amount paid for a covered student is the greater of two sums. The first is $17,500. The second is the charge found by using the Veterans Affairs table of 2010-2011 in-state maximums, published on October 27, 2010, as if that table still governed the student's program.
plaw-112-27-2011: Public Law 112-27 is the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2011, Part IV, approved on August 5, 2011. It pushes the aviation tax dates out by roughly eight weeks. Fuel taxes and ticket taxes for the Airport and Airway Trust Fund now run to September 16, 2011 instead of July 22, 2011. The trust fund's spending authority moves from July 23, 2011 to September 17, 2011. The tax changes take effect on July 23, 2011.
plaw-112-28-2011:
Public Law 112-28, approved on August 12, 2011, gives the Consumer Product Safety Commission greater authority and discretion in enforcing the consumer product safety laws. Its first section deals with lead limits in children's products under the Consumer Product Safety Improvement Act of 2008.

The limits now apply only to a children's product made after the effective date of the limit in question, a change called prospective application. The act adds a functional purpose exception. The Commission may excuse a product, material, or part that needs lead. It may act on its own move or on a petition. The excuse holds where making the item without excess lead is not practicable or not technically workable, and a child is not likely to mouth or swallow it.
plaw-112-29-2011:
The Leahy-Smith America Invents Act is Public Law 112-29, approved on September 16, 2011. It amends title 35 of the United States Code to reform the patent system, the largest such rewrite in decades.

The table of contents shows the breadth. Early sections set a first inventor to file rule, remake the inventor's oath, and allow a defense based on prior commercial use. Others create post-grant review proceedings and a Patent Trial and Appeal Board, and allow third parties to file material before a patent issues. Later sections cover fee setting, office funding, satellite offices with one named for Detroit, and priority examination for important technologies.
plaw-112-3-2011: Public Law 112-3 is the FISA Sunsets Extension Act of 2011, approved on February 25, 2011. The operative text extends two sunset dates, in the USA PATRIOT Improvement and Reauthorization Act of 2005 and in the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004. In each, February 28, 2011 becomes May 27, 2011. The powers covered concern access to business records, lone terrorists as agents of foreign powers, and roving wiretaps. The act's own purpose line instead names December 8, 2011.
plaw-112-30-2011:
The Surface and Air Transportation Programs Extension Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-30, approved on September 16, 2011. It extends surface and air transportation programs while Congress worked on longer laws for each field.

Title I extends the surface programs. Subtitle A covers the federal-aid highway programs and their administrative expenses. Subtitle B extends highway safety programs run by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration and the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration, plus added programs. Subtitle C covers public transportation: planning funds, a special rule for city area formula grants, capital investment grants, and grants for areas that are not urbanized.
plaw-112-31-2011: Public Law 112-31, approved on September 23, 2011, names a courthouse in Jefferson City, Missouri. The United States courthouse at 80 Lafayette Street is to be known as the Christopher S. Bond United States Courthouse. The references clause says any mention of that courthouse in a federal law, map, rule, or record counts as a mention of the Christopher S. Bond United States Courthouse.
plaw-112-32-2011:
The Combating Autism Reauthorization Act of 2011 is Public Law 112-32, approved on September 30, 2011. It renews the Combating Autism Act of 2006, which set up federal work on developmental disabilities surveillance and research.

Three sections of Part R of the Public Health Service Act gain new end years, 2014 in place of 2011. A report deadline moves from four years after the 2006 act to two years after this act, and a study span grows from four years to six. The funding clause authorizes $22,000,000 for each of fiscal years 2012 through 2014 for the developmental disabilities surveillance and research program.
plaw-112-33-2011:
Public Law 112-33 is the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2012, approved on September 30, 2011. It makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2012, the stopgap funding that keeps agencies running when the year's regular bills are not yet law.

Section 101 funds projects and activities carried on in fiscal year 2011, at the rate and under the terms of the 2011 laws. The acts named are the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2011 and the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011, the two halves of Public Law 112-10. The rate for operations is then cut by 1.503 percent. Section 102 bars the Defense Department from using these funds to start new production or raise production rates.
plaw-112-34-2011:
The Child and Family Services Improvement and Innovation Act is Public Law 112-34, approved on September 30, 2011. It amends part B of title IV of the Social Security Act to extend the child and family services program through fiscal year 2016.

Title I extends the Stephanie Tubbs Jones Child Welfare Services Program, swapping the years 2007 through 2011 for 2012 through 2016. State plan rules change as well. Plans must cover response to emotional trauma, including trauma tied to a child's maltreatment and removal from home. They must include protocols for the proper use and watching of psychotropic medications, and a description of work to cut the time children under 5 spend without a lasting family.
plaw-112-35-2011: The Short-Term TANF Extension Act is Public Law 112-35, approved on September 30, 2011. It extends the block grant program of aid to needy families, under part A of title IV of the Social Security Act, through December 31, 2011. Activities continue in the manner allowed for fiscal year 2011. Grants may be paid quarterly through the first quarter of fiscal year 2012, at the level of the matching quarter of fiscal year 2011. It also shifts the maintenance of effort years in section 409(a)(7).
plaw-112-36-2011:
Public Law 112-36, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011, carries the short title Continuing Appropriations Act, 2012. It is a stopgap funding law for fiscal year 2012. Congress passed it because the regular spending bills for that year were not yet done.

The act funds federal work at the rate set in the fiscal year 2011 spending acts. It covers work run under the defense act and the full-year act for 2011, named in section 101. Money comes from the Treasury and from agency receipts and funds. The text then sets a rate cut, which the sample shows only in part.
plaw-112-37-2011:
Enacted in 2011 by the 112th Congress, Public Law 112-37 is the Veterans Health Care Facilities Capital Improvement Act of 2011. The law deals with building and leasing major medical sites for the Department of Veterans Affairs. It also extends some expiring rules and changes some powers of the Secretary.

Early sections back fiscal year 2012 major medical facility projects and leases. They also change past project approvals and fund the work. Later sections limit how Congress must approve some site buys. They also curb the use of bid savings to widen a project's scope.
plaw-112-38-2011: Schertz, Texas, is home to the site renamed by Public Law 112-38 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. The Postal Service site at 1081 Elbel Road in Schertz must be known as the Schertz Veterans Post Office. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name. The act does nothing else.
plaw-112-39-2011: Naming a Texas mail site is the whole job of Public Law 112-39, approved in 2011 by the 112th Congress. The Postal Service site at 5014 Gary Avenue in Lubbock must be known as the Sergeant Chris Davis Post Office. Federal laws, maps, rules, records, and other papers must use that name when they refer to the site.
plaw-112-4-2011: Public Law 112-4 is a joint resolution of the 112th Congress from 2011, called the Further Continuing Appropriations Amendments, 2011. It amends the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011, which had kept the government funded. The resolution moves the end date in section 106 to March 18, 2011. It also adds new sections on war funds and on earmark language, though the sample cuts off mid-way through that part.
plaw-112-40-2011:
Trade relief for poor countries sits at the center of Public Law 112-40, passed by the 112th Congress in 2011. The act extends the Generalized System of Preferences, a program in the Trade Act of 1974. That program lets some goods enter the United States with low or no duties.

Section 1 moves the program's end date from December 31, 2010, to July 31, 2013. The change takes effect for goods entered on or after the fifteenth day after the act passed. Goods entered in the gap can still get the old treatment. Their entries are settled again as if they had come in on that fifteenth day.
plaw-112-41-2011:
Public Law 112-41, enacted by the 112th Congress in 2011, puts the United States-Korea Free Trade Agreement into United States law. Title I approves the deal and covers its start date. It also covers how the deal fits with federal and state law, plus dispute steps and claim handling.

Title II turns to customs work. Its sections cover tariff changes, rules of origin, and customs user fees. Those rules decide which Korean goods get the deal's lower rates. They also set how customs staff check where a good was made. The act was approved on October 21, 2011.
plaw-112-42-2011:
Colombia trade terms are the subject of Public Law 112-42, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011. Its short title is the United States-Colombia Trade Promotion Agreement Implementation Act. Title I approves the trade deal and covers when it starts. It also covers the deal's fit with United States and state law.

Title II covers customs. The listed sections deal with tariff changes and rules of origin. They also cover how trade disputes are run and how claims are judged. In short, the act gives the Colombia deal legal force inside the United States.
plaw-112-43-2011:
Public Law 112-43 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011, carries out the United States-Panama Trade Promotion Agreement. Title I approves the deal and sets its start rules. It also states how the deal relates to United States and state law. Other sections cover steps taken before the deal starts and how disputes are handled.

Title II sets the customs side. It covers tariff changes and extra duties on some farm goods. It also covers rules of origin, which decide if a good counts as Panamanian. Those rules control which goods earn the deal's lower rates.
plaw-112-44-2011: Keeping the United States Parole Commission at work is the aim of Public Law 112-44, passed in 2011 by the 112th Congress. The act amends the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984. Each mention of 24 years in the key section now reads as 26 years. That change adds two years to the time the Commission keeps its role. The act also orders a report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees within 180 days. The report starts with a count of offenders, but the sample cuts off there.
plaw-112-45-2011: Public Law 112-45, enacted in 2011 by the 112th Congress, sorts out control of the C. C. Cragin Dam and Reservoir. Section 1 covers a land withdrawal and reservation for the Cragin Project. The covered land runs to about 512 acres. It takes in about 300 feet of the dam crest and spillway, a reservoir pool of about 250 acres, and a linear corridor. The act also defines the project and names the Salt River Project district in its terms.
plaw-112-46-2011:
Ski land on national forests gets wider use under Public Law 112-46, the Ski Area Recreational Opportunity Enhancement Act of 2011. The 112th Congress passed it to amend the National Forest Ski Area Permit Act of 1986. That older act governs ski area permits on National Forest System land. The Secretary of Agriculture issues those permits.

The stated purpose has two parts. First, snow sports beyond nordic and alpine skiing may be allowed on permit land. Second, the Secretary may allow fitting added recreation in any season, all year. Sample text stops while stating that second aim.
plaw-112-47-2011: In Barrigada, Guam, a post office building takes the name set by Public Law 112-47 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. The site at 489 Army Drive in Barrigada must be known as the John Pangelinan Gerber Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of that full name.
plaw-112-48-2011: A Pasadena mail site gains a new name under Public Law 112-48, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011. The Postal Service site at 281 East Colorado Boulevard must be known as the First Lieutenant Oliver Goodall Post Office Building. References to the site in federal laws, maps, rules, records, and other papers count as references to that name.
plaw-112-49-2011: Public Law 112-49, passed in 2011 by the 112th Congress, names one post office in Massachusetts. The Postal Service site at 45 Meetinghouse Lane in Sagamore Beach must be known as the Matthew A. Pucino Post Office. Any mention of that site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of the new name.
plaw-112-5-2011:
Highway and transit programs get more time under Public Law 112-5, the Surface Transportation Extension Act of 2011. The 112th Congress passed it while a longer, multiyear law was still pending. It extends federal-aid highway, highway safety, motor carrier safety, and transit programs. The Highway Trust Fund pays for those programs.

Section 1 also tells the Transportation Secretary to reconcile funds. Amounts for fiscal year 2011 must be cut by sums already given out under the two 2010 extension acts. That cut covers the span from October 1, 2010, to March 4, 2011. Title I then extends the highway programs.
plaw-112-50-2011: Public Law 112-50, enacted by the 112th Congress in 2011, names a Postal Service site in Hawaii. The site at 4354 Pahoa Avenue in Honolulu must be known as the Cecil L. Heftel Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, record, or other paper counts as a mention of that full name.
plaw-112-51-2011:
Moving suits against federal staff to federal court is clarified by Public Law 112-51, the Removal Clarification Act of 2011. The 112th Congress amended title 28 of the United States Code. The target is section 1442, which covers removal of cases against federal officers or agencies. The act aims to clear up and improve those rules.

One change widens what counts as a civil action or criminal prosecution. Any case where a court order is sought or issued counts, at least in part. That reach covers subpoenas for testimony or papers. The sample stops in the middle of that new rule.
plaw-112-52-2011: One Utah water district may pay its federal debt early under Public Law 112-52 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. The Interior Secretary must allow early payment of repayment contract number 6-05-01-00143. The United States and the Uintah Water Conservancy District signed it on June 3, 1976. It covers repayment for town and industrial water delivery works. Early payment must let the United States recover the present value of all sums it would have been paid.
plaw-112-53-2011: Pay rates for hurt veterans rise under Public Law 112-53, the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2011. The 112th Congress amended title 38 of the United States Code. From December 1, 2011, the Secretary of Veterans Affairs must raise the sums in effect on November 30, 2011. The raise covers disability pay for veterans with service-linked harm. It also covers dependency and indemnity pay for survivors of some disabled veterans. The list of sums starts with wartime disability pay.
plaw-112-54-2011:
Business travel across the Pacific is the focus of Public Law 112-54, passed by the 112th Congress in 2011. Its short title is the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Business Travel Cards Act of 2011. The act lets the Homeland Security Secretary set up a card program. The Secretary of State works with Homeland Security on it.

For seven years, ending September 30, 2018, the program may issue APEC Business Travel Cards. The cards go to people active in APEC business, such as business leaders and United States officials. A person must first be approved and in good standing in a trusted traveler program.
plaw-112-55-2011:
Public Law 112-55, the Consolidated and Further Continuing Appropriations Act, 2012, funds much of the government for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2012. The 112th Congress passed it in 2011. Its full title names the Departments of Agriculture, Commerce, Justice, Transportation, and Housing and Urban Development. Related programs are covered as well.

The act is split into four divisions. Section 4 of the contents gives a statement of appropriations. Division A covers farm, rural, and food and drug work. Division B covers commerce, justice, and science. Division C covers transportation and housing. Division D adds further continuing funds for 2012.
plaw-112-56-2011:
Three unlike parts share one act in Public Law 112-56 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. Title I is the Three Percent Withholding Repeal and Job Creation Act. It ends the 3 percent withholding on some payments that government bodies make to vendors. The act also changes how modified adjusted gross income is worked out.

That income change affects who can get certain health care programs. Title II is named VOW to Hire Heroes. Its first parts set up a retraining aid program for veterans. They also make the Defense Department's Transition Assistance Program a must for service members.
plaw-112-57-2011:
Peace Corps volunteer safety drives Public Law 112-57, the Kate Puzey Peace Corps Volunteer Protection Act of 2011. The 112th Congress amended the Peace Corps Act. The act calls for sexual assault risk-reduction and response training. It also calls for a sexual assault policy, an Office of Victim Advocacy, and a Sexual Assault Advisory Council.

New section 8A orders the training as part of what all volunteers get. The President must build and run full training on risk and response. As far as is workable, it must follow best practice in the field. Experts are consulted while the training is built, the sample notes.
plaw-112-58-2011: Two filing clocks pause for troops posted abroad under Public Law 112-58 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. It amends section 216 of the Immigration and Nationality Act. That section covers removing the conditional basis of permanent resident status. While a spouse serves abroad on active duty, the 90-day span to file the petition is tolled, or paused. The 90-day span for the personal interview is paused in the same way. Couples may still file during the service if they choose.
plaw-112-59-2011:
The Montford Point Marines receive the Congressional Gold Medal under Public Law 112-59 of the 112th Congress, passed in 2011. Section 1 sets out the facts behind the honor. On June 25, 1941, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8802. That order opened the Marine Corps to the first African-American enlistees.

The findings trace what came next. The first Black recruits trained at Camp Montford Point, near Jacksonville, North Carolina. Howard P. Perry of Charlotte was the first Black private to set foot there, on August 26, 1942. By April 1943, Black drill instructors led the platoons in training. Black Marines later landed on Iwo Jima.
plaw-112-6-2011: Public Law 112-6 is a joint resolution of the 112th Congress from 2011, called the Additional Continuing Appropriations Amendments, 2011. It amends the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011, which had kept the government funded for fiscal year 2011. The resolution moves the end date in section 106 to April 8, 2011. It also adds new sections that set specified rates for named accounts. One gives the Agricultural Research Service a rate of $1,135,501,000 for salaries and costs.
plaw-112-60-2011: A Woburn mail site gains a new name under Public Law 112-60, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011. The Postal Service site at 462 Washington Street in Woburn, Massachusetts, must be known as the Officer John Maguire Post Office. References to the site in federal laws, maps, rules, records, and other papers count as references to that name.
plaw-112-61-2011: Public Law 112-61, the America's Cup Act of 2011, helps the United States host the 34th America's Cup sailing races. The 112th Congress passed it so certain eligible vessels could take part in work tied to the contest. Section 2 defines the 34th America's Cup as the sailing races starting in 2011. They answer a challenge to the defending team from the United States. The term can also cover one more year of races if a United States club defends the cup well.
plaw-112-62-2011: Appeal deadlines in civil cases with federal parties are clarified by Public Law 112-62, the Appeal Time Clarification Act of 2011. Section 2 gives the findings. Most civil appeals allow 30 days to appeal. The span is 60 days for all parties when the United States is a party. Congress finds the 60 days should also apply when a party is a federal agency. The same holds for a federal officer or worker sued for acts tied to duty.
plaw-112-63-2011:
Public Law 112-63, enacted by the 112th Congress in 2011, bears the short title Federal Courts Jurisdiction and Venue Clarification Act of 2011. It amends title 28 of the United States Code to clear up the reach of the federal courts. Title I is called Jurisdictional Improvements. Title II is called Venue and Transfer Improvements.

Title I covers how resident aliens are treated. It also covers the citizenship of firms and insurers with foreign ties, plus removal and remand steps. Title II covers venue in general, repeals section 1392, and covers change of venue. Each title ends with its own start date.
plaw-112-64-2011: Public Law 112-64, passed in 2011 by the 112th Congress, is the National Guard and Reservist Debt Relief Extension Act of 2011. It deals with the chapter 7 bankruptcy means test. Qualifying Guard members and reservists called to active duty or homeland defense for at least 90 days after September 11, 2001, are exempt from the abuse presumption. The act changes one word pair in the 2008 act behind the relief. It strikes 3-year and inserts 7-year, which adds four more years to the shield.
plaw-112-65-2011: Membership rules for Blue Star Mothers of America change under Public Law 112-65, a 2011 act of the 112th Congress. The act revises the group's federal charter in section 30504 of title 36. A mother now means a woman who filled the role of birth, adoptive, step, or foster mother, grandmother, or legal guardian. The old limit tied to World War II or the Korean hostilities is struck. A United States citizen living outside the country can also qualify.
plaw-112-66-2011: Public Law 112-66, approved by the 112th Congress in 2011, adds one power to the American Legion's federal charter. Section 21704 of title 36 gains a new fifth power. The Legion may give guidance and leadership to groups and local chapters set up under the charter. The same clause bars the Legion from control of those groups. It may not shape their specific acts and conduct either. The rest of the act only renumbers the powers that follow.
plaw-112-67-2011: One date changes in Public Law 112-67, a joint resolution of the 112th Congress approved on December 16, 2011. The resolution amends the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2012, which is Public Law 112-36. It strikes the date in section 106 and inserts December 17, 2011. That one-day move kept federal funding in place for fiscal year 2012. Both chambers passed the resolution on the day it was approved.
plaw-112-68-2011: Public Law 112-68 is a joint resolution of the 112th Congress, approved on December 17, 2011. It makes one change to the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2012, which is Public Law 112-36. The date in section 106 is struck and December 23, 2011, takes its place. The swap kept short-term funding for fiscal year 2012 in force for six more days. The House passed it on December 16 and the Senate a day later.
plaw-112-69-2011: Leasing park land to river pilots is allowed by Public Law 112-69, the Fort Pulaski National Monument Lease Authorization Act. The 112th Congress passed it in 2011. The Interior Secretary may lease land inside Fort Pulaski National Monument to the Savannah Bar Pilots Association, or a group that takes its place. The lease caps at 30,000 square feet of land and buildings. The site sits on Cockspur Island, where the group has worked since 1940. Rent must rest on fair market value.
plaw-112-7-2011: Airport funding gets a short stay under Public Law 112-7, the Airport and Airway Extension Act of 2011. The 112th Congress amended the tax code to stretch the Airport and Airway Trust Fund. Fuel taxes and ticket taxes were set to end on March 31, 2011. Section 2 moves each of those end dates to May 31, 2011. The changes take effect on April 1, 2011. The act also extends the airport improvement program in title 49, as its opening line states.
plaw-112-70-2011: Public Law 112-70, the Box Elder Utah Land Conveyance Act, hands federal land to a small Utah town. The 112th Congress passed it in 2011. The land is about 31.5 acres of National Forest System land in Box Elder County. A map dated June 23, 2011, shows the ground as parcels A, B, and C. If the town of Mantua asks within one year, the Agriculture Secretary must convey all federal rights in the land. The town pays nothing, and the deed is a quitclaim deed.
plaw-112-71-2011: Congress consents to a two-state deal change in Public Law 112-71, a joint resolution of the 112th Congress from 2011. Missouri and Illinois had amended their compact on the Bi-State Development Agency. The change lets bonds from that agency mature in up to 40 years. Section 1 gives consent to the state acts behind the change, one from each state in 2010. The change takes effect on the day the resolution passed. Congress keeps its right to alter or repeal the consent.
plaw-112-72-2011: Hoover Dam power shares are reset by Public Law 112-72, the Hoover Power Allocation Act of 2011. The 112th Congress passed it to further allocate dam power and widen who can get it. Section 2 amends the Hoover Power Plant Act of 1984. It strikes the word renewal and moves a key date from June 1, 1987, to October 1, 2017. It then inserts a new Schedule A. The schedule lists each contractor with summer and winter capacity and firm energy sums.
plaw-112-73-2011: Public Law 112-73, the Civilian Service Recognition Act of 2011, honors federal civilian staff who die from job-linked harm. The 112th Congress passed it in 2011. An agency head may give a United States flag for a worker who dies of harm tied to federal work. The harm must stem from a crime, an act of terrorism, a natural disaster, or a like cause set by the President. A request must come first, from kin such as a spouse or child.
plaw-112-74-2011:
Public Law 112-74, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2012, is the big year-end spending act of the 112th Congress. It was approved on December 23, 2011. The contents list shows Division A as the Department of Defense Appropriations Act, 2012. That division has nine titles, from military personnel and upkeep to overseas contingency operations.

Division B is the Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act, 2012. Its first titles cover the Corps of Engineers, the Interior Department, and the Energy Department. The act sets how its funds may be used and how long they last. The sample ends part-way through the contents list.
plaw-112-75-2011: Public Law 112-75, passed in 2011 by the 112th Congress, renews the law behind the United States Commission on International Religious Freedom. Its long short title adds the words Reform and Reauthorization to that body's name. It reauthorizes the International Religious Freedom Act of 1998. Section 2 then rewrites the term rules in that act. Each member now serves a 2-year term. No person may serve more than 2 terms in any case, even if first named before this act.
plaw-112-76-2011:
Gold medals for the dead of September 11 are ordered by Public Law 112-76, the Fallen Heroes of 9/11 Act. The 112th Congress passed it in 2011. It awards Congressional Gold Medals to honor the men and women who died in the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. The findings name the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania.

Congress finds those deaths changed the nation for good. It praises the officers, emergency workers, and staff who rushed to the World Trade Center and died there. It gives the same praise to those who answered the attack on the Pentagon.
plaw-112-77-2011:
Disaster aid for fiscal year 2012 is funded by Public Law 112-77, the Disaster Relief Appropriations Act, 2012. The 112th Congress approved it on December 23, 2011. Title I is headed Disaster Relief. Its first account adds money to the Disaster Relief Fund of the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The sum is $6,400,000,000, left open until spent.

The fund pays for major disasters declared under the Stafford Act. The act names that sum as disaster relief under a 1985 budget law. Next, the Army Corps of Engineers gets added funds for the Mississippi River and Tributaries account. Those funds pay to repair harm, though the sample cuts off mid-line.
plaw-112-78-2011:
Public Law 112-78, the Temporary Payroll Tax Cut Continuation Act of 2011, keeps several short-term policies alive. The 112th Congress passed it in late 2011. Title I extends the payroll tax holiday. Title II extends unemployment pay rules for a short span. It also covers extended jobless aid under the Railroad Unemployment Insurance Act.

Title III extends health rules for a short span. It sets a Medicare physician payment update and a two-month stay for some hospital class rules. The act's own head note adds one more charge. It also provides for review of the Keystone XL pipeline.
plaw-112-79-2011: Public Law 112-79, the Sugar Loaf Fire Protection District Land Exchange Act of 2011, swaps land in Colorado. The 112th Congress passed it for land in the Arapaho-Roosevelt National Forests. The district in the act is the Sugar Loaf Fire Protection District of Boulder, Colorado. Federal land means two parcels shown on maps dated November 12, 2009. One parcel runs about 1.52 acres. The other runs about 3.56 acres. The sample stops as the act starts to define the national forest.
plaw-112-8-2011: Public Law 112-8 is an act of the 112th Congress from April 2011, called the Further Additional Continuing Appropriations Amendments, 2011. It amends the Continuing Appropriations Act, 2011. The end date in section 106 moves to April 15, 2011. New sections then set specified rates for named accounts. One gives $9,800,000 for Transportation planning and research. A second gives $2,927,500,000 for Federal Aviation Administration facilities and equipment. The sample ends as more rates are listed.
plaw-112-80-2011: One year changes in Public Law 112-80, a 2011 act of the 112th Congress on a charity stamp. The act amends title 39 of the United States Code. It extends the Postal Service's power to issue a semipostal that raises funds for breast cancer research. A semipostal is a stamp sold above face value for a cause. Section 414(h) had set the end year as 2011. The act strikes that year and inserts 2015.
plaw-112-81-2011:
Public Law 112-81, approved on December 31, 2011, is the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2012. The 112th Congress used it to back spending for military work of the Defense Department. It also covers military building and defense work of the Energy Department. The act sets troop strength levels for that year as well.

Section 2 splits the act into five divisions. Division A covers Defense Department grants of power, and Division B covers military building. Division C covers Energy Department national security work. Division D holds the funding tables. Division E renews the SBIR and STTR programs.
plaw-112-9-2011:
A long short title about 1099 taxpayer protection heads Public Law 112-9 of the 112th Congress, passed in April 2011. Its main work is a repeal. Congress had widened the reporting rules for payments of $600 or more. The wider rules reached payments made to firms. They also reached payments for property and other gross proceeds.

Section 2 strikes those added parts of section 6041 of the tax code. The repeal applies to payments made after December 31, 2011. Section 3 starts a second repeal, on reporting by landlords. The sample cuts off before that section's text begins. The act was approved on April 14, 2011.
plos-pbio-0020211:
Juergen Tautz, Shaowu Zhang, Johannes Spaethe, and their team tested how honeybees judge distance in PLOS Biology in 2004. Bees tell nestmates how far food is through their waggle dance. To do that, a bee must measure the trip, a skill called odometry, based on how the world streams past its eyes.

The team flew bees over varied ground and watched how their estimates changed. Rough, rich scenery made trips feel longer than smooth ground did. That fits an eye-flow measure rather than energy spent. The study shows a tiny brain solving a navigation task with a simple, robust rule, a result that interests both biologists and robot designers.
plos-pone-0000011:
Matthew Falagas, Konstantinos Fragoulis, and Ioannis Karydis compared drug prices across medicine in a 2006 PLOS ONE study. New antibiotics draw special worry: bacteria keep evolving resistance, so fresh ones are badly needed, yet firms say developing them pays poorly. The authors asked whether new antibiotics actually cost more than new drugs in other fields.

They set the price of new antibiotics beside drugs from other therapeutic categories, from heart medicine to cancer care. Price gaps, where they exist, feed the debate over why so few antibiotics reach the market. The comparison gives policy makers a factual base for arguments about incentives, patents, and the true cost of staying ahead of resistant germs.
plos-pone-0000111:
Donatella Bulone, Laura Masino, David J. Thomas, and their team studied protein clumping in PLOS ONE in 2006. Stretches of repeated glutamine, called polyQ, appear in several brain disease proteins, like the one in Huntington's disease. The longer the stretch, the more readily the protein clumps into toxic fibers.

The authors show the protein around the stretch matters as much as the stretch itself. The right context can delay clumping by holding the protein in a store of early, loose clumps called protofibrils. That delay changes how the disease clock might run. It also suggests a therapy idea: stabilize the harmless store, and the toxic fibers may never form.
plos-pone-0000211:
José M. Pérez, Iván L. Calderón, Felipe A. Arenas, and colleagues published this microbiology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Potassium tellurite is a compound long known to poison bacteria, used for over a century to select them in the lab. Yet why it kills was an old puzzle, an ancient enigma, as the title says. The authors work on how tellurite harms bacterial cells.

Tellurite still appears in microbiology labs and in some industrial settings. Pinning down its toxic mechanism explains both its killing power and how some bacteria resist it. The paper brings modern molecular tools to a question that dates back to the early days of bacteriology.
plos-pone-0000311:
Victor Frak, Isabelle Croteau, Daniel Bourbonnais, and colleagues published this motor control study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Prehension is the act of reaching and grasping. The authors report that merely simulating a grasp, imagining or preparing the action, modifies actual prehension. This is evidence that the brain represents an object's graspable features together with the action of grasping it.

Mind and hand share one representation, in this account. That joint coding explains why thinking about a grip changes the grip itself. The finding matters for rehabilitation and for understanding how the brain plans skilled movements.
plos-pone-0000411:
Patrick Peretti-Watel and colleagues examined how stigma against people with HIV may feed the epidemic in France, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Discrimination can push people to hide their status, avoid testing, or skip care. The team gathered evidence on how common such discrimination is and how it connects to the spread of HIV.

If fear of mistreatment keeps people from knowing or sharing their status, the virus gains room to spread unseen. Documenting that chain matters for policy: fighting stigma becomes part of fighting the epidemic itself, alongside medicine. The study grounds that argument in French survey and social evidence rather than assumption.
plos-pone-0000511:
Christopher B. Guest and colleagues studied how diabetes changes the way immune cells swallow fat, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. In artery walls, cells called macrophages gorge on stored cholesterol, known as cholesteryl ester. They swell into the foam cells of artery plaques. The team found this fat swallowing is turned up in macrophages from diabetic mice.

Two surface sensors, CD36 and SR-A, do most of the swallowing. Diabetes sharply raises heart disease risk, and fat-stuffed artery cells are a strong suspect link. Naming the sensors that do the work gives drug makers clear targets. The study ties a whole-body disease to a cell's appetite, tested one sensor at a time.
plos-pone-0000611:
Bernhard Voelkl and Ludwig Huber tested what monkey imitation really copies, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Marmoset monkeys watched a demonstrator perform a novel technique to get food. The team examined imitation as faithful copying of the novel technique: whether the observers reproduced the method itself, not just the result.

True imitation, copying actions rather than outcomes, is a milestone in the evolution of learning and culture. Marmosets are cooperative breeders with rich social lives, a promising place to look for it. Careful tests matter because animals often appear to imitate while actually using simpler tricks, and telling the difference defines what social learning means.
plos-pone-0000711:
John F. Bruno and Elizabeth R. Selig measured how coral cover has declined across the Indo-Pacific, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Many factors had recently caused mass coral deaths in all the world's tropical oceans. Yet little was known about the timing, rate, or spatial variability of the loss. The Indo-Pacific holds a major share of the world's reef-building corals.

The authors set the region's figure at 75 percent of the world's reef-building coral territory, making its trend the global story. Their analysis covers timing, extent, and comparisons between subregions. A firm baseline matters for conservation: without knowing how fast cover fell, no one can tell whether protection is working.
plos-pone-0000811:
Sanjay Chandriani and Don Ganem sorted the host's responses during aggressive infection by a cancer-linked herpesvirus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Lytic infection by Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus brings an extensive shutoff of host gene expression. The shutoff runs chiefly through accelerated messenger RNA turnover, driven by the viral SOX protein, which destroys host messages. A small number of host mRNAs had previously been found to escape or rise.

By measuring host transcript accumulation during infection, the authors reveal several classes of host responses. Some genes resist the shutoff, others are actively induced. Those classes point to defenses the cell mounts, and to host factors the virus cannot do without.
plos-pone-0000911:
Stephen Proulx, Sergey Nuzhdin and Daniel Promislow looked for direct selection on genetic robustness in yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Theory says living things should evolve ways to keep a healthy form despite shocks from outside or from their own mutations. Several routes to that steadiness were already known.

What was missing was proof that selection acts on robustness itself, not just on traits it protects. Reading the yeast transcriptome, the full set of active genes, the authors argue the signature is there. The claim matters for how we think traits stay stable over generations. It also bears on why some mutations stay hidden until stress reveals them.
plos-pone-0001011:
Joachim Goedhart, Joop Vermeer, Merel Adjobo-Hermans and colleagues built new glowing protein pairs to detect a doubled immune factor, in PLOS ONE in 2007. FRET is a technique where one glowing protein passes energy to another when they sit very close. The classic pair uses blue and yellow green fluorescent proteins.

Newer red shifted proteins could work better, with less background. The team built FRET couples from them and used the pairs to detect homodimers of p65, two copies of an immune control protein joined together. Better probes mean cleaner live cell images of proteins meeting. That feeds many fields at once.
plos-pone-0001111:
Matthew Witt and Brendan Godley used ship tracking data to map fishing at sea scale, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Saving marine ecosystems needs a full picture of fisheries alongside maps of biodiversity. The UK government's vessel monitoring system tracks large UK registered fishing vessels by satellite.

Witt and Godley investigate patterns of fishing activity in that data. Knowing where effort concentrates, season by season, is the base layer for seascape scale conservation, protecting whole seascapes rather than single spots. Fishing maps also expose where protected areas would bite and where they would merely displace boats. The paper shows a surveillance system doubling as a science tool.
plos-pone-0001211:
Growing tissues in three dimensions, rather than as flat layers, is a goal of tissue engineering. Takuya Matsumoto and colleagues demonstrated a patterning method in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Their system uses a strained fibrin gel, a gel made from a blood-clotting protein, pulled so its fibers align.

The authors show three-dimensional cell and tissue patterning in the strained gel. Cells placed in such a scaffold can be guided into organized arrangements that mimic real tissue. Techniques like this are valuable both for studying how cells behave in tissues and for building cell and matrix composites for repair.
plos-pone-0001311:
In regions where malaria is seasonal, some people carry the parasite at very low levels. The levels are too low to see under a microscope. Those hidden infections can restart transmission. Badria El-Sayed and colleagues ran a randomized, open-label trial in eastern Sudan, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Treating these symptom-free carriers could be a useful way to control malaria.

The trial compared artesunate plus sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine with the same regimen plus primaquine. The goal was to clear sub-microscopic P. falciparum infections and gametocyte carriage. Gametocytes are the parasite stage mosquitoes pick up. Their comparison tests whether adding primaquine clears the reservoir better.
plos-pone-0001411:
Jairam Lingappa and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on couples where one partner has HIV and the other does not. Most HIV spread in Africa occurs in such couples, who often do not know their state. These couples face a high rate of new infection. The team mapped how common such couples are by region.

They also tracked how many joined a trial of ways to block spread. Rates of mixed state couples varied a lot from place to place. That spread shapes where trials and care will do the most good. The data help aim scarce funds at the couples and regions at highest risk.
plos-pone-0001511:
Guido Michels and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the heart's pacemaker current. A set of channels drives the steady beat of the heart. Those channels were thought to have helper proteins that tune them, but few helpers were known. The team tested one such helper, called KCR1, in heart cells.

They show KCR1 curbs the pacemaker current and so slows heart rhythm. A brake on the beat is as vital as the drive itself. Faults in such brakes could underlie rhythm ills that now lack a cause. The work names a fresh target for rhythm drug research.
plos-pone-0001611:
Laura Wilding Crawford and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on pancreas shape faults in mice. A decade of work had named many factors that build the pancreas. Yet how its islets, the insulin hubs, take their right shape was still not known. The team read gene use in a mouse model where islet shape goes wrong.

Their gene lists flag paths that steer islet form as it grows. Faults in shape can blunt insulin release even when cells are present. That makes shape a real part of diabetes, not a side note. The lists give labs set leads for the next round of mouse tests.
plos-pone-0001711:
Ben Lopman and Simon Gregson reconstructed the history of HIV in Harare, Zimbabwe, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. HIV prevalence there had recently begun to fall, driven by high AIDS mortality and fewer new infections. To understand that turn, officials need to know when new infections, or incidence, peaked, and that date cannot be observed directly.

The authors used back-calculation, working backward from mortality statistics to infer past incidence. The full text gives the death data, the model, and their estimate of the peak year. Dating the peak helps judge which prevention efforts and behavior changes actually bent the epidemic's curve in one of the countries hit hardest by HIV.
plos-pone-0001811:
Laura D. Mydlarz, Sally F. Holthouse, Esther C. Peters, and their co-authors studied immune cells in sea fan corals in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Climate warming is making marine and land organisms, and even humans, more susceptible to emerging diseases. Coral reefs are among the ecosystems most impacted by climate stress, and coral immunity is ancient, inherited from the earliest multicellular animals.

The team examined granular amoebocytes, coral immune cells, and how they react to pathogen and climate stressors. The full text gives the cell responses under each stress. Knowing how coral defenders behave under heat and infection may help predict reef die-offs and protect the species that respond best.
plos-pone-0001911:
Ningli Cheng and co-authors tested how three genes interact in blood cancer in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. One gene, Bcl-2, can slow cell death, which can help cancer grow, yet in some settings it slows cancer instead. A second gene, p27, acts as a brake on cell division, and a third, Bax, pushes cells to die.

The team bred mice lacking the p27 brake, with or without changes in the other two genes, and watched for T-cell lymphoma. As the title states, loss of p27 teamed with Bcl-2 to drive the cancer, but not with Bax. Gene pairs, not single genes, set the risk here.
plos-pone-0002011:
Christian Voigt and co-authors asked why Amazon bats visit mineral licks, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Many tropical animals in Africa, Asia, and South America trek to salt or mineral licks to eat clay or drink clay-rich water. Two ideas compete: the clay adds scarce nutrients to the diet, or it soaks up plant toxins the animals eat.

The team studied bats of the Amazon rainforest that visit such licks. Food or detox: each idea makes unlike predictions about which bats come and when. Settling the question explains a striking habit and what it says about nutrient limits in rainforest food webs.
plos-pone-0002111:
Dennis Hansen, Christopher Kaiser, and Christine Muller applied a classic ecology model to endangered island plants, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The Janzen-Connell model states that plant-specific enemies, such as seed-eating pests, hit offspring hardest close to the mother tree. Most past tests asked how the model explains diversity in rich forests.

The trio turn it to a practical aim: seed dispersal and establishment of endangered plants on oceanic islands. They also discuss ecological analogues, stand-in species that can take the role of extinct seed carriers. Old theory, put to work for conservation on islands that have lost their dispersers.
plos-pone-0002211:
Wook Kim and co-authors checked whether common mitochondrial lineages raise prostate cancer risk in Korean men, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited from the mother and does not shuffle between generations, so its lineages, called haplogroups, are clean markers of ancestry. Some studies had hinted that mitochondrial variation might link to cancers, including prostate cancer.

The team compared haplogroups between patients and healthy men in the Korean population. They found no association between the common lineages and prostate cancer. A solid negative answer still helps, since it tells future studies to look elsewhere for the genetic roots of this cancer.
plos-pone-0002311:
Chris Paffen, Marnix Naber, and Frans Verstraten asked where in the brain a visual flip begins, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In binocular rivalry, the two eyes receive different images at the same spot. Perception alternates: only one image is seen at a time, then it switches. The phenomenon is a clean tool for studying how conscious perception is selected.

The team traced the spatial origin of a perceptual transition, the moment one image gives way to the other. Finding where the switch starts helps decide whether rivalry is settled in early visual areas or by higher decision centers. The answer bears on how the brain resolves any conflicting input.
plos-pone-0002411:
Ross-Ibarra and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Jeffrey Ross-Ibarra, Stephen I. Wright, John Paul Foxe, among others. Its subject is patterns of Polymorphism and Demographic History in Natural Populations of Arabidopsis lyrata. Many of the processes affecting genetic diversity act on local populations.

However, studies of plant nucleotide diversity have largely ignored local sampling. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002511:
Hadjantonakis joined co-authors to publish a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. Named on the byline are Anna-Katerina Hadjantonakis, Elinor Pisano, Virginia E. Papaioannou, among others. Its subject is tbx6 Regulates Left/Right Patterning in Mouse Embryos through Effects on Nodal Cilia and Perinodal Signaling. The determination of left/right body axis during early embryogenesis sets up a developmental cascade that coordinates the development of the viscera.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002611:
Kitamura led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Masahiro Kitamura, Keisuke Nakashima, Yusuke Kowashi, among others. Its subject is periodontal Tissue Regeneration Using Fibroblast Growth Factor -2: Randomized Controlled Phase II Clinical Trial. The options for medical use of signaling molecules as stimulators of tissue regeneration are currently limited.

Preclinical evidence suggests that fibroblast growth factor (FGF)-2 can promote periodontal regeneration. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002711:
Ellen Kreijveld and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was immunological monitoring of renal transplant recipients to predict acute allograft rejection following the discontinuation of tacrolimus. Authorship is credited in the record to Ellen Kreijveld and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.
