Md Mehedi Hasan and colleagues describe CLIN-LLM, a diagnostic support system designed to be cautious where ordinary chatbots are reckless. Their 2026 framework reads a patient's symptoms and vital signs, names likely diseases with a stated confidence level, and drafts treatment suggestions grounded in real doctor-patient dialogues rather than free invention.

Cases the system finds uncertain, about one in five, are automatically routed to a human expert. Built-in checks screen antibiotics and dangerous drug combinations. In tests the system classified diseases from text with high accuracy and cut unsafe antibiotic suggestions sharply compared with a leading general chatbot, while clinicians rated its treatment drafts sound. The team targets clinics with few specialists, where guarded automation could help most.
plos-pone-0348811:
Jabia Mostofa Chowdhury builds a three-dimensional computer model of how an eye drug spreads and fades after injection into the gel of the human eye. The drug blocks abnormal vessel growth in wet macular disease, but human measurements inside the eye are scarce. The 2026 model tracks flow and diffusion under four body scenarios, varying gel state and exit routes for the drug.

Predicted drug lifetimes inside the eye ran from under three days to over four, matching the broad range reported in people. Levels near the macula, the drug's target, could be checked against the floor needed to suppress vessel growth. A tested model like this can explore dosing schedules on a screen instead of in patients' eyes.
plos-pone-0349011:
Roman Holík and colleagues ran a twelve-week jump training trial in thirty-seven young male footballers aged ten to eighteen, asking whether growing bodies at different maturity stages respond differently. Players were sorted by a standard maturity estimate into before and after their growth spurt, then assigned by chance to twice-weekly plyometric sessions or normal training. Speed, agility, jumps, and leg stiffness were tested before and after.

Jump training improved sprinting in both maturity groups, and it alone lifted broad jump and single-leg triple jump, while leg stiffness rose in trainees and sagged in the older control players. Agility improved everywhere regardless of group. Formally, maturity never changed the training effect. The authors endorse jump training across adolescence for speed and explosive power, without needing to time it around the growth spurt.
plos-pone-0349111:
John Owuoth and colleagues measured how often HIV spread among young adults at high risk in Kisumu County, western Kenya, where infection rates run far above the national average. They enrolled six hundred nineteen HIV-negative adults aged eighteen to thirty-five who reported multiple recent partners, many from fishing villages. Participants were tested every three months for up to two years.

Eleven new infections appeared during the follow-up, giving an incidence just under one per hundred person-years, with most infections in the first year. Comparing those who did and did not acquire HIV pointed to risk factors prevention programs can target. Local incidence numbers like these tell health teams whether their efforts are reaching the right people.
plos-pone-0349211:
Jonas Rusnak and colleagues tested whether the drug bulevirtide, which blocks a bile acid transporter in the liver, changes artery disease in mice. They used mice bred to develop atherosclerosis, fed a Western-style diet. Groups received bulevirtide, rifampicin, both drugs, or no drug for four weeks.

Both drugs raised bile acid levels in the blood, and the combination raised them most. Yet cholesterol, other blood fats, plaque size in the aorta, and immune cell content in plaques did not change. The result separates two ideas: raising bile acids in blood is not, by itself, enough to shrink artery plaques in this model.
plos-pone-0349311:
Gabriel Laporta and colleagues studied how deforestation changes infection in the palm-dwelling insects that carry Chagas disease in the southwestern Brazilian Amazon. These triatomine bugs live in palm crowns and harbor the Chagas parasite and a harmless relative. Field teams surveyed twenty landscape units in 2022 and 2024, collecting bugs from palms at measured distances from homes, with forest cover mapped by drones and satellites.

The two parasites answered the landscape differently. The Chagas parasite became more likely as forest cover fell and homes came closer, while its relative followed a contrasting pattern. The result connects land policy to disease risk in a direct way: clearing forest near houses appears to raise the odds that the insects near people carry the dangerous parasite.
plos-pone-0349411:
Shima Rezaei and co-authors followed tomato plants in fish-based growing systems over two years to learn why some plants wilt and die. In these aquaponic setups, fish waste feeds the plants, but sludge can build up around roots and starve them of oxygen. During the first year, coupled systems with poor drainage lost about a fifth of their yield to wilt.

Adding settling tanks and timed pumps fixed the flow, and coupled systems then outyielded the separated ones by a wide margin. Some wilting remained, and sick roots held far less oxygen plus more microbes linked to root disease, while healthy roots carried helpful bacteria. Keeping roots oxygen-rich emerges as the central lesson for long-running systems.
plos-pone-0349511:
Kukiat Tudpor and a team of researchers fed a powder made from partly defatted house crickets to rats bred to have high blood pressure, asking whether the food could protect their bones. Fourteen female rats took the powder daily for four weeks or received a plain substitute, after which their thigh bones were scanned and bent until they flexed to test strength.

Treated rats kept stronger bones than controls, withstanding more force before giving way, even though the inner structure of the bone looked unchanged. Their blood pressure also rose less over the month than that of untreated rats. Cricket powder is rich in protein and minerals, and the results hint it may support bone strength where high blood pressure and weak bones occur together.
plos-pone-0349611:
Toshiko Furukawa and Takuya Iimura built a mathematical model of one of nature's classic trades. Legume plants give carbon to Rhizobium bacteria in their roots, and the bacteria return nitrogen the plant cannot capture alone. Their model adds a strict energy budget, since every exchange costs ATP, the cell's energy currency, and any imbalance is settled by changing bacterial biomass.

Using measured energy costs and the carbon-to-nitrogen ratios of both partners, the model makes three predictions that match real observations. Among them, the plant supplies relatively little carbon while the bacteria supply generous nitrogen, and the shares shift predictably as each partner's body ratio changes. The model explains why this trade stays fair enough to persist.
plos-pone-0350011:
Tuodi Zhang, Songtao Shen, and Yingyi Xu optimized a hybrid system that cleans rural sewage while generating a trickle of electricity: a planted wetland wired as a microbial fuel cell. Winter cold makes rural treatment harder, and electrode settings decide performance. Their 2026 study tuned three electrode parameters statistically for a reed-planted vertical-flow system treating village wastewater.

The hybrid beat a plain wetland clearly. The plain system's outflow missed China's strictest rural discharge limit for organic pollution, while every hybrid configuration met it. At the best settings, the system removed about eighty-nine percent of the pollution load, matching the model's prediction closely. The authors present the tuning recipe as guidance for decentralized village sewage treatment in cold seasons.
plos-pone-0350111:
Nicholas O. Schulte and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on squeezing the most species from seawater DNA sampling without overspending. At an intertidal site off Point Conception, California, they compared two filter types, large capsules and small syringe discs, under one lab workflow. Gene markers stood in for vertebrates and for broader animal and plankton life. Each filter's DNA was copied ten times, to ask whether more copies or more samples find more species.

Discs found more vertebrate species than capsules at every comparison level, partly because the workflow processed a smaller effective share of each capsule's larger extract. For the broader marker, the filters performed about equally. Adding copies of one sample accumulated species about as well as adding fresh field samples along their uniform shoreline. Pooling copies worked too. Cheaper, simpler filtration, they conclude, can match or beat pricier setups when the workflow is held constant.
plos-pone-0350611:
O'Shea and colleagues set out a study plan in 2026 on heat, aging, and Alzheimer's disease in South Florida. Five hundred adults aged fifty and older will have their home addresses linked to satellite heat maps. The team will test recent and long-term heat exposure against thinking scores, blood markers, and brain scans.

Heat may also act through inactivity, isolation, and inflammation, which the study will measure. Tree cover near homes will be checked as a possible shield. If neighborhood heat truly tracks brain decline, planting and cooling plans become health policy, especially for older adults in fast-warming cities.
plos-pone-0350811:
Xuejin Ye and co-authors studied a simple blood index in intensive care patients with acute kidney injury in 2026. The index multiplies white cell count by blood sugar, joining two signs of stress and inflammation, and the team asked whether it predicts death.

They drew on two large hospital databases covering more than one hundred thousand admissions. Patients in the highest quarter of the index died more often at one and three months than those in the lowest. The link held after adjusting for other risks and across patient groups. A cheap index from routine tests could help flag kidney patients in danger early.
plos-pone-0351011:
Adanze Nge Cynthia and colleagues mapped what helps and what blocks health care for migrants from Sub-Saharan Africa living in Europe. Fourteen studies passed their checks after searches of five large databases. Most used interviews and close observation. Themes were drawn out by sorting findings across studies rather than counting visits alone.

Three big themes stood out. Gaps in insurance, shaky legal status, and heavy paperwork blocked care in study after study. Undocumented people, women, and people living with HIV faced layered risks. Language gaps and poor cultural fit added further strain. Only one study focused on ageing and long term care choices, a blind spot as these communities grow older in Europe.
plos-pone-0351111:
Mingqiang Wang simulates how railway fasteners muffle inspection sound waves in this 2026 study. Ultrasonic guided waves can scan long stretches of rail for hidden cracks. They travel the full cross-section as they go. Real rails, though, are clamped down by fastener systems. Those clamps bleed wave energy and shorten the inspection range. Wang built a three-dimensional model coupling the fastener's static grip with the wave's fleeting dynamics. A standard preload force squeezed the fasteners in the simulation.

Comparisons were stark. Fastened rail lost wave energy far faster than free rail. Stress maps showed where the clamping concentrated force. Two mathematical styles of modelling the contact were also tested against each other. For rail operators, the physics sets realistic expectations: inspection systems must be calibrated for fastened track, not laboratory rail. Understanding exactly how the clamps drink the signal helps engineers place sensors and interpret echoes on working lines.
plos-pone-0351211:
Quan Zhou and colleagues used a large 2018 survey of healthy ageing in China to study older adults who live apart from their children. More than five thousand such empty nest elders, aged sixty and older, were included. Questions covered arm function, exercise habits, and thinking ability. About fifteen percent showed impaired thinking.

Limited arm function linked with higher odds of poor thinking, even after other factors were counted. Exercise sat in the middle of that link, carrying part of the effect: weak arms may cut activity, and less activity may dull thinking. Because data came from one point in time, cause cannot be proved. Keeping arms strong and daily activity up may still support the ageing mind.
plos-pone-0351311:
Rural officials need current maps of buildings to catch illegal construction and plan disaster response. Jingling Zhong and colleagues built a deep learning system that finds rural buildings in drone and satellite images despite tangled backgrounds, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Three ideas drive the system. Attention modules read buildings at several sizes while muting vegetation and shadow noise. A feature pyramid reroutes information so large and small buildings are both caught. And a learning strategy squeezes value from the few hand-labeled images available by mining the hardest examples. Wide experiments showed gains over standard detectors, offering village governments faster, cheaper mapping.
plos-pone-0351411:
Lingna Huang and colleagues studied women who had induced abortions at a large maternity hospital in Fujian, China. They compare patients from before and after the country adopted its three-child policy. Their 2026 study asks whether the policy changed why pregnancies were unintended and which contraceptive methods women had been using.

Hospital records cover one year on each side of the policy change. They show that not using contraception stayed the leading cause of unintended pregnancy, though its share fell. Among women who did use contraception, condoms and withdrawal remained the most common choices despite their higher failure rates. The authors conclude that little shifted in method choice, so health services still need to tackle non-use and reliance on weak methods.
plos-pone-0351511:
Rahme Nese Safakli and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on whether malaria drugs strain the heart's energy system, a safety question for mass drug campaigns. The team worked with human heart muscle cells grown from stem cells, tuned to resemble atrial tissue. They exposed the cells briefly and for longer periods to single malaria drugs and combinations, then measured how well the cells' mitochondria breathed.

Mefloquine, alone and in combinations, reduced mitochondrial respiration, signaling weaker energy production. Long exposure to halofantrine cut the cells' maximum breathing rate and their spare capacity. Four other standard malaria drugs left mitochondrial function intact at both time scales Ivermectin, an anti-parasite drug used in malaria programs, looked harmless briefly but reduced coupling efficiency over longer exposure. The pattern is presented as early safety evidence for treatment programs, with a call for work on the reasons behind the harmful cases.
plos-pone-0351911:
Shomaila Mehmood, Pankaj Bhatia, and Samson Jamesdaniel test a rescue for hearing threatened by chemotherapy, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Cisplatin saves lives, especially in children, but it permanently damages hearing in many patients, and only one preventive drug is approved, for children only. The team gave mice cisplatin alongside MnTBAP, a compound that mimics the body's own antioxidant enzymes, and then measured hearing with electrical and acoustic tests and inspected the inner ear's cells.

Cisplatin alone scarred the system: a damage marker rose in hearing cells and their nerve partners, both cell types died back in the cochlea's middle and base, and hearing thresholds climbed. With the antioxidant aboard, those changes were prevented: hearing sensitivity held, and the cellular damage reversed. The mouse evidence strengthens the case that oxidative chemistry drives this side effect, and that a mopping up drug might one day protect adult patients too.
plos-pone-0352111:
Jingmei Zhou and colleagues improved an animal-inspired search algorithm to sharpen indoor positioning by ultra-wideband radio, the technology behind precision tags in warehouses and hospitals. Walls bend and block the signals, and the standard first-guess method wobbles badly off line of sight. Their upgrade chains that first guess to a grey wolf optimizer toughened with chaotic scrambling, a smoother convergence curve, and shifting weights between exploration and focus.

In complex test environments the improved algorithm settled on the true position faster and landed closer than five rivals, including the standard methods and the unimproved wolf pack. Indoor positioning sounds minor until a robot, a dementia patient, or a forklift depends on it. Better math on the same radios means upgrades without new hardware on the walls.
plos-pone-0352311:
Caiyun Liu and colleagues pooled clinical trials to ask whether adding antibiotics helps treat peri-implantitis, an infection that eats at the bone around dental implants. The usual first step is a deep mechanical cleaning of the implant surface. They searched major databases and combined twenty-two randomized trials comparing cleaning plus antibiotics with other care.

Across the trials, adding antibiotics improved several gum measures, including shallower pockets, better attachment, and less bleeding and plaque. The gains over cleaning with other add-ons were uneven, and the trials differed a lot from one another, which weakens certainty. Still, for dentists weighing whether the drugs are worth it, the pooled evidence leans toward a real, modest benefit on top of thorough cleaning.
plos-pone-0352511: Gu and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how power companies prepare for huge blackouts. Utilities keep a reserve fund and stock emergency gear, and the two choices trade off against each other. The team worked out a joint plan that sizes the fund and places resources together, for several kinds of large blackouts. Better joint planning could shorten the next big outage.
plos-pone-0352811:
Yukari Nakajima and three colleagues test whether two growth factors can speed wound healing. Their 2026 experiment used forty healthy laboratory mice. Each mouse received two circular full-thickness skin wounds. Injections near the wound delivered one growth factor, the other, or both together. A control group received plain saline. One factor targets blood vessel growth, the other lymphatic vessels. Healing was photographed and measured for fifteen days.

The honest headline is a null result. Wounds in every group healed almost identically. Neither factor, alone or combined, beat saline. Counts of new blood and lymphatic vessels inside the healing tissue also matched across groups. One detail did emerge. Larger collecting lymph vessels failed to regrow across wounds, while tiny capillary lymphatics did regenerate. Publishing clear negatives like this saves other laboratories from repeating an attractive but ineffective treatment idea.
plos-pone-0353111:
Llewellyn and colleagues set out a pilot trial plan in 2026 on home exercises for high blood pressure. The plan enrolls seventy treated adults in Newcastle, England, split between a home program and usual care. The home group will do wall squats, a still-hold exercise, three times weekly with remote supervision for twelve weeks, then continue with behavior support.

The pilot judges whether people join, stay, and find the program acceptable over twenty-four weeks. Blood pressure at the clinic and across the day will also be tracked. A workable home option could widen treatment choices for people who dislike gyms or drugs alone.
plos-pone-0353311:
Irvin and colleagues, in a 2026 study, work to improve polygenic risk scores for high blood pressure. Such scores add up many small genetic effects into one risk number, and they often perform unevenly across ancestry groups. The team compared two scoring methods and asked whether extra biological notes on each variant, and a fairer reference panel, could help.

Scores were tuned in a large stroke study with European American and African American participants, then tested in a second study of hypertension genetics. In European Americans, the improved approaches explained several times more risk than the standard setup. In African Americans, gains were real but smaller, so the gap between groups narrowed only partly. Adding notes on what each variant does, and using a reference panel drawn from multiple ancestries, both helped. The authors frame this as progress toward genetic risk tools that serve more than one population well.
plos-pone-0353511:
An editorial note from The PLOS One Editors in 2026 concerns a study comparing salmon availability for two killer whale groups in summer feeding areas. Readers should note this flag on the record. A reader had questioned how the findings were interpreted and how fully prey and feeding information was explained.

Editors followed up with the authors and sought advice from a board member skilled in population data. They concluded that the findings remain supported. The note adds context on earlier research, study limits, and why sites were chosen. It closes gaps in the published explanation rather than changing results, and it lets readers weigh the whale feeding claims with fuller information.
plos-pone-0353611:
Helen Sharp and four colleagues published this 2026 pilot trial for children whose behavior problems survived standard parent training. Their new therapy, RICAP, brings children into reflective work with parents. One hundred and five families first received the established Incredible Years program; children still above the clinical line were randomized to the new therapy or usual clinic care.

Eight months on, parents and teachers disagreed: teacher reports favored usual care on some measures. Sharp stresses the trial proves the two-stage design is feasible, and warns future trials to expect reporter differences.
plos-pone-0353911:
Wang and colleagues, in a 2026 experiment, measure how firefighters' fans clear smoke from a building with an awkward layout. Smoke destroys visibility fast and makes rooms unsurvivable, so crews use fans to push or pull air through openings. Their test space was a two-story structure with bent, non-linear halls joined by a stairwell.

Using harmless artificial smoke, the team compared blowing air in, sucking air out, and a combined push-pull setup, repeating each run several times. The combined mode cleared the space to near-full visibility fastest, cutting clearing time by about a quarter against blowing in and a third against sucking out. Even so, the combined gain fell short of what simply adding the two single effects would promise. The authors offer their numbers as a baseline for training and for clearing smoke after the flames are knocked down, not as a guide for raging fires.
plos-pone-0354311:
This entry is an Expression of Concern issued in 2026 by the editors of PLOS One, and it should be read as a warning label, not as research findings. It concerns an earlier article that claimed a small RNA called MiR-125b slows a pig virus by dampening an immune pathway. After publication, readers raised doubts about the methods and several figures.

The editors list the problems plainly. The test materials were designed from the wrong monkey species' sequences for the cells used. Panels in two figures appeared to overlap or repeat across different conditions, and one figure lacked a detectable background. Board members added that key checks were missing, including proof the treatment worked. The authors answered, supplied corrected versions of two figures and extra data files, and explained their image handling. The editors state they are issuing the notice because the core doubts about the experiments remain unresolved.
plos-pone-0354511:
Louis Tshimanga and co-authors present in 2026 a leaner design for outlining brain tumours in three dimensional scans. Transformer based models read global context well but demand heavy computing, which many labs lack. Their design keeps a standard convolutional encoder and pools a fixed small set of tokens from its feature maps, so token count no longer grows with image size.

On a major glioma challenge dataset the model matched a leading heavy rival on the standard overlap score while using far less memory, time, and parameters. Its attention maps also showed plainly where it looked. Easier training on modest hardware could widen who can develop such tools.
plos-pone-0354611:
Satwik Motaganahalli and co-authors present in 2026 a pilot trial plan on how long antibiotics should run for diabetic foot ulcers where a bedside probe touches bone. That finding suggests bone infection, but in low risk outpatients the test often overcalls it, and bone infection care is heavy. Patients without early X-ray signs will receive either a short or a standard longer course.

Main aims are feasibility and safety: recruitment, staying in the trial, sticking to the plan, harmful events, and hospital stays. Later X-rays and any need to restart treatment or operate add early clinical hints. Results will shape a larger trial on safer, shorter treatment.
plos-pone-0354711:
Yuxin Nong and seven colleagues follow nearly ten thousand people with diabetes in the UK Biobank to ask whether dirty air harms their smallest blood vessels, reporting in 2026. Microvascular complications, damage to eyes, kidneys, and nerves, are among diabetes' most disabling outcomes. The team linked long-term pollution exposure estimates to health records over a median follow-up of more than twelve years.

About one participant in five developed a microvascular complication, and those breathing the most polluted air faced clearly higher risk than those breathing the cleanest. The pattern held for both nitrogen dioxide and larger airborne particles and survived a battery of checks. Risk seemed to rise even at fairly low exposure and showed up early. The authors argue clean-air measures belong in diabetes prevention plans, not just lung health policy.
plos-pone-0354811:
Weixuan Wang, Junhui Wu, and Shaomei Shang published this 2026 analysis of chronic kidney disease in the world's oldest adults. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2021 database, they tracked cases, deaths, and lost healthy years for people aged seventy-five and over across more than two hundred countries, from 1990 to 2021.

Burden patterns differed widely by region and level of development, so a single global response fits poorly. Wang urges health systems facing fast population aging to tailor kidney screening and care to their own older residents, using this country-level map to place resources.
plos-pone-0355111:
Yuhong Xue and co-authors upgrade in 2026 a popular detection model to find cracks in road surfaces more reliably. Cracks vary in shape, hide in busy backgrounds, and need fine detail, so standard models miss many. Their version fuses normal and heat images early, uses a windmill shaped filter to pull crack features, and adds a wider viewing layer for large cracks.

On a cross border road damage dataset the upgraded model scored higher on accuracy and related measures than the original and other leading models. The authors present it as a dependable tool for automatic road inspection in smart transport systems.
plos-pone-0355211:
Khorshed Alam and co-authors tested brain-inspired computing for spotting intrusions on networks of small connected devices. Such devices cannot run heavy security software, so detection must be light. Their 2026 study built detectors on reservoir computing, where a fixed recurrent pool does most of the work and training stays minimal.

The team tried two reservoir designs on a recent dataset of well over a million network flows, covering many attack types. Both designs performed close to the standard deep learning models used for comparison. They did so while using far fewer computing resources. Alam and colleagues argue reservoir models deserve more attention as a fast, lean option for guarding device networks in real time.
plos-pone-0355411:
Lihui Zhou, Xiansheng Liu, and Shuai Jin build a forecasting model for the temperature of key components inside high-speed train electrical cabinets, in this 2026 study from China. A component running hot can signal overload, poor contact, or failing insulation, and catching the rise early prevents breakdowns and fires. The team assembled time-series data on component temperatures alongside environmental and operating conditions, then pitted a memory-based deep learning network against three established forecasting methods.

The deep network won on both accuracy and stability across standard error measures, tracking long trends and short swings in temperature alike. The authors also tuned its architecture and the length of history it reads, since those choices shaped performance. They present the model as reliable technical support for condition monitoring and early fault warning in equipment whose failure would strand a train.
plos-pone-0355611:
Ke Yang and colleagues present in 2026 a light computer vision system for reading codes engraved on surgical tools. Clear reading matters so each tool can be traced, yet shine off metal, blur, and faint marks make the codes hard to find. Their design adapts a text spotting network with a smaller backbone and adds modules for edge alignment and for focusing on useful channels.

On their own tool dataset the system scored highly and beat its base design by several points, while running fast with few parameters. It also did well on a public scene text set. Hospitals could use such a reader to track tools with less manual work.
plos-pone-0355711:
Arifa Qazi and Attaullah Memon work on a core problem in control engineering in this 2026 paper. Their problem is making a nonlinear system follow a desired reference and shrug off changing disturbances, without measuring everything inside it. Their design pairs a high-gain observer, which estimates the system's hidden states from its outputs, with a controller built on inverse optimal principles and a compensator that keeps steady-state error at zero.

The scheme is meant to keep the optimality and toughness of state-feedback control while working from realistic, partial measurements. The authors tested it in simulation on a nonlinear DC motor, a standard stand-in for real actuators. Against baseline controllers, their design showed stronger robustness and better transient behavior. They present it as a practical route to high-performance control in machines whose behavior refuses to stay simple and linear.
plos-pone-0356611:
Xuguang An, Jin Zhang, Xiaofei Hou, and Chenghao Yang describe a planned clinical trial of brain stimulation for depression that has resisted standard treatment, published as a study protocol in 2026. The trial will enroll seventy patients whose blood tests show raised inflammation, and will test a strong form of alternating current stimulation applied through the scalp.

Half the patients will receive real stimulation for four weeks and half a sham version, with neither patients nor raters knowing which. The team will track depression scores, response and remission rates, brain wave changes, and safety signals such as abnormal heart or brain activity. If stimulation helps this inflamed subgroup, it would support matching depression treatments to biology rather than trial and error.
plos-pone-0356811:
Ana Lúcia Nunes Diniz and colleagues traced childhood tuberculosis in Rio de Janeiro State from 2010 to 2023. They used national notification records. They also used a statistical method that finds the years where trends bend. Their 2026 analysis focused on cases in children and teenagers. It set the pattern against social indicators for the same years.

After earlier declines, reported incidence turned upward from 2020 through 2023. The sharpest rise came in children under five. This is the group most vulnerable to severe disease. The same years saw the state's development index slip. Inequality and infant deaths climbed. The authors cannot prove the social slide caused the tuberculosis rise. But they argue child-focused surveillance and outreach should strengthen when living conditions worsen.
plos-pone-0357011:
Arne Stolp and colleagues published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE introducing a new way to measure how political views slant people's judgment of evidence. Biased evaluation is often confused with simply holding a political position. Drawing on signal detection theory, a method from psychology, they built a scale that separates a person's accuracy at telling strong evidence from weak evidence from the pull of their ideology.

Two studies with German samples, covering climate and energy policy plus domestic security and migration, gave early support for the scale. Biased judgment turned out to be distinct from education and political knowledge, so it cannot be explained away as ignorance. It also showed some consistency across the two issue areas, suggesting a general habit rather than topic-specific reactions. In the German setting, the bias seemed tied more to social identity and values than to party loyalty alone.
plos-pone-0357311:
Negawo Lelissa and Tewodros Mulugeta published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on fake and watered-down farm chemicals in Ethiopia's Wolmera district, near Addis Ababa. As farming expands, demand for pesticides and fertilizers grows, and with it the market for adulterated products. The authors interviewed several hundred farmers, field agents, and cooperative workers about how common the problem is, what forms it takes, and what damage it does.

Respondents confirmed that adulterated products circulate in local markets, with herbicides, fungicides, and insecticides the most commonly faked. Dilution and under-filled packages were the tricks most often reported. Farmers described damaged crops, lost yields, and wasted money, and said the experience eroded their trust in farm chemicals generally. The authors call for a working regulation system, technology that can spot counterfeits, and real accountability for fraud along the supply chain.
plos-pone-0357411:
Kristina M Kokorelias leads a team of eight publishing the plan for a review of how compassion is defined in dementia caregiving research, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Compassion is praised constantly in care settings, yet researchers use the word loosely, blending it with empathy and emotional labor until it means almost anything. The planned scoping review will map empirical studies of unpaid family caregivers, asking how it, including self compassion, is framed, defined, and turned into measurable practice.

The protocol follows established scoping methods and reporting guidance, searching four major health and psychology databases. Qualitative, quantitative, and mixed studies all qualify, while purely theoretical pieces do not. The payoff the authors promise is a foundation: clear meanings on which future programs for exhausted family caregivers, and honest tools to measure whether those programs work, can finally be built. In a field running on goodwill, definitions are infrastructure.
plos-pone-0357611:
Siyi Song and colleagues test how fitness-themed social media posts affect young women in China, in a 2026 online experiment. Posts of this kind promise drive and discipline but often praise one narrow body shape. Earlier work focused mostly on Western users, so the team asked whether the same harms appear in a Chinese setting with different beauty norms.

More than four hundred women aged from the late teens to mid twenties viewed exercise posts, thin-focused posts, or calm nature scenes. Both image sets lowered how much viewers valued their own bodies and what those bodies can do, with the thin-focused set doing the most harm. Song and co-authors urge readers and platforms to treat workout content as a possible risk, not pure motivation.
plos-pone-0357811:
Ali Shakhshir and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on appendicitis severity in Palestine, asking what can be learned from the removed appendix itself. Clinicians know the usual signs of complicated appendicitis, gangrenous or perforated, but the organ's gross measurements are rarely studied, and Palestinian data were missing. At a Jerusalem charitable hospital, the team reviewed a decade of appendectomies, keeping just over a thousand confirmed cases in four severity grades.

Many features differed across grades, from vomiting and operation length to white cell counts and hospital stay. In the adjusted model, one finding was expected: a hard fecal stone in the appendix more than doubled the odds of complicated disease. Another was not: higher white cell counts oddly went with lower odds. Age, sex, and a common inflammation marker showed no independent link. Overall prediction stayed weak, cautioning against reading severity off any single measure.
plos-pone-0357911: Borráz-León and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study with an odd mix: wealth, health, cats, and a parasite. Toxoplasma gondii is a common parasite often carried by cats. The team compared country-level data from ninety-three nations with how well people said they felt. Such broad comparisons can hint at links worth testing closely, though they cannot prove cause on their own.
plos-pone-0359311: Shi and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how soil-like matter forms without life. They fed glycine, a simple amino acid, into reactions that build humic-like substances, the dark matter that enriches soil. Two clays, montmorillonite and kaolinite, were compared as helpers in the process. How clays steer this chemistry bears on soil health, carbon storage, and ideas about early Earth.
plos-pone-0359411: Erfanifar and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE plan for a review on self-injury among teens in Iran. The review will search past work for what raises the risk of self-injury without suicidal intent, and what protects teens from it. Such behavior is a warning sign that calls for care, not punishment. A planned map of risks and protections can guide counselors and families toward the factors they can change.
plos-pone-0359511: Wang and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study asking whether sports facilities can stand in for exercise itself. The question sounds odd: can having gyms and courts nearby give some of the wellbeing that exercise brings? The evidence came from four waves of a large Chinese family panel survey. The answer matters for city planners weighing what public facilities do for health.
plos-pone-0360411:
Ge Song, Siti Hajar Halili, and Zamzami Zainuddin wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on university teaching. Their setting is EFL classrooms, where students learn English as a foreign language. The authors look at interactive response systems, tools that let students answer and react during class through devices.

Going beyond engagement, the study also examines student attitudes and technology acceptance, meaning whether learners find the tools welcome and worth using. A system students resist will fail no matter how active it makes a lesson look. Language teachers and course designers can use these findings when deciding whether response technology belongs in their classrooms.
plos-pone-0360511:
Junji Shimauchi and colleagues built and tested prediction models in 2026 for patients seen by a hospital Medical Emergency Team. These teams are called to wards when a patient suddenly worsens, and within minutes they must judge who needs intensive care and who may not survive. The authors asked whether information available at that moment could predict two outcomes: the need for ICU level intervention, and death within fourteen days.

Their retrospective cohort study developed the models from past cases and checked them by internal validation. A reliable early warning would help teams act sooner for the patients at greatest risk, and plan honestly with families. Prediction at the moment of crisis, rather than on admission, is the gap this work addresses.
pmc-10767911:
Milacic, Beavers, Conley, and co-authors describe the 2024 edition of the Reactome Pathway Knowledgebase. Reactome is a free, expert-checked store of how molecules act together inside cells. It covers normal body processes and also processes that go wrong in disease, all checked by hand.

Each process is stored as an ordered chain of molecular events, from a signal arriving to a cell response. That structure lets researchers place their own data on known pathways and spot what changed. As a core shared resource, Reactome helps labs compare results and build on the same trusted map.
pmc-12972711:
Jerrard and colleagues publish a protocol in this 2026 paper for a scoping review about the words intensive care teams use. Critically ill patients need tightly coordinated multidisciplinary care, yet the concepts underpinning that care, what teams mean by familiar terms, are defined inconsistently, which corrodes communication. Concept analysis studies exist to pin such terms down, but nobody has mapped which ones have been analyzed.

The planned review will search four major databases plus dissertation archives, from inception onward, for concept analysis studies concerning the management of critically ill adults at any stage of the care pathway. Duplicate independent screening and extraction are specified, with results charted in tables and mapped visually across the pathway from admission to recovery. The authors, who registered the protocol openly, aim to show which concepts are settled, which are contested, and where definitional gaps invite future analysis.
pmc-13199411:
M Yasser Alsafadi and colleagues audited a hospital system's electronic order set for home IV antibiotics in a 2026 analysis. OPAT lets patients finish intravenous antibiotics at home after discharge. Safe care needs clean data and tight follow-up, yet the team suspected the order set in the Epic record system was leaking both.

Across three years and close to ninety-five hundred treatment episodes, flaws stood out. Free-text entries replaced structured fields, key fields sat empty, and microbe results were not linked. Those gaps made it hard to track care, watch for harm, and study outcomes. Missed drug-level checks and murky instructions added safety risk. The authors list design musts for a rebuild.
pmc-13210311:
Volunteer counselors who treat children who have lived through trauma can absorb trauma themselves, and a 2026 study led by Priya Dahiya looks for workplace shields in Kenya. The research article studies organization-level factors tied to low secondary traumatic stress among lay counselors giving trauma-focused therapy in a rollout trial in western Kenya.

Separate analyses covered 120 community health volunteers and 117 teachers trained for the program. A pattern-matching method found several working mixes for low stress, and the winning recipes differed between the two counselor groups. Strong oversight ties helped both, while how leaders acted and rollout climate combined in other ways by role, so the authors advise tailoring support to each workforce.
pmc-13212611:
E. Lorzadeh and co-authors test in 2026 whether a short questionnaire can measure how many flavonoids people eat. Flavonoids are plant compounds linked to health, but tracking them usually needs long food lists that tire respondents and invite error.

Eighty Australian adults completed the 23-item tool repeatedly over a year, alongside detailed 24-hour recalls each quarter. The short tool gave moderately matching rankings for total flavonoids and several subgroups, though it overestimated amounts by a wide margin. Repeat answers stayed fairly consistent across the year. The authors judge the tool usable for ranking intake, while warning that absolute values need further correction work.
pmc-13212811:
Yunhong Wu and Rick Chappell present in 2026 a statistical method for estimating survival when patient risk is known to rise steadily over time. Their setting is hard: some patients enter studies late, while others leave before the event of interest occurs.

The pair build an estimator that merges a classic proportional hazards approach with an older method that assumes a monotone hazard. They prove the estimator settles on the right answer with enough data and describe its long-run behaviour. Simulations showed stable, nearly unbiased estimates even in small samples, with gains from adjusting for patient traits. A well-known retirement community dataset illustrates the method in practice.
pmc-13213711:
Lynn Honeckman, writing alone in 2026, tells how a young dog with fierce aggression got a full workup and, in time, got better. The nine-month-old Australian Shepherd bit people again and again, at home and out, and her owners weighed giving her up or putting her down.

Blood tests and brain checks found no illness to blame. The behaviour review named built-up fear, poor impulse control, guarding of food and toys, and too little contact with the world as a pup. She had also left her mother young and had sick spells early on. Care mixed strict safety rules, kind training, and two drugs for mood and calm. Bites eased in six weeks and stopped within a year.
pmc-13214411:
Anaseini Ratu, Katherine L. Anders, and Karin Leder write in 2026 about how Pacific Island countries can base mosquito-borne disease control on solid evidence. Dengue outbreaks strike the region often, and a World Health Organization framework for evidence-informed decisions frames their discussion.

They use the release of Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, a method that blocks virus spread, as their test case. Several Pacific countries adopted it before a full local evidence system existed, leaving gaps in data on impact, surveillance, and long-term support. The authors propose squeezing more from existing surveillance, time-series analysis, and blood studies. Culturally grounded discussion methods can supply missing local knowledge and connect researchers with decision makers.
pmc-13215411:
Muhammad-Safuan Zainuddin and co-authors review clinical evidence in a 2026 paper linking oxidative stress to Alzheimer's disease and asking whether flavonoids could help. Flavonoids are plant compounds known for antioxidant activity.

The review gathers biomarker studies from brain tissue and body fluids, where signs of oxidative damage generally run higher in patients and track disease severity, though methods differ between studies. Animal work shows flavonoids can restore antioxidant defences and calm inflammation in the brain. Human trial evidence, however, remains thin. The authors treat oxidative stress as a promising target that still needs firmer clinical proof.
pmc-13215511:
Mahboobeh Nouri and co-authors report a 2026 study of a new sprayable treatment against Verticillium dahliae, a soil fungus that wilts more than 400 plant species. The treatment packs short DNA strands into tiny capsules made from whey protein.

In dishes, the loaded capsules slowed fungal growth while plain protein did nothing. On tomato seedlings in a greenhouse, treated plants showed about half the disease of untreated infected controls after thirty days. The authors present the method as a targeted, low-impact option for wilt control.
pmc-13216111:
Péter de Lima Wachholz and co-authors present a 2026 pilot study of ezetimibe, a cholesterol-absorption blocker used in human medicine, for dogs with high blood lipids. Diet is the usual first step for these dogs, and drugs that lower cholesterol specifically are lacking.

Twenty-three dogs were assigned to a low-fat diet alone, ezetimibe alone, or both together, with blood tests at the start, midway, and after thirty days. Cholesterol fell significantly in both groups receiving the drug but not in the diet-only group. Triglycerides did not change significantly in any group. Owners reported no side effects. The authors conclude the drug was well tolerated and effective for cholesterol under these study conditions.
pmc-13216611:
Jun Koarashi and co-authors present a 2026 study measuring how much ancient carbon escapes when tropical peatlands in Central Kalimantan, Indonesia, are drained and burned. These swamps store carbon for millennia, and radiocarbon dating lets the team tell old carbon from new.

The comparison covers an intact swamp forest, a drained forest, and a drained, repeatedly burnt site over the period 1996 to 2014. Drainage and fires together released roughly 30 to 41 kilograms of carbon per square metre. Fires did most of the damage, freeing peat up to 3,000 years old and starting slow oxidation of still older layers. Scaled to Indonesia's disturbed peatlands, the implied release reaches billions of tonnes, with decomposition continuing every year.
pmc-13217211:
Alshehhi and colleagues update what is known about food protein-induced enterocolitis syndrome, a severe food allergy in children. Unlike classic allergy, it does not run through IgE antibodies, and its causes stay unclear. It usually starts in the first year of life, often after rice, oats, or cow's milk, foods many babies meet early.

An acute episode begins one to four hours after eating, with repeated vomiting, diarrhoea, and limpness. Bad cases drain fluids until blood pressure falls. Because the picture looks like sepsis or stomach flu, babies are often misdiagnosed at first. The review gathers current thinking on causes, testing, and day-to-day management for families.
pmc-13217911:
Yang Liu and co-authors report a 2026 study of influenza vaccine performance in older adults in Jiaxing, China. The team followed patients aged 60 and over who sought care for acute respiratory symptoms across three flu seasons, from 2022 to 2025. Their question was how much protection the seasonal vaccine actually gave this age group.

Using a test-negative design with 3,214 participants, the researchers compared vaccination status between patients who tested positive for influenza and those who tested negative. Adjusted effectiveness came to 42.5 percent overall, peaking at 47.2 percent in the 2024-2025 season. Protection ran higher in women, in people without underlying illness, and in the first 90 days after vaccination, when it reached 52.3 percent. The authors conclude that timely annual vaccination still offers moderate, worthwhile protection for older adults.
pmc-13218311:
Somying Pumtong and co-authors review the staffing behind antimicrobial stewardship programs in a 2026 systematic review with a first meta-analysis. How the work is divided among professions, and how much staff time hospitals commit, had never been gathered, notably outside wealthy countries.

Infectious disease doctors and pharmacists mainly oversaw prescribing, infection control nurses handled monitoring and training, microbiologists led diagnostic stewardship, and hospital epidemiologists ran surveillance and reporting. Staffing levels varied widely across hospitals and reporting styles. Early pooling hinted that larger hospitals report more doctor and pharmacist time, though differences between studies make that pattern tentative.
pmc-13219111:
Lena H. Nguyen writes a 2026 commentary on a study reading the mosaicism behind a form of epilepsy. Focal cortical dysplasia type two, a patch of cortex, is a major cause of drug-resistant epilepsy. pmc-13221111:
Qiming Xu and colleagues search public gene data for early warning markers of diabetic kidney disease in a 2026 analysis. Their patterns separated patients from controls well in test curves. Mouse models and patient samples then confirmed the expression changes. These candidates could support earlier detection, and they point to pathways worth probing for treatment.
pmc-13221911:
Xi Xiao and colleagues track sexually transmitted infections among people with HIV in China across fourteen years, in a 2026 multicenter cohort study. Records covered 32,961 people who started antiretroviral therapy between 2010 and 2024 at two southern treatment centers. Five major infections were traced through linked clinic and laboratory records, including repeat episodes.

About one participant in seven had at least one infection after starting therapy, and overall incidence rose over the period. Syphilis stayed the leading infection, followed by HPV. Younger age, male sex, and being a man who has sex with men predicted infection. The authors argue HIV and STI prevention should be delivered together rather than apart.
pmc-13222511:
Efstratios Kouskos and co-authors report a twisted, dead appendiceal mucocele causing an acute abdomen, in a 2026 case report. CT scanning showed a cystic mass behind the uterus, about nine centimeters long, with calcified walls.

Pathology confirmed the mucocele. Recovery was uncomplicated, and she remained well three months later. A cystic pelvic mass with acute pain should raise this rare possibility.
pmc-13224311:

Those regions then become informed priors for standard Bayesian fitting. Tested on two independent brain-recording datasets, the combined approach predicted data better than either method alone. pmc-13225111:
Ansh Kapil and a large collaboration test a 2026 software method that predicts who gains from a targeted stomach cancer drug. Software instead measures HER2 levels across tumour slides from two trials.

Patients flagged positive by these measures lived significantly longer on the drug in the first trial. pmc-13232811:

The women share of applicants rose nationwide across the period by several points. After the court reversal, that rise ran slower in restrictive states than in protective ones, by a modest yearly gap. Enrolled student shares showed no clear split between the two groups. Small yearly gaps can compound into a thinner, less even doctor pipeline in states already short of physicians.
pmc-13232911:

Writing notes takes clinicians much time, and open conversation datasets are scarce. Meditron-7B and Llama3-8B earned the strongest scores on standard overlap and meaning measures, with Mistral-7B close behind. pmc-13233011:

The agent viewed the previous two hours of data and chose among small dose steps, earning rewards for keeping glucose between 70 and 180 milligrams per deciliter. pmc-13233511:

pmc-13235411:

Their insider view aims to help other systems expand pharmacist scope safely.
pmc-13235511:

pmc-13236611:

pmc-13237811:

pmc-13238111:

Their comparison flags the genetic differences that make some fruits crisp and others soft, giving breeders markers to select on.
pmc-13239711:

pmc-13240111:

pmc-13240211:

pmc-13240911:

pmc-13241511:

pmc-13241611:

pmc-13242511:

pmc-13242811:

pmc-13244511:

pmc-13246411:

pmc-13246811:

pmc-13247311:

pmc-13248111:

pmc-13248211:

pmc-13249611:

pmc-13249711:

pmc-13249911:

pmc-13250111:

pmc-13250211:

pmc-13251111:

pmc-13251711:

pmc-13252911:

pmc-13254311: Lisanne Bogaard, Juraj Mesik, and Andrew Oxenham issued a 2026 author correction to their study of how listeners pick out voices in polyphonic music. The correction fixes an error in calculating the sensitivity index d-prime, which affected a subset of Experiment 2 data where performance sat at ceiling or floor. The authors state the changes do not alter the main results or conclusions, so this notice can only be described at that level.
pmc-13254811:
Neven Aref and Hannah Wesley test vitamin E in a denture liner in a 2026 lab study. Soft liners cushion dentures but can grow rough and host fungi. A commercial acrylic liner was mixed with vitamin E at three low levels and compared with a plain control for cell safety, antifungal action, and surface roughness.

The middle mix gave the best results, with the highest cell survival at 48.0 percent and the lowest roughness. Cell survival fell at the highest level but stayed above the control. No mix blocked the fungus Candida albicans. The authors call the findings early and urge fuller testing.
pmc-13255211:
Zhigang Wang and colleagues study a protein pair behind kidney scarring in diabetes in a 2026 paper. Diabetic kidney disease is a leading cause of kidney failure, and its hallmark is fibrosis, or stiff scar tissue. The team used sugar-stressed kidney cells and diabetic mice fed a high-fat diet.

A growth factor called FGF11 was high in diseased kidneys, and blocking it cut cell growth and scarring. Silencing a partner protein, USP22, sped FGF11 breakdown and eased kidney injury in mice. Restoring FGF11 undid that gain. The authors propose the USP22-FGF11 pair as a drug target.
pmc-13255711:
Carmen Hannemann and co-authors report a 2026 laboratory study of iRhom2, a protein that helps macrophages release the inflammatory signal TNF-alpha. Macrophage-driven inflammation starts atherosclerosis, the plaque buildup behind heart attacks and strokes. The team studied macrophages lacking iRhom2 to see what changed.

The altered macrophages still engulfed particles, survived stress, and multiplied normally. They put out less TNF-alpha and more of the calming signal IL-10, though. Fluid from these cells also made blood vessel cells produce fewer of the sticky molecules that recruit more immune cells. The authors suggest blocking iRhom2 could quiet the earliest stage of vessel inflammation while leaving everyday macrophage duties intact, a profile that safer anti-inflammatory strategies would need.
pmc-13256011:
Jiahao Liu and colleagues report a 2026 study of GALNT7, an enzyme that attaches sugars to proteins, in gastrointestinal stromal tumors. These tumors run on abnormal KIT signaling, and resistance to KIT-blocking drugs remains a serious problem. The team combined bulk, protein-level, and single-cell data to find which sugar-adding enzymes matter most.

The mechanism ran through KIT itself: GALNT7 attached a specific sugar mark that stabilized the KIT protein and kept its growth signals on. A sugar-blocking compound reversed these effects and shrank grafts. The authors nominate GALNT7 as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13256911:

A redesigned variant of the enzyme doubled its activity and lasted twice as long at warm temperature. Careful tuning of reaction conditions then pushed NMN yield above ninety-four percent. Adding a second enzyme to recycle ATP, the cell energy carrier, lifted yield still higher at a stronger feed level. Readers interested in greener manufacturing get a concrete route toward larger-scale production. The results also show how small protein changes can improve an industrial process.
pmc-13257411:
Lorena Ciumărnean and co-authors present a 2026 case report of severe metabolic collapse during kidney cancer care. A fifty-four-year-old woman had metastatic clear cell kidney cancer with sarcomatoid features, an aggressive variant. Earlier checkpoint therapy had already caused gland inflammation and thyroid failure before later drug treatment.

She arrived dehydrated with repeated vomiting, deep weakness, and dangerous blood chemistry, including high potassium, low sodium, and low sugar. Kidney injury and low blood counts compounded the picture. Fluids, electrolyte correction, and supportive care restored chemistry and kidney function. Muscle weakness raised concern for an immune nerve or muscle event, though potassium alone could explain part of it. Oncologists get a warning case on layered toxicity. Careful differential diagnosis and team management are the authors' central plea.
pmc-13257811:
Ching-Han Tseng and co-authors trace both-eye progression of wet macular degeneration in a 2026 real-world case series. The timeline from first-eye diagnosis to second-eye conversion was reconstructed, along with visit habits and injection counts. Baseline features of the still-healthy second eye were tested as predictors.

Second eyes converted in about two years when the first eye stayed active, versus more than six years when the first eye quieted. Once both eyes needed treatment, yearly injections jumped more than threefold. Patients whose first eye settled visited less often, which may have widened the detection gap. Surface abnormalities in the second eye at baseline strongly predicted conversion. Retina clinics gain a vigilance rule: quiet first eyes should not relax second-eye surveillance, especially with early surface changes present.
pmc-13258311:
Nisachon Siripaiboonpong and co-authors link gum disease with carrying many long-term conditions in a 2026 analysis of two giant cohorts. UK Biobank supplied half a million people, and a United States nutrition survey added ten thousand more with clinical gum examinations. Multimorbidity meant living with at least two chronic diseases.

About half of participants in both cohorts carried multiple conditions. Gum disease raised the odds of multimorbidity modestly in the United Kingdom data and more clearly in the American data. Links strengthened in adults under sixty and grew in a dose pattern with gum severity. Blood inflammation markers explained part of the association in mediation tests. Public health readers gain population-scale support for mouth-body integration. Dental care belongs in chronic disease prevention talks, especially for younger adults.
pmc-13258611:
Conghui Li and colleagues put wheat seedlings through drought, salt, and heat, alone and in punishing pairs. Real fields increasingly deliver these stresses together as the climate warms. Using the cultivar Yannong 1212 in water culture, their 2026 study measures growth, chemistry, and gene responses side by side.

Single stresses slowed sprouting in proportion to dose, but paired stresses hit far harder. Leaves yellowed, pores closed, and the green machinery inside cells was damaged. Seedlings stockpiled protective sugars and proline while antioxidant enzymes rose and fell by stress type. Drought combined with heat proved the most damaging pairing of all.
pmc-13258811:
Marika Kanthe and co-authors surveyed every metabolic dietitian in Sweden about a relaxed diet for phenylketonuria. People with PKU must limit phenylalanine, an amino acid most foods contain. European guidance now allows many low-protein foods freely, but their 2026 survey asks whether Swedish practice follows.

All thirteen dietitians replied, and eight recommended the free-food approach. Even so, about a third of foods the handbook calls free were still commonly counted in Sweden. For many items, colleagues flatly disagreed about whether counting was needed. Worry about patients overdoing phenylalanine drove much of the caution, the authors report.
pmc-13260511:
Chen-Fang Kang and co-authors present a 2026 study of a non-destructive checking method for semiconductor structures made of AlGaN and GaN, materials used in high-power electronics. Their framework combines second harmonic generation microscopy, an optical method sensitive to broken crystal symmetry, with pixel-level anomaly detection. The approach was compared with standard detectors such as YOLOv8 and Mask R-CNN. It showed far better spatial overlap and sensitivity, resolving more than five thousand micron-scale defect-affected regions within a single field of view. Many of those regions were largely out of reach for box- or mask-based methods. Optical defect features were also supported by correlation with light-emission based defect measures.
pmc-13260711:

Records captured blood values, complications, treatments, and outcomes for mothers and newborn babies.

Median platelet count at diagnosis was low. Maternal complications occurred in 19.8 percent of cases, most commonly premature rupture of membranes at 4.9 percent of cases. Newborn complications affected 12.4 percent, mainly preterm birth and restricted growth in the womb, each at 3.8 percent of newborns. Overall, eighty percent of pregnancies were uncomplicated. Cases that began during pregnancy had a higher complication rate, at 28.5 percent, than cases present before pregnancy, at 23.2 percent of cases.
pmc-13262511:
Babak Saravi and colleagues audited in 2026 whether demographic cues in a prompt can sway image-reading language models giving dental advice. They sent 705 panoramic dental X-rays from a public set to three commercial multimodal models. Each image arrived under twelve prompt conditions varying stated race, ethnicity, and sex, plus controls.

The audit totaled 25,380 model calls, each returning ten structured recommendation fields. All three models shifted their advice when demographic labels appeared. One model reacted most broadly, moving treatment invasiveness, outlook, and confidence across groups. The shifts were systematic yet small, each under six percent of a rating step. Agreement between models under plain prompts hovered near chance, a larger worry than the label effects. The authors ask for routine demographic audits before such tools reach clinics.
pmc-13262711:
Davide Ruggero writes a 2026 commentary on targeting protein production in cancer. Tumor studies often find that RNA levels poorly predict protein levels, so the making of proteins, called translation, helps set a cancer cell's identity. A study in the same journal issue blocked a key translation factor called eIF4E in prostate cancer.

Blocking eIF4E rewired which proteins the cancer cells made, the study found. It suppressed traits of the basal cell type, which resists hormone therapy, and pushed cells toward the luminal type, restoring hormone sensitivity. Ruggero argues that cancers broadly depend on selective translation to stay flexible and resist drugs. Attacking those dependencies could turn resistant cell states into treatable ones.
pmc-13262811:
Xinying Quan and co-authors study a little-known protein in stomach cancer in a 2026 journal article. The protein, THSD7B, had been linked to several cancers, but its role in gastric adenocarcinoma, the main stomach cancer type, was unclear. The team checked its levels in public tumor data sets and then altered it in cancer cells and in mice.

THSD7B levels were higher in tumor tissue than in normal tissue and tracked with patient survival. Genes linked to it clustered around cell adhesion, how cells grip their surroundings, and internal cell scaffolding. Lowering THSD7B in cells slowed growth, movement, and invasion, while raising it did the reverse. In mice, it promoted tumor growth, marking it as a candidate marker.
pmc-13263411:
C. Yarkutay Turkkan and co-authors report a 2026 journal article testing a simple blood ratio as a supporting marker in Cushing's syndrome. In this disorder the body makes too much cortisol, a stress hormone. Standard diagnostic tests are imperfect, so the team studied the blood urea nitrogen to creatinine ratio in 229 people in Istanbul.

Patients with Cushing's syndrome, its subclinical form, and both hormone-driven subtypes had higher ratios than healthy controls. Specific cutoff values separated each patient group from controls. The ratio also tracked with cortisol levels and standard test results, and it changed after treatment. The authors suggest it can support diagnosis when main tests are unavailable or unclear.
pmc-13263811:
Shi-Ying Long and a large surgical team reported in 2026 long-term pregnancy results after a delicate microsurgery that reconnects the sperm duct to the epididymis. Their patients had blockages from infection, injury, or unknown causes rather than vasectomy, where the blocked interval cannot be dated. The series covered 197 men treated with a vessel-sparing version of the operation.

The connection stayed open in about eighty percent of men checked at eighteen months. Among couples followed for an average of nearly five years, almost three quarters achieved natural pregnancy. Notably, about two in five couples still waiting after the first year conceived during years one to three. A partner aged thirty-five or older and a left-sided varicocele each predicted lower success. The authors advise waiting two to three years before turning to lab-assisted conception.
pmc-13263911:
Kristina Countryman and colleagues examined in 2026 whether clinicians ask pregnant women about cannabis unevenly by race, within a trial cohort already flagged for substance use risk. Their 176 participants, about a quarter of them Black, reported use and clinician conversations at four points. Guidelines urge universal screening in pregnancy.

Adjustment for background factors put their odds near four times higher. The gap persisted even after accounting for prior cannabis use itself. The authors read the pattern as screening bias rather than diligence. They call for system-level fixes so universal screening actually lands universally.
pmc-13264311:
Xin Liu and colleagues compare acupuncture approaches for chronic prostate and pelvic pain in a 2026 network meta-analysis. Drug treatment often disappoints in this condition, and needle-based therapies are widely used as support. Most trials compared acupuncture methods against medicines rather than sham needles, which limits certainty about specific effects.

Needle therapies, alone or with medication, improved symptom scores more than conventional drugs in those active comparisons. Warm needle acupuncture ranked highest for both total improvement and response rate in the ranking analysis. Electroacupuncture also performed favorably across outcomes. The authors present rankings as guidance for practice and for designing stricter sham-controlled trials.
pmc-13264411:
Congcong Chang and colleagues review a peony-derived compound as a possible treatment for intestinal diseases in a 2026 article. Bowel inflammation, everyday gut disorders, stress-related gut injury and colon cancers share overlapping drivers. Colon-targeted delivery and derivative design are raising exposure where it matters. Human evidence remains thin, so the authors frame promise carefully and call for clinical trials with set dosing and safety checks.
pmc-13264611:

Nearly all used smartphones, and most in both groups would use a health app and join a reward-based bonus scheme. Interest barely varied by age or cultural background. The authors back apps, wearables, and online learning for shipboard health.
pmc-13264911:
Christina Psaros and colleagues outline a 2026 pilot trial protocol in South Africa on HIV self-testing for partners of pregnant and postpartum women. The pilot will measure enrolment, kit delivery, testing, and prevention uptake at three months. Interviews will explore how couples experienced the approach.
pmc-13265011:

Each person applied the serum to one half of the face and a plain base to the other, before and after injections, so the comparison stayed within the same skin.

pmc-13265211:
Huijuan Zhang, Guanghua Wu, and Chunxu Liao study how survival chances change over time in primary breast lymphoma, in a 2026 registry study. pmc-13265411:

The approach suits live imaging needing flexible geometry and little handling.
pmc-13266611:

pmc-13266711:
Rundong Zhang and colleagues set a 2026 diagnostic quiz built around a man in his seventies with fast-growing, painful plaques. pmc-13267611:

pmc-13267811:
Manhui Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 review of bloodstream infections in newborns at a large Chinese hospital. Newborns, above all early and small babies, catch infections easily. The authors back local tracking to guide drug use.
pmc-13268411:

pmc-13268511:

Bias risk was moderate, driven by small samples. The authors call for bigger, better studies before ultrasound guides care.
pmc-13268711:

Looking closer, pain that interfered with specific activities (housework, visiting friends, public transport, shopping) tracked with narrower life-space. pmc-13268911:
Haoxuan Deng and co-authors report in 2026 a case of a benign smooth muscle tumor that grew inside veins all the way into a woman's heart. Only short-term images exist so far, and the authors flag the missing long follow-up as a weakness, since this rare tumor can return. pmc-13269311: A correction notice from 2026, led by Jong Kwon Lee and co-authors, fixes errors in their journal paper on whole genome sequencing. The paper covered 25 families with suspected inborn errors of immunity, meaning immune defects present from birth. Figure 1 had misaligned shapes and arrows that distorted it. Table 2 showed wrong values in its final column instead of article identifiers. Figures 2 and 3 were updated for clarity.
pmc-13269411:

The first examined over a thousand brief synchronization events in ninety-one people and found frequency ratios matching the scheme closely, with group-level precision even as single frequencies wandered. The second sifted nearly a quarter-million rhythm peaks and found the predicted dips and crowding, then replicated the pattern in a separate dataset. Lacy reads the match as evidence of a standing mathematical scaffold for brain oscillations.
pmc-13269611:

At 12 weeks, resin still led, at four point six nine against eight point five zero. Raters also scored resin higher for looks and reduced cloudiness. pmc-13269811:

pmc-13270611:
Georgia Vesma wrote a 2026 small-scale qualitative study, one based on interviews and survey answers rather than counts alone, about peer review of research that crosses subject fields. Reviewers reported papers outside their expertise and weak editor guidance. Editors reported that a wider shortage of reviewers made the process harder still.
pmc-13270711:
Carlotta Marie Wehrkamp led a 2026 journal article on centromeres, the central parts of chromosomes, in oats and their relatives in the Avena genus. New near-complete genome assemblies let the team compare these repeat-rich regions across species with different numbers of chromosome sets.

pmc-13271211:

pmc-13271811:

pmc-13271911:

pmc-13272011:

pmc-13272311:

pmc-13272511:

pmc-13272711:
