pmc-13273211:
Sebastian Kalytta and colleagues validated a deep learning method for brain scan correction in a 2026 study. SPECT imaging, used to measure dopamine transporters in Parkinson's disease, needs correction for signal loss in tissue. That correction usually needs a CT scan, which adds radiation.

Their method creates a synthetic CT from an MRI scan using a trained network, so no real CT is needed. In twelve patients with Parkinson's disease, binding measures from the new method matched CT based results almost exactly in both deep and outer brain areas. Older uniform correction overshot, and no correction undershot by wide margins. An outside dataset of eighteen people confirmed the pattern. The authors call the method a valid radiation free option.
pmc-13273511:
Nashira I Brown and co-authors studied beliefs and distress linked to sunburn among Florida adults in a 2026 analysis. Melanoma causes most skin cancer deaths, and most cases are preventable, yet sunburn stays common. The team asked which beliefs and feelings best predict having been sunburned.

Their cross-sectional study covered 1,172 adults with at most modest sun sensitivity, using data gathered from 2015 to 2018. People who worried more about melanoma and rated their own risk higher were more likely to report a sunburn in the past year. Belief that prevention steps actually work ran lower among the sunburned. Weekend sun exposure and deliberate outdoor tanning also predicted burns. Several other beliefs and distress measures did not, which surprised the authors.
pmc-13273711:
Jose David Amorocho-Morales and colleagues built a new risk model for heart attack in a 2026 Colombian cohort study. Heart disease is the top killer worldwide, and long horizon risk scores often perform poorly in regions like theirs. The team aimed for accurate short term prediction from routine health records.

They analyzed more than 382,000 patients with millions of encounters from an integrated heart care system. A gradient boosting classifier was paired with an interpretable survival ensemble to estimate six and twelve month risk. Accuracy and calibration were strong, with predicted and observed heart attacks nearly matching. The model re-ranked many patients compared with older scores like Framingham. An outside delayed check still separated risk bands in order. Local recalibration is advised before use.
pmc-13274311:
Juxiang Shao and co-authors wrote a 2026 review article on printing thermoelectric materials from inks. Thermoelectric materials convert heat directly into electricity and back, useful for harvesting waste heat and for cooling. Making them the usual way is rigid and wasteful, while printing allows flexible shapes at scale.

The review covers how the inks are formulated and bound, then printing methods such as inkjet and screen printing. Printed devices shown include energy harvesters, thermal managers, and sensors. Performance hinges mostly on ink quality, the authors stress. They close by sketching future directions, including possible medical uses in tissue repair and disease treatment, where gentle heat and power control could help.
pmc-13274911:
Amanda Ling Jie Yee and colleagues present a 2026 tutorial article on building a one-day quality improvement workshop with the learners themselves. Quality improvement, the discipline of making care safer step by step, is vital but rarely taught hands-on. The team used Kern's six-step curriculum framework, informed by experiential learning theory, to co-design the day with medical students and resident physicians.

Thirty-one learners attended, mixing expert talks, small-group project design, and peer presentations on audits, ethics, and practical rollout. About seventy-seven percent completed both pre- and post-workshop surveys. Self-rated understanding of the Plan-Do-Study-Act cycle, the core improvement loop, rose significantly, from a median of two on a ten-point scale before the workshop. Interviews explored attitudes and relevance to future practice.
pmc-13275011:
Tess Thompson and co-authors reviewed what research says about caregivers and health care paperwork burden in a 2026 scoping review. Patients with long term illness face forms, insurance fights, and scheduling chores, and family caregivers quietly absorb much of that work. Almost nothing had been gathered about their experience of it.

Eighteen United States studies met their rules, most of them qualitative and most about cancer caregiving. Using a standard framework, they sorted burden into learning costs, compliance costs, and psychological costs. The three blurred together in caregivers' accounts. Insurance navigation in particular caused distress and even harmed caregivers' own health. Few studies used any theory. The authors call for theory guided work and for interventions that lift burden from patients and families alike.
pmc-13275711:
Ibrahim Adabara and co-authors propose a policy-enforced AI framework for network intrusion detection in a 2026 study. Security AI often chases accuracy while offering little accountability or rule compliance. Their design pairs a deep learning detector with a governance layer tied to the NIST AI risk framework.

A policy engine written in a plain declarative language checks each decision against set rules. Tests used a public dataset holding more than two million network flow records. Detection performance matched standard baselines while every decision met the policy schema. Governance scores also rose, which the authors present as evidence that accountable automation need not cost detection power.
pmc-13276311:
James Haag and co-authors present a 2026 methods article on measuring radiation damage in metals more accurately. Under radiation, tiny cavities form inside metals and make them swell. Microscopists usually assume each cavity is a sphere when estimating its volume from flat images.

The authors show that this shortcut can understate volume by a quarter or overstate it by nearly three quarters, depending on the cavity's true shape. Real cavities are often many-sided solids whose shape follows the metal's crystal structure. Their revised method, shortened to CAVV-T, uses crystal orientation to track true void volumes. They tabulated the corrections for common shapes in two crystal systems. A test on neutron-irradiated nickel demonstrated the approach. The team hopes it will sharpen confidence in swelling data used to judge reactor materials.
pmc-13276511:
Joel Daniel Castañeda-Espinoza and co-authors test plant extracts against mosquito larvae in a 2026 laboratory study. The extracts came from the fruit, seeds, and stems of Hippocratea excelsa, a climbing plant. Target species were three disease carriers: Aedes aegypti, Culex quinquefasciatus, and Anopheles albimanus.

Extracts were prepared with three solvents and tested across a range of strengths. Hexane extracts killed every larva of all three species within twelve hours at higher strengths. Half the larvae died at only a few parts per million, which shows strong potency. Chemical analysis named seven main compounds in the stem extract. The authors propose these extracts as candidates for natural mosquito control.
pmc-13277211:
Yue Yang and colleagues catalogue a family of growth-regulating genes in a Chinese lily, in a 2026 genome study. The bHLH transcription factors steer plant development, hormone signals, and stress responses. Lilium davidii variety unicolor is valued in China for food and medicine, yet its family had never been mapped.

Two hundred fourteen genes were found in the genome and sorted into twenty-three subfamilies. Duplicated gene pairs were few, suggesting limited large-scale expansion of the family. Many genes switched on briefly under hormone or stress treatment, with a few responding strongly to salt or abscisic acid. Four genes were confirmed to support salt tolerance, offering breeding targets for hardier lilies.
pmc-13277411:
Tae-Youn Kim and a large guideline panel present part five of the 2025 Korean resuscitation guidelines, published in 2026. The section covers cardiac arrest in special circumstances, where standard algorithms may need adjusting. Each recommendation is graded for strength and for certainty of the supporting evidence.

For arrest from high blood potassium, insulin with glucose is suggested, while routine bicarbonate or calcium lacks support either way. Clot-busting treatment may be considered when a lung clot is suspected or confirmed. Naloxone is not advised routinely for opioid-related arrest once full life support is under way. The section also covers prone patients, drowning, severe hypothermia, pregnancy, and anaphylaxis.
pmc-13278511:
Shirin Akter Begum and co-authors map HPV genotypes in cervical lesions at a Dhaka hospital, in a 2026 study. Lasting infection with high-risk human papillomavirus drives most cervical precancer and cancer. Knowing which types dominate locally helps shape vaccine and screening policy in Bangladesh.

Three hundred women with confirmed lesions joined the study between 2022 and 2024, split between precancer and invasive cancer. Among cancer cases, most tested positive for high-risk HPV, and type 16 dominated by a wide margin. Type 18 and several less common types appeared at low rates, and some women carried multiple types. Squamous cell carcinoma was the main cancer form in both positive and negative groups.
pmc-13278711:
Jay Kakadiya leads a 2026 study of United States death trends for hepatocellular carcinoma, the main type of liver cancer, from 1999 to 2020. Causes are shifting from viral hepatitis toward alcohol-related and metabolic liver disease. Using a national death database, the team split deaths into infective and non-infective groups and tracked age-adjusted rates by sex, race, and region.

Overall liver cancer mortality rose substantially, driven by non-infective causes. Infective mortality rose until 2013, then fell significantly, while non-infective rates climbed throughout. Rates were higher in men than women. Infective deaths were highest among Asian Americans, while non-infective deaths hit Hispanic and American Indian groups hardest. Western states led overall.
pmc-13279211:
Shramana Ghosh and colleagues published a 2026 study of Asp f 10, a protein released by the mold Aspergillus fumigatus, as a blood marker for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis. The condition, a severe allergic lung reaction to the mold, is hard to tell from other allergic diseases. The team first screened proteins the mold secretes under host-like conditions, then produced Asp f 10 in the laboratory. They tested blood samples from patients with the disease, from patients with severe asthma sensitized to the mold, and from controls.

IgG antibodies against Asp f 10 were significantly raised in both patient groups, and an accuracy analysis gave IgG an AUC of 0.90, far above IgE's 0.54 against the same protein. The mature protein was a stable, active enzyme that cut gelatin, yet it did not trigger histamine release from cells. Adding Asp f 10 IgG testing to existing panels could sharpen diagnosis of Aspergillus-related lung disease.
pmc-13279511:
Lenka Kollar Moskalova and colleagues report a 2026 study of humic substances fed to honey bees. Humic substances are dark, soil born compounds sold as a natural health aid for people and animals. Their effect on bees was little known. New worker bees were kept in lab cages for seven days. One group got plain sugar syrup and the other got syrup with a small dose of a humic product.

Tests read immune gene use, germ fighter proteins, cell guard enzymes and blood cell types. Two defence genes rose with the feed, one that fights cell rust and one that starts a dark pigment defence. Two germ fighter genes fell. Fat damage marks and guard enzyme acts were also tracked. The mixed shift shows humic feed tunes, not just boosts, bee defence.
pmc-13279811:
Daniel Kuznicki and colleagues report a 2026 study of gene control faults in the BCL2 gene in lymphoid cancers. BCL2 upregulation, or raised gene output, drives lymphoma growth and shapes drug response. Past models blamed a chromosome swap or loss of small RNA brakes. Faults in the gene promoter, the control zone before the gene, were little explored. Noncoding zones are hard to read and often skipped in genome scans.

Large genome sets showed a lymphoma specific hotspot of faults in the BCL2 promoter. The faults linked to raised output from one gene copy alone, apart from the chromosome swap. They break protein binding sites in the control zone and shift gene form balance. In diffuse large B cell lymphoma, they also linked to worse survival. Promoter faults stand as an independent marker of BCL2 level for care calls.
pmc-13279911:
Masoumeh Bathaee and colleagues report a 2026 mouse study of cress seed compounds in a multiple sclerosis model. Multiple sclerosis is a nerve disease where immune attack strips myelin, the fat coat on nerve fibres. Garden cress seeds hold glucosinolates, plant compounds with anti swelling acts. The main one in cress is glucotropaeolin. Mice got cuprizone, a toxin that strips myelin, in their diet for eight weeks.

Seven groups held normal mice, toxin mice, a standard drug group and four seed fraction groups. One fraction was rich in glucosinolate and one was a volatile oil part, each at two doses for twenty one days. Acts tests showed symptom gains, and tissue checks showed better remyelination, meaning new myelin coats. A myelin gene called Olig2 shifted with care. The seed parts guard nerves most by myelin repair in this model.
pmc-13280311:
Firoozeh Alavian and Arefeh Hajimohammadi give a 2026 review of nanoparticles that target Alzheimer pathways past amyloid and tau. Alzheimer disease is a complex brain decay illness. Two protein clumps, amyloid and tau, dominate past drug hunts. Swelling, power core flaws and lysosome faults, where lysosomes are cell recycling sacs, offer fresh paths. Nanoparticles can cross the blood brain barrier and aim at set targets.

Lipid, chitosan and gold particles carried anti swelling and antioxidant compounds like curcumin and resveratrol in animal studies. Those loads cut brain swelling and boosted power core function. Particles tagged for mitochondria, the power cores, cut rust stress and raised energy output. Polymer and carbon structures aided lysosome function and cell balance. All proof stays preclinical, in animals and dishes, so human trials must still prove worth.
pmc-13280911:
Nathaphon Yu King Hing and colleagues published a 2026 study showing enzymes in a carbon-dioxide-proof bacterium organize into metabolons, complexes that pass molecules from one enzyme to the next. The bacterium, Priestia megaterium SR7, lives in supercritical carbon dioxide, an extreme valued by carbon-fixing engineers. The team focused on the pyruvate node, the hub where carbon traffic splits among energy production, replenishment, and building blocks.

Cross-linking followed by protein tests caught four enzymes around that hub interacting in the test tube, including pyruvate kinase and lactate dehydrogenase. Computer models of the pairs suggested likely contact faces. Carbon-13 labeling tests in living cells showed metabolite pools thinning as expected if compounds are channeled inside complexes rather than released into the cell. The authors argue this grouping is a real layer in its central metabolism. If confirmed, such complexes could help route carbon better in industrial strains.
pmc-13281511:
Atanu Ghosh and colleagues published a 2026 photophysics study showing an iron complex can do electron-transfer chemistry from a short-lived upper excited state. Iron-based light absorbers could replace rare ruthenium and iridium in photoredox catalysis, but their useful charge-transfer states collapse into metal-centered states within a trillionth of a second. Using an iron(II) pyridinium carbene complex and ultrafast spectroscopy, the team timed that collapse and mapped the energy landscape.

The higher state survived about 3 picoseconds before relaxing. Temperature-dependent measurements identified the receiving state and showed ground-state recovery sits near the barrierless regime of Marcus theory, letting the authors estimate the state's redox power. Armed with those numbers, they tuned the pathways so electron transfer fires from the upper state first. The authors present this balancing act as a strategy for putting cheap iron complexes to work in light-to-chemical energy conversion.
pmc-13281611:
John Cafferkey and colleagues explored immune effects of two fluids for sepsis in a 2026 letter. Sepsis is a runaway body response to infection that can kill. First care gives a salt fluid by vein, but a blood protein fluid is also used. The protein fluid is claimed to calm immune harm. The letter reports a side study of a small trial in emergency rooms. Twenty-six patients gave blood at the start and twice in the first day.

Fourteen patients got the protein fluid and twelve the salt fluid. Lab tests counted immune cell types and signal proteins in blood. Gene activity in white cells was read as well. Health outcomes in the two groups were alike. The authors frame the work as a probe of how fluids may shape immunity. Such clues could guide a larger trial of the protein fluid.
pmc-13282211:
Meng-Hua Tao and co-authors report a 2026 study on whether lacking steady access to enough food links to a fatty liver condition in adults. The condition, shortened to MASLD, involves excess liver fat tied to metabolism problems. The team used a national United States health survey from 2017 to early 2020. It included five thousand seventy-six adults who had a liver stiffness scan.

Food insecurity, meaning unreliable access to enough food, was linked to higher odds of the liver condition overall. That link appeared mainly in non-Hispanic White adults and in women, but not in men. Diet partly explained the link in White adults, through added sugar and low fruit and vegetable intake. The authors suggest food programs that cut added sugar and raise whole fruit and vegetable intake could soften this risk. They stress that patterns differ by group, so one-size advice may miss those most affected.
pmc-13282311:
Cody L Nathan and co-authors present a 2026 study of seizures in patients with a rare brain tumour type called pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma. Such tumours often cause epilepsy, but outcome patterns were little studied. The team reviewed twenty-five patients treated at one centre between 2004 and 2025. They linked seizure outcomes to tumour traits, clinical features, and brain activity findings.

Nineteen patients had tumour-related epilepsy, and seizures were the first symptom in most. Nearly a third had earlier focal seizures that went unrecognised. After first surgery, before any tumour return, most became seizure free. At latest follow-up, about two thirds stayed free. A tumour marker loss, called ATRX loss, linked to better long-term seizure freedom. When seizures returned, the tumour had usually returned on scans within a month. The authors stress careful seizure histories, since early focal events are easy to miss.
pmc-13283211:
Eye movements alone might flag mental stress outside the lab, the premise Maike Laut and fellow engineers test in 2026. Pupil size and gaze shifts can signal stress, but most tools need lab tasks or many sensors. The team tested whether eye data alone can work across tasks.

Two datasets were used: a virtual goalkeeper task and a virtual job interview. Deep learning models read the raw eye time series for stress patterns. Top scores neared a 96 percent F1 level under good conditions in the best setup. Scores varied widely across datasets with signal quality and task design. Eye-only tools may offer a lighter path to stress tracking in real settings.
pmc-13283811:
Jiawen Li and Xingwen Xie reviewed in 2026 how gut balance and immune crosstalk shape ankylosing spondylitis, a long-term inflammatory disease of the spine and the points where tendons attach to bone. The gene HLA-B27 is a known factor, yet gut disturbance has drawn growing attention through a gut-joint axis. Patients show lower gut microbe diversity and shifts in community make-up.

The review links those shifts to a leakier gut barrier, immune priming, and a key inflammatory route involving IL-23 and IL-17 signals. Unusual lymphocyte types that live near barriers may be switched on and travel to joints, feeding inflammation and odd bone growth. Gut chemical products, such as short-chain fatty acids, also help tune the barrier. The authors separate proven immune drugs from early microbe-based ideas.
pmc-13284111:
Tingyu Su and colleagues combined many data types in 2026 to hunt prognostic markers in clear cell kidney cancer, the main kidney cancer form, which carries a poor outlook. Genome, methylation, and immune data from public databases were merged, then checked with single-cell sequencing, genetic causal analysis, computer gene knockout, and lab tests.

One gene, CRHBP, stood out as switched down in tumours, with lower levels at later stages and a link to better survival when levels held up. A partner signal, UCN2 from the testes, showed a causal risk effect and tied inversely to vessel growth and low oxygen in tumours. Computer docking flagged an existing drug, dabrafenib, as a candidate binder for both targets. Lab checks confirmed the expression shifts in human and mouse tissue.
pmc-13284411:
Deepa Singal and co-authors report a whole-population study, published in 2026, on mental health among autistic people in Manitoba, Canada. Using linked health records from 2018 to 2022, the team compared autistic children, teens, and adults with all other residents. They tracked doctor-diagnosed disorders and suicide attempts across three age groups.

Autistic people had higher rates of almost all conditions studied, with much higher adjusted risk for schizophrenia, conduct disorder, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in the pooled results. Risk of a suicide attempt was also more than three times higher than in the comparison group, the authors report. The scale of the gaps supports stronger, age-aware mental health support and suicide prevention for autistic people.
pmc-13285011: Nian Liu and co-authors publish a correction, dated 2026, to a study of vitexin compound 1 and melanoma cell growth. Errors were found in the right panel of Figure 4a and in a supplementary figure. The notice reprints the affected figure material on DNA damage and reactive oxygen species and presents the correct figures. No change to the study topic is stated in the notice.
pmc-13285711:
Yongcheng Ge and colleagues review robot-assisted oral examination in a 2026 survey of the field. Dentists now test robots that combine cameras, sensors, and smart software to inspect the mouth in a standard way. The review maps the main parts of these systems and the problems that still block routine use.

A search of PubMed and ScienceDirect through September 2025 yielded 134 included studies from a much larger first pool. Key parts include high-resolution imaging inside the mouth, fusion of data from several sensors, force sensing, and self-guided movement. These tools can sharpen image capture and make exams more alike across clinics. Gaps in safety checks, speed, and clinical testing remain, so wider use will need steady refinement.
pmc-13285911:
Guangling Li and colleagues survey stroke knowledge, attitudes, and habits among young patients in China in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. Stroke now strikes more adults under 45, who face decades of risk for a second event. The team asked what these patients know about their condition and whether that knowledge shapes daily prevention habits.

An online survey in Shanxi Province drew replies from 445 patients aged 18 to 45 in the first half of 2025. Attitudes scored well and habits scored in the middle range, while knowledge lagged behind both. Model tests showed knowledge fed straight into habits and also worked through attitudes to lift them further. The gap between knowing and doing points to focused teaching, through phone tools and local workshops, as the clear next step.
pmc-13286011:
Ralph Andrews and Paul M Dockree propose a framework tying breath, brain waves, and perception in a 2026 theory article. Breathing does more than fuel the body: each cycle seems to open and close small windows in which sights and sounds reach awareness. Their Rhythmic Embodied Perception framework joins those windows across three levels, from cell signals to felt experience.

Slow breath cycles tug on brain rhythms in sight and attention networks, creating quiet phases when input most easily breaks through. Chosen slow breathing steadies those rhythms through a brainstem system that sets alertness, stretching the clear windows longer. The model makes sharp, testable calls: detection should swing with breath phase, and paced breathing should tighten breath-brain links. Old yoga accounts of breath and attention find a modern echo in the scheme.
pmc-13286411:
Alpaslan Kaban and colleagues search for a group of womb cancer patients who can safely skip extensive staging surgery. Their 2026 study reviews 250 women with the common endometrioid type of tumor that had invaded less than half the womb wall. Finding spread beyond the uterus normally requires wider surgery, so a reliably low-risk profile matters.

Eighteen women had such spread. Tumors of the higher grade spread at nearly four times the rate of the lower grade, and tumors wider than three centimeters also spread far more often. Both features predicted spread independently of each other. Women with small, low-grade tumors carried the lowest risk. The authors support sparing that group the full staging operation.
pmc-13286911:
Ju Hee Oh and colleagues refine a shock-based delivery method, electroporation, for editing genes in fragile primary mouse blood cells without using viruses. Their 2026 study optimizes settings on a commercial platform for three cell types: killer T cells, macrophages grown from bone marrow, and blood stem and progenitor cells.

Two pulse programs delivered genetic material into activated T cells with high efficiency while sparing viability and growth. Macrophages tolerated the process well and kept their identity while target genes were knocked out efficiently. The best program also worked in stem cells, giving steady delivery and reproducible editing. A shared, modular workflow, the authors argue, lowers the barrier to quick genetic experiments in immunology.
pmc-13288111:
Dimitri Desvillechabrol and co-authors present LORA in 2026, a ready-made workflow that assembles genomes from long-read sequencing machines using several proven builder tools under one roof. Builders differ in strength by species, and hand-run assembly is hard to repeat, so the pipeline automates choices and records each step.

Built on a task-running framework, it works on a laptop or a big cluster. Checks cover build quality and completeness, name stray species by gene matching, and produce clickable reports. Trials on bacterial and single-cell eukaryote data from both major long-read machines show typical results and common traps. The tool ships inside an open-source package.
pmc-13288211:
Hai-Jun Li and a large team show a light-driven trick in 2026. Ring-shaped starting molecules carry a carbon triple bond and a bulky boron group. Shining light makes each ring swallow an extra carbon. The result is a seven-membered ring fused into a larger boron-dusted frame. Such expansions used to need unstable reactive fragments.

The clean reaction breaks a strong ring bond, inserts the carbon, and shifts a hydrogen atom in a linked sequence. Maths modelling points to short-lived allene and boron radical forms along the path. The authors claim the first expansion of this classic type driven by a stable alkyne. The route opens fresh designs for boron-bearing carbon frames.
pmc-13288611:
Shilan Li and colleagues study immune cells in a childhood airway disease in a 2026 paper. Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis causes wart-like growths that keep returning in children's airways. Human papillomavirus drives the disease, yet why the immune system fails to clear it is unclear. The team compared 97 young patients with 124 controls using blood and tissue tests.

One T cell family, marked by the V-beta 3 receptor chain, had expanded in patients with aggressive disease. Those cells carried strong activation and killing markers and gathered inside the growths themselves. Tumor tissue also showed raised levels of PD-L1 and TGF-beta, both known immune dampeners. Chemical signals that recruit T cells were turned up as well. The authors suggest the cells arrive in force but are held back by the suppressive setting. Targeting that balance could one day reduce how often growths return.
pmc-13288711:
Belayneh Jejaw Abate and colleagues chart uneven cesarean delivery across sub-Saharan Africa in a 2026 multi-country geospatial analysis. Pooling Demographic and Health Survey data from 2015 to 2024 gave 201,481 weighted cases across 28 countries, which they tested for clustering and modeled with several spatial regression methods.

Delivery by cesarean clustered strongly on the map. Hotspots covered countries such as Uganda, Rwanda, Kenya, South Africa, and Ghana, while cold spots included Ethiopia, Nigeria, Angola, and Madagascar among others. A prior cesarean, maternal age of thirty-five or more, birth spacing behavior, and insurance coverage predicted use, with effects shifting by place. Matching policy, referral routes, and financing to local patterns is their prescription.
pmc-13288911:
Michael K Steinhoff and colleagues use nuclear magnetic resonance to track lithium movement inside a garnet battery material in 2026. The material, shortened to LLZTO, is a solid electrolyte candidate for safer batteries. Coating its powder with alumina by atomic layer deposition was known to stir up lithium during coating. The team measured lithium relaxation times to see how coating thickness changed bulk behavior before firing.

Relaxation patterns varied a lot between samples with different coating histories. The team traced that spread to diffusion triggered during the deposition process itself. In other words, a surface treatment reached deep into the powder and altered lithium mobility throughout. Such hidden changes could shift later battery performance without any visible sign. The authors offer spectrally resolved relaxation measurement as a sensitive check during production. It can flag when a coating step has quietly changed the material.
pmc-13289211:
Nehal Refaat Raouf and colleagues study fall risk in rural Egypt in 2026. Their survey ran in two villages in Minia. It held 325 adults aged 60 and up. Talks ran from September to December 2024. A checked Arabic form set fall risk.

Over half, 57.8 percent, faced high fall risk. Many health and home traits tied to risk at first. Five traits held up in final models. Age 75 and up raised the odds. Three or more diseases raised them a lot. Poor self-rated health also raised them. Low activity and home hazards counted too. The authors urge screens in rural clinics. Home safety checks should join them.
pmc-13289311:
Alixandra Rachman and coauthors evaluated a 2026 follow-up survey of Yale's online Climate Change and Health Certificate Program. Started in 2018, the course trains professionals across fields to act on health harms from a warming climate. The study tracked members of the first nine cohorts, from 2018 to 2023, well after training ended.

A total of 205 alumni answered, rating knowledge, confidence, work changes, and wider results. Over 90 percent said they grasped most knowledge areas, but only about seven in ten felt sure using key skills on the job. Still, 91.1 percent had changed how they work, and many joined new climate efforts outside class. Grouping methods found distinct paths from learning to action, useful for improving future cohorts.
pmc-13290711:
A plasma-cell drug is tried as a last resort for a transplant complication in a 2026 letter by Parthenopi Despina Avaniadi and colleagues. They report six kidney transplant recipients whose focal segmental glomerulosclerosis came back after transplantation and resisted standard care.

Every patient had biopsy-proven recurrence with widespread podocyte damage, and all were dialysis-dependent before their transplants. Standard rescue steps, plasmapheresis and anti-CD20 therapy with rituximab (escalated to obinutuzumab in one case), failed to hold remission for any of them. The team therefore turned to daratumumab, which targets plasma cells, as rescue therapy. The letter frames the series against a thin and mixed evidence base, where which patients benefit from the drug remains unsettled.
pmc-13290811:
Transplant tolerance may get stabler soldiers: Arimelek Cortés-Hernández and colleagues describe in 2026 a recipe for growing donor-specific regulatory T cells that keep their identity. Such cells are rare in blood, hard to purify, and prone to drift during long expansion, which has stalled their clinical use.

The protocol first grows regulatory T cells with donor dendritic cells plus interleukin-15, interleukin-2, and retinoic acid, then sorts the CD25+CD27+CD70− subset and expands it with antibody stimulation, rapamycin, and TGF-β. Three weeks yielded a 434-fold expansion at over 95% purity, with the FOXP3 stability marker largely demethylated. The cells suppressed T cell growth in a donor-specific way even after inflammatory challenge and made none of the inflammatory cytokines that signal drift. Cortés-Hernández and colleagues nominate them for long-term transplant tolerance therapy.
pmc-13291211:
Blistering skin in a child can be scabies in disguise. Anupa Khadka and Vikash Paudel report a 2026 case of this rare form. Scabies mites cause fierce itching. Big blisters are rare and often fool doctors.

Their patient was a 12-year-old boy. He had itchy blisters mostly on his hands. A few scratched bumps sat on his trunk and thighs. A skin scope showed the classic jet-with-trail sign between fingers. That sign confirmed scabies under world criteria. Two rounds of mite cream, one week apart, cleared the skin. No marks stayed at four weeks. A scope check can spare needless tests, they argue.
pmc-13291311:
A cell death guard helps plants fight a root rot foe. Yujing Fang leads a 2026 study in Arabidopsis plants. The guard protein BI-1 sits in the cell’s inner web. A foe factor called RTP1 weakens plant defense.

Mutant plants lacking RTP1 made far more BI-1 early on. Plants lacking both lost their cell death control. They also fell sick more under attack. Defense gene activity dropped in double mutants. A burst of reactive oxygen vanished as well. RTP1 binds BI-1 and lowers its levels. Two stress switches turn the BI-1 gene on. This tug-of-war may guide crop protection design.
pmc-13291711:
A new drug eased hard lung hypertension in a tough case. Yujin Nishioka and colleagues report this 2026 case from Japan. Their patient was a 53-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis. Her lung arteries narrowed while vein disease lurked too.

Three oral drugs failed to hold her disease back. Lung pressure climbed steeply despite that care. Standard infused drugs risked flooding her lungs. Sotatercept was chosen to dodge that risk. Her walking distance and heart strain marks improved. Lung pressure eased down as well. Pauses for high hemoglobin did not undo gains. No lung flooding occurred during care.
pmc-13292011:
Awais Mehmood and Romesa Tahir write a 2026 letter questioning a biomarker claim in heart attack subtypes. The letter responds to a study that flagged the gene CDK7 as higher in NSTEMI than STEMI attacks in a Bangladeshi group. That distinction matters if CDK7 becomes a test separating the two. Mehmood and Tahir focus on the study's measurement method instead. Its gene readings were normalized against a single housekeeping gene, GAPDH.

GAPDH, they note, is a poor anchor here because oxygen shortage itself raises its expression. STEMI attacks block arteries fully and starve tissue harder than NSTEMI attacks do. A shifting anchor could fake the very difference the study reports. Reporting guidelines for this assay type ask for at least two validated reference genes. The writers suggest steadier candidates and free tools that pick them. They propose a quick check on the raw values to settle the question.
pmc-13292111:
Tengfei Li and co-authors set out a 2026 Cochrane protocol for comparing drug-free treatments for anxiety and depression in Parkinson's disease. Mood problems affect roughly 40 to 50 percent of people with Parkinson's and deepen dependence, decline, and mortality risk. The protocol states the review's aim plainly: judge how well non-drug options work and how safe they are.

Because it is a protocol, no results are reported yet. The background explains how Parkinson's disrupts dopamine, serotonin, and noradrenaline circuits feeding the limbic system and amygdala-driven fear pathways. It also notes that women and younger-onset patients often carry heavier mood symptoms. The finished review is meant to guide care for a symptom group that drugs alone handle imperfectly.
pmc-13292311:
Susan O'Donovan, Laura Ward, and Ruth Melia map a 2026 scoping review of EMDR therapy for trauma tied to childbirth. Guidelines already recommend eye movement desensitization and reprocessing for post-traumatic stress after birth, but how it is applied to this group stayed murky. Following PRISMA-ScR methods, the team searched six databases and grey literature through about August 2025.

Twenty-nine sources qualified, spanning trials, qualitative studies, systematic reviews, and grey material. Across them, EMDR looked promising for easing birth trauma symptoms. Yet study designs and outcome measures varied widely, and long-term follow-up was scarce. Evidence on partners and on diverse ethnic groups was also thin. The authors call for stronger designs, shared measures, and research that follows families over time before firm guidance can be written.
pmc-13292511:
Bennett Tochukwu Amaechi and colleagues run a 2026 bench test on whether adding calcium hypophosphite supercharges hydroxyapatite toothpaste against early tooth decay. One hundred twenty bovine tooth blocks were split among four pastes: hydroxyapatite alone, hydroxyapatite plus 1 percent calcium compound, the calcium compound alone, and standard 1450 ppm fluoride. A microbial model first grew early lesions, then two weeks of pH cycling with daily paste treatments tested repair.

Every paste remineralized significantly. The combination won clearly, reaching 95.7 percent remineralization against 67.3 for fluoride, 69.4 for hydroxyapatite alone, and 80.4 for the calcium paste in the reported means. The authors credit the additive's ready calcium ions. They say the pairing could strengthen fluoride-free remineralizing pastes, pending mouth-based trials.
pmc-13293411:
M. S. Amithalal leads a 2026 study making silver nanoparticles with leaf extract from Falconeria insignis, a plant not used this way before. Green making avoids harsh chemicals, using plant compounds to form and coat the tiny particles.

A color shift and light tests confirmed particle formation, with a peak in the 300 to 350 nanometer range the authors report. Crystal size averaged 19 nanometers, and shapes were mostly uneven rather than round. Surface groups from plant proteins and phenolics helped form and cap the particles. The particles killed Staphylococcus aureus far better than plain extract or silver salt, hinting at medical uses.
pmc-13293511:
Qingya Pan and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, a vision method to track how tumors shift as a patient breathes during lung radiotherapy. Exact motion data can cut radiation dose to healthy tissue, yet standard four-dimensional scans are slow and labor-heavy.

A chest phantom held eight fake nodules of varied shape and shade, shifted by 10 pixels in four directions and turned by set angles. An improved feature-matching method, called SIFT, was compared with a correlation method. Both tracked straight shifts equally well, with no clear gap by direction. Only the feature method handled turning distortion well, suggesting value for breathing motion checks.
pmc-13293611:
Ying Yao and Simon Hanslmayr comment, in a 2026 article, on new human brain recordings showing that nerve cell firing tunes to rhythm frequency, not just rhythm phase. Brain waves help coordinate activity, and spikes were long known to favor set moments in each wave cycle.

The study under discussion, by Jourahmad and colleagues, found firing also tracks moment-to-moment shifts in wave speed. Three readings are weighed: waves may drive firing, firing may help set wave speed, or both may follow a shared state change. Frequency tuning thus adds a fresh dimension to how brain rhythms may organize activity.
pmc-13293711:
Hiroki Karita and colleagues report, in a 2026 case study, joint brain-spine and gut surgery for an adult with Currarino syndrome. The syndrome is a rare birth condition marked by a missing lower spine bone, a growth before the spine, and bowel malformation. A 45-year-old woman learned of it in pregnancy.

Over time the growth enlarged, blocking her rectum and causing belly pain. Surgeons freed her tethered spinal cord and removed the mass in one combined operation, placing a flap of belly fat tissue to stop spinal fluid leaks. No leak occurred, and after effects were limited to brief bladder trouble and left foot numbness.
pmc-13294411:
Kirsten A Kalverda leads a 2026 pilot of live lung microscopy at the bedside in breathing failure. Chest scans cannot show early microscopic rebuilding after the wet phase of lung injury syndrome, which tracks with poor recovery. Ventilated intensive care patients already set for lung washing got an added confocal laser probe through the bronchoscope, giving near-tissue views of air sacs in real time.

Thirty-three patients joined, with median age 64 years and 61% men in the reported shares. Nearly all met formal injury syndrome criteria. The pilot judged success by getting at least one readable air sac video per session and by tracking harms within a day, with scan comparisons and one autopsy check as extras.
pmc-13294811:
Muhammad W. Amjad and colleagues use ultrasound to steer a healing fat molecule into injured heart muscle, in a 2026 animal study. After a heart attack, restored blood flow still triggers oxidative stress and inflammation that scar the heart and weaken it. A nitroalkene fatty acid can calm both processes, but little of it reaches the heart when given plainly. The team packed it into gas-filled lipid nanoparticles and burst them at the target with focused ultrasound.

In rat models of reperfusion injury and heart scarring, the targeted delivery cut fibrosis significantly more than the same drug given through a vein. Heart output improved, and tissue markers of scarring and inflammation moved in favorable directions, with imaging confirming less scar. The authors present the platform as a combined diagnosis-and-treatment route worth developing for ischemic heart disease.
pmc-13294911:
Huimin Lin and a large team review a screening approach for heart-harming ingredients in Chinese herbal medicines in a 2026 article. Some herbs long viewed as safe can still damage the heart, often without warning. Bioaffinity chromatography, which fishes out compounds that bind chosen biological targets, may catch such risks earlier.

Known harm routes include disturbed heart ion channels, damaged mitochondria, cell death, and metabolic upset. Five forms of the technique are explained, from antibody and lectin columns to cell membrane and receptor based versions. The authors propose using binding based screening for early warning and mechanism work, shifting safety checks from reaction after harm to prediction beforehand.
pmc-13295611:
Charalampia Pylarinou and a large team design reasoning software agents for surgical care in a 2026 article. Older multi-agent systems follow fixed rule trees and stumble on new situations across the long surgical journey. Their framework swaps fixed rules for language model agents that reason, fetch evidence, and check their own thinking.

Six agents cover care before, during, and after heart-lung surgery, each with a defined tool set and authority limits. Every decision that changes the care path must pass a confidence gate with human approval. A supervisor agent settles competing resource requests, aiming to cut false alerts while keeping patients safe in unclear cases.
pmc-13295711:
Elizabeth Adeogun and co-authors measure how gene therapy viruses grip heparin, in a 2026 study of binding heat. Adeno-associated viruses ferry genes into cells for therapy, and makers need better ways to purify them at scale. Heparin, a sugar chain, is a candidate grip for sorting, yet virus amounts are so low that standard heat tools struggle to read the binding.

The team set design rules that let a heat-based method, isothermal titration calorimetry, work at these low amounts. Grip strength rose as the heparin chains grew longer, and the team counted how many chains bind each virus. Buffer mix and acidity shifted the grip as well. The rules should help design sorting steps that catch the virus by its surface.
pmc-13296011:
Scorpion venom peptides as possible medicines are reviewed in 2026 by Man Wang and co-authors. Long prized as probes for nerve channels thanks to their sturdy folded shapes, these molecules now draw interest for antioxidant and protective effects as well.

The review sorts peptides by structure, explains how they tune ion channels, and highlights one molecule, SVHRSP, with protective effects in Parkinson's models. Engineering tricks such as ring closing, nano delivery and computer design aim to fix delivery problems. The authors caution that key findings come from one group and human proof is still lacking.
pmc-13296811:
Xavier Pochon and co-authors field-test, in 2026, TorpeDNA, a cheap compact sampler that collects environmental DNA from seawater so species can be detected without catching anything. Most gear is costly and fussy, so the team trial theirs in three settings from Brittany to a two-thousand-kilometre Pacific crossing.

Profiles matched those from fine laboratory filtration closely, capturing main microbe and plankton groups and known geographic patterns, including ocean animal DNA. Differences traced to filter pore size and water volume, affecting rare and sediment-bound kinds. The authors present the device as fit for large-scale and citizen monitoring.
pmc-13296911:
Atsuya Kameda and colleagues present a rare adolescent case of bent forearm bones without any fracture in a 2026 case report. A sixteen-year-old girl injured her forearm in a bicycle accident, then gradually lost rotation movement. Careful three-dimensional analysis showed her radius and ulna had bowed in different directions.

Surgeons planned separate corrections for each bone, using the healthy arm as the reference. Different cutting techniques were chosen for the radius and the ulna, with rotation checked during the operation. Two months later her rotation range had improved dramatically, and she returned fully to badminton at three months. The case shows why three-dimensional planning matters when both bones deform together.
pmc-13297111:
Murong Wang, Chunying Liu, and Xin Wei review the immune system's role in glaucoma in a 2026 article. High eye pressure remains the main treatable risk factor, yet immune abnormalities keep appearing across glaucoma subtypes. Autoantibodies, cytokine shifts, and altered immune cell sets all feature in the clinical evidence gathered.

Mechanisms span glial-driven inflammation, pattern-recognition signalling, adaptive immune attacks, and complement overactivity. Together they may keep retinal ganglion cells dying even when pressure is controlled. Treatments aimed at these pathways protect nerve cells in animal and laboratory models, the authors report. Patient evidence is still limited, so immune therapy is framed as a precision direction rather than a present standard.
pmc-13298011:
Qian Wang and colleagues built a 2026 machine-vision system that sorts harvested potatoes from soil clods and stones. Their detector adapts YOLOv10n with an added attention module and a dynamic blur strategy for training. A programmable controller and pneumatic actuators remove flagged items while the belt runs.

Comparisons with other lightweight models and orthogonal tests weighed belt speed, spacing between items, and the classification threshold. Belt speed mattered most, followed by spacing and then threshold. Under the best combination found, overall sorting accuracy and impurity removal were both high, while few good tubers were rejected by mistake. The results support stable automatic sorting under postharvest conditions.
pmc-13299711:
Zinc pills lifted blood zinc in weak-muscled boys and men who lacked it, and bone strength inched up in one band of them. Thaís Borges and her team report that in a 2026 study of Duchenne muscular dystrophy. They checked 34 patients three times in eight months. Four of those months brought zinc pills of 5 to 15 mg a day.

At the start, 36.7% of patients lacked zinc in the blood. Bone marks in the round did not shift by much. In the band whose bones were sound at the start, whole-body bone strength rose a touch. The team treat that band find with care, since plain growth in the young can fake such a rise. In the zinc-short band, blood zinc rose by a clear mark. The team back blood zinc checks as part of care for this group.
pmc-13299811:
Rimma Gamirova and others report an infantile case of GM1 gangliosidosis, a lysosomal storage disorder with epilepsy, in a 2026 genetics paper. The child carried two different harmful changes at the very same codon of the GLB1 gene, one from each parent. That exact pairing had not been described before, per the authors.

Both changes alter a residue that holds the enzyme's catalytic domain together, so severe loss of enzyme activity is expected. Earlier cases with changes at this position consistently showed the rapidly progressive infantile form with multisystem involvement. The authors propose the codon as a critical lab hotspot in the gene.
pmc-13300011:
A 2026 outbreak of Andes virus aboard the Dutch cruise ship MV Hondius anchors a review by Laura Scorzolini and three colleagues on infection risks tied to ecotourism. The authors trace how one exposure to rodent waste in Argentina likely seeded cases that then spread between passengers in close quarters.

Andes virus stands out among hantaviruses because people can pass it to each other, and its long incubation period hampers quick detection. The authors urge surveillance that links animal, environmental, and human health data, plus travel medicine that prepares clinicians for exposures in wild settings. Cruise ships, they argue, act as amplifiers rather than sources, so early recognition matters.
pmc-13300211:
K Witte and colleagues report primary results, published in 2026, from the CORE-CPP study of conduction system pacing for people who qualify for cardiac resynchronization therapy. Standard resynchronization uses two ventricular leads, while conduction system pacing uses the heart's own wiring through a single lead in a dual-chamber pacemaker. The analysis drew on Medicare claims from 2017 to 2023 linked with device registration records.

The cohort held 2,207 conduction system pacing patients and 5,693 patients with conventional resynchronization pacemakers. The newer approach was non-inferior on thirty-day complications and reinterventions, and on heart failure hospitalizations at twelve months. It was also linked to lower all-cause mortality over that year. Reintervention rates were similar overall, and the authors conclude the single-lead approach is a credible alternative in this population.
pmc-13300711:
Elizabeth Brouwer and co-authors price out extremity arterial injury care in the United States in a 2026 analysis linking hospital chargemaster records with insurance claims. Graft repair follows about forty-five percent of these injuries, and the patient's own vein is the preferred material, yet injury specific cost data have been missing. The study followed 964 adults repaired between January 2018 and March 2023, tracking the first hospitalization and eighteen months of later care.

Mean hospital charges reached about three hundred seventeen thousand dollars, of which roughly seventy-six thousand was actually reimbursed. Fractures, graft infection, and amputation each added large sums during the stay, and early complications kept driving costs afterward, with graft infection the costliest thread of all. Patients repaired with their own vein used the least follow-up care and stayed most stable. The authors argue graft choice and complication prevention carry heavy financial weight.
pmc-13301311:
D Della Rocca and co-authors ask whether pulsed field ablation makes lab scheduling more predictable than heat based methods, in a 2026 real world study. Their European center analyzed 1,845 atrial fibrillation ablations, mixing first time and repeat cases across pulsed field, cryoballoon, and radiofrequency approaches. They measured not just room and procedure times but how widely those times scattered, since scatter is what wrecks a day's list.

Pulsed field cases were faster on average, roughly fifty-eight minutes of procedure time against seventy-six for cryoballoon in first time vein isolation. Their times also varied significantly less on every statistical test used. Adjusted models kept the advantage for both first time and repeat work. Longer cases clustered around extra ablation targets, implanted devices, mapping use, and prior heart surgery. The authors argue predictability is a resource: steadier times mean tighter scheduling, better throughput, and fewer overruns for the lab.
pmc-13301711:
L Crepin and co-authors trace how fat creeps into the atrial wall, fingering a resident cell as an accomplice, in a 2026 study. Fat around the heart expands, and scar tissue takes its place, forming the atrial cardiomyopathy that feeds fibrillation in metabolic disease. Using gene mapping and cell sorting in right atrial samples, the team located macrophage groups by neighborhood. Mouse work separated two groups, each deleted in turn in animals fed a fattening diet.

Deleting the resident Lyve1 positive macrophages left atria dystrophic: fat cells sat shrunken and sparse, muscle cells swelled, and no matrix scaffolding remained after a month of the diet. Deleting the recruited CCR2 macrophages did the opposite, preventing fibrosis and the cardiomyopathy itself. The authors conclude the resident group controls atrial fat build up while the recruited one drives scarring, a split that reframes inflammation as cellular jobs rather than plain damage.
pmc-13301811:
A brain blood-flow scan before heart surgery might flag who wakes up delirious, Astrid Bergmann and colleagues suggest in a 2026 study. They enrolled 108 patients over seventy set for heart surgery with a bypass machine, scanning both middle brain arteries with an automated Doppler device. Eighty-seven patients stayed in the final count, with confusion checked over three days.

Fourteen patients, sixteen percent, became delirious, and every one had shown abnormal flow readings before surgery. No patient with a clean scan did. Yet ninety-four percent of all patients showed abnormal flow inside the skull despite normal neck artery scans. The authors urge larger multicenter tests of this early signal.
pmc-13302611:
M Foti and a multicentre team map, in a 2026 study, exactly where pulsed field ablation lesions land after vein isolation for atrial fibrillation. The back wall of the left upper chamber sits close behind the veins, and stray lesions there might help or harm. High-density voltage maps made right after treatment revealed the true footprint.

One hundred thirteen patients treated at fourteen centres all achieved complete vein isolation. The average ablated area around the veins was sizeable, and more than half of patients showed unintended back-wall involvement on the fresh maps. About a quarter met the study's narrowing pattern and a small share showed full back-wall closure. During follow-up of roughly nine months, that involvement showed no link to rhythm recurrence.
pmc-13303111:
A metabolic index predicts who recovers poorly after stroke thrombectomy, especially when backup blood flow is weak, Yishu Wang and colleagues find in a 2026 hospital study. Records of 209 patients treated with endovascular therapy between 2022 and 2025 supplied triglyceride-glucose index values, imaging of collateral vessels, and ninety-day function scores. Sixty-four patients ended with poor outcomes.

The index independently nearly doubled the odds of a poor result per unit rise. Its bite concentrated in patients with poor collateral circulation, a significant interaction. Adding the index to clinical variables lifted the model's discrimination to an area under the curve of 0.834. Cheap admission labs, the authors argue, can flag high-risk recoveries early.
pmc-13303811:
Lujain Fouad Khalaf and co-authors test, in a 2026 case-control study, whether past infection with a common lung bacterium tracks with acute coronary syndromes. Chlamydia pneumoniae has long been suspected of feeding artery inflammation, yet proof stays murky. Blood antibodies revealing past exposure were measured in heart patients and matched controls at an Alexandria hospital.

No participant showed signs of fresh infection, so the question concerned older exposure only. Antibodies were present in eighty-three percent of the forty-seven cases against sixty percent of the fifty-three controls. The link survived adjustment for standard risk factors, though the numbers were small and the estimate imprecise. Inflammation marker levels were high in nearly all cases regardless of antibody status, and the authors demand prospective proof.
pmc-13305111:
Petr S. Sokolov, Lydia V. Ermakova, and co-authors report, in a 2026 materials study, a new way to build pixelated radiation detectors for X-ray imaging. Flat-panel detectors convert X-rays to light in a scintillator layer before sensors read it out. Existing plate designs lose light through translucency or low density, blurring the image.

Using light-based 3D printing, the team formed green bodies, then sintered them into two-layer ceramic elements. The base layer is transparent, non-glowing garnet, while the top layer holds scintillating pixels about two hundred thirty micrometers square. Tests under ultraviolet light and alpha particles showed spatial resolution near four tenths of the pixel size. The authors present the integrated process as a route to sharper medical and neutron detectors through finer printed pixels.
pmc-13306111:
Zepeng Zheng reported a severe skin ulcer illness after caesarean birth in a 2026 case report. A 24-year-old first-time mother had emergency surgery at 29 weeks and 4 days after cord prolapse, then developed painful ulcers around the wound by day seven.

Antibiotics failed and cleaning surgery worsened the wound through a trauma response, enlarging it to 21.5 × 11.0 cm in reported measures. Diagnosis on day eleven rested on appearance, sterile cultures and tissue findings, and strong immune-suppressing treatment followed. The patient left hospital on day thirty, with full skin closure reached later in follow-up care.
pmc-13306411:
Julia C. Andrade spun all water based tiny fibres from PVP blends in a 2026 study. Two mix partners were tried one by one, a seaweed gum and a vitamin, to split how each shapes the spin run.

Base mixes held 20% PVP, with gum at 1 to 5 percent or vitamin at 1 to 10 percent in the reported plan. Gum raised how well the mix carried charge, while the vitamin left it near flat. UV light shone on fibres as they formed, and skin and strength tests closed the check set for both blends.
pmc-13307211:
Kehoe argues that joint design work in mental health often shuts out the people it claims to hear. She calls this wrong epistemic injustice, which means some kinds of knowledge get pushed aside. Lived experience, meaning what patients know first hand, is often valued least.

Kehoe sets out a three-step cycle built on ideas from restorative practice, which focus on truth and repair. Step one asks groups to name harms and tell the truth. Step two works on repair and trust between staff and patients. Step three moves to shared design of future services. The aim is fair say, not just a seat at the table.
pmc-13307311:
Sebastian Knoll and co-authors report in 2026 on a paired molecule that joins ferrocene to a Dawson type oxide cluster, with no noble metal used at all. Visible light splits charge inside the pair, as an electron moves from the iron based part toward the cluster.

The team tracked that light driven step with several forms of spectroscopy and with computer based quantum chemistry. The split charge could then switch on organic peroxides in both directions and free oxygen based radicals. Results offer a design guide for light active pairs built from common, low cost elements for solar fuel and catalysis work.
pmc-13307411:
Yi-Kai Hu and co-authors ask in 2026 where cancer stem cells in liver tumours come from, using single cell data from 109 samples and 44 patients in five public groups. They also sorted stem and non stem cells from a lab line and tracked gene marks over two weeks of growth.

Mutation counts and family trees placed stem cells at the far ends of tumour growth, not at its root. About 78 percent of the gene marks that set stem cells apart stayed in place after the cells changed form, a kind of locked in memory. A 16 gene score built from those marks flagged early return of disease.
pmc-13307611:
Jean Baltzer and co-authors explore in 2026 whether how a knee moves during walking before surgery can guide total knee replacement planning with robot help. Of 30 patients booked for surgery, 26 had a full gait check before the operation, and 17 had a repeat check six months later.

Knees that leaned more inward during walking showed wider looseness on the outer side when straight and tighter looseness inside when bent. In a small inward leaning subgroup, pre surgery motion plus planned looseness foresaw post surgery motion very well. Walking scores also tracked with how patients rated their new knee, which hints at a path to more personal planning.
pmc-13308611:
See Jie Yow and co-authors study in 2026 how threat context shapes whether neutrophils burst and die after inflammasome firing, a step that frees defence signals. Neutrophils often free those signals without bursting, and the switch that lets them burst has stayed murky until now.

A growth factor called GM-CSF licensed bursting after two sensor types fired, by boosting an early priming step in the cells. A strong bacterial primer did the same, while a weaker one did not reach that bar. Bursting also needed a self loop through a tumour necrosis factor receptor, plus a membrane protein for the final tear. One sensor type stood apart and gained nothing from the factor.
pmc-13309011:
Brittany Peterson and co-authors cost out in 2026 a national door to door azithromycin drive to cut child deaths in Niger, from trial roots in 80 Dosso towns. They paired fine cost counts with field notes to price a twice a year round for children aged 1 to 59 months in non urban areas.

At 90 percent cover, the yearly national bill would run to 12.5 million dollars, or 1.59 dollars for each dose handed out in their model. Sparse regions cost far more per dose, up to 3.61 dollars at the top end of the range. Training ate 16.4 percent of all costs, so shared training with other health drives could trim the bill for states.
pmc-13309711:
Manish Rai, Rajeshwari Gore, and Piyush Setu describe in 2026 the anaesthetic care of an eight-year-old girl who has severe spastic quadriplegic cerebral palsy who needed cataract surgery with a lens implant. Her stiffness, bent joints, and speech limits cloud every step of anaesthesia. A full pre-anaesthetic review and family talks came before the surgery.

Early troubles centred on placing a drip line and placing her rigid limbs safely. Beyond those hurdles, the work and healing ran smoothly under general anaesthesia. The child weighed only nine kilos, far below growth norms, which shaped drug and gear choices. Breathing-in risk from excess fluids also hangs over such cases in general. The authors conclude that careful checks, fitted drugs, and a team approach can still deliver a calm course. Each child may react in her own way, they caution, so planning must be her own.
pmc-13309811:
Imran Ahmad and Yousaf Jamal Mahsood run a randomised trial in 2026 comparing two injection strategies for diabetic macular swelling in eyes that already carry an artificial lens. Eighty-two patients at a Peshawar teaching hospital split evenly between monthly bevacizumab alone and a combined first treatment adding steroid placed behind the eye wall. Vision and macular thickness were measured over four months.

Both groups improved significantly in sight and thickness from their starting points. The combination group finished with better vision scores and a thinner macula than the single-drug group. Its steroid dose was given once, at the first visit, alongside the standard drug. Swelling at the centre of vision is the main sight threat in diabetes, so extra drying power matters. The authors propose the single combined opening treatment as a stronger start for this patient group.
pmc-13310211:
Luke Tattersall examines how variants of a cell sensor shape bone cell behavior in a 2026 study. The sensor, P2RX7, responds to ATP, a molecule plentiful around bone, and helps govern bone balance. Natural variants and shortened forms of the sensor can strengthen or weaken its action.

Full and shortened sensor forms, alone and paired, plus three single-letter variants, were placed into bone-forming cells. Calcium entry, pore opening, cell growth, enzyme activity, mineral laying, and bone gene activity were all measured. Variant effects differed by form and pairing, with known gain and loss variants behaving distinctly. The author uses the pattern to explain how inherited sensor differences may shift bone mass and turnover.
pmc-13310911:
Liang Gao led a 2026 study on which E. coli traits turn harmless newborn colonization into invasive infection. The germ can pass from mother to baby at birth and sometimes cause life threatening illness. Gene traits that split those paths were unclear in proven mother baby pairs.

Pairs totaled 43 in number, with 27 invasive cases and 16 colonization cases confirmed by genome match. One strain type appeared only in invasive cases. Capsule and iron uptake genes were far more common in invasive strains, and a model named four strong predictors. All top strain isolates carried the three key genes together. Gene checks may flag risky strains early.
pmc-13311111:
Guolin Song and colleagues profile a drug resistant germ in a psychiatric hospital in a 2026 study. Corynebacterium striatum can infect long stay patients, yet telling true infection from harmless carriage is hard. Isolates from psychiatric inpatients were tested for drug response and gene makeup.

Thirty isolates were gathered, and most resisted many drugs. Gene reading found stacks of resistance genes plus traits for iron uptake and sticking to tissue. Family trees showed wide diversity with loose ties to ward place. A five item infection score sorted infection from carriage better than any single marker in early tests. Outside checks are required.
pmc-13311211:
Kenza Qitout and co-authors present a 2026 dataset built to help computers find Barbary macaques in zoo images. The monkeys are an endangered North African primate, and tracking them by eye takes much staff time.

The set holds 1742 labeled photos with 6689 single monkey sightings, filmed from many angles, times of day, and seasons at a French zoo. Each sighting carries an outline mask and an age label, which goes beyond simple box labels. The team trained several YOLO models on the data to test how well they work. The set gives conservation and zoo teams a shared base for building automatic watch tools for primates.
pmc-13311311:
Minmin Wen and co-authors, in 2026, analyze a survey study on thyroid hormones, heart disease, and a measure of body aging in older adults. The aging measure is called phenotypic age acceleration.

Data came from the 2007 to 2010 rounds of the United States NHANES survey. Among people aged 60 and over, higher free T3 levels tied to lower heart disease odds. The aging measure carried about a fifth of that link in the analysis, at 21.13 percent for free T3 in this model. Total T3 showed a like pattern. The results hint that slowing body aging could help guard the older heart.
pmc-13311911:
Anita Caruso and co-authors in 2026 present a study on emotional distress and guilt in women carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations, and how those feelings shape choices about having children.

Carriers face high lifetime breast and ovarian cancer risks, and prevention steps carry heavy physical and mental loads. The study measures guilt forms, including survivor guilt and a sense of total responsibility for passing on risk. Distress ran stronger around telling others the result than around the test itself, on the authors' account, and depression rates passed those in the general population. Support for carriers should treat guilt as a core issue.
pmc-13312811:
Dian Fu and co-authors analyze, in a 2026 retrospective study, whether what men eat relates to semen quality when infertility stems from varicocele. This vein disorder is a leading cause of male infertility and works largely through oxidative stress, so the team asked whether antioxidant and micronutrient intake tracks with sperm measures in affected men.

Diet records and semen tests from 380 men treated between 2018 and 2023 were compared across intake levels for vitamin C, vitamin E, zinc, selenium, CoQ10, and L-carnitine. The highest intake group showed better sperm concentration, motility, and shape. Zinc and CoQ10 best predicted concentration, vitamin E and L-carnitine predicted forward motility, and vitamin C intake ran opposite to sperm DNA damage. The authors argue nutrition deserves a central place in managing varicocele-related infertility.
pmc-13312911:
Levi T. Flom and co-authors characterize, in a 2026 mouse study, the brain cell groups, or ensembles, that light up for two competing rewards at once. Addiction research links drug seeking to small ensembles of neurons tagged by their activity, usually studied one reward at a time. The team built a place preference test where one chamber meant cocaine and the other meant chocolate.

Using genetically engineered mice whose active neurons can be permanently labeled, 33 males and 33 females learned both associations. After conditioning they favored the cocaine chamber when no reward was present. Ensembles tagged in cortex and nucleus accumbens during testing matched the size of those from single-reward training, and context-tagged cells grew larger than home-cage controls. Ensemble size, though, did not track how strongly each mouse preferred a chamber, a caution for reading preference off cell counts.
pmc-13314411:
Silvia Mihaela Ilie and colleagues find a viral fingerprint that may flag breast cancers ripe for immune therapy, in a study from 2026. Old retroviruses sit in our DNA, making up about 8 percent of the genome as stated in the report. When cancer cells wake them, the immune system can react as if a virus were present.

The team used public RNA data from The Cancer Genome Atlas for breast tumors and matched normal tissue, counting retrovirus activity with a tool called Telescope. They built a signature of 19 such viruses whose activity tied to signs of this viral mimicry inside tumors. Luminal breast cancers with high signature scores looked more immune-active and more likely to answer immune therapy. The marker could help pick patients for drugs that free the immune system.
pmc-13314511:

pmc-13318111:

pmc-13319711:

pmc-13320011:

pmc-13320411:

pmc-13320511:

pmc-13320711:

pmc-13321211:

pmc-13322911:

pmc-13325911:

pmc-13338611:

pmc-13339011:

pmc-13339111:

pmc-13340211:

pmc-13340311:

pmc-13341411:

pmc-13341511:

pmc-13343611:

pmc-13344011:

pmc-13345811:

pmc-13345911:

pmc-13346111:

pmc-13350711:

pmc-13351711:

pmc-13376311:

pmc-13391711:

pmc-13394611:

pmc-13397511:

pmc-13397611:

pmc-13397711:

pmc-13398711:
