It also held up against brute force, statistical probing, chosen-plaintext tricks, added noise, and cropping. The authors aim it at image protection across cloud and internet-of-things settings.
pmc-13408911:
Jin Muk Kang and colleagues turn the world's leftover immunity to COVID-19 into a cancer vaccine booster in 2026. Dendritic cell vaccines against cancer often flop because tumour antigens provoke weak help from CD4 T cells. Their platform, PROTEXI, loads dendritic cells with tumour targets for killer T cells alongside helper epitopes from the coronavirus spike protein, which most immune systems already remember.

In mouse melanoma and breast cancer models the vaccine slowed tumour growth and extended survival, drawing T cells into previously cold tumours and broadening the attack through epitope spreading. It also paired well with other immunotherapies in resistant models. In humanised mice, spike help boosted responses against two human tumour antigens and cut tumour burden. The strategy suggests yesterday's antiviral memory can be drafted into tomorrow's cancer therapy.
pmc-13409011:
Victorien Faivre-Rampant and colleagues compare in 2026 two laboratory stand-ins for standing up: tilting the whole body head-up, and sucking blood toward the legs with lower-body vacuum. Both drain blood from the chest, but they differ in heart orientation and where fluid pools. Thirty young adults, half healthy and half with type 1 diabetes, experienced both in random order at graded intensities while sensors tracked fluid shifts and heart function.

Carefully matched settings produced equal drops in chest blood volume, yet tilting pooled blood in the abdomen while vacuum pooled it in the pelvis. The heart's stroke volume fell further during tilt, though faster beating defended overall output, whereas output sagged at strong vacuum. Participants with diabetes ran consistently faster heart rates but preserved the other measures. The study warns that the two common tests are not interchangeable.
pmc-13410111:
Husnu Cagri Genc and colleagues report in 2026 on three signaling molecules in people with stomach cancer. The molecules, called PANX1, P2RY2, and TLR3, take part in cell chatter and immune defense. Long-term stomach inflammation is tied to this cancer, so such signals might mark its presence.

Blood and gene tests covered 45 patients and 45 healthy people of similar makeup. Only PANX1 stood out: its blood level ran higher in patients and stayed tied to disease after other factors were weighed. Gene activity shifts for all three fell short of clear statistical support. Each marker alone sorted patients from controls poorly, so none is ready as a stand-alone test.
pmc-13410611:
Bin Liang and colleagues mapped the genes behind productive rice stems in a 2026 study of 270 rice lines. Effective tiller number, the count of stems that actually bear grain, shapes yield. Few of the genes found so far have reached breeding programs, so the team scanned more than a million DNA markers for links to that trait.

They found 214 linked markers on eight chromosomes and 12 linked regions, including a new gene, OsIAA3, whose extra activity raised stem counts in test plants. The paper also supplies tested DNA markers and favorable gene variants, giving breeders practical tools for picking higher-yielding rice without waiting through full field seasons.
pmc-13410711:
Valentina Quintero-Santofimio leads a multinational team reporting in 2026 on how workplace exposures wear down lungs over time. Dusts, fumes, and farm chemicals drive chronic lung disease, above all where rules are weak. Their data come from the Burden of Obstructive Lung Disease study across 17 sites.

Following 4,237 people for a median of ten years, the team linked exposure records with breathing tests and symptoms. Moderate to high exposure to mixed vapors, gases, dusts, and fumes tied to a faster fall in a key breathing ratio. Pesticide exposure showed a similar tie and also raised the risk of wheeze. No such links appeared for solvents or metals, and patterns held for both sexes.
pmc-13410811:
Xin Qin and colleagues develop in 2026 light-activated iridium compounds that kill kidney cancer cells through two death routes at once. Kidney cancer often returns, spreads, and shrugs off drugs. Triggering several regulated death paths together is a newer way to break that resistance.

The two compounds home to mitochondria, the cell's power stations. Under white light they wreck those structures, spilling DNA and calcium into the cell. Leaked DNA fires an immune alarm and one fiery death pathway, while calcium overflow drives a second, swelling death pathway. In animals, treated tumors shrank, distant tumors also cleared through immune action, and safety looked good. One drug thus sparks a whole network of attack.
pmc-13410911:
Thong Huu Tran, Hien Thi Thu Nguyen, and Trung Huu Tran review in 2026 how well bedside warning scores predict death or intensive care need in poorer countries. Scores built in rich health systems may misread patients where staffing, labs, and case mix differ. Their review pooled studies from emergency departments in those settings.

Twenty-six studies with over 45,000 patients fed the analysis. For predicting death in hospital, the NEWS family of scores caught more cases but raised more false alarms, while a rival score, MEWS, proved stricter and missed more. For intensive care admission, NEWS gave the most balanced showing. No score excelled everywhere, so local checking before adoption is the authors' advice.
pmc-13411211:
Jonathan Suess and Nicolas Cornelissen present in 2026 a two-enzyme assembly line that builds the energy-carrying building blocks of nucleic acids from simple starting pieces. Making these triphosphate blocks chemically gives poor yields at the last step. A universal green route would serve labs and drug makers alike.

One enzyme, borrowed from fruit flies, takes the first step using a pinch of ATP. The second enzyme, from a gut bacterium, spends cheap polyphosphate to finish the job and recycle the ATP. Only trace amounts of ATP are needed to keep the loop turning. The one-pot system made all standard blocks plus eleven modified ones, including a key ingredient for mRNA medicines at milligram scale.
pmc-13412011:
Tim Mackey and co-authors describe, in a 2026 prototyping study, a blockchain platform built to keep Indigenous communities in charge of their research data. Past misuse of Indigenous health data has pushed demands for Indigenous data sovereignty, meaning communities set the terms for collection, storage, and use. The project paired UC San Diego with the Native BioData Consortium over two years.

A community advisory board guided design through public meetings, conference sessions, and repeated rounds of co-design. The resulting proof of concept, called b-IDS, combines a web front end, an Ethereum network running smart contracts, and an off-chain database linked to genomic repositories. The authors argue the design supports timely oversight, shared decisions, and consent that communities control.
pmc-13412311:
Jinwen Chen and colleagues studied a long noncoding RNA, GAS6-AS1, in childhood neuroblastoma in 2026 to test its worth as a warning marker. Neuroblastoma is the most common solid tumor outside the brain in children. Its course varies widely, so the team measured the RNA in tumor tissue and tracked growth, spread, and survival links.

High GAS6-AS1 levels marked worse features and poorer outcomes on their own, and silencing it slowed tumor cell growth and spread by freeing a small RNA, miR-3200-3p. The paper nominates GAS6-AS1 as both a prognosis marker and a possible drug target for this childhood cancer.
pmc-13413711:
Thamer S. Almoneef and Maged A. Aldhaeebi design in 2026 a small four-port metasurface antenna that works on three X-band channels for MIMO links. Such systems need several ports that barely talk over each other, all in a tight space. Their build tiles a grid of 32 by 32 shaped cells and feeds it at four ports. It aims at three set channels in the X band, near nine to ten gigahertz.

A built test piece matched the computer models well at all three channels. Low crosstalk showed the ports stay apart, so each channel stays clean. Gain passed 12 decibels at each channel and peaked near 13 in their tests. Scores for channel spread and loss stayed strong too. The authors put the design up for radar and fast wireless use.
pmc-13414011:
Sang-Uk Byun and co-authors mix green quantum dots into a red conversion layer in 2026 and get brighter, purer red light for displays. Quantum dot screens excite red and green dots with blue light, but red-only layers leak blue and waste photons unless made thick. The team dispersed both dot colours in silicone rubber, sweeping the recipe and thickness while tracking spectra, leakage, and conversion efficiency.

A red-only layer needed 38 micrometres to reach 16.7 percent efficiency with heavy red loading. The mixed layer beat it at just 5.6 micrometres, scoring 19.3 percent while blocking blue leakage more firmly in their measurements. Extra blue absorption, plus green dots re-emitting energy that red dots then soak up, likely explains the gain. Thinner, brighter conversion films could simplify display making.
pmc-13415911:
Viktorija Lodeikina, Liga Kuksa, Iveta Ozere, and Reinis Riekstins report genital and urinary tuberculosis that looked like testicular cancer, in a 2026 case. A man aged forty-one had chronic epididymal inflammation, a testicular mass, and a left kidney swelling toward destruction. Removal of the testicle showed granulomatous inflammation with no cancer.

Urine molecular testing found tuberculosis complex DNA, and one urine culture later grew the bacterium. The kidney, fully destroyed, was removed and confirmed as tuberculous on examination. Lung imaging showed mild apical changes, while airway samples stayed negative. Combined imaging, tissue, molecular, and culture evidence clinched a tricky diagnosis.
pmc-13416111:
Rosanna Huchzermeier and co-authors test whether deleting a pollutant sensing receptor in kidney tubules changes artery plaque in mice, in 2026. The aryl hydrocarbon receptor responds to tryptophan breakdown products and drives inflammation, and kidney patients face high cardiovascular risk. Their mice lacked the receptor only in kidney epithelium and ate a high fat diet for twelve weeks.

Plaque outcomes matched control mice exactly. Surprisingly, kidney inflammation and scarring also stayed unchanged without the receptor. A high fat diet alone may not provoke a strong receptor driven response in kidney lining, the authors conclude. The negative result narrows where this receptor matters for disease.
pmc-13416711:
Joseph Cho and a large team introduce EchoAI-Peds, a deep learning system for heart ultrasound in children, in a 2026 report. Birth defects of the heart affect about one in a hundred births worldwide. Earlier tools often handled one task or one view, so this model reads whole studies with many videos at once.

Training used more than 700,000 videos from over 12,000 Stanford studies done between 2014 and 2021. The system detects 28 defects, structural problems, repairs, and procedures together. Accuracy stayed high on a separate Philadelphia cohort from 2024 and 2025, and it beat two adult trained models by a wide margin.
pmc-13416811:
Pedersen and colleagues examine the case files behind rapid tranquillisation, the forced sedation used to calm disturbance in psychiatric wards, for signs ethnicity shapes decisions. Minority patients receive this practice more often, but the paperwork has rarely been read closely. Their 2026 qualitative study selects nineteen tranquillisation cases from Danish forensic inpatient units between 2021 and 2025. Cases are sorted by patients' country of birth. The team compares the build up, negotiation, and follow up.

Headline use looked similar across groups, but the process differed. Rising distress in minority patients was written down later, often just before sedation. Majority patients' escalation was charted over longer stretches. Notes on planning, offers of voluntary medication, and debriefs were thin and thinner still for minority patients. Repeated sedation cycles appeared in both groups. The disparities, the authors argue, accumulate through process gaps rather than biased calls, where training and documentation reform should aim.
pmc-13418311:
Gajdusek and colleagues report the first mixed reality planning used to close a leak beside a heart device. The device, a plug in the heart's left atrial appendage, guards against stroke in atrial fibrillation patients who cannot take blood thinners. Leaks are common and raise clot risk. This one sat in a hard rear upper spot. Their 2026 case concerns a 69 year old man whose plug, placed in 2023, left a cavity with two way flow on scans.

The team rebuilt his anatomy as a hologram in a HoloLens headset and walked it before the procedure. They picked a lower rear puncture path and a telescoping catheter plan. In October 2024 they closed the leak with coils under ultrasound guidance, following the rehearsed route. Planning in 3D, the authors argue, turns a blind corner into a mapped one, and they offer the workflow for other structural repairs.
pmc-13418511:
Kong and colleagues profiled immune cells in 2026 from pigs vaccinated against a major swine virus. Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus costs the pig industry heavily, and why some vaccines protect fully is unclear. The team combined single-cell gene readings with T cell receptor profiling in animals that ended up fully, partly, or not protected after virus challenge.

Protected animals held distinct CD8 subsets marked by clonal expansion, meaning many copies of the same cell, and strong killing programmes. Unprotected animals instead piled up worn-out CD8 cells bearing exhaustion markers such as CTLA4. Swapping the virus's structural protein region reshaped the cell mix toward the protective pattern and improved outcomes. Full activation also needed signals from macrophages and help from CD4 cells.
pmc-13418611:
Marcus Jia-Ming Ng and colleagues modify a classic back muscle flap to cover a severe leg wound, in a 2026 surgical report. The latissimus dorsi flap, moved with its blood vessels as a free flap, is a workhorse for large traumatic leg defects. Sometimes muscle alone cannot cover all exposed bone in circumferential wounds.

Their twist repositions the flap's skin paddle segment, guided by its perforating vessels, as an extra local flap within the main flap. That bonus skin reaches critical exposed areas the muscle misses. The authors present the method as simple and reproducible for extensive wounds needing every bit of coverage.
pmc-13419211:
ZhaoLiang Zhu and Xin Huang model what happens to buried plastic-and-steel pipelines when a strike-slip fault shifts the ground beneath them. These hybrid pipes pair a plastic body with a steel frame for strength, and they cross active fault country in many regions. The team built a detailed three-dimensional computer model of pipe and soil moving together.

Layered modeling with locked contacts reproduced how the plastic and steel share the strain. Past failures tend to start where the glue layer between materials breaks down, letting steel wires corrode and snap until the pipe leaks. The simulations trace that failure chain under different fault slips. Engineers can use the results to set safer crossing angles and burial depths where pipelines must span a fault.
pmc-13419311:
Zhuang Liu and colleagues studied 871 Chinese college students in 2026 to test how academic stress, depression, and parent-child bonds interact. Stress and distant family ties each predicted higher depression, yet whether closeness buffers stress or sharpens it was unresolved.

Close parent-child ties did not cushion stress as hoped; instead they tracked with heightened sensitivity to academic pressure in the interaction analysis. The paper complicates simple advice to lean on family, suggesting campus support must address how closeness itself shapes stress responses. Campus counselors can use the pattern to tailor support for stressed students.
pmc-13419411:
Kinsey McClure Johannemann and colleagues test a pharmacist-led rule that screens every starting order for IV vancomycin, a strong antibiotic often begun on suspicion alone. The quasi-experimental study compares matched winter periods, January to March 2024 against the same months in 2025, across sites in one health system. Chart review covered 200 patients, split evenly between the two periods.

Appropriate starting orders jumped from 55 percent before the rule to 97 percent after it took effect, a firm statistical gain. Use totals and blood level checks per patient days were tracked as side measures. Death rates within 30 days did not shift between periods, suggesting tighter control cost no safety. The authors present the rule as a practical model for other hospitals fighting antibiotic overuse.
pmc-13420211:
Liujing Zhang and colleagues test a probiotic strain called CP-9, a form of Bifidobacterium animalis, in healthy infants. Their 2026 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examines gut microbes, immune markers, and safety in babies aged six to thirty-six months.

Infants received CP-9 or a placebo for three months, with growth, blood counts, immune markers, and stool microbes measured before and after. All infants grew appropriately in height and head circumference. The probiotic significantly raised gut Bifidobacterium levels and shifted a pathway that builds polyunsaturated fatty acids. Blood and inflammation markers stayed in normal ranges, stools improved, and rates of allergy or respiratory infection did not rise. The authors conclude CP-9 showed no obvious short-term safety concerns in this age group.
pmc-13420511:
Alexander J Lepak and colleagues trial a point-of-care multiplex test for sore throat at an academic urgent care clinic, where throat infections drive heavy visit volume. The test names several germs from one swab at the visit itself, rather than days later from a lab. Clinicians and patients were surveyed before and after rollout on how the test felt in practice.

At least one germ showed up in 149 of 200 patients, some 74.5 percent of the group in the reported share, with patterns split sharply between children and adults. Prescribing of antibiotics was tracked beside the detections to see whether answers changed habits. Both clinician and patient groups reported high satisfaction and judged the test useful for decisions. Fast naming may curb antibiotics given just in case, a quiet driver of resistance.
pmc-13420611:
Della A. Forster and colleagues evaluate a culturally tailored midwifery program for First Nations mothers in Victoria, Australia, where outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander families run far worse than for others. The program, Baggarrook Yurrongi, gives each woman continuity with known midwives across pregnancy, birth, and the early weeks, at three large Melbourne maternity services. Culture sits at the center of the model rather than at its edge.

Later data covered 62,499 non-First Nations births and 1038 First Nations births in the totals reported, and 669 of the eligible First Nations women, some 64.5 percent of that group, received the model of care. Outcomes before and after rollout were compared without randomization. The authors call for ongoing outcome tracking and cost proof to support wider rollout.
pmc-13420711:
Gonçalo Araújo and colleagues describe a neck bypass built to keep blood flowing to brain and arm while a tumor at the top of the lung was cut out whole. Such superior sulcus tumors often grip the subclavian artery, threatening both territories at once. Their patient was a 47-year-old woman treated first with induction therapy, which shrank the tumor before surgery.

The operation rerouted blood from the carotid to the arm artery and moved the vertebral artery to preserve its flow. Key nerves, including the phrenic nerve along the scalene muscle, were found and spared during the dissection. A scan before discharge showed both reconstructions open and flowing well. The case gives chest and vascular teams a joint playbook for a tumor few centers see.
pmc-13421111:
Richard A Bryant and colleagues set out the protocol for UNITY, a longitudinal survey of mental health in Ukrainian children and their caregivers during the war. Russia's full invasion in 2022 has placed the whole population under sustained stress, yet research has centered on adults. Child conduct problems, better reported by caregivers, have been especially neglected.

The study will recruit 3,000 children through schools across 22 regions of Ukraine, in three planned waves with more to follow after the war. Caregiver and child reports together give the fuller picture the authors argue for. Findings will guide services for a generation growing up under fire, in schools and clinics alike. A shared protocol also lets later studies in other conflicts copy the design.
pmc-13421211:
Aviel Avraham Azulay and co-authors describe, in a 2026 report, how a cardiothoracic team managed high-velocity gunshot wounds to the chest during a mass casualty incident. All patients were injured on October 7, 2023, each by a single military rifle round passing through lung tissue.

The cohort held 11 men aged 19 to 49, nine soldiers and two civilians. Six needed emergency chest surgery within the first day for ongoing bleeding, controlled mainly by deep suturing of lung tissue or temporary packing. The authors also track blood clots in veins, regional pain control and early psychiatric support. Their aim is practical: to show how damage-control priorities and follow-up care can be tailored after such an event.
pmc-13421511:
Zainab Alaithan and colleagues tailored carbon adsorbents in 2026 for removing anthracene, a carcinogenic polycyclic hydrocarbon, from industrial effluents. Nitric acid treatment and metal ion-exchange were tested on activated carbon and carbon black to see which surface changes actually lift uptake.

Acid boosted carbon black removal from 69 to 74 percent but cut activated carbon from 60 to 50 percent as micropores collapsed. Metal loading hurt both materials and the best carbon black held 70 to 74.5 percent removal across five reuse cycles. Wastewater engineers gain design rules that favor surface area and pore structure over metal decoration.
pmc-13422011:
Hernández-Ayala, Guzmán-López, and Galano ask how trofinetide, the first approved drug for Rett syndrome, works, since its mechanism was never pinned down. Docking tests the fit, and hundred nanosecond motion simulations check whether the drug stays seated.

The drug sat stably in the binding pockets of the transporter and the muscarinic receptor. It also sat inside the enzyme's catalytic cleft. On GABAA and AMPA it only skimmed surfaces. A proline fragment of the drug kept anchoring it. These are testable hypotheses, the authors stress, for lab follow up and for designing successors.
pmc-13422311:

Middle-ear effusion affects most children at some point. Standard checks mislabel up to a quarter of cases. That leads to operations, ear drum punctures and tube placements, that were never needed.

Their hospital's own records confirmed a twenty-nine percent false-positive rate across more than four and a half thousand procedures. On donated human tissue, the team injected salt solution behind the eardrum and imaged it with a customised hyperspectral endoscope that maps water content. The water index read the fluid with about eighty-nine percent sensitivity and eighty-three percent accuracy. The authors propose the method to cut unnecessary surgery.
pmc-13422811:
Ofosu and a large Canadian team lay out in 2026 the DECIDE-T study protocol. The plan rolls out one shared digital care pathway across a whole province for children needing a tracheostomy, a breathing tube placed in the neck. Such pathways have shortened hospital stays at single centers.

The pathway, built into the electronic health record, covers everything from the decision to operate through acute care, the move home, and eventual tube removal. The evaluation compares care before and after rollout at multiple centers without a separate control group. It runs in four phases: assessing each site's barriers, matching strategies to them, launching the pathway while tracking clinical, cost, and reach outcomes, and sharing the lessons. Surveys, interviews, audits, and patient records feed the analysis, with costs judged from the public system's viewpoint.
pmc-13423311:
Aliasghar Keramatinia leads a nine-author bioinformatics study proposing anxiety as a risk factor for gastric cancer. The stomach cancer burden is usually blamed on genes, Helicobacter pylori infection, diet, obesity, and alcohol, and the team asked whether anxiety shares molecular machinery with the tumour.

Starting from public gene-expression data, they filtered 658 changed genes against cancer databases to find core gastric cancer genes, then checked overlap with anxiety-linked genes. Five genes surfaced in both sets: CHEK2, SLC2A1, EZH2, STAT1, and MMP9, each switched on more strongly in tumour data. Survival databases supported their relevance. The authors conclude that anxiety and gastric cancer share dysregulated genes, hinting at a molecular route between the two.
pmc-13423811:
Minghao Wang and five colleagues, including senior author Vy M Dong, present a copper-catalysed method for attaching aryl groups to pyrazoles at either of two neighbouring nitrogen atoms, on demand. Pyrazoles appear in many blockbuster medicines, yet standard coupling chemistry favours one attachment point, shutting off whole families of candidate structures.

The trick uses highly strained aryne partners and tunes how copper grips the pyrazole, steering the new bond to one nitrogen or the other under mild conditions. Mechanistic work maps how size and electronic effects decide the outcome. The authors frame the switchable selectivity as a general blueprint for taming nitrogen-rich rings, speeding the late-stage diversification that drug discovery depends on.
pmc-13423911:
Braivo and colleagues reported in 2026 a pilot screening program for early type 1 diabetes in high-risk children in Latvia. About half of newly diagnosed Latvian children arrive with diabetic ketoacidosis, a dangerous acid build-up from insulin lack, so early warning matters. The team invited brothers and sisters of patients, aged 2 to 17 years, for two-stage blood testing for diabetes autoantibodies at a children's hospital in Riga.

Braivo screened 83 children in the first stage, and about a third had at least one positive result. In the second stage, half of those tested negative for all four antibodies, while a few children carried two or three. All had normal blood sugar at testing. During follow-up, two children developed full diabetes and one more reached the stage just before it. The authors argue screening can flag risk early enough to act.
pmc-13424011:
Favor and colleagues published a 2026 study on Spanish-language resources for rare-disease patients in Alabama. Rare genetic diseases already leave families hunting for support and clear information. For Spanish speakers, language gaps pile onto that burden every day. The team interviewed eleven experts who work with these patients and families.

Experts said Spanish-speaking medical staff and interpreters are too often missing. Written and online resources in Spanish exist but reach patients only patchily. Where Spanish resources do exist, their quality drew praise from the experts. The trouble is uneven rollout, not poor content, in their account. The authors urge wider translation access and standard use of what exists. Standard steps for using those resources would cut the burden further.
pmc-13424211:

They grouped mothers by blood glucose, fed some a ketogenic diet, and measured fetal growth, insulin release, and the insulin-producing beta cells of the fetal pancreas.

Mild maternal diabetes produced oversized fetuses whose beta cells multiplied, matured early, and released excess insulin under a strongly activated growth pathway. Severe diabetes instead shrank beta cell mass and impaired their function, leaving fetuses growth-restricted in the womb. The ketogenic diet normalized fetal growth in the mild group by preventing the extra beta cell growth and early maturation. It only partly restored beta cell function in severe diabetes and did not rescue growth there, though it uncoupled insulin levels from body weight.
pmc-13424511:

Patients, caregivers, health workers, traditional and religious leaders, advocates, and policymakers built the package together, first ranking possible non-drug components by vote, then workshopping how it would actually run.

Fifty-one people joined virtual preparation sessions and forty-five a five-day workshop in Enugu, drawn from all six regions of the country. The group settled the package's parts, who delivers each one, where care happens, and how patients step up to facility-based basic palliative care when needed. Expert review polished the result into a form programmes could adopt directly.
pmc-13427511:
Han G. Ngo, Sayed Golam Mohiuddin, and Mehmet A. Orman show that glycerol metabolism powers antibiotic tolerance in resting Escherichia coli in a 2026 study. Stationary-phase bacteria survive antibiotics without genetic resistance, a persistence problem whose metabolic basis under nutrient limits was murky. Protein surveys, gene tests, metabolic checks, and single-cell imaging together mapped how dormant cells stay alive.

Breaking the core energy cycle reset resting cell function and cut lipid and glycerol handling, which lowered tolerance. Glycerol freed from cell membrane fats emerged as a key fuel for persistence. Breaking that pathway disturbed membrane energy, protein clump handling, and cell division changes. Persisters then became far easier for antibiotics to burst open. Still cells that shrug off drugs are a root cause of cures that fail late, so a fuel path they lean on is a prize worth the hunt in this field.
pmc-13428311:

The materials were high-translucent resin composites, used where fillings must blend with natural teeth. Disc samples were kept first in distilled water for 30 days, then in coffee for 30 more days.

Coffee caused clear colour change in all five materials. Beautifil II stained the most, while Opallis T Neutral stained the least both after water and after coffee. Filtek Z350 XT Trans kept the highest translucency after coffee storage. Two materials lost a large share of their translucency in coffee, while Opallis T Neutral barely changed on that measure too. The authors rank Opallis T Neutral as the most stable overall.
pmc-13428411:
Isabella Eiter and colleagues report 21 months of universal coronavirus testing for everyone admitted to a large German hospital during the pandemic. From April 2020 to December 2021, each new patient and accompanying person got a throat swab test on arrival.

Of 111,271 people screened, 705 tested positive, and 236 of them had not been diagnosed before the admission test. Among the new finds, 110 people had no symptoms and no known contact with a case. The test wrongly flagged almost no one, with accuracy for ruling out infection near perfect in screening use. Finding one positive person cost about 8,083 euros on average, which Eiter weighs against the infections screening prevented.
pmc-13429111:
Tommy S. Korn and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, a consumer headset as the main screen for cataract surgery. The Apple Vision Pro headset was linked to a digital surgical microscope, with the normal eyepieces and a wall monitor standing by as backup. Forty-five patients at one center had their cloudy lenses removed while the surgeon worked from the headset view. Success meant finishing without switching away for device reasons and without device-caused complications.

Forty-four of the 45 operations finished on the headset. One case switched after a brief image freeze, with no harm to the patient. Average surgery time ran about fifteen minutes, and vision a month later was excellent on standard charts. Surgeons reported low workload, and staff noted little disruption. The authors frame the setup as feasible in a guarded setting, not yet ready for routine adoption everywhere.
pmc-13430611:
Monica Viviano and colleagues reviewed small drug-like molecules that block a family of enzymes called PRMTs in a 2026 survey of the field. These enzymes add methyl tags to arginine building blocks in proteins, a step that helps steer gene activity, RNA handling, and repair of DNA harm. Faulty enzyme action has links to cancer growth and other illness.

The review sorts blockers by where they grip the enzyme, whether at the fuel pocket, the protein pocket, or both at once. Some forms, above all those aimed at one family member, show strong action in cells and have moved into early human tests. Others serve as lab probes for single members. Newer tricks pair blockers with tumor traits or tag the enzyme for removal by the cell.
pmc-13431011:
Zhou and colleagues reported in 2026 on glyphosate, a widely used weed killer, and kidney tubule injury in people with low everyday exposure. Traces of the chemical reach the general public through food and the environment, and it may build up in the body. The team looked back at 110 patients who had kidney biopsies and were not exposed at work, sorting them by a tubule injury score.

Zhou found that urine glyphosate levels rose with the injury score, and patients in the third-highest exposure band had far higher odds of moderate to severe injury than the lowest band. A curve analysis confirmed the link was not a simple straight line, and urine levels predicted worse injury fairly well. Reviews and network analysis pointed to cell harm and genetic damage as likely routes, which supports concern about kidney effects at low doses.
pmc-13431711:
Primož Strojan and a large panel weighed in 2026 whether throat cancer that has not spread should meet surgery first or radiation with drugs first. No large head-to-head trial has ever settled the choice, so guides list both routes across stages without a clear pick. The panel sorted proof by disease stage and by a viral marker that shapes outlook.

Matched-patient studies, the best proof on hand, show much the same survival for both routes, in marker-positive and marker-negative disease alike. Surgery alone tends to leave the lightest harm load. Surgery plus later radiation and full drug-radiation courses land near each other, though their harms differ in kind. Marker-positive patients report better life quality after care in most reports. The panel also scans softer-dose plans and immune drugs that may shift the balance.
pmc-13432011:
Dias and colleagues mapped lung cancer incidence in 2026 against social, economic, and environmental indicators in Pará, a state in Brazil's Amazon region. Their ecological study drew 700 new cases from a national hospital cancer registry. Post-op problems are common, yet early warning tools that doctors can understand were scarce. The team studied 245 patients at three centers in China.

One center's 185 patients formed the training set, while two other centers supplied 60 patients for outside testing. Overall, 27.8 percent had a complication within thirty days. Six predictors, led by post-op C-reactive protein and pre-op total protein, were picked by screening and regression. Eleven models were trained, with the best chosen by discrimination and checked for calibration and clinical value. Surgeons gain a transparent risk tool for rectal surgery care.
pmc-13454311:
Xinrui Zheng and a large team of chemists report, in 2026, a catalyst that turns waste plastic into useful aromatic chemicals without noble metals. Their material is a layered zeolite made with steam, named SA-HZSM-5 in the study. The feedstock was high-density polyethylene, the stiff plastic used in bottles and containers.

At 260 degrees, the catalyst converted about 85 percent of the plastic, with aromatics making up about half of the product. Roughly 85 percent of those aromatics were single-ring types that industry values. The team used neutron and infrared tools to watch how the catalyst works. They found paired acid sites that guide chain fragments toward ring formation. The authors present the material as a strong route for plastic upcycling.
pmc-13454611:
Ahmad Karadagi and fifteen colleagues report, in 2026, that adding human genes helps pig kidneys survive longer in monkeys, a step toward easing the human organ shortage. The donor pigs lacked three sugar tags that trigger fierce rejection, a design once thought ideal on its own. What remained unclear was which added human genes best calm protein mismatches.

The team transplanted kidneys carrying four different human gene sets into nonhuman primates. Added genes quieted early immune activation signals in the grafts. Survival stretched markedly compared with kidneys lacking the additions. Two anti-inflammatory genes, TNFAIP3 and HMOX1, stood out, pairing with fewer invading immune cells in biopsy checks and calmer rejection-linked gene patterns. The authors say gene choice, not just sugar removal, will decide how well pig organs serve future patients.
pmc-13454911:
Zhenzhe Liu, Zhong Wei, Zhensheng Li, and Liqiang Zhou review, in 2026, a gene-switch protein called ELK3 and its growing role in cancer. ELK3 belongs to the ETS family of transcription factors, proteins that turn genes on and off. Faulty switches of this kind help tumors grow, spread, and resist drugs.

The review maps ELK3's structure and how healthy and tumor tissues control it. It then traces the protein's hand in blood vessel growth, cell shape change, and invasion across several cancers. Pathways that feed into ELK3, and those it feeds in turn, get detailed treatment. The authors weigh ELK3's value as a diagnostic marker and as a drug target. They argue that its central position in tumor programs makes it worth the hard chemistry that targeting such switches demands.
pmc-13455011:
Matzke, Li, and Malik warn that a shortcut for deep evolution can smuggle lab artifacts into the family tree. Protein structure changes slowly. Codes that summarize a protein's 3D shape could resolve splits where sequence data blur. New tools make such codes cheap: AlphaFold predicts shapes and Foldseek translates them into a structural alphabet. Their 2026 paper shows the catch and imports systematics concepts to tame it.

The same amino acid chain can yield different structure codes depending on where the model came from and whether partner chains were included. A protein, like a fossil specimen, passes through stages that shape what gets coded, which the authors frame with the terms semaphoront and hypodigm, borrowed from work. Their rule is simple: use one replicable pipeline for every protein in a study, so matrix differences reflect evolution, not method. The concepts cost nothing and protect the tree claims built on them.
pmc-13455211:
Farzaneh Ghorbani and others took stock of cytokine-induced killer cell care for cancer in 2026, from forty-eight published trials. Cytokine-induced killer cells kill tumours well with less need for strict MHC match, through T-cell grip plus natural killer-like, MHC-free killing. Boost tricks include gene engineering, checkpoint drug pairs, and dendritic cell pairs.

The review finds CIK care cuts post-care relapse in adjuvant use and lifts chemo gains in advanced disease, with better survival scores in many cancers. Hurdles include tumour-site immune dampening, short in-body life, product drift, and care-plan choice. Next steps hinge on set make rules, precision biomarker-led care plans, and checked next-gen engineered products. Cancer doctors gain a full CIK care synthesis.
pmc-13455311:
Kara Hollins and colleagues test a mapping tool for judging whether health equity work reaches the neediest places in a 2026 study. The COPE project set up local equity teams in 20 Kansas counties, but counting meetings or clients alone says little about where help lands. The team scored community assets, community projects and help to single clients, then set those scores against a census measure of local deprivation.

Across 1,786 groups, 355 community projects and 3,241 clients, roughly two thirds of each sat in high-deprivation areas, and mean asset scores ran clearly higher there than in less deprived areas. That pattern suggests the coalitions did steer effort toward greatest need rather than spreading it thin. Planners elsewhere could borrow the same map-based score to check reach and depth, instead of trusting raw counts of activity.
pmc-13457011:
Ryota Sasaki, Masako Kinoshita, Abbas F. Sadikot, and Ichiro Nakagawa review, in a 2026 article, deep brain stimulation for epilepsy that drugs cannot control. Stimulation offers a softening option when removing brain tissue is impossible or has failed. Many targets have been tried, from thalamus hubs to the hippocampus and cerebellum, and picking among them is the hard part.

The front thalamic nucleus carries the strongest proof, with lasting seizure cuts in randomized trials and long follow-ups. A midline thalamic target suits generalized epilepsy best, above all the severe Lennox-Gastaut pattern. A side thalamic region called the pulvinar is rising for seizures in the back and temporal parts of the brain. Smaller studies cover the rest, with uneven results. The authors tie each target to the seizure network it can reach, urging selection by network, not habit.
pmc-13457211:
Min Xu and four colleagues published this 2026 study building an ultrasound model to separate endometrial cancer from endometrial hyperplasia with polyps. Polyps are benign overgrowths that can look similar to cancer. Both cause abnormal bleeding, and telling them apart guides surgery. The team combined clinical features, image measurements called radiomics, and deep learning features from vaginal ultrasound scans into one model.

Records came from 340 patients at two hospitals, including 149 cancer cases, with one hospital's patients held back as an outside test set. Four clinical factors proved to predict cancer on their own: testosterone, estradiol, abnormal bleeding and whether periods had stopped. The combined model scored 0.991 on the accuracy curve in training, 0.94 in internal validation and 0.955 in the external test group. It beat every single-source model, and the authors packaged it as a nomogram for clinical use.
pmc-13457511:
Phillippo and colleagues in the United Kingdom built in 2026 a stats frame to pool drug trials on life span when drug gains shift with time. Health boards pool trials in nets to rank drugs they can't test head to head. Stock math holds each drug's edge fixed for all time. New immune drugs break that rule: their risk curves bend in rich ways. The frame bends the base risk curve with flex strips, while a smart prior keeps the bends tame and smooth.

Drug marks can ride the strips, so an edge may wax or wane by month. The prior holds across knot picks and time scales, a rare trait. The frame ships in a free code pack that takes pooled or raw trial data. A lung cancer net shows the frame at work. Boards gain life calls that track how drugs truly act.
pmc-13457811:
Xiangxiang Cao and co-authors review how combining several layers of molecular data, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, could improve breast cancer care. Their 2026 paper argues that most reviews treat these layers separately, while real treatment decisions need them joined with what is known about the tumor's surroundings. Breast cancer accounts for 11.6 percent of new cancer cases and 6.9 percent of cancer deaths worldwide, and spread to distant organs causes over 90 percent of its fatalities.

The review focuses on how tumors reprogram their microenvironment, the mix of cells and signals around them, and how that drives resistance to therapy. It highlights liquid biopsy, testing blood for circulating tumor DNA, stray tumor cells, and exosomes, as a way to watch for leftover disease after treatment. The authors present this combined approach as a roadmap toward treatment matched to each patient's tumor.
pmc-13457911:
Carmine Michele Mele and colleagues follow 169 women who had breast lift-plus-implant surgery using polyurethane-coated implants placed above the muscle. The coating grips tissue early, which should hold the implant's position better than smooth shells in the prepectoral pocket. Their 2026 study covers operations from 2019 to 2023, 338 breasts in total, with selective fat grafting for asymmetry or thin coverage, and checks patients out to 24 months.

The key measure, nipple-to-jugular distance, fell from 27.4 centimeters before surgery to 21.5 at one month and crept only to 22.3 centimeters by two years, signaling a stable lift. One capsular contracture case was solved by swapping the implant. Satisfaction ran high, with 78 percent of patients giving the top rating at one year. The authors present the coated, prepectoral approach as a dependable alternative to traditional techniques, with few complications and shape that lasts.
pmc-13458411:
Marziye Maqami and colleagues test how minerals, litter and microbes jointly control soil carbon cycling in a 2026 lab-jar study. Soils are often treated as simple chemical reactors, yet mineral pores, organic inputs and microbe life shape carbon breakdown. A multi-factor trial over 90 days varied clay type, fibrous palygorskite versus bentonite, clay content, calcium carbonate, litter type, wheat versus alfalfa, and microbe origin, native versus lab-made.

Clay acted as the primary filter, with more clay raising released carbon, while palygorskite gave faster release and stronger late biomass bounce-back than bentonite. Protein-rich alfalfa drove rapid, large release, while high-carbon wheat slowed breakdown and heightened clay response. Native microbes lost more carbon overall but slower, synthetic microbes released carbon faster on that clay, and lime tuned timing. Soil models gain an order: mineral habitat first, litter and microbes next, calcium as tuner.
pmc-13458811:
Juri Iwata and colleagues compare seven-year outcomes of two valve types in women receiving transcatheter aortic valve replacement in a 2026 registry study. Women with aortic stenosis often have a small aortic annulus, which can leave balloon-expandable valves with smaller openings and higher pressure gradients, yet long-term comparisons with self-expanding valves were scarce. From the OCEAN-TAVI registry, 1,827 women treated with balloon-expandable valves and 805 with self-expanding valves were matched one-to-one into 744 pairs each.

Balloon valves kept smaller effective orifice areas and higher mean gradients throughout follow-up, yet matched analysis showed lower seven-year mortality at 51.5 versus 57.4 percent and lower stroke at 10.8 versus 16.7 percent, with similar heart failure readmissions. Multivariable analysis found valve type not independently tied to outcomes, so both valve types remain acceptable options for women, mostly with small annuli.
pmc-13458911:
Ashraf Maghrabi and colleagues reported in 2026 on patients in a Middle Eastern cohort whose sleeve gastrectomy was later converted to a Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Surgeons turned to conversion chiefly for stubborn reflux, weight regain, or anatomical problems after the first operation. The group followed 32 women, whose average age was 46 years.

One year after conversion, body mass index had fallen sharply in each indication group, with the largest drop among patients treated for reflux alone. Reflux symptoms eased in 85 percent of patients, diabetes went into remission in 58 percent, and complications affected about nine percent. Laparoscopic and robotic cases looked similar, though the two groups were treated in different periods, so that comparison needs care.
pmc-13459111:
Colin Hill argues in a 2026 commentary that viruses of the gut deserve a central place in microbiome science rather than a footnote. Most gut research reads only the bacterial community, yet the gut holds an estimated hundred trillion bacteriophages, viruses that infect bacteria. These phages kill their hosts or settle inside them, and only a tiny share has ever been grown in a laboratory.

Hill notes that phage classification is hard because phages lack a universal marker gene, and one abundant gut order contains members sharing very little DNA. New computer tools are starting to sort this diversity. Readers get a case, built from a decade of the author's work, for weaving phage biology into accounts of gut health and disease.
pmc-13459211:
Ayhan Senol and Seyhmus Kavak studied which patients are most likely to die in hospital after a gallbladder drainage procedure used when surgery is too risky. The procedure, percutaneous cholecystostomy, threads a drain through the skin into an inflamed gallbladder. Their 2026 study reviewed 266 adults treated at one center between 2022 and 2025. It tested clinical, lab, and scan findings against survival, including a new imaging severity score they built from gallbladder features.

Twenty patients died in hospital, an overall mortality rate of 7.5 percent in this cohort. Older age, an underlying cancer, high levels of a tissue damage enzyme called LDH, and stubbornly high inflammation three days after drainage each independently predicted death. Their combined model separated survivors from non survivors well in internal testing. The imaging severity score instead predicted slower settling of inflammation, not death. The authors call all findings exploratory.
pmc-13460211:
Xiaodong Zheng and colleagues evaluated in 2026 keyhole lung cancer surgery performed without a breathing tube in patients whose lungs already work poorly. Letting patients breathe on their own avoids one-lung ventilation and airway instruments, yet risks low oxygen and chest flutter during surgery. The retrospective study compared 162 patients, eighty-six non-intubated against seventy-six intubated, then matched sixty-two pairs to balance the groups.

After matching, operating time and cardiovascular complications were similar. The non-intubated group shed chest tubes sooner, woke from anesthesia in about half the time, and showed lower rates on several recovery measures. The authors present spontaneous ventilation surgery as feasible and safe for carefully selected patients with weak lungs, fitting enhanced recovery goals.
pmc-13461111:
Jose Tiran-Saucedo, Yvette K. Leon-Camacho, Arturo C. Berber, and Claudia V. Melendez-Gonzalez report in 2026 twelve years of real-life experience with OM-89, an oral immune modulator made from processed Escherichia coli, for women with recurrent urinary tract infections. Records came from a specialist clinic in Monterrey, Mexico, covering 208 women who took one ninety-day cycle or several cycles of the preventive treatment.

One cycle held infections off for a mean of a little over five years, and repeat cycles averaged slightly less. Resistance in bacteria cultured afterward fell significantly in most urine samples and in a smaller share of vaginal samples. The authors present OM-89 as a safe non-antibiotic strategy for breaking the cycle of recurrence, a valuable option as antibiotic resistance climbs worldwide.
pmc-13461311:
Ye and colleagues studied in 2026 how ethical leadership relates to eudaimonic wellbeing at work, a deeper form of wellbeing built on good relationships and personal growth. Surveys came in two waves from 310 employees in Chinese project and property management firms. The team tested whether feeling part of the organisation carries the effect, and whether a caring ethical climate changes its strength.

Ye found ethical leadership tied positively to staff identification with the organisation. It also linked to personal growth and to positive relations with others. Identification partly carried the link to both wellbeing outcomes, which means leaders help both directly and by making staff feel they belong. A caring ethical climate strengthened every one of these links. The authors frame fair, principled leadership as a wellspring of relational and growth wellbeing, with the surrounding climate deciding how far the benefit travels.
pmc-13461411:
Yang Zhou and colleagues cataloged in 2026 the apyrase gene family in Chinese cabbage, enzymes that trim extracellular ATP and help plants keep chemical balance under stress. Chinese cabbage is highly sensitive to drought and temperature swings, pressures growing under climate change. The genome-wide study identified thirteen apyrase genes and mapped their evolutionary relationships, shared structural motifs, and the regulatory switches sitting in front of each gene.

Gene activity testing then showed distinct patterns by tissue and sharp changes under drought, heat extremes, and cold. Some family members switched on under one stress and off under another, suggesting division of labor across the family. The authors offer the catalog as a molecular framework and a shortlist of targets for breeding hardier cabbage.
pmc-13461511:
Xin Zou and colleagues compared two bone drugs, denosumab and zoledronic acid, over 36 months in patients with primary osteoporosis. Osteoporosis thins bones until they break easily, and both drugs slow the cells that eat bone away.

The records covered 413 patients, 198 on denosumab injections twice a year and 215 on yearly zoledronic acid drips, all with calcium and vitamin D. Bone density rose at spine, hip neck, and total hip in both groups, but gains ran larger on denosumab at every site. Bone breakdown markers also fell further on denosumab, and pain scores improved more there. Side effects were far rarer on denosumab, about 5.6 percent against 20 percent, Zou reports, pending prospective confirmation.
pmc-13461711:
Pantović and co-authors argued a 2026 policy analysis that models for linking scientific diasporas fail in fragile countries such as Venezuela. Standard models assume a stable national science system and working ties between the state and researchers abroad. Venezuela instead faces a long state crisis and a scattered research community.

Drawing on diaspora research, science diplomacy, and knowledge circulation studies, Pantović looked at how engagement is planned, done, and blocked in such settings. Focus groups with members of the Venezuelan scientific diaspora spoke of long crises and periods of spread shaping their lives. The authors cast diaspora scientists as non-state actors who could bridge national and international agendas. They urge flexible engagement models fitted to each context, with concrete policy steps.
pmc-13462811:
Sung-Won Park and co-authors tuned drone spraying against garlic leaf blight, a fungal disease where the pathogen is already dodging some fungicides. Drone application saves labor but droplet patterns differ from ground rigs, so chemical choice and dose need re-testing. In their 2026 study, freshly isolated Stemphylium fungi were screened against five fungicides in the laboratory. The most promising were compared in pot trials using spraying equipment that mimics drone output, and the winner was flown over real garlic fields.

The isolates had lost sensitivity to one standard fungicide entirely and varied against the rest. In pots, metconazole controlled the disease best at 76.67 percent efficacy, with ipflufenoquin second at 56.67 percent. Under field conditions, drone applied metconazole at its labeled concentration outperformed the alternatives, achieving 45.54 percent control with the lowest disease progress curve. The mobile rig successfully predicted drone performance.
pmc-13463011:
Gyeong-Ju An reviewed Korean research in 2026 on how living liver donors adjust after giving part of their liver. Living donation made up 72.9% of Korean liver transplants in 2024, and most donors give to family, so their recovery shapes whole households. Donor livers regrow within a year, yet donors' own physical and emotional recovery had drawn far less study than recipients' survival.

The integrative review pulls together the scattered Korean studies of donors' body, mind, and social recovery over time. Foreign reviews put 80 to 93% of donors back to pre-surgery quality of life within six to twelve months, but Korean family norms and care systems may shift that path. A joined-up picture should help coordinators counsel future donors with honest, timed detail about life after donation.
pmc-13464011:
Molly E Lumnitzer and six co-authors name AFF3 as a guard of rest in naive CD8 T cells. These killer T cells must sit quiet yet ready, burning little fuel until a virus calls. With age that quiet state slips, and responses to infection weaken.

Cells missing AFF3 burned more fuel at rest than normal cells did. When a virus struck, those cells piled up poorly and failed to switch on sugar burning as needed. AFF3 levels fell with age in both mouse and human cells, alongside loss of the quiet state. The authors propose AFF3 as a lever for restoring youthful T cell strength in older people.
pmc-13464311:
Hamaguchi and colleagues studied in 2026 a little-examined group at a Japanese university hospital. These patients were aged 85 or older and carried do-not-attempt-resuscitation orders. Yet they were not critically ill on arrival. Records from 2022 to 2024 were reviewed. The team compared 72 such patients against more than a thousand similar admissions without the order. An early-warning score of four or less defined not critically ill.

Only about six in every hundred eligible patients had the order. Those who did were older and less able to handle daily activities. They were slightly sicker by score, with lower hemoglobin and albumin and higher inflammation markers. They went home less often and stayed longer. They also died in hospital more often. Their chance of transfer to a post-acute care facility was about double. The raised risk persisted after adjustment, suggesting the order marks broader vulnerability, not just a resuscitation preference.
pmc-13464911:
Lica-Miler and colleagues wrote a 2026 review of vaptans, a class of water-balance drugs. These drugs block a hormone signal that tells the kidneys to hold water. The review traces how the drugs grew from lab-made copies to pills taken by mouth. It covers tolvaptan, conivaptan, and mozavaptan in depth.

Tolvaptan stands out as a drug that slows polycystic kidney disease, not just treats symptoms. Vaptans also help when blood sodium drops too low from hormone imbalance. Gene differences help explain why patients respond in uneven ways to the same dose. Two gene variants get close attention for their effects on drug handling. The authors close with safety checks doctors should run during treatment. The review also tracks how the body takes in, breaks down, and clears each drug.
pmc-13465511:
Yi Su and five co-authors tune the IGF1 gene up and down in primary muscle cells from Yili horses, a breed famed for speed and stamina. The growth factor had been tied to exercise response, yet its direct muscle actions in horses stayed unclear. Cells received extra gene copies or silencing RNA in matched dishes.

Extra IGF1 sped cell growth and movement across the dish, while silencing it braked both. The PI3K/Akt pathway carried the effect, with its key switch showing stronger activation under high IGF1. Cell shape and working traits followed the same up-down pattern. The findings hand breeders and vets a cell-level target for muscle building and injury recovery programs in sport horses.
pmc-13465611:
Maria Rodrigues Cardoso and a large team study whether time of day changes how the Alzheimer drug donepezil crosses a key barrier around the brain, in work published in 2026. The barrier between blood and spinal fluid runs its own daily clock, which shifts the activity of transport proteins in its walls. Chitosan nanoparticles serve here as carriers meant to improve drug delivery.

Using a lab model of that barrier, the group compared plain drug with drug packed inside the nanoparticles at different clock phases. They built and measured the particles first, then tracked how much drug crossed under each condition. The aim is a combined timing-plus-carrier strategy that could sharpen dosing schedules for brain disorders.
pmc-13466211:
Eugen-Silviu Bud and colleagues report on guided surgery paired with a jaw-widening procedure for adults whose upper jaw is too narrow, in a 2026 observational study. The method, miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion, can stall when the seam between the jaw halves has fully matured. Small cuts through the bone surface, planned on scans, are meant to ease that opening.

Fifteen adults with mature jaw seams received the treatment using guides printed for each patient's anatomy. Follow-up scans checked whether the seam opened and how much width was gained. Records also tracked complications and whether the small implants stayed firm. The authors weigh accuracy and safety gains from digital planning against the added surgical step.
pmc-13467111:
Young Suk Shim and colleagues sequence a signaling gene in one hundred Korean girls with early puberty of unknown cause. Their 2026 study hunts for genetic contributors beyond the known single-gene cases. One hundred matched healthy girls served as controls. All thirty-four coding stretches of the NOTCH2 gene were read letter by letter.

Fifty-five variants turned up, eleven of them changing the protein. One variant in a pairing region never appeared in patients. It sat in a small share of control copies, raising a careful guess that it might protect against early puberty. Three other changes appeared only in single patients. The authors stress that none of this proves cause without replication elsewhere.
pmc-13468211:
Lv and colleagues mapped the genomes of 109 rice varieties from Zhejiang Province, China, in 2026 to support breeding and conservation. They resequenced each variety and scored field traits over two years, looking for diversity patterns, signs of past selection, and genes tied to useful traits.

The panel held about 4.75 million high-quality DNA variants and split sharply into the indica and japonica subspecies, with signs of past gene flow between them. Three genome regions showed strong selection signals, and one holds a sugar transport gene that may have driven subspecies divergence. Association mapping found nine regions affecting heading date, tiller number, and grain size. Follow-up work pinpointed promising gene variants for grain weight, grain width, and stalk length, giving breeders concrete molecular targets.
pmc-13469111:
Evandro Martin Lanzoni traced potassium treatments in 2026 inside copper-indium-gallium-selenide solar absorbers, a high-efficiency thin-film technology. Alkali post-deposition treatments lifted cell efficiency, yet their action at surfaces and grain edges stayed fuzzy because each edge differs. The team grew mm-scale domains on gallium arsenide to watch the same edge before and after treatment.

Surfaces and edges alike showed copper depletion with strong (112) facets, and K coating pushed copper inward, leaving a K-rich surface layer. K moved at different speeds through grain cores versus edges, and band bending at edges stayed nearly nil after treatment. The atomic view should guide further output gains in thin-film solar cells.
pmc-13469311:
Xue Chen and colleagues report in 2026 on a puzzling change in the H9N2 bird flu virus, which lives in poultry and can spill over into people. Since 2021, the virus has largely lost its ability to clump chicken red blood cells, a property that routine flu testing depends on. The team traces that loss to two changed building blocks in the virus surface protein called hemagglutinin.

Working from virus records, lab assays, and animal tests, the group shows that cells from turkeys or guinea pigs restore detection where chicken cells fail. The changed protein also binds more weakly to one kind of sugar receptor on cell surfaces. In mice the altered virus grew less in the lungs, while chickens stayed strongly infected. The authors urge testing labs to add other cell types so spreading viruses are not missed.
pmc-13469611:
H Al-Khalaifah and colleagues tested natural feed additives in 2026 for producing low-cholesterol eggs without losing laying performance. Eggs are a staple protein, and healthier eggs could serve consumer demand and local food security. Five hundred Lohmann hens ran two trials: ten single-additive diets from weeks 34 to 69, then a combined mix at week 75.

Fermented red mold rice at 8 grams per kilogram cut yolk cholesterol most, by 35 to 45%. Ziziphus leaves and probiotic cut it by 20 to 40%, with no harm to production, feed efficiency, or egg quality. Immunity and antioxidant enzymes improved, and the combined mix cut cholesterol by about 25% with no sensory loss. Economic analysis backed commercial use of these local additives.
pmc-13469811:
Talgar Bayan, Bibarys Mukhambetiyar, Askar Boranbayev, and Adnan Yazici share in 2026 a dataset logging the cost of adding a blockchain to federated learning on small edge devices. Ten Raspberry Pi boards acted as learning clients, sending updates to a workstation server over forty training sessions. Every round was written to a public layer two blockchain contract, with model files pinned to distributed storage.

Two activity recognition benchmarks and two software setups were covered, twenty sessions each. One setup handled chain and storage tasks in line, while the other overlapped uploads with training and reused fee estimates. Files record accuracy and device heat, memory, and processor load for each round, plus timing logs for every chain operation. The authors offer the traces for benchmarking edge learning and device resource studies.
pmc-13469911:
Hu and co-workers in China built in 2026 a single pass computer model that cleans photos shot in dark rain, a twin ill that breaks most tools. Brighten the shot, and rain streaks and grit bloom. Scrub the rain hard, and the dim scene melts. Their model, DHP-Net, leans on hue, the color tone map of a shot, which stays firm when light and rain foul the rest. Hue maps at three scales feed a stacked fix core, with a side part that sorts cross color clashes.

On the set test bank for this ill, the model hit top scores for both sharp truth and build truth, clear of past tools. On true dark rain shots, its work also read best to the eye. The authors pitch hue led fixing for night cams on cars and streets, where rain and dark come as a pair.
pmc-13470111:
Michelle Musiol, Milen Nachev, Kaan Kumas, Kurt Buchmann, and Bernd Sures measure in 2026 how a marine worm accumulates trace elements across its life in different hosts. The nematode Anisakis simplex grows as a larva in North Sea herring and as an adult in harbour seals. Parasites are known indicators of pollution in fish, yet data from mammal hosts has been scarce.

Both stages held higher levels of several elements than their hosts did, with strong concentration factors for non essential elements in seals. Adults carried more of most essential elements than larvae, while silver ran the other way. Isotope readings suggested adults may feed partly on the seal meals rather than seal tissue alone. The pattern shows that life stage and feeding route shape what the worm records about its environment.
pmc-13470311:
Hovland and colleagues in the United States told in 2026 of an ankle wreck that pairs two harms teams near never see at once. One was a smashed shin top inside the joint. The other was a torn Achilles cord. Their patient, a man of 78 with Parkinson's disease, fell from a ladder. First X-rays at the emergency ward were read as no break, and he went home with what looked like scrapes and pain.

A bone doctor's check, with deep scans and a hands on exam, found both harms. Each alone is grave; both at once had not been told in print before. The team fixed the break with plates and screws, and sewed the cord in the same stay. The authors urge full exams in hard ankle falls, above all in older folk.
pmc-13472811:
Chidambaram and colleagues present a 2026 deep learning system, BrainFusionNet, for sorting brain tumors on MRI scans into four classes: glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumor, and no tumor. These classes look alike on scans, sharing brightness patterns and varied shapes, which makes the task clinically hard. The system builds on a pre-trained image network with an attention module that focuses on informative regions.

Training used a hybrid loss that combines smoothed standard loss with a focal term that emphasizes hard cases, plus a two-phase schedule that first freezes early layers, then trains the whole network. At reading time, five altered versions of each scan vote together, a trick called test-time augmentation, to steady the answer. Such systems aim to speed triage where radiologists are few; careful external testing decides whether the reported accuracy survives new hospitals.
pmc-13473111:
Zhongna Fu and seven colleagues tested in 2026 a new hospital air cleaner that uses a high-oxygen membrane, comparing it with a plasma air cleaner already in use. Natural airborne bacteria served as the test organisms, and trials ran in wards both empty and occupied, so the team could see how real ward life changed performance. They also checked whether room size, temperature, humidity, starting bacterial load, or staff movement altered the result.

With no one in the room, the membrane machine killed 88.4 percent of airborne bacteria, clearly above the plasma machine's 82.5 percent. Once the ward was occupied, the gap vanished, at 80.0 percent against 78.7 percent, a difference too small to be statistically meaningful. Room conditions and staff activity did not measurably change the membrane machine's performance in these tests. The authors conclude it beats plasma cleaning in empty rooms only, and it cannot yet stand alone against airborne infection.
pmc-13473411:
Lin and colleagues reviewed in 2026 mobile lung cancer screening units that bring low-dose CT scans to high-risk communities. Such units can cut access barriers for underserved groups, but earlier reviews looked only at detection outcomes. This review covered eighteen studies to March 2025, assessing screening results, costs, and what helps or hinders delivery.

Suspected cancer rates ranged widely across programmes, from about one to sixteen percent of those screened. Confirmed cancers ranged from a fraction of a percent to about four percent. Five studies found the mobile approach economically efficient, with early detection far cheaper per case than late-stage treatment. Implementation factors clustered in areas such as the intervention's traits and the outer setting. The authors conclude mobile units benefit early detection, especially for underserved populations.
pmc-13473511:
Arash Ghazbani and eleven colleagues estimated in 2026 how common sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and strength with ageing, is among older Iranians. Using the Iranian Multicenter Osteoporosis Study from 2021, the team examined 705 adults aged 60 and over, averaging 67.2 years, with just over half women. Sarcopenia meant low muscle mass plus low strength, while severe sarcopenia added low physical performance, and survey weighting gave nationally adjusted estimates.

The weighted prevalence reached 13.8 percent and rose steeply with age. A body mass index below 25 carried the strongest link and the largest share of cases, at 51.0 percent, followed by high fat mass at 42.39 percent, with low physical activity at 28.71 percent and small calf circumference at 16.55 percent also contributing. The authors highlight low weight, excess fat, and inactivity as the main modifiable targets, and call for prompt nationwide action on muscle health in older adults.
pmc-13473611:
Gilbert Audira and four colleagues used in 2026 automated video tracking to measure fighting behaviour in two cricket species, field crickets and house crickets. Aggressive behaviour shapes survival and mating success, yet cricket studies still rely on slow, bias-prone human observation, and fights between species had never been compared with fights within a species. The team applied DeepLabCut, a markerless pose-estimation tool that tracks body parts from video, to paired crickets.

The trained model tracked body parts with an average likelihood of 0.94, and its aggression scores matched manual scoring, at average sensitivity of 0.8 and precision of 0.7. Male field crickets fought most fiercely, with frequent overt combat, high movement, and complex motion, while house crickets showed little aggression except among males. Between species, both sexes still fought, but less intensely than field-cricket males among their own kind. The method opens large, reproducible studies of animal social behaviour.
pmc-13474511:
Renyu Zhang and many colleagues map genes behind the split between maize and its wild ancestor teosinte in 2026. Crosses between a maize line and a wild Mexican form let the team track twenty traits at once. They found 93 single gene spots plus nine paired effects shaping those traits. Linked traits often shared the same spots, which shows common roots for many form changes.

One ear-length spot was cloned and named EL3-2, and it codes for a gene control switch. That switch appears to steer many traits at once across growth stages. Signs of past selection clustered near trait spots, tying breeding history to form. The map helps breeders pick traits with fewer side effects.
pmc-13474811:
Guangcheng Sun and four colleagues charted in 2026 two decades of research on left ventricular assist devices for heart failure. They analysed 871 publications from 2004 to 2024 with mapping software, tracking countries, institutions, authors, and themes.

Output grew steadily, with the United States leading at 187 papers and Columbia University the most productive institution. Core themes covered device improvement, clinical outcomes and complications, patient selection and prognosis, and long-term quality of life. The field has matured steadily over twenty years, and the map gives newcomers a useful guide to where the open questions lie.
pmc-13475611:
Jeffery reviewed in 2026 the evidence on therapist self-disclosure, when therapists share personal details with clients. Disclosure can strengthen the working bond and engagement, but it can also harm. The review gathered recent studies on its effects, risks, and cultural aspects. Findings were read against classic person-centred ideas: congruence, unconditional positive regard, and accurate empathy.

Recent studies strongly supported several classic recommendations: put client benefit first, keep clear limits, disclose on purpose, and return focus to the client. Doubt persisted about what content to share, how intimate to be, and why. The review found those questions resolve best through sensitivity to the client and context, rather than fixed rules. Culture and power need direct attention, the author argues. The paper offers a brief person-centred framework for quick decisions.
pmc-13476311:
Ali Hussein Abdulkarim and co-authors tune car seat climate control in 2026 with coils built under the seat surface. Seat-level heating and cooling can comfort riders while using less energy than whole-cabin systems. A test rig measured how a seated person and the seat trade heat. Neural networks learned to predict system output from sensor readings.

Prediction error stayed tiny, and the match between predicted and real values neared perfect. Average gaps for cooling, heating, and efficiency all sat below half a percent. The model handles both warming and cooling in one setup, a gap past work left open. Learned control could trim cabin energy use on the road.
pmc-13476711:
Dewan and colleagues reviewed in 2026 whether smaller breathing bags help or harm adults receiving CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, after cardiac arrest. Smaller self-inflating bags have been proposed to stop rescuers squeezing too much air into the lungs. The team searched four databases for human and simulation studies comparing small bags with standard adult bags, and graded the certainty of what they found.

Dewan found no randomised trials at all. One observational study of nearly two thousand arrest patients linked the small-bag period to lower survival with good brain outcome and lower event survival than the standard-bag period. Two simulation studies gave mixed results on whether small bags hit target air volumes more reliably. Certainty was very low for every outcome. The authors advise against routine swapping to small bags during CPR on this evidence.
pmc-13477111:
Alexandre Sebestyen and co-authors probe blood-clotting therapy choices in 2026 in French cardiac operating rooms using a set case. The case featured unclear bleeding with normal clotting tests. Anesthesiologists and surgeons rated therapy use at three surgical stages. A fictional colleague opinion was inserted to test social sway, and agreement scores were measured.

Agreement within each profession rated poor on a standard scale. Therapy use jumped sharply after chest closure, and the colleague prompt lifted use further in both groups. Surgeons voiced lower satisfaction and stronger worry about late transfusion. Bleeding judgment in the room is part data, part peer signal.
pmc-13478211:
Arash Akbarzadeh and six colleagues built in 2026 gene-based classifiers to detect stress and life stage in juvenile sockeye salmon. They exposed fish to combined heat, low oxygen, and salinity challenges across smolt stages, measuring gill gene expression with a microfluidic chip.

Random forest classifiers detected heat stress, low-oxygen stress, salinity acclimation, and smolt stage with accuracy from 85.5 to 100 percent. Stress signals faded within three days for low oxygen but lingered longer for heat. The classifiers advance field-ready monitoring, including possible non-lethal gill biopsies, for salmon facing climate change.
pmc-13478511:
Tana-Hernandez and colleagues studied sheep abortions in Uruguay in 2026, typing the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, a leading cause of pregnancy loss in ewes. They compared the abortion strains with types reported before in local people. Two strains from separate abortion cases were then grown out for full genome reads and infection tests, to learn whether sheep strains form one family or many.

The abortion samples proved highly diverse, meaning the parasites did not descend from a single recent clone in these flocks. The two strains carried types never described before, and they behaved very differently in infection tests, with wide gaps in harm-causing traits between them. Genome reads found changes at known harm-linked spots, including different copy counts of a gene called ROP5. Tree analysis pointed to several separate origins for the sheep strains found in Uruguay.
pmc-13478811:
Robert Beaglehole, Ruth Bonita, and Ben Youdan published a 2026 analysis of New Zealand's fast-falling smoking rates and what they mean for tobacco harm reduction. Smoking declined slowly for years under the country's Framework Convention measures. From 2018 to 2019 the pace changed sharply, coinciding with wider vaping uptake after rules were clarified and vaping was endorsed as a quitting aid.
