Statistical joinpoint analysis confirms a genuine acceleration rather than a blip. Declines ran strongest among Māori and younger adults, the groups with the highest vaping uptake. Daily adult smoking now sits below seven percent, concentrated among Māori, older, and disadvantaged groups. Youth smoking stays at record lows, and youth vaping has fallen after tighter rules. The authors argue harm reduction can speed decline when paired with strong regulation.
pmc-13479411:
Adam Leonard and colleagues present a 2026 integrative review of youth-friendly health services applied to tuberculosis care for adolescents and young adults. This age group faces high tuberculosis risk through biology, mobility, HIV exposure, and services designed for children or older adults instead. The World Health Organization recommends youth-friendly care, yet tuberculosis programs have rarely adopted its principles.

The review gathered qualitative, quantitative, and conceptual studies covering ages 10 to 24 in high and medium burden countries. Two reviewers screened four databases and appraised quality with standard tools. Themes were organized deductively around the youth-friendly framework across the whole care path, from testing through treatment completion. The synthesis aims to give tuberculosis programs a practical model for keeping young patients engaged until cure.
pmc-13479911:
Lucy Stocks and coauthors published a 2026 article examining whether artificial intelligence should support or substitute for human facilitators in healthcare simulation debriefing. Debriefing, the guided reflection after a training scenario, is where much of the learning happens, yet skilled facilitators are scarce and sessions generate more data than humans can review.

Four integration modes are described: metric-based AI tutors, large language model assistants, conversational chatbot debriefers, and hybrid systems. Each is examined for how it works, where it is already used, what it adds, and where it falls short. The authors weigh risks such as shallow feedback and lost human judgment against gains in consistency and scale. Their framing helps simulation centers choose augmentation deliberately rather than drifting into replacement.
pmc-13480211:
Shota Inoue and seven colleagues reported in 2026 a staged rescue for a rare, deadly aortic dissection with heart vessel blockage. A torn ascending aorta with a clotted false channel had collapsed the true channel and choked the left main coronary artery.

In a 58-year-old man who arrived with stomach and back pain and then fell into shock, doctors placed a bare-metal stent in the ascending aorta to reopen the true channel. Coronary stenting through the aortic stent restored heart blood flow and steadied pressure, bridging the patient to definitive surgical repair. The case shows aortic stenting can buy time for heart intervention before surgery in selected dissection cases.
pmc-13481611:
Jingyu Liu and co-authors describe a 2026 study of a protein called ASAP3 in cancer of the food pipe. This cancer type kills many patients and lacks good drug targets. The team stained tumour samples for ASAP3 plus four partner proteins and charted links to patient traits and survival.

High levels of all five proteins tracked with poor outlook. In cell work, silencing ASAP3 slowed growth, movement, and invasion of cancer cells. In mice, silenced tumours grew smaller with lower growth activity. Tracing the chain showed ASAP3 works through a partner called NEMO to switch on a master inflammation pathway, which then drives spread traits. The authors pitch ASAP3 as both a warning marker and a drug target worth testing in this cancer.
pmc-13483311:
Michael Wenninger and eight colleagues published this 2026 report on an mRNA vaccine against elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus 1A, the leading killer of young Asian elephants once they lose their mothers' antibodies. Two juvenile male calves, aged six and seven, arrived at Cincinnati Zoo from Dublin Zoo confirmed free of prior infection. Both received the experimental multi-antigen vaccine in October 2024 and a booster the following month, under a programme spanning four institutions.

Blood tests showed strong antibody production against four viral surface proteins after vaccination, though levels began falling by day 102 after the booster. In early 2025 both calves became naturally infected, one in February and one in March. Their viral loads stayed below 6,000 genome equivalents per millilitre of blood, and neither showed blood abnormalities or any sign of illness. The infections cleared without treatment. The authors present this as the first evidence of clinical protection from an EEHV1A vaccine.
pmc-13483411:
Vikrant Palande and co-authors report a 2026 search for immune signs that track virus clearance after a therapeutic vaccine for HPV16, the type behind over half of cervical cancers. Twelve women with low-grade cervical changes got a DNA shot aimed at a viral gene plus a fusion protein shot across eight weeks. Blood and immune cell sampling followed the course.

Shots raised antibody levels and killer T cell replies in most women. By month six the virus had vanished in five of eleven women who could be checked. Antibody strength alone did not predict who cleared. One blood signal measured before treatment, MCP-1, ran high in women whose virus lingered. T cell receptor variety and shared receptor patterns also failed to separate the groups, though vaccine-targeted reads rose most in clearers. The hunt for a simple clearance marker goes on.
pmc-13483611:
Jiachen Li and colleagues compare two chest openings for fixing a heart defect that sits just below the great arteries. Their 2026 retrospective study covers 74 patients aged 14 and older treated between January 2016 and December 2024. One group had repair through a small cut under the right arm, while the other had the traditional cut through the breastbone.

Starting health was similar in both groups. The under-arm approach needed longer heart-lung machine and clamping times, yet produced notably less fluid drainage after surgery. Ventilation time, intensive care stay, hospital stay, and heart function at discharge matched between groups. Long follow-up recorded no deaths, repeat procedures, leftover leaks, or complete heart block in either group. The authors conclude the smaller opening trims surgical trauma without losing safety.
pmc-13483911:
Chenyang Zhang tests how layered coal and rock blocks break under realistic three-direction stress and unloading in deep mine roadways. Published in 2026, the laboratory program squeezes 100-millimeter cubes at five coal-to-rock ratios while listening for cracking sounds and running matching computer simulations. Excavation-style unloading and different layer thicknesses drive the comparison.

As coal share rose, failure shifted from steady splitting and shearing in rock-heavy blocks to sudden coal-driven collapse. Middle mixes failed in X-shaped shear patterns governed by the layer interface, and they crackled with warning signals during unloading more strongly than pure materials. Stored energy peaked at a 67 percent coal share even while peak strength kept falling. Burst danger therefore follows energy storage more than strength alone, a distinction mine engineers should design around.
pmc-13486711:
Zhao and team compared three ways of fitting overnight contact lenses that reshape children's corneas to slow short-sightedness, including one fitted by artificial intelligence. Children with asymmetric corneas are hard to fit, and a decentered lens worsens vision quality. Their 2026 study covered 139 children split among conventional, established, and AI-personalized lens designs, measuring lens position and optical distortions after one month of wear.

The AI-fitted lenses sat closest to center, decentering by about 0.60 millimeters on average in the reported measurements. A conventional design decentered most, at about 0.84 millimeters on the same measure. All designs raised optical aberrations somewhat, but the conventional group gained more of two distortion types than the AI group. Zhao concludes personalized AI fitting suits asymmetric corneas best among the options tested.
pmc-13486811:
MacInnes and co-authors identify a new controller of early red blood cell development. Their 2026 paper studies IMP1, a protein that reads chemical marks on RNA messages and shapes which proteins get made. Embryonic red cells produce distinctive globin types, the oxygen-carrying chains, before switching to fetal and then adult forms, and the controls behind that first stage were poorly understood.

Using gene removal in early erythroid cells, protein profiling, and RNA capture methods, the team showed IMP1 helps set the fetal character of these cells. Embryonic globin output was governed directly by IMP1 after the RNA stage, rather than through gene switching alone. The authors present IMP1 as a previously unrecognised posttranscriptional regulator, meaning it acts on RNA messages after they are produced, in the earliest blood-forming stage.
pmc-13486911:
Mia Miller measures what happened to takeaway alcohol prices in Darwin right after Australia repealed a minimum price floor. Published in 2026, the observational study scrapes every product from three large retailer websites between October 2024 and March 2025. The Northern Territory floor of 1.30 dollars per standard drink, set in 2018, ended on March 1, 2025.

Within one month, no beer or spirits and only small shares of wine and cider fell below the old floor price. Large-format wine was the exception, with about two thirds of big-vessel wines priced under the former floor. Most cheap products had already been on sale before repeal rather than being new arrivals. Panel statistics in the full report test broader price shifts. Immediate chaos did not materialize, yet the cheapest segment deserves continued watching.
pmc-13487311:
Appavoo and co-authors fused three kinds of breast imaging into one network that predicts how lesions grow over time. Mammography, MRI, and ultrasound each see different aspects of a lesion, and simple concatenation wastes their overlap. Their 2026 model aligns the three streams with a correlation-learning module, weighs them with cross-modal attention, and forecasts growth with a memory network tuned for both straight-line and curved growth patterns.

On the mammography benchmark used, the fused model reached about 92 percent classification accuracy in the reported testing. Confusion lingered between benign and malignant borderline cases, with a few dozen samples misclassified each way. The design deliberately separates steady normal growth from accelerating malignant growth in its temporal module. Appavoo presents the network as interpretable support for tracking lesions across scans rather than judging one image alone.
pmc-13487911:
Xidong Zhang and co-authors study anemia around heart surgery in a 2026 retrospective cohort from a single center. Records covered 315 adults operated on between 2020 and 2025, with anemia judged by World Health Organization criteria before surgery and on days one, three, and seven afterward. Outcomes included longer hospital stay, lung infection, and low cardiac output syndrome, a serious drop in heart pumping.

Almost half of the patients were anemic before surgery. Anemia still present on day seven was independently linked with all three poor outcomes, while day one anemia showed a different pattern. The authors argue that tracking hemoglobin over the full first week matters more than a single early reading for judging risk.
pmc-13488011:
Ndonwi Elvis Ngwa and co-authors test gene variants linked to diabetes, obesity, and high blood pressure in Black South Africans in a 2026 cross-sectional study. The sample held 560 adults aged twenty-five to seventy-four, who gave lifestyle details, had body measures and blood pressure taken, and completed glucose tolerance testing. Variants in genes tied to appetite, blood pressure control, and insulin signaling were typed in the laboratory.

One variant in a diabetes gene was linked with lower odds of type 2 diabetes, even after adjustment for age, sex, and body size. A variant near an appetite gene tracked with higher blood pressure and hypertension risk, though the signal weakened after adjustment. The authors call for replication in larger local samples.
pmc-13488411:
Yamamoto and colleagues film skipjack tuna spawning in three dimensions inside an aquarium tank, in 2026 marine biology research. Skipjack reproduce by group spawning, yet detailed descriptions of the behavior itself were lacking. Stereo cameras let the team estimate each fish's body size and measure swimming movements precisely during spawning events. They could distinguish a pursued leader fish, presumed female, from the followers chasing it, presumed male, in the tank's social setting.

Leaders chased by several followers proved rare, even though that configuration should make sperm release visible. Single followers instead chased leaders of many sizes, including smaller, likely immature fish. When multiple followers did join, the leader darted and turned at higher speeds than in single chases. Yamamoto proposes a sequence: one male starts pursuing a female, her acceleration when ready to spawn draws in additional males. Linking swimming performance to reproduction, they argue, clarifies how this mating system works.
pmc-13488911:
Newton Nyirenda leads a large team reanalyzing a United States blood pressure trial for dementia risk in a 2026 post-hoc study. The marker under study, estimated pulse wave velocity, is computed from age and average blood pressure and stands in for artery stiffness. Records covered 8,536 participants with no dementia at entry in the SPRINT-MIND trial, followed for new probable dementia judged by expert review.

During follow-up, 323 participants developed probable dementia. Risk stayed lowest at gentler velocity values, then climbed once values passed a threshold a little above ten meters per second in the reported curves. The top quarter carried most of the excess risk, which suggests a step pattern rather than a smooth slope. Tracking over two years also split patients into distinct aging paths.
pmc-13491611:
Bahattin Saz, Ozgun Yusuf Ozyilmaz, and Ozge Doganay Ozyilmaz present in 2026 a modeling study of stress in full-arch dental implants. Replacing every upper tooth with a fixed bridge loads implants in ways that decide long-term success. The team compared titanium and zirconia implants under three bridge materials, using finite element analysis, a computer method that maps force through a structure.

Twelve models paired each implant material with either a cantilever, a rear section jutting past the last implant, or a fully supported design. Each model took a slanted load of 200 newtons at a molar. The PEKK plastic bridge produced the highest stresses and the most movement, above all with the cantilever. Zirconia implants carried more stress than titanium but stayed within safe limits. Rigid bridge materials and designs without the jutting section come out ahead.
pmc-13491711:
Khatmah Alanazi and Samantha Curle study in 2026 how Saudi medical students cope with learning medicine entirely in English, a language that is not their first. Students must master difficult material and a foreign tongue at the same time across three public universities. The researchers combined interviews with fifty female students, questionnaires from 289 students, and observations in classrooms, study groups, and laboratories.

Students leaned on a shifting toolkit that changed as their English improved. Many translated terms into Arabic, watched Arabic explanatory videos, drilled vocabulary with flashcards, and worked through lecture slides together in groups. Classroom observations confirmed these habits were central rather than occasional. The authors recommend that programs openly legitimize mixing languages and build visual resources into teaching, which would also prepare students for multilingual clinical work.
pmc-13491911:
Yanyan Bai and three colleagues recount in 2026 how a new belt-like stitching technique saved the uterus of a mother bleeding unstoppably during a cesarean delivery. The woman, just past forty weeks and diabetic, had a placenta fused densely to the womb wall with patches growing into its back surface. Blood loss reached two and a half liters while standard measures failed one by one.

Crews tried manual placenta removal, forceps, ordinary stitches, contraction drugs, artery ties, figure-of-eight sutures, and packing, none of which stopped the bleeding. A quadruple modified belt suture then compressed the whole uterine segment evenly and achieved control. Careful follow-up care prevented infection, clotting, and tissue death, and scans three months later looked normal. The authors lay out the technique as a reproducible emergency protocol.
pmc-13493711:
Monestier and co-authors use France's national health database to describe how stage III melanoma was treated between 2019 and 2023. In stage III, skin cancer has spread to nearby lymph nodes but can still be removed surgically. The 2026 study covers 2,612 patients who started extra drug treatment after surgery to lower the chance of the cancer returning. Three options were compared: the immunotherapy drugs nivolumab and pembrolizumab, and a paired targeted therapy.

Nivolumab was the most common choice, given to well over half the patients, while the targeted pair went to younger patients on average. After about three years, roughly half of each group remained free of recurrence. That means the cancer had come back for around one in two patients despite treatment. When melanoma did return, immunotherapy combinations were again the main response. The authors argue better patient selection and earlier detection of recurrence are still needed.
pmc-13495311:
Jordan Uguet leads a large team in a 2026 pilot trial of a standard breathing protocol for bronchoscopy in intensive care patients on ventilators. Passing a scope down the airway during the exam raises pressure, cramps air delivery, and can drop oxygen or jolt blood pressure. Practice varied widely, so the team set a low-flow routine and tested it in a before-and-after design.

The routine cut the incoming air flow, held the end-breath pressure steady, and slowed the rate. Peak airway pressure fell by nearly half against usual care, and time spent triggering pressure alarms collapsed. Air volume per minute and carbon dioxide levels held about even, and oxygen and low blood pressure events did not worsen. The authors call the protocol workable and safe in the short term, and a base for a larger trial.
pmc-13495411:
Bing Song and colleagues unravel, in a 2026 study, how the testes steer musk making in the muskrat. Male muskrats in season secrete a musk much like that of musk deer, prized in scent and medicine, yet the control chain was unknown. The team read genes and small molecules in scent glands and testes from two-year-old males in and out of the scenting season.

Tissue shape differed sharply between seasons. Fifteen gland genes were tied to building the main musk parts through fat, cholesterol, and steroid paths. Seven testis genes governed sex hormone making and signaling. Joined analysis showed the testes raising a carrier molecule and switching gland genes through hormone signals, in effect phoning instructions to the gland. The authors map a testis-led control system for musk output, a base for farming or lab work on musk supply.
pmc-13496011:
Otto Van de gaer and colleagues report a validation study, published in 2026. It tests bacterial identification by long-read gene sequencing. The work took place in a routine hospital laboratory. Standard culture misses some bacteria. Slow-growing or non-culturable ones escape it. The team tested a Nanopore workflow. It reads the full 16S rRNA gene directly from samples. This gene is a standard bacterial identity marker.

Spiking tests and quality-control strains checked the workflow. So did 54 real clinical samples. The workflow named the bacterial genus correctly in over ninety-eight percent of strains. Species accuracy exceeded eighty-five percent. It matched nearly all culture-positive samples. It found extra relevant pathogens in several culture-negative ones. This supports routine clinical use.
pmc-13499211:
Gauresh Palekar leads a 2026 report on real-world results of implanting bone-forming cells, called osteoblasts, into hips dying from lost blood supply, a condition named osteonecrosis of the femoral head. The treatment pairs cell implantation with core decompression, a drilling procedure that relieves pressure in the bone. Centres across India contributed records for patients treated between April 2017 and April 2022, with follow-up from two to seven years.

The cohort held 319 patients and 502 treated hips, most at middle stages of disease, and average follow-up ran about three and a half years. Pain scores eased and hip function scores rose by amounts patients would notice in daily life. About one patient in ten later needed a full hip replacement, with the middle time to replacement near six and a half years. The authors read the figures as support for preserving the natural joint in earlier stages.
pmc-13499311:
Nikolina Vrdoljak and colleagues probe in 2026 a metabolic enzyme that acute myeloid leukaemia cells rely on in an unusual form. Leukaemia cells shift toward sugar fermentation for energy, and they swap a highly active enzyme form for a weaker one, called PKM2, which also helps switch genes on in the nucleus. Levels of this form were higher in leukaemia cells while overall enzyme activity ran lower than in healthy blood cells.

Genetic and drug experiments in cell and animal models showed a striking pattern, since pushing activity down and pushing it up both harmed the cancer. Either move disturbed the protein's natural grouping, kept it out of the nucleus, lowered a key growth gene's output, and ended in cell death. The finding marks the enzyme's balanced state, rather than its simple presence, as the vulnerability worth targeting.
pmc-13499711:
J G Jennifer Lydia and co-authors run in 2026 a randomised double-blind trial comparing two spinal anaesthetic drugs for surgery below the navel. Newer drugs in this family were developed to be gentler on heart and nerves than the older standard. Ninety patients were assigned to receive one of two drugs into the spinal fluid. Assessors tracked how fast numbness and muscle block began and faded, blood pressure effects, pain scores, and need for extra pain relief.

The levobupivacaine group numbed faster and stayed numb far longer than the ropivacaine group, with sensory block averaging well over four hours against under three in the reported means. Muscle block also lasted longer, and later pain was lower with less early rescue medication, at the cost of slower return of leg movement. Both drugs proved heart-stable, supporting either as a safer alternative to the older agent.
pmc-13500711:
Křivohlavý and co-authors test a tempting shortcut: reading the heart's pumping strength from the eye. Cardiac output, the volume the heart moves each minute, normally needs ultrasound or invasive catheters, while retinal oximetry photographs the eye's blood vessels and estimates oxygen levels painlessly. Their 2026 pilot study enrolled healthy volunteers and stable cardiac patients, fourteen people in the final analysis, who had eye imaging and heart ultrasound on the same day.

The two measurements moved in opposite directions with surprising strength. As the oxygen gap between retinal arteries and veins widened, cardiac output fell, a correlation the authors describe as strong for a sample this small. The pattern fits physiology, since a weaker pump makes tissues extract more oxygen, widening the artery-vein gap everywhere including the eye. Larger prospective studies must test whether the eye can report on the heart.
pmc-13501311:
Röhrig and colleagues released version 3.0 of Attracting Cavities, the molecular docking engine behind the SwissDock webserver, in a 2026 software paper. Docking predicts how a small drug-like molecule fits into a protein target and how tightly it binds. Unlike newer co-folding methods, it still gives physical insight into the interaction regardless of whether the ligand or pocket is novel.

Röhrig reports enhanced sampling features, new functionalities, and technical improvements. Together they dock better in less time and handle more kinds of problems, building on earlier additions such as covalent docking and hybrid quantum-classical docking. Benchmarked head-to-head against AutoDock Vina, a widely used rival, the new version produced better docking results across multiple test sets. The physics-based scoring, pairing a standard force field with an implicit solvent model, is unchanged, and the update will be available through the webserver.
pmc-13501811:
Belinda Twesigye leads a sixteen-author team reporting a 2026 training programme that strengthened clinical trial monitoring across the East African Community. Trials are multiplying in the region while trained monitors remain scarce. The project ran in Burundi, Kenya, Rwanda, South Sudan, Tanzania, and Uganda between February 2024 and February 2025. Stakeholder consultations shaped a six-module curriculum, and each country cohort completed five weeks of blended learning: a two-day workshop, four weeks of online study, and a two-day wrap-up.

Two hundred people trained, drawn from national regulators, ethics committees, research teams, and monitor pools; 50.5 percent were women, and Uganda supplied the largest share at 30.5 percent of the cohort. Knowledge scores jumped from 61.8 percent before training to 84.3 percent after, a gain of 22.5 points on the test scale. The share clearing the 60 percent pass mark leapt from 37.5 percent to 95.6 percent of participants. Whether knowledge becomes practice awaits follow-up.
pmc-13502311:
Caram and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare case of solitary bone plasmacytoma, a single tumor of plasma cells, hiding in the upper jaw of a 76-year-old woman. The lesion looked like a routine root infection near two front teeth, with a draining tract. Standard root canal treatment brought no improvement, which prompted referral for a tissue sample.

Caram's biopsy showed sheets of abnormal plasma-like cells with a heavy white cell infiltrate. Marker tests confirmed the cells were all of one clone, matching plasmacytoma. Full body checks ruled out multiple myeloma, the widespread form of this cancer, leaving the solitary diagnosis. The patient received 20 radiation sessions and stays stable under joint follow-up. The authors warn that lasting root-area lesions may not be dental at all, and early spotting matters because a solitary tumor can be a first sign of myeloma.
pmc-13503111:
Moedt and colleagues test two urine proteins as response markers for kidney drugs. Their 2026 paper examines clusterin, which signals tubule injury, and epidermal growth factor, which signals repair, in samples from two large randomised trials of chronic kidney disease. The standard marker, albuminuria, mainly reflects damage to the kidney's filters and fluctuates considerably.

After six weeks on atrasentan, an endothelin blocker, the urinary clusterin ratio fell by about 46 percent, consistent with reduced tubule injury. In the second trial, dapagliflozin, a diabetes and kidney drug, slowed the decline of the growth factor ratio over one year, with the largest relative gains in diabetic kidney disease. Biopsy data linked the urine growth factor signal to gene activity inside the kidney. The authors propose both proteins as mechanism-based markers for personalising treatment.
pmc-13503911:
Saeed Mokhtari Masoumi Alamdarloo and others meta-analyze conversational agents for low mood, anxiety, and stress. In 2026, the review synthesizes forty-eight randomized controlled trials covering 28,071 people, spanning both artificial-intelligence and rule-based agents, using robust variance estimation to handle within-study dependencies. Restricted access leaves many people without timely mental health care.

Effects were small to modest but clear: same-form mean gaps of minus 0.27 for low mood, minus 0.20 for anxiety, and minus 0.26 for stress, with larger gains in medical groups and shorter programs. Risk of bias was largely low and publication bias negligible. Chat-based agents emerge as scalable support, though long-term effectiveness and integration remain open.
pmc-13504211:
Khoshi Ari Muhammed and Eman Dhahir Arif survey Salmonella germs at a chicken wet market in Iraq, in a 2026 study. Salmonella spreads through food and lives in the gut of chickens, so market tools and water can carry it to buyers. The team sampled a broiler market in Sulaymaniyah province over six months.

They gathered 210 samples across the market, drawing on gut contents, water, knives, and chopping boards, plus swabs from workers' hands and bird bodies. Culture found Salmonella in about half. Gene tests named the species in most culture hits, and over three fifths of those were the Typhimurium type, many carrying a key invasion gene. Boards showed the highest species rate. The local strain grouped with world strains, which hints at shared roots across borders.
pmc-13506111:
Atul Goel argues for rethinking ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament, a condition where a spinal ligament slowly turns to bone and squeezes the cord. The usual story treats the bony growth as the disease and surgery as cutting space around the cord. Goel proposes the opposite order: hidden instability in the spine comes first, and the ossification is the body's attempt to brace the loose segment.

Under his view, ligament thickening, disc shrinkage, and bony spurs belong to one protective response. Removing bone without steadying the segment may worsen the underlying problem. He points to patients who improved after stabilisation alone, with no removal of the ossified mass, as the cord settled once abnormal motion stopped. Critics may worry about large masses left in place, yet Goel answers that compression is real but secondary. The essay asks surgeons to treat instability as the root target.
pmc-13511711:
Rossella D'Alessandro and eight co-authors screen thinking, emotional, and behavioral health in children with Duchenne muscular dystrophy at one center, in 2026 work. The disease, tied to the X chromosome, wastes muscle step by step, yet missing forms of a protein also act in the brain. Twenty-one children took a broad test battery while the team reviewed clinical history and cognitive scores.

Screening surfaced attention trouble, inward emotional vulnerability, poor emotional control, and autism-linked features beyond the motor picture. Among children with cognitive data, nearly half scored in the low range for full intelligence, with one genetic subgroup hit hardest. Patterns varied a great deal between children. The authors call the work early and exploratory, and they argue for multi-domain screening plus personal assessment plans so support can match each child's mix of needs.
pmc-13511811:
Rocco Carcione, Valentina Mastrobuono, Riccardo Pagliarello, Elisabetta Bennici, Alessia Cemmi, and Silvia Massa formulate food hydrogels from natural polymers and berry processing leftovers, in 2026 work. The gels use pectin plus an extract made from spray-dried strawberry and blueberry preparation waste, turning by-products into food matrices. One version also carried living plant cells. The team probed light spectra, acidity, moisture, micro-structure, swelling, and drying over time.

Calcium chloride proved key to holding the gel network firm. Plant cells changed how the gel held and released water without breaking the basic gelation route. Gels stayed physically and chemically stable after twenty days in cold storage. The authors present the materials as sustainable carriers for biological parts and active compounds in new food products built on waste valorization, meaning turning leftovers into value.
pmc-13513611:
Hyunjee Kim, Olga Frunze, Sang Mi Han, Soon Ok Woo, Jewon Jung, and Hyung-Wook Kwon compare how diet quality shapes gene activity in honey bees, in 2026 work. Readings were taken before and after acute heat stress. Bees rank among the world's key pollinators, and rising heat strains them hard. Colonies received natural diets of honey or bee bread, or artificial diets of sugar syrup or pollen substitute, and metabolic plus immune genes were tracked around a heat shock.

Each diet left a distinct molecular fingerprint at rest and under heat. Bees on the richer natural diets regulated metabolic and stress pathways in a more coordinated way. Sugar syrup bees switched immune genes on more strongly under heat, a sign the authors read as deeper physiological disturbance. The work suggests full nutrition helps bees hold their regulation together in heat waves, a point for feeding practice in a warming climate.
pmc-13515011:
Laura Maghiar and fourteen colleagues argue, in a 2026 review, that antimicrobial peptides could fight peri-implantitis, the biofilm-driven inflammation that eats away the bone holding dental implants. Cleaning cannot fully decontaminate an implant surface, and antibiotics act bluntly while breeding resistance. Peptides offer a two-way alternative. Positively charged molecules that rupture microbial membranes tend to kill broadly without quickly selecting resistance. The body's own defence peptides also calm inflammation and help tissue knit closed.

Framing the implant's gum crossing as a healing wound barrier, the authors draw lessons from skin repair research on peptides such as LL-37 and the beta-defensins. They focus on coating the collar where the implant meets the gum, since disease starts there, and extend the idea to zirconia and hybrid parts. Stability, cell toxicity, cost, and regulation all stand between concept and clinic.
pmc-13515411:
Davoud Amiri and four colleagues review, in a 2026 article, the metabolic side of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder. ADHD is usually framed as a problem of attention circuits in the front of the brain. Yet the hypothalamus, the small hub governing appetite, sleep, stress hormones, and body rhythms, may also play a part in why patients differ so much. The team searched five databases for human studies on these links.

Findings tie ADHD to higher obesity risk, immune and inflammation changes, shifted appetite hormones, delayed body clocks, and unusual stress-hormone responses. Obesity, inflammation markers, and diabetes risk carried the strongest numbers, with appetite hormones close behind. Direct proof of inflammation in the hypothalamus itself stays thin, so Amiri's team treats that pathway as a plausible hypothesis for a subgroup, not settled cause.
pmc-13518711:
Efstathios Vounotrypidis leads a seven-author prospective trial, published in 2026, of an extended depth of focus lens implanted during cataract surgery. Every patient had earlier undergone vitrectomy, an operation that removes the gel inside the eye, to repair a detached retina. Such eyes are usually denied lenses that correct focus at several distances.

Twenty-seven patients and 43 eyes received the Vivity lens once the retina had stayed attached. Six months later, corrected distance vision improved sharply in the repaired eyes, and near and intermediate results were usable. Satisfaction ran high, with only two patients reporting halos. The findings suggest careful selection can make this lens a safe option after retinal repair.
pmc-13518811:
Amanda Maria Kostro and five colleagues run a 2026 randomized trial in early knee osteoarthritis, testing tailored exercise, orthopedic shoe inserts, and both together. Worn cartilage and uneven loading disturb balance in this condition, while foot problems such as flat feet may worsen knee strain. Earlier comparisons lacked objective balance measures.

Patients split into exercise (43), insoles (43), mixed (39), and control (41) groups, then stood on a force platform, eyes open and then closed. The mixed group improved most on sway measures, and pain, daily function, sports ability, and quality of life all gained. Exercise and insoles each helped, yet Kostro and co-authors found the combination strongest for rehabilitation.
pmc-13518911:
Xiao Wei leads a nine-author team introducing ViscoClamp in 2026, a peptide gel designed to steady the squishiness of the tissue immediately around cells. Living tissue remodels constantly, so the mechanical cues cells feel drift over time. Chronic sugar damage, called glycation, worsens that drift and undermines healing.

A rule-based design agent searched peptide options for one that threads into the natural matrix and binds calcium plus glycation products. ViscoClamp squeezed wide swings in glycation input into stable cell-scale mechanics, while still letting stem cells remodel and mineralize. In sugar-rich jaw defects across rats, rabbits, dogs, and macaques, the gel restored bone-forming activity and improved repair.
pmc-13519011:
Seira Arakane, Yu Sato, Masanori Hashino, and Shintaro Maeno dissect the hidden diversity inside a supposedly uniform heat-loving bacterium in 2026. Geobacillus stearothermophilus is a workhorse for food sterilization testing and industrial processes, treated for decades as one tidy species. Comparing 36 strain genomes exposed clear internal structure.

Two major genomic groups emerged, differing in origin and equipment. Food-linked strains carried smaller genomes with fewer metabolic genes, while strains from natural hot habitats kept larger genomes and broader abilities, including genes for using carbohydrates and fatty acids. A few strains sat between the groups, suggesting gradual splitting. All still meet species thresholds, so divergence is accumulating quietly inside one name.
pmc-13520311:
Huanhuan Zheng and colleagues test in 2026 whether spectral CT scans can show how well oesophageal cancer responds to drug treatment given before surgery. Spectral CT can estimate iodine uptake in a tumour, which may reflect blood supply and living tumour tissue.

Scans before and after treatment were compared in 87 patients with squamous cell cancer of the oesophagus. Tumour size and iodine measures after treatment were lower in responders than in non-responders. Combining normalised iodine with tumour area gave the best sorting of response. As a pilot study, the work offers an early imaging option that avoids extra biopsies.
pmc-13520411:
M. Slikkerveer and colleagues describe in 2026 a newborn boy with drug-resistant seizures linked to a new SCN2A gene change, treated with lacosamide under close blood-level monitoring. The seizure drug is licensed only from age two years, so newborn use is off-label and dosing guidance is absent.

Born early at 33 weeks, the infant kept seizing despite several medicines. Lacosamide was added with repeated trough level checks and heart monitoring. Reaching the target blood level needed a far higher dose than expected, split into four daily doses, with no side effects seen. The single case supports cautious, monitored use while wider studies are awaited.
pmc-13520711:
Rishita Shah and JJ L Miranda turned a weakness of chatbots into a classroom lesson on honest citation. Published in 2026, the work starts from a familiar flaw: general-purpose language models invent references and misuse real ones. Fake-citation rates were reported from about one fifth to over nine tenths of references. Teachers need material that builds both AI literacy and writing skill at once.

The authors repurpose model errors as worked examples, asking students to spot fabricated references, correct misused real ones, and choose primary versus secondary sources well. Seeing errors firsthand shows a key limit of generative AI better than any warning could. The exercise also gives students a structure for practicing sound source use. Readers get a ready framework for teaching citation rigor in an age of fluent but unreliable machine text.
pmc-13522011:
Hiroji Iwata and colleagues report in 2026 long-term outlook from the NEOS trial for postmenopausal early breast cancer, combining response to pre-surgery hormone therapy with a 21-gene recurrence score. The analysis covered 226 patients drawn from the earlier assay study.

Hormone treatment shrank tumours at least partly in just over half the patients. In low and middle score groups, adding chemotherapy showed no clear survival edge over hormone therapy alone. In the high score group, hormone therapy alone fared worse on overall survival, although responders to initial hormone treatment showed no clear gap. Event counts were small, so caution applies.
pmc-13522511:
U Nikhil Sagar leads a 2026 genome study aimed at breeding more nutritious groundnuts, also called peanuts. Kernels were measured for iron, zinc, and protein across seasons in a diverse mini-core collection, and whole genomes were scanned for DNA markers linked to those traits. Wide variation appeared for all three nutrients, giving breeders useful raw material.

Fifteen marker links were found in pooled data, with more in single-season analyses, pointing to dozens of candidate genes. Several candidates govern iron and zinc balance, while others relate to protein control. Accessions carrying favorable gene versions clustered in certain groundnut types. Three practical DNA markers were validated, offering tools to select nutrient-rich lines in future breeding programs.
pmc-13523211:
Atefeh Shamsi and Imane Bagheri explore social isolation among mothers of autistic children in Yazd, Iran, in a 2026 qualitative study. Twenty-two mothers of children aged four to twelve took part in semi-structured interviews. Their accounts were analyzed inductively to build themes grounded in their own descriptions of daily life and social contact.

One overarching theme, social isolation, rested on three categories. Mothers pointed to stigma and being judged by others. They also lacked enough support, both formal and informal. Caregiving strain pushed many into defensive withdrawal. Mothers described judging looks, wrong beliefs about autism, thin family and service support, and demanding therapy schedules that pushed them to withdraw protectively. The authors call for public awareness that respects local culture, teaching for families, and support that is easy to reach. They note that a single-city interview study transfers with care to other settings.
pmc-13523311:
Agnieszka Mania-Końsko and co-authors describe a distinctive rash and mouth inflammation syndrome in a young child in a 2026 case report from Poland. A five-year-old boy was admitted with prolonged fever, erosive sores of the mouth and lips, and a pink rash. The illness came with infection by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, a common cause of chest infections. The pattern fits a relatively new diagnostic entity distinct from several severe skin reaction syndromes.

Treatment combined systemic and local steroids, an antibiotic, a mucus-thinning drug, pain relief, and a local antifungal, with follow-up two months later at a university clinic. The authors walk through presentation, diagnostic steps, and the conditions that must be ruled out. They recommend suspecting this syndrome when pneumonia appears alongside mucosal and skin eruptions in young patients.
pmc-13523411:
Jochen Grohmann and colleagues report the first case of heart wall erosion after a patch-like septal closure device in a 2026 case report. A twelve-year-old patient had a significant atrial septal defect, a hole between the upper heart chambers. The child also had pulmonary hypertension, severe scoliosis, and Down syndrome. A Gore occluder was placed after test balloon closure went smoothly. The device position looked reasonable at implantation.

Follow-up imaging later showed a blood-filled fluid collection around the heart next to the correctly positioned device, indicating erosion of the right atrial wall. The authors conclude that any closure device can in principle erode the atrial wall, since remodeling after unloading and wall texture vary unpredictably. Because risk is highest in the first one to six months, they insist on consistent outpatient follow-up whatever device is used.
pmc-13523511:
Ye Song, Yangsheng Yu, Bo Zhang, and Xiao Zhang report 2026 laboratory work uncovering a chain of proteins that fuels sugar use in colorectal cancer. Abnormal glycolysis, the breaking down of sugar for energy, is a hallmark of this cancer. The team traced how one gene, EFNA3, becomes overactive and helps tumors grow while evading immune attack.

Silencing EFNA3 in cancer cells lowered glycolysis, growth, movement, invasion, and blood vessel signaling, while strengthening killing by natural killer and CD8 T cells. Mouse tumors with silenced EFNA3 spread less and drew more anti-tumor immune cells. Upstream, a transcription factor switched EFNA3 on, a scaffold protein stabilized that factor's message, and the ligase PRKN normally restrained the scaffold through tagging for disposal. Restoring PRKN blocked the chain, suggesting a treatment angle.
pmc-13524711:
Diana Clynes and colleagues report, in a 2026 letter, a global survey of kidney patients, caregivers, and advocates about dialysis education and choice. Modality use and patient experience vary worldwide with education, professional training, and policy. The survey asked how people learned about options, how involved they felt in decisions, and why a modality was chosen.

An electronic survey run in July and August 2024 by a patient association and a home dialysis roundtable drew 967 respondents. Home dialysis recipients received extra questions about that route. Respondents included dialysis patients, care partners, transplant recipients, and people with advanced kidney disease, although about 42 percent did not state their role, a limitation the authors note. The project ran as quality improvement, exempt from formal ethics review at the senior author's institution.
pmc-13525911:
Andrew Kent and colleagues offer a narrative review, published in 2026. It covers how medicines for chronic pain affect the heart and blood vessels. The authors examine anti-inflammatory drugs and acetaminophen. Opioids, antidepressants, and gabapentinoids are covered. Joint injections are also reviewed. For each class, pain relief is weighed against cardiac risk.

The authors searched several databases through April 2026. Risk rises with dose and duration. It is not fixed for a given drug. Risk concentrates in older patients. Those with existing heart disease are also at higher risk. Each class threatens different outcomes. Anti-inflammatory drugs raise heart attack and heart failure risk. Some opioids disturb heart rhythms.
pmc-13526111:
Vicent Balanzá-Martínez and others examine, in a 2026 longitudinal family study, whether sex shapes higher-order thinking in schizophrenia and in unaffected first-degree relatives. Sex differences in the illness itself are well documented, yet evidence on executive function and working memory in the chronic stage was disputed. The team predicted sex effects would be negligible.

A total of 266 people, comprising 113 people with schizophrenia, 58 unaffected relatives, and 95 healthy controls, completed a full neuropsychological battery twice over one year. No significant sex differences appeared in executive or working memory performance in any group. Patients still performed markedly worse than relatives and controls on most tasks. The authors say the null result extends earlier evidence to relatives, suggesting the cognitive deficit travels with illness risk rather than with sex.
pmc-13527911:
Jiahao Yu and five colleagues compare two keyhole approaches for removing tumors from the mediastinum, the space between the lungs, in a 2026 retrospective study. One group had robot-assisted surgery and the other had video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery, a camera-guided technique. Matching on age, health scores, tumor size, and other factors left 102 patients, split evenly between the groups.

Robotic surgery lost less blood during the operation, and those patients needed chest drains for about a day less and left hospital about a day sooner. Pain scores and complication rates were similar in both groups, with serious complications uncommon either way. The robotic operations cost roughly 4,400 dollars more, so the authors advise weighing the modest recovery gains against the higher price for each patient.
pmc-13529611:
Gao-jue Wu and four colleagues test a cap-assisted injection therapy for severe bleeding hemorrhoids in a 2026 study. The method uses an endoscope cap to see clearly and a long needle to place sclerosing medicine precisely. Eighty-two patients with grade three internal hemorrhoids took one treatment. Bleeding was their main complaint. Scores at three months judged success.

Overall success reached about eighty-five percent. Bleeding eased in about ninety-six percent of patients. Prolapse improved in only about fifty-eight percent. Over twenty-four months, bleeding returned in about a quarter of those followed. Strong bleeding intensity before treatment predicted both leftover bleeding and return. High bleeding frequency after treatment also flagged return. No severe complications occurred. The authors back the method for bleeding control. They advise closer watch on high scorers.
pmc-13529911:
Vahid Zarghami proposes a 2026 design framework for biodegradable scaffolds that break down in step with healing bone. Large bone gaps often fail to close on their own, so a temporary support must carry load early and then yield as new tissue forms. Timing that handover is the central problem.

Four material families receive review: metals, ceramics, polymers, and mixed composites. Matching math models link each family to defect sizes and care settings, followed by a four-step planning method for individual patients. A proposed synchronization index scores how closely implant loss follows a target healing curve, pending future testing.
pmc-13530111:
Wenjue Tang leads a 2026 hunt for exosome-linked markers in childhood glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumor with poor survival. Exosomes are tiny packets cells release to signal neighbors, and their cargo can drive tumor growth. Two public gene datasets supplied the starting material.

Machine learning narrowed the field to three genes: FGF9, TGFBR1, and PLCB4. One ran high in tumors while the other two ran low, and each tracked with distinct immune cell patterns in the tissue. Computer drug screening pointed to a known enzyme-blocking compound as a possible candidate worth laboratory follow-up.
pmc-13530211:
Zohreh Yaghoubitajani and colleagues review in 2026 whether brief micro-exercises ease neck and shoulder pain for desk-bound workers. Tiny movement breaks fit into a workday without special equipment, which makes them attractive for offices. Three databases supplied randomized trials published through July 2025 for pooling.

Nineteen trials with 2,732 workers met the entry rules. Pooled results showed clear pain relief for the neck, the shoulder, and both combined, plus gains in neck function and quality of life. Muscle activity showed no clear change, while work outcomes were mixed. Wide variation between trials and signs of publication bias urge caution.
pmc-13530611:
Tuyishime and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 51, a cadaver anatomy study of lateral extra-articular tenodesis in children's ligament reconstructions. It asks whether the reinforcing band can be anchored without damaging the thigh bone's growth plate. The usual landmarks sit uncomfortably close to that plate in growing knees.

Seven skeletally immature cadaver knees, ages eight to sixteen, were dissected and X-rayed with pins marking the two candidate anchor origins. The anterolateral ligament's origin sat on average only about one and a half millimeters beyond the growth plate, and in one specimen right at it. The lateral collateral ligament's origin averaged about five millimeters clear. Both origins were also close to each other, with variable front-to-back ordering between specimens. The authors conclude the anterolateral landmark is consistently the riskier anchor point near the plate.
pmc-13530811:
Bugbee presents in 2026, as conference poster 49, outcomes of osteochondral allograft transplantation in the patients thought most likely to do well. The procedure grafts fresh donor cartilage and bone into a damaged knee. This cohort was young, non-obese, with small lesions from injury or a cartilage-bone disorder.

The series covered 109 patients and 116 knees, mean age about twenty, with grafts averaging five and a half square centimeters. About one knee in five needed some reoperation, but only one graft, under one percent, actually failed and required revision, at a little over five years. Graft survival stood at one hundred percent at five years and just over ninety-eight percent at ten years in this selected group. At a median five and a half years, pain and function had improved and about ninety percent of patients were satisfied.
pmc-13531211:
Danny Dvir leads a 2026 first-in-human report on mechanically splitting a native aortic valve leaflet before valve replacement. A displaced leaflet can block a coronary artery opening during the procedure, a rare yet deadly event. Two patients with severe narrowing and high blockage risk received the splitting device first.

The catheter cut each target leaflet in a controlled way through the leg artery. Replacement valves then seated with clear coronary flow and strong function on imaging. Neither patient suffered a neurological event. The authors call for wider study of the approach in native valve disease.
pmc-13531611:
Rao and Riegal wrote a 2026 editorial on how professional soccer reshapes the heart, framing their commentary around the principle that form follows function. They discuss the largest echocardiographic study of adult male professional soccer players in North America. It covered 1,368 Major League Soccer players with an average age of 26 and a racially mixed roster, where ultrasound heart screening is routine.

Rao summarizes the findings: chamber dimensions, wall thickness, and heart mass often exceeded general population limits, yet true enlargement by size-indexed criteria was uncommon. No player reached the wall thickness zone that overlaps with inherited heart muscle disease. Most players showed normal geometry, right-sided enlargement was common and tracked with left-sided size, and pumping function stayed normal in nearly all. The editorial stresses that sport-specific reference values are essential so healthy athletic remodeling is not mistaken for disease, and real disease is not missed.
pmc-13531811:
Shaowei Liu and co-authors examine in 2026 whether routine preventive services shield older Chinese adults from heat-linked depression. Survey waves from 2016 to 2020 covered 7,464 people, linked to city weather records counting extreme heat days each year. Depression scores came from a standard nine-item scale.

More accumulated heat days meant worse depressive symptoms. Health education strongly softened that link, and personal health record management helped as well, while screening showed a weaker effect. Protection concentrated among men, rural residents, and the middle region. The authors frame local preventive services as climate adaptation capital for aging towns.
pmc-13531911:
Wisteria Deng and co-authors review in 2026 how rigid interpretation of social situations feeds mental illness. People constantly read ambiguous social cues, and trouble starts when first readings refuse to update against new evidence. The review gathers work on depression and psychosis within everyday social settings.

Depression showed narrow rigidity, clinging to negative readings of unclear events. Psychosis showed broader rigidity across pleasant and unpleasant material alike. Measurement tools increasingly test revision inside social scenes rather than abstract puzzles. Targeting stuck social readings may open fresh therapy routes for both conditions.
pmc-13534511:
Shunqing Yuan and colleagues study in 2026 how the level of artificial intelligence use affects carbon emission intensity in Chinese firms. Firms face strong pressure to cut emissions, and AI can either raise energy use at first or improve efficiency later. Provincial panel data were tested with fixed-effects models and pathway analysis.

The link formed an inverted U shape, with emissions rising early, then falling past a turning point as use deepened. Gains ran through greener innovation, better energy use, and industry upgrading. Effects were stronger in the eastern region, so policy should vary by region and energy mix.
pmc-13536611:
Fang Liang and colleagues sequence in 2026 the chloroplast genomes of three Barringtonia trees, two of them threatened coastal species. These trees anchor tropical shore forests, yet no chloroplast genomes existed for the genus. The team assembled and annotated the full green-cell genomes for all three species.

The genomes were alike in size and gene content, with no large rearrangements. A few fast-changing regions stood out as useful markers for population studies. Family tree tests grouped the three firmly in one lineage, giving conservation work its first genomic base for these trees.
pmc-13538311:
Jinbao Zhang and colleagues explore lived experience of long-term care insurance in Guangzhou, China, in a 2026 interview study with twenty-four older recipients and family members. Home-based insurance programs aim to help older adults stay in their communities, yet unmet needs persist. Interviews traced how specific policy features eased or failed to ease daily care gaps, using a care network lens.

Four features eased unmet needs, covering enrollment into formal care, choice of caregiver, agency nurses joining care networks, and caregiver training. Gaps remained where benefits fell short, program information stayed scarce, and personal care goods were hard to obtain. The authors advise policymakers to build these lessons into future insurance design so home care matches real family needs more closely.
pmc-13539411:
Lin and colleagues joined two Taiwan datasets in 2026 to probe why only some people with heart rhythm problems go on to develop cardiomyopathy, a weakening of the heart muscle. One dataset was the national insurance database covering 2000 to 2015, and the other was a biobank with gene data, thyroid hormone measures, and lifestyle records. Thyroid problems and inherited risk were their main suspects.

In the insurance cohort, a new rhythm diagnosis came with more than double the risk of later cardiomyopathy, with atrial fibrillation, a fast irregular rhythm, showing the strongest link. In the biobank, a gene-based risk score for thyroid trouble was strongly tied to actual thyroid dysfunction, and diabetes, blood fats, and diet shifted that tie. The authors frame the two lines as parallel evidence for heart-endocrine interplay, while noting the unlinked cohorts bar any claim of cause.
pmc-13539811:
Masoumeh Paknia, Maryam Dehestani-Ardakani, and Heidar Meftahizade report a 2026 laboratory protocol for multiplying a pink-leaved ornamental plant, Syngonium podophyllum 'Pink Allusion', from small stem pieces. Ordinary cuttings multiply slowly and can carry disease, so growers need a cleaner route.

Three linked trials tuned the growth chemicals for shoot formation, rooting, and greenhouse settling. One mix gave the most shoots per piece, a rooting chemical called IBA gave the most roots, and every plantlet survived the move out of the laboratory. Peat-based mixes beat cocopeat mixes for leaf and root growth. The authors offer the recipe for large-scale nursery production.
pmc-13539911:
Jai-Hong Cheng and seven colleagues report a 2026 cell study asking whether vitamin D3 and shockwave treatment together push bone-forming cells to mature faster than either one alone. A protein called Pdia3 carries the vitamin's quick signal at the cell surface, yet its link to shockwaves was unclear.

Mouse bone precursor cells received the vitamin, shockwaves, or both, and the combined treatment raised enzyme activity, mineral deposits, and surface Pdia3 the most. Blocking the cell's internal actin fibres removed the benefit, while shockwaves helped those fibres rebuild and move Pdia3 outward. A signalling chain through protein kinase C completed the picture the authors propose.
pmc-13540811:
Leitao Wen, Cong Shen, Yuedong Han, and Xiu'e Wang chart, in a 2026 imaging study, how the walls of children's airways change shape from birth to adulthood. Their measure, wall area proportion, compares airway wall area with the total of wall plus open channel, and healthy reference values for Chinese youth were missing.

Chest scans from 795 healthy children and teenagers were measured automatically across airway generations. Wall proportion fell with age beyond the second airway branch, more steeply in boys. Sex made little difference before sixteen, after which boys showed lower values in the windpipe, lobes, and upper airways. The tables give clinicians a baseline for spotting abnormal airway thickening.
pmc-13540911:
Clémence Tropis leads a 2026 study arguing that body fat itself helps drive the confusion and memory problems that can follow surgery in people with obesity. Postoperative neurocognitive disorder can linger for months and raises later dementia risk.

Obese patients having heart or orthopaedic surgery showed more early cognitive change and lower test scores than lean patients. A mouse model pairing diet-driven obesity with a leg fracture reproduced the worsening. Treatments that cut inflammation, removed fat tissue, or restricted calories each protected the obese mice from the cognitive slide. The authors propose targeting obesity-linked inflammation before surgery as a prevention strategy.
pmc-13542111:
SeonYong Lee and six colleagues map, in a 2026 landscape study, how heron and egret breeding colonies across South Korea assemble into types, and which surroundings at which distances explain each type. Colonies sit in patchwork landscapes, and national-scale multi-scale evidence was scarce.

Nest counts from 176 colonies were clustered with a self-organising map, yielding six distinct assemblages. Large species dominated inland forest colonies, while smaller species clustered in coastal and mixed urban-rural areas. Built land, managed greenery, and water cover ruled the immediate surroundings, grasses and trees mattered at middle distances, and broad land use still counted at ten kilometres. Conservation planning, the authors argue, must work at all scales at once.
pmc-13542211:
Yan-li Zhang, Chao Ran, and Wei Li build a prediction chart in 2026. The chart forecasts treatment effect in a fungal lung infection. The infection is pulmonary cryptococcosis. Its CT look overlaps with other diseases. The tool mines texture patterns from scans. The eye cannot quantify those patterns alone.

Records covered 255 patients at two centres. Sets were split into training and validation groups. One set came from a second centre for external checks. A support vector machine performed best among the models. It used selected scan features as inputs. Adding clinical variables made a combined nomogram. That chart matched the scan-only model. It clearly beat a clinical-only model.
pmc-13543011:
Jeenat Mehareen and co-authors published a 2026 study measuring how much extra people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease spend on medicines, and who pays. Using British Columbia health databases spanning 2001 to 2020, the team matched more than 207,000 patients with physician-diagnosed COPD to over 400,000 people without the disease. Excess cost was the adjusted difference in all medication spending, split between the public PharmaCare programme and private sources such as out-of-pocket payments.

Patients with COPD spent an extra 1,336 Canadian dollars per patient-year on medications. About forty percent of that excess, 528 dollars, was privately financed, and private spending grew much faster than public spending across the two decades, at roughly 8 percent a year. Patients also personally bore half of their inhaler costs. The authors warn that the private share of drug costs quietly shifts the burden of chronic lung disease onto patients.
pmc-13543511:
Sara Sousi and colleagues published a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of remote care for pregnant women with diabetes. The condition, whether pre-existing or gestational, raises risks for mother and baby, and virtual consultations plus home monitoring spread quickly during recent years. Whether that shift helped or hurt the quality of antenatal care is unsettled, so the review will search seven databases for studies from 2005 to 2025 covering virtual visits and remote monitoring.

Quality will be judged by a six-part framework whose parts are patient-centredness, effectiveness, safety, efficiency, timeliness, and equity. Two reviewers will screen and extract independently, bias will be appraised with Cochrane tools, and subgroups will separate diabetes types and intervention styles. Being a protocol, the paper itself reports no results. Its value is a transparent plan whose findings should guide safe, fair roll-out of remote antenatal diabetes care.
pmc-13543611:
Yuxi Ma and Min Liu published a 2026 study comparing HPV infection patterns and cervical cell changes in women with and without HIV in Shanghai. The team enrolled 238 women confirmed HPV-positive at a public health centre between 2019 and 2023, just under half of them also living with HIV. Genotypes were catalogued, cell abnormalities compared, and risk factors for cervical dysplasia in the co-infected group were modelled.

The HIV-positive group carried more high-risk HPV and more multiple infections, including higher rates of two particular genotypes, and vaccine-covered types were commoner there too. Cell abnormalities were significantly more frequent with HIV. Within the co-infected group, a viral load above one thousand copies per microlitre of blood raised dysplasia odds roughly tenfold, marking uncontrolled HIV as the danger to watch. Cervical screening intensity, the authors imply, should follow HIV control.
pmc-13544111:
Owino and colleagues produced the first county-by-county estimates of the combined human and livestock burden of Rift Valley fever in Kenya, covering 2014 to 2024. Rift Valley fever is a mosquito-borne virus that sickens people and causes deaths and abortions in farm animals. Their 2026 analysis uses a One Health measure that adds years of healthy life lost by people to losses expressed as animal equivalents.

Owino found the burden heavily concentrated in northern Kenya, with Marsabit county highest by a wide margin, followed by Baringo and Wajir, while several central counties recorded almost none. The pattern split by sector: Marsabit carried the largest livestock burden, while Nairobi carried the largest human health burden. Because losses cluster so sharply in space, the authors argue that vaccination, surveillance, and outbreak preparation money should target the high-burden counties rather than spread evenly nationwide.
pmc-13545111:
Vi and co-authors surveyed a 2026 nationwide snapshot of myopia awareness in Australia, where short-sightedness usually starts in childhood and can end in permanent visual damage. Slowing its progression early is possible, but only if families know treatments exist. The online survey ran across September and October 2024.

After excluding eye care workers, 1,565 responses were analysed from residents across the country for this study. Seventy-nine percent had heard the term myopia, yet understanding of risk factors, complications, and treatments stayed patchy, Vi reports. Only fifteen percent knew treatments exist that slow myopia progression in children over time. Common misconceptions about causes and lifetime risks, such as retinal detachment, fed complacency about the condition. The authors call for public health campaigns promoting early detection and treatment.
pmc-13546711:
Anak Agung Gde Oka Dharmayudha and colleagues tested in 2026 whether leaf extract from the Spondias pinnata tree can keep dog semen healthy during chilled storage. Their breed was the Kintamani, a Balinese dog of conservation interest. Semen from four dogs was pooled, diluted in a coconut-water-based extender, and split into a plain batch and three batches with rising extract doses. Quality was checked over 72 hours in the refrigerator.

The lowest extract dose worked best, preserving sperm movement and survival better than the plain extender, while the DNA held up well for at least three days in every batch. Higher doses gave no extra benefit. The authors present the recipe as a cheaper, locally sourced option for short-term semen storage.
pmc-13547111:
Torwane and colleagues interview fourteen committed opponents of community water fluoridation to learn what actually holds their opposition together, aiming to give health communicators something better than fact sheets. Participants from Britain, Australia, and the United States were recruited through the Fluoride Action Network's Facebook page, the movement's main online hub. They were interviewed by video call across the first half of 2025 for this 2026 qualitative study.

Anti-fluoride networks plus social media were the most trusted information source, named by the large majority, while mainstream science and health authorities ranked low. Opposition rested less on disputing the dental evidence than on mass medication without consent, distrust of institutions, industrial-waste worries, and memories of being dismissed by professionals. The authors conclude engagement must answer values and trust, inside the networks where beliefs circulate, not merely repeat the evidence louder.
pmc-13547911:
John Politis and colleagues argued asthma care stands at a turning point. Published in 2026, the viewpoint traces drivers of change: deeper disease knowledge, steroid harms in view, and immune-targeted drugs that make lasting calm a real goal. Patient-centered care with virtual health and AI also drives change. In Australia, up to 10 percent of people live with asthma.

These drugs can bring lasting calm, flagging type 2 eosinophilic disease found in half to most mild cases and nearly all severe ones. Yet primary care faces thin funds, short visits, split handling, and guideline churn, while typing and fixable traits get short shrift. AI and virtual tools plus patient voices promise to ease these chokepoints. The authors urge careful use so advances lift results without trading safety.
pmc-13548711:
Martina Smorti and colleagues explore what helps teenagers and young adults with heart muscle disease come to terms with their condition, in a 2026 pilot study. Acceptance research in this age group has focused on private identity, yet these years hand disease management from parents to the young person within a web of relationships. Sixty-eight Italians aged sixteen to thirty, recruited through a patient association, rated their acceptance and the support they felt from family, friends, and partners.

The final statistical model explained about a sixth of the differences in acceptance. Feeling strongly supported by family went with greater acceptance. Carrying an implanted defibrillator device went with lower acceptance, perhaps as a daily reminder of risk. Support from friends and partners showed no clear independent link. The authors suggest family-focused help belongs inside transition care as young patients take over their own management.
pmc-13548911:
Daniel Houghton and colleagues watch the very same platinum nanoparticles before and after harsh fuel cell stress tests, in a 2026 microscopy study. Platinum particles drive fuel cell reactions but sit on carbon supports that corrode, muddying any judgment of the particles themselves. The team mounted particles on corrosion-proof boron-doped diamond, transparent to the electron beam, and built automated software to track each particle's size, position, and neighbors across the test.

Roughly two hundred particles per image were followed. Between forty and fifty percent barely changed area at all, a few grew, and the rest shrank by less than an atomic layer through brief dissolving. Particles wandered on average only a third of a nanometer. The authors credit a strong platinum and diamond bond and pitch diamond as a durable catalyst support for punishing conditions.
pmc-13550311:
Linna Lu and colleagues build a ten-gene risk score from the cell's recycling centers to forecast survival in acute myeloid leukemia, in a 2026 computational study. Lysosomes digest and recycle cell contents, and their genes are disturbed in this blood cancer. Comparing leukemia and control samples from public databases, the team isolated lysosome genes tied to outcome, then used survival statistics and machine learning to assemble a model from cancer atlas data.

The ten-gene score split patients into high and low risk groups with clearly different clinical features, active pathways, immune surroundings, and drug sensitivities, and it held up in outside datasets. Laboratory checks on three of the genes in leukemia and marrow cell lines matched the computed direction. The authors suggest the signature could steer choices between immunotherapy and chemotherapy, pending clinical testing.
pmc-13550811:
Heather H. Cheng and twelve colleagues lay out PATROL, a multicentre early-detection study for prostate cancer in people at genetic risk. Carriers of inherited risky variants in genes such as BRCA2 and BRCA1 now warrant closer screening under current guidelines. Yet the best early-detection plan for carriers still needs refining. Their 2026 paper sets out the study design.

The study enrolls people aged 40 or older carrying a risky variant in an eligible gene, with no prior prostate cancer. Each year brings a physical exam and a PSA test, with MRI at baseline optional and advised when PSA tops the protocol cutoff. Biopsy is offered for any clinical concern or a PSA above age-based cutoffs. Samples will be banked to test new clinical and research markers.
pmc-13551811:
Gabriella Barratt Heitmann, leading fifteen colleagues, published a 2026 analysis of weather and vivax malaria in the Peruvian Amazon, where this malaria species dominates and blocks elimination goals. Monthly case counts from 136 communities between 2017 and 2024 were paired with hourly climate reanalysis data. Distributed lag models, which spread an exposure's effect over following weeks, tested minimum and maximum temperature and rainfall over a two to sixteen week lookback.

Warmer minimum and maximum temperatures each raised malaria incidence by about a tenth at lags of seven and nine weeks in the reported comparisons. Heavy weekly rainfall raised incidence by nearly a third at eleven weeks, and river-adjacent communities showed stronger links than highway ones. Incidence dipped during El Niño periods, adding a climate signal for timing control efforts.
pmc-13551911:
Francis Duhamel Nang Nang, with eleven colleagues, published a 2026 study of high blood pressure in adults with HIV in Yaounde, Cameroon. The study ran at an urban HIV clinic from January to March 2024. It covered 460 adults on antiretroviral therapy. The team modeled blood pressure with a method suited to common outcomes. They also probed how treatment length interacts with age.

High blood pressure affected 43.3 percent of the group. Mean age was about fifty, and most participants were women. Family history of high blood pressure was the strongest factor. Older age and obesity also counted. Treatment length linked to pressure before adjustment, yet not after. The team reads age as the driver behind that first link.
pmc-13553711:
Daniel Ostler-Mildner and colleagues built a sound-based screening tool for a throat pouch disorder that often goes undiagnosed for years, publishing the work in 2026. Zenker's diverticulum causes swallowing trouble, yet confirming it usually needs a specialist centre and video X-ray, which smaller clinics may lack. The team recorded neck sounds during swallowing with a portable device, gathering data from 23 patients and 27 healthy volunteers.

Their two-stage deep learning model first spots swallows in the recordings, then sorts each swallow as healthy or pathological. Patient-level accuracy reached about 89 percent, with a similarly strong balance of precision and recall. The authors present the approach as a first noninvasive screen that could speed referral, cut diagnostic delays, and lower costs in swallowing care.
pmc-13554811:
Yu-Chang Liu, Tsung-Cheng Kuo, and How-Ran Guo study pesticide use and liver injury in two farming regions of Taiwan in a 2026 field study. The areas grow water caltrops and mangoes, crops needing regular spraying. From random samples of two hundred residents per region, 331 adults aged forty and up took part. Liver blood tests were compared between users and non-users.

Pesticide users showed abnormal liver tests more often than non-users. Risk ran far higher in residents carrying hepatitis B or C infections. Spraying upward, toward tree canopies, emerged as an independent risk factor on its own. Its share of blame rivalled that of hepatitis B in this population. The authors urge safer spraying practice, above all for infected workers.
pmc-13554911:
Rafael Alejandro Iraheta Castaneda leads a seven-author team reporting a heart transplant for runaway electrical storms in Chagas disease in a 2026 case report. Their sixty-two-year-old patient had lived a decade with an implanted defibrillator for the parasitic heart condition. Repeated dangerous rhythms resisted drugs and a prior burn procedure, building into a refractory storm. Transplant offered the last route to control.

During surgery the new heart failed severely, a known transplant complication called primary graft dysfunction. A heart-lung machine took over through a leg vessel, eased by a balloon pump and a direct drain from the heart's upper chamber. Guided by the body's responses, the team weaned support as the graft recovered. The authors back transplant for such storms.
pmc-13557811:
Sinan Yavuz and nine colleagues reviewed in 2026 the hospital records of children admitted with asthma attacks to a tertiary centre in the United Arab Emirates. Asthma attacks send many children to hospital, and spotting which ones will turn severe matters for triage. The retrospective study covered children aged 2 to 13 admitted between January 2018 and July 2023, and statistical models hunted for signs that predicted a severe course.

Chest recession, visible breathing distress, preventive medication use, and family allergy history all linked to severe attacks in early analyses, while obesity unexpectedly linked to lower odds. In the refined model, faster breathing, younger age, and lower blood oxygen stood out as predictors of severe or life-threatening episodes, with heart rate also differing between groups. The authors offer these bedside signs as a practical early warning set for emergency teams.
pmc-13558511:
Xinlyu Huang and seven colleagues ran a randomised trial in 2026 of a new hyaluronic acid filler with numbing agent mixed in. The target was the folds that run from nose to mouth.
