Filler injections hurt and fade, so a premixed product promises comfort plus staying power. Their multicentre trial enrolled 324 Chinese adults with moderate to severe folds and compared the new gel against an established product, with assessors kept blind to who received what.

At six months, the share of patients improving by at least one wrinkle grade was higher with the new gel. It sat inside the non-inferiority margin in both analysis sets. Pain scores were comparable at first but higher at two hours after touch-up injections. Adverse event rates were similar, with firmness and swelling at the site most common. The authors conclude the premixed gel works as well as the standard, with numbing built in.
pmc-13558611:
Minghui Ou and nine colleagues uncovered in 2026 a partnership between skin fat cells and white blood cells that defends against staph infection, and showed how obesity breaks it. Fat cells under the skin release an antimicrobial peptide, yet obese animals suffer worse skin infections despite thicker fat. Using two mouse infection models plus diet-induced and genetic obesity, the team tracked the peptide through fat cell development and infection.

Healthy fat cells raised the peptide early in their development, then faded as they filled with lipid, and obese mice mounted a weaker peptide response with poorer local bacterial control. Neutrophils, the first-responder white cells, turned out to trim the peptide with their own enzymes into shorter fragments that kill bacteria better. The authors name this handoff a key amplifier of skin defence and a possible point of repair in obesity.
pmc-13558711:
Miguel Thomas and colleagues used single-cell sequencing in 2026 to ask why some injuries in adult mammals regenerate while most simply scar. Mesenchymal stem and stromal cells tend the repair in every tissue, and the team suspected that early shifts in their variety decide the outcome. Their mouse model stages regenerative and non-regenerative repair side by side in genetically identical adults, letting the early cell states be compared cleanly.

Distinct clusters of these stromal cells marked the two repair paths from the start. Unsupervised analysis organised their jobs into three coordinated functions: shaping tissue structure, steering inflammation and immunity, and managing metabolism. The authors bundle the trio into a framework they call SIM and argue that repair succeeds when the three act as one tissue-level response. The work reframes regenerative medicine around coaching cell states early, before scar programmes lock in.
pmc-13560211:
Chong Ge and colleagues catalog the BES1-like gene family in the tung tree, an oil-producing species whose male-heavy flower balance limits seed yield. Their 2026 genome-wide study is the first to characterize these brassinosteroid signaling genes in Vernicia fordii. Multi-omics methods combined family phylogeny, promoter analysis, and expression profiling across tissues and stages.

Seven family members fell into three distinct clades with simple structures and clade-specific motifs. Two segmental duplication pairs showed how the family expanded, and promoters carried hormone- and stress-responsive elements. Expression split by sex and stage: one gene dominated female flowers and fruit, another marked male flowers specifically, and a third switched on early in floral development. That early gene sat in the nucleus and co-expressed with a regulator of male structure degeneration. The authors offer the map for precision breeding aimed at flowering synchrony and productivity.
pmc-13560311:
Joshua Okyere, Bibha Simkhada, and Padam Simkhada set out a protocol for reviewing whether health education raises breast cancer literacy and screening uptake among women in sub-Saharan Africa. Their 2026 protocol responds to low screening use blamed largely on poor cancer knowledge across the region. Existing intervention studies scatter across strategies, delivery styles, and cultural settings.

Eligible studies are randomized trials and quasi-experimental work in women aged fifteen and older that test an educational intervention. Six databases plus grey literature will be searched. Two reviewers will screen, extract, and judge quality independently, using Cochrane and Joanna Briggs tools as appropriate. Results will be narrated, and pooled statistically where studies resemble each other enough. The authors expect the review to compare delivery methods and guide funding for culturally fitting programs that lift screening.
pmc-13561611:
Zi-Ying Wang and colleagues test a perforator flap method for rebuilding the breast after wide removal of granulomatous lobular mastitis tissue. Their 2026 single-center retrospective study covers 108 patients treated between January 2022 and May 2024. Three real-world paths were weighed: resection with flap rebuilding, resection alone, and drainage without resection.

Forty-three patients received the intercostal artery perforator flap. Their surgeries ran longer, bled more, and drained longer than the other groups' work. Complication rates, though, did not differ clearly across the groups. Against resection alone, flap patients reported better cosmetic outcomes and higher satisfaction. No flap patient recurred within one year of follow-up, a difference the authors flag as exploratory given the design, modest numbers, and short window. They present the flap as feasible and safe for selected patients needing resection.
pmc-13562511:
Isidore Houaga and colleagues built high-quality genome maps for five African cattle breeds, a resource long missing for the continent's herds. Africa holds about 150 cattle breeds, nearly a quarter of the world's cattle, yet most reference genomes came from European or Asian breeds. Using PacBio HiFi sequencing, a method that reads long stretches of DNA accurately, the team assembled genomes for Lagune, Gudali, Iringa Red, Singida White, and Mpwapwa cattle.

The new assemblies are the most complete African cattle genomes yet, with completeness scores above 99.68 percent and long unbroken stretches of sequence. They should sharpen gene mapping, variant detection, and breeding studies that older references blurred. For researchers tracing disease tolerance and adaptation, the authors present these genomes as a foundation for livestock science across Africa and beyond.
pmc-13563711:
Chenyuan Li and three colleagues chase a protein-shredder part that helps breast cancer spread and blunts a main chemotherapy drug. The part, PSMD8, belongs to the proteasome, the cell's waste-disposal machine. Their 2026 study found PSMD8 overproduced in breast tumours compared with nearby tissue, marking patients with poorer outlooks. Turning the gene down in cancer cells slowed their growth and their shape-shifting spread programme, in dishes and in animals, and it made the drug paclitaxel bite harder. Turning it up did the reverse.

The mechanism runs through a partner protein, KIF10, which PSMD8 shields from destruction. Silencing KIF10 erased PSMD8's tumour-promoting effects, including the drug resistance. The pair's signal fed into the ERK growth pathway, and blocking ERK partly undid the harm. The authors nominate PSMD8 as a target whose removal might both slow breast cancer and restore the power of an existing drug.
pmc-13563811:
Liangze Ma and nine colleagues ask whether loneliness and low mood, separately and together, forecast stroke in older adults. Both have been blamed through behaviour and biology, yet their joint weight was unclear. Their 2026 study used two national ageing cohorts: China's CHARLS with 10,555 people followed from 2011, and England's ELSA with 5,321 followed from 2012. At the start, each person was sorted into one of four types by social participation and depressive symptoms, then watched for a first stroke.

Depressive symptoms alone raised stroke risk in China, at a hazard ratio of 1.40, while low participation alone showed no firm link in either country. The danger concentrated in the combined type: socially disengaged and depressed people carried ratios of 1.56 in China and 1.87 in England against the engaged, symptom-free group. The authors argue screening should look for the pairing, since misery alone flags risk but isolation plus misery flags the most.
pmc-13563911:
Gabriela Gonçalves Amaral leads a 2026 mixed-methods assessment of how well vaccine cold storage worked in primary care vaccination rooms across Brazil. Fieldwork from 2021 and 2022 combined a national survey using a conservation assessment scale with interviews of managers and nursing staff at several levels of the health system.

National performance was rated inadequate, although urban rooms and places with stronger coverage for one childhood vaccine did somewhat better. Interview accounts pointed to structural, logistical, and organizational problems behind the weak scores. The account helps readers see both measured performance and the practical reasons staff gave for keeping vaccines safely cold.
pmc-13569211:
Isaac Carrasco and colleagues test, in a 2026 open-label multicentre study, probiotic ear drops containing lactobacilli for dogs with red, waxy, non-infected ear inflammation, a common problem often tied to allergy. Thirty-seven privately owned dogs received drops every forty-eight hours for twenty-eight days, with ear, itch, lesion, and quality-of-life checks at start, two weeks, and four weeks.

Lesion and itch scores fell clearly by the final visit, and owners reported better quality of life in eighty percent of dogs. Improvement appeared regardless of other medicines or the microbes first found. With no comparison group, the drops look like a helpful add-on rather than proven stand-alone treatment, a distinction the authors keep in view.
pmc-13569411:
Daniele Avenoso leads a 2026 phase II multicenter trial of a gentler high-dose conditioning regimen, treosulfan plus fludarabine, before donor stem cell transplant. Patients were adults aged forty to sixty-five with acute myeloid leukemia in first remission. Eighty-two patients were followed for a median of about twenty months to judge leukemia-free survival and safety against standard harsher regimens.

About eighty-two percent remained leukemia-free at one year, and relapse by one year was under fifteen percent. Donors were mostly matched unrelated volunteers. Safety was described as excellent in the results available. The regimen offers transplant centers a less toxic preparation that still protects against leukemia returning.
pmc-13569611:
Woo-Jung Song and colleagues test, in a 2026 study of the U-BIOPRED asthma cohort, whether cellular senescence is enriched in the airways of people with severe asthma. Senescence is the aging-like shutdown of cells that also releases inflammatory signals. Gene activity scores for two senescence pathways were compared across airway samples and checked in a second cohort.

Scores ran higher in bronchial biopsies from severe asthma than from milder disease or healthy volunteers, and one pathway was confirmed in the validation cohort. Higher scores tracked with frequent flare-ups, steroid use, nasal polyps, and worse lung function. A subgroup of signals tied to lung injury and repair stood out, suggesting aging biology helps drive the hardest asthma.
pmc-13569911:
Henriques-Calado and colleagues report a 2026 study that followed 333 psychiatric patients in Portugal who experienced homelessness, over twenty years.  The team split patients into four groups by how long homelessness lasted, from under one year to over fifteen years, and compared diagnoses, hospital use, and survival.

About three in ten patients died during follow-up. The early-stage and prolonged groups fared worst, with deaths near half, tied to alcohol disorders and organic psychosis. The persistent group, homeless longest, had the longest psychiatric follow-up and lower late mortality, a survivor effect the authors note after eighteen years. Patients with alcohol misuse, anxiety, or personality disorders, and younger patients, had the fewest hospital stays. Risk by stage could help services target the middle years, where death risk peaks.
pmc-13571711:
Briones Alvarado and co-authors reported a 2026 case report of a sixty-two-year-old man whose both diaphragms weakened suddenly from Parsonage-Turner syndrome, an inflammatory nerve disorder also called neuralgic amyotrophy. He had recently had a knee replacement and arrived with sudden breathlessness and left shoulder pain. A small lung clot was found, but it could not explain his full picture.

Breathing tests showed lung capacity falling by twenty-seven percent when he lay flat, a classic diaphragm weakness sign. Ultrasound confirmed both diaphragms moved far less than normal, worse on the left side, while their thickness stayed preserved. Briones Alvarado notes the pain then weakness sequence fits the syndrome's pattern of nerve attack after surgery. Breathing muscle pressures were markedly reduced at testing, and diaphragm movement improved only slightly at one month.
pmc-13572311:
Lin and co-authors analysed a 2026 brain imaging study of how young people with mental health symptoms process emotional faces they are told to ignore. Adolescence is a high risk period for psychiatric disorders across many diagnoses at once. Data came from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study of eleven to twelve year olds.

Nearly five thousand youths performed a demanding memory task in the scanner while emotional faces appeared as irrelevant decoration. Lin measured how distinctly the visual network represented each emotion category in the brain activity patterns. Greater distinctiveness under high memory load linked to worse task performance and more psychopathology symptoms in the group. The effect appeared already in primary visual cortex, the earliest visual area, and predicted symptoms a year later.
pmc-13573411:
Md. Ramjan Sheikh, with seven colleagues, ran a 2026 study of how bread wheat copes with lead in its environment. Lead pollution chokes plant growth by sparking oxidative stress and jamming cell work. Wheat types differ in how much lead they can bear, yet a joint read of body, chemistry, and gene responses was missing.

Plants faced lead acetate doses from zero up to the top test level in a graded series. The team measured growth and body signs, defence chemistry, and gene activity side by side. That three-way read shows which wheat lines hold up and which pathways switch on as dose climbs. Strong lines can point breeders to traits worth keeping, such as better damage control or lead shut-out at the root. The authors frame the data as a base for picking parents for tougher wheat.
pmc-13574711:
Won Dong Shin, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 winged drone that flies and crawls on a single motor. Drones that both fly and move on land can reach more places, yet most carry many motors that add weight and complexity. Ground movement in such designs also tends to stay weak.

One actuator drives this drone, through a new transmission that can flip its spin direction. That flip switches the craft between modes: rolling on the ground, jumping up, and taking flight. The same single drive thus covers land travel, air travel, and the passage between them. Cutting motors trims mass, which stretches working range. The authors frame the design as a lean path to multimodal robots for mixed terrain. Tests back each mode in turn.
pmc-13575011:
Sridevi Rajeeve leads a 2026 real-world study of a cell therapy for multiple myeloma, a cancer of plasma cells in the bone marrow. The therapy, cilta-cel, uses a patient's own altered immune cells. It was first cleared for late-stage use and later moved into earlier lines of care.

Records covered 120 adults treated after one to three prior lines of therapy. Most received bridging treatment while the cells were prepared. Among those checked for response, 98 percent responded, and nearly all patients tested reached deep clearance of disease markers. At last follow-up, 94.2 percent stayed free of progression. Results held across bridging regimens, though follow-up was short at a median of 5.8 months.
pmc-13575111:
Jie Li leads a 2026 study of an implantable device that aims electric fields at glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour. Electric field therapy can disturb tumour cell division, yet the skull weakens fields applied from outside the head. The team built a thin-film device that sits like an artificial membrane over the brain.

Ultrasound from outside switches the film on, turning sound into local electric fields inside the skull. Lab tests showed about 68 percent slowing of growth in glioblastoma cell lines. In mice with brain tumours, tumour burden fell by about 72 percent. Field loss stayed below 20 percent at working frequencies, far better than external electrode systems. Healthy nerve tissue was spared in the tests reported.
pmc-13575211:
Saba Babakan, Hoda Jafarizadeh-Malmiri, and Nader Rahemi optimise a fast way to make pectin nanoparticles in a 2026 study. Pectin, a natural gelling agent from fruit, can be formed into tiny particles for food, drug, and cosmetic products. Their method sets the particles with magnesium ions and speeds heating with microwaves.

A statistical tuning method found the best recipe: a magnesium-to-pectin volume ratio of 0.1 and 155 seconds of heating. The result was particles about 390 nanometres wide with an even size spread and a stable surface charge. Freeze-dried powder particles came out rod-shaped, smooth, and without crystal structure. Thinner solutions flowed more easily, with lower thickness and density. The authors present the powder as a bridge between natural polymers and nanotechnology products.
pmc-13575411:
Kah Hup Chew and three colleagues compare how well three filling materials seal the sides of cavities against bacterial leakage in a 2026 lab study. Leakage at the edge of a filling lets bacteria in and drives new decay. The materials were an alkasite, a standard resin composite, and a glass hybrid.

Standard side cavities were cut into 66 extracted human molars and filled by group. A two-chamber setup exposed the fillings to Streptococcus mutans, a decay-causing bacterium, for 40 days. Every material leaked eventually. The alkasite leaked more slowly than the composite, with a clear statistical gap between those two, and microscope images showed the state of each filling's edge. The authors note the limits of a lab setup when judging real-world durability.
pmc-13576311:
Fernando J Mota de Almeida leads a 2026 Swedish registry study of a tooth-wasting condition called external cervical resorption, where tissue activity eats away the neck of a tooth. Outcome data mostly came from specialist clinics, leaving everyday practice unmapped. The national dental registry offered a population-wide view.

The study found 14,881 affected teeth recorded between 2009 and 2018. Extraction was the first treatment for 42.8 percent, while the rest were treated conservatively, with or without surgery. Conservatively treated teeth survived at 82.7 percent after five years, 74.9 percent after ten, and 67.8 percent after fifteen. Older age, fewer remaining teeth, molar teeth, and surgery each raised later extraction risk. Root canal treatment near the start made no clear difference to survival.
pmc-13578511:
Floor R Pijl and colleagues costed the first thirty days of hospital care after brain tumor surgery at a single regional referral center in 2023. Using detailed bottom-up costing, they tracked 322 adult patients with a mean age of 61 years. The median hospital stay was three days, and mean in-hospital costs reached 6,988 euros per patient.

Surgery type, pre-operative functional status, total stay, intensive-care stay, and complication grade each drove costs independently. Repeat surgery, readmission, and death within thirty days pushed costs higher still. The authors suggest targeted steps such as selective intensive-care admission, faster recovery pathways, and complication prevention could make brain tumor care more efficient.
pmc-13582011:
Victoria EJM Palasantzas and colleagues grade an immortal liver cell line as a stand in for fatty liver disease research, in a 2026 study. The field leans on a cancer derived line that behaves little like a healthy liver cell. The candidate line, grown from real human liver cells, was set against that standard on genes, fat loading, and drug response.

The two lines differed sharply in chromosome layout, in disease risk gene forms, and in how their genes answered a fat bath. A new approved drug for the inflamed form of the disease cut stored fat in the candidate line but not in the cancer line. Its gene shifts ran through energy making paths. The authors warn that model choice can flip a study's answer.
pmc-13582711:
Luan Lawson and colleagues track how medical students grow as self directed learners across the first two school years, in a 2026 study. A sixteen item survey measured four traits: adaptive learning, resilience, curiosity, and drive. Students answered at entry, after year one, and after year two, with sixty five students matched across all three rounds.

Scores dipped on adaptive learning in year one, while the other three traits held steady. By the end of year two, scores rose across the board, passing the entry marks. The authors read the dip as the shock of a harder learning world before students build the thinking tools to run it. Schools get a baseline rhythm for when to coach these skills.
pmc-13586111:
Maissa Chakroun and colleagues find a gentler way to pull apart clumped spore and crystal bundles in a pest-killing bacterium. Bacillus thuringiensis makes protein crystals that poison insect larvae, paired with hardy spores, and makers must count each part to keep batches steady. One variety, used against mosquitoes, clumps so tightly that standard separation fails and counts run low.

The team tried sound waves, a detergent, and lipopeptides, fatty soap-like molecules made by bacteria themselves. The lipopeptide wash won by far, raising live spore counts up to eight thousand fold and lifting crystal recovery to sixty percent. A related variety that stays naturally loose turned out to carry the gene for making its own lipopeptides, which hints that nature uses the same trick. The authors offer the wash as a cleaner swap for harsh methods.
pmc-13587211:
Erica Yim and colleagues set drug response in child bladder infections at one Korean hospital in 2015 to 2020 beside the same hospital's data from 2003 to 2008. They looked back at 571 kids with germ-proven acute bladder infections. Germ type, drug response, resistant-enzyme rates, and scan results were all weighed anew.

Gut germs caused 98.2 percent of infections, with Escherichia coli alone at 89.1 percent. Drug response fell a lot for a few drugs used each day, and enzyme-proof germs grew far more common. Scan faults showed no clear link to germ type. Local drug-use watch must go on, so first-choice drugs for kids stay wise.
pmc-13591711:
Arzu Or Koca and four colleagues mine, in 2026, a huge Turkish work screening dataset for links between heavy metals and hormone or metabolic health. Metals such as lead, cadmium, and arsenic can disrupt hormones. Records covered 34,595 people seen at a national work and environment hospital over two years. Metal levels in blood and urine were classed as normal or high, then set against thyroid, sugar, fat, and liver tests.

Among those tested, thyroid trouble appeared in about one in seven, and diabetes or pre diabetes in about one in five. Some high metal groups showed worse fat or liver patterns, yet many gaps faded after strict correction for false alarms. The team calls the results early signals, and urges routine thyroid and sugar checks for exposed workers.
pmc-13592411:
Seongmin Ga leads a 2026 team designing a carrier that bursts gene silencing RNA out of the cell's recycling sacs before they digest it. Under two percent of such RNA normally escapes. Their liposome wears a flu virus proton channel on its surface, tethered to the RNA by a nucleic acid linker. The channel pumps protons inward, swelling the sac until it ruptures.

Treated RNA reached the cell interior far better, with less of it ending in the digesting compartments, and gene silencing strengthened. Extra RNA packed inside the bubble let the team silence two genes at once. Ga and colleagues present active pH control of the sac as a flexible platform for RNA drugs aimed at genetic disease and cancer.
pmc-13593711:
Michael Wilkinson and Jenny Myers survey the search for a true treatment for pre-eclampsia, the dangerous pregnancy disorder marked by high blood pressure and organ strain. Care today manages blood pressure and times the delivery, but nothing yet modifies the disease itself, and their review weighs repurposed drugs alongside newer biologic strategies for the preterm form.

The diabetes drug metformin showed a trend toward longer pregnancies in a randomized trial, with larger trials under way. Heartburn medicines and an anti-inflammatory drug looked strong in early laboratory work but have not yet helped patients, possibly because too little drug reaches its target. Newer approaches aim at the placenta directly, including gene-silencing injections against a growth factor signal and antibody treatment that calms complement attack. Matching treatments to molecular subtypes of the disease is, the authors argue, the missing step.
pmc-13594311:
Minghang Yu and colleagues identify EHMT2, an enzyme that tags DNA-packaging proteins with a repressive mark, as a brake on the maturation of natural killer cells, the immune system's front-line tumor killers. Their 2026 study links the enzyme's level to weaker killer function across human tissues and cancers.

Deleting the gene only in mouse natural killer cells pushed the cells to full maturity, raising their output of interferon-gamma and their killing power in dishes and in living animals. Combined gene and mark profiling showed the loss lifted repression from whole programs for development and attack. Drugs blocking the enzyme copied these effects in human killer cells grown from cord blood stem cells and in cells from adult blood. The authors propose EHMT2 blockade as a way to sharpen cell-based cancer immunotherapy.
pmc-13596711:
Viji Remadevi and colleagues tested pirfenidone, a drug approved against lung scarring, in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, where growing cysts are joined by progressive scarring that itself drives kidney failure. Their study began with single-nucleus sequencing of human polycystic kidneys to find where the scar material comes from.

Fibroblast cells proved to be the dominant source of fibrous matrix, and in cultured human disease cells pirfenidone quieted matrix genes and slowed growth, movement, and contraction. In a mouse model of the disease the drug reduced scarring, matrix buildup, and the scar-forming cell population, and kidney function improved. Kidneys grew less enlarged, though cyst counts fell only in females. The authors position pirfenidone as a partner to cyst-targeted drugs, arguing the scar deserves treatment in its own right.
pmc-13611711:
Fenghe Wang, Haotian Hao, and Jiahe Miao introduce a special issue of eight papers on cleaning polluted soil and water. Pollution of these linked systems threatens nature, drinking water, farming, and health. A pollutant's fate depends on acidity, minerals, organic matter, and microbes. Cleanup methods are judged by removal performance, mechanism, limits, and real-world practicality.

Six articles and two reviews make up the issue. Topics include electrokinetic removal of copper and lead from loess, mine tailings restored with fertilizer plus plants, and resource recovery from antibiotic waste. Other papers cover microbes degrading petroleum and chlorinated compounds, chloride stripping from strongly acidic wastewater, boosted breakdown of carbon tetrachloride in groundwater. A final paper tracks how hexavalent chromium migrates and transforms between soil and groundwater. Arsenic cleanup methods round out the set. The editors present a cross-section of current strategy.
pmc-13612211:
Mingxuan Liang leads an eleven-author team writing a 2026 letter on what happens in leukemia cells before whole chromosomes start duplicating. Extra chromosome copies appear as the sole abnormality in a slice of myeloid cancers, yet the genes that invite them were unknown. The team compared cancers with normal chromosome counts against trisomy cases across three cohorts, covering 1,650 normal-karyotype and 229 trisomy patients.

Thirteen genes were mutated more often in trisomy cases in their own acute myeloid leukemia cohort, led by ASXL1, SRSF2, and MACF1. Combining all three cohorts strengthened four names: ASXL1, SRSF2, STAG2, and EZH2. These are regulatory genes, running splicing, chromatin, and cohesion rather than the division machinery itself. The pattern suggests quiet, cumulative disruption of gene regulation loosens chromosome handling until gains follow. The authors present the enrichment map as a starting point for understanding how numerical instability begins.
pmc-13614311:
Federico Ravera leads a team introducing a design framework named LUFFY. It picks molecules that could serve as working parts of molecular field-coupled nanocomputing. In that scheme, logic passes between molecules by electric fields rather than by moving charge. Such computing could use very little power, yet finding molecules with stable logic states is hard. The team began with 32 molecules that can actually be made in a lab.

For each candidate, the framework samples the molecule's possible shapes and studies how its charge responds to an input field, in both plain and oxidized states. Energy-averaged models fold shape variety into the score rather than pretending molecules sit still. The result is a fair way to rank candidates before anyone spends months making and testing them. Designers of post-silicon logic get a shared test bench for an idea still in its infancy.
pmc-13616311:
Dongmei Luo and colleagues use single-cell gene profiling to find a faulty B cell group behind primary immune thrombocytopenia, an autoimmune disease where antibodies destroy the blood platelets needed for clotting. The team profiled blood cells from four patients, four people with high platelet counts, and four healthy donors, then screened the results with machine learning. One B cell subset appeared almost only in patients.

Digging into its control network named a master regulator, RUNX3, and flagged a fat-building pathway that runs through an enzyme called UGCG. Tests in mice with the disease confirmed the enzyme's rise, and blocking it eased the B cell fault. A named cell subset, its control switch, and a druggable enzyme together give this puzzling disease a concrete set of targets for the first time.
pmc-13616411:
Nivedita Singh and colleagues work out, atom by atom, how a protein tag called FAST switches its fluorescence on when a dye ligand docks, enabling a chemically gated energy-transfer trick. Such tags let biologists make glow appear only where a chosen molecule is present, yet the switching mechanism was unclear. Crystal pictures of the tag empty and loaded show the pocket blocked by the protein's own head section when empty.

When the ligand arrives, that blocking section swings aside, opening a water-lined cavity that grips the dye. Different dye variants settle at slightly different angles and glow with single or multiple lifetimes in living cells. Lifetime patterns thus report the tag's local state, not just its presence. A clear structural story lets designers tune tags for sharper, switchable imaging inside cells.
pmc-13616911:
David Noyvert and seven colleagues report a 2026 study of how human astroviruses cut their large polyproteins into working parts. These RNA viruses infect gut and nerve cells, and they must slice one long protein chain at exact points to build their replication machinery. The team mapped those cut sites in a classic strain and in a nerve-infecting strain called MLB2.

Using protein-end analysis in infected cells plus lab-made polyproteins, they found paired cut sites at both ends of the viral protease and mapped cuts in the variable region and the VPg protein. Mutant viruses unable to cut at key sites could not replicate properly, proving the cuts are essential. The map clarifies how classical and newer astroviruses differ and highlights steps that antiviral drugs might target.
pmc-13617311:
Raul Velez-Montoya and seven colleagues test whether ultraviolet-C light can disinfect eye surgery instruments quickly in the office. They used seven steam-sterilized lid speculums, tools that hold the eyelid open. Most were deliberately contaminated with Staphylococcus epidermidis taken from a real case of post-surgical eye infection, then exposed to a commercial ultraviolet emitter for times ranging from thirty seconds to ten minutes.

Bacterial growth fell steadily as exposure lengthened, and after five minutes no recoverable bacteria grew at all, a complete reduction under these laboratory conditions. A speculum left out in a busy area for a day also came back clean after five minutes of light. The authors call the study exploratory: spores, fungi, and viruses were not tested. Still, they suggest ultraviolet treatment could be a practical extra step for reusable instruments between office procedures.
pmc-13617811:
Fengyang Li and twelve colleagues develop a cocktail subunit vaccine against Glaesserella parasuis, the bacterium behind Glässer's disease, a costly killer of young pigs. Existing vaccines protect poorly across the bacterium's many serotypes. The team screened fourteen candidate antigens by computer prediction and mouse testing, measuring immune responses and survival, to assemble a mixture that might cover diverse strains.

Three antigens, VacJ, PtsG, and GAPDH, paired with an adjuvant called Gel-01, formed the final cocktail. Vaccinated mice mounted strong antibody and cellular responses and survived lethal challenges with serotypes four and five, the dominant strains in China. Immune serum also slowed both strains in the laboratory, and a pilot study in piglets looked good. The authors say the cocktail shows strong promise under lab conditions, while large field trials in pigs are still required.
pmc-13618411:
Ana Paula da Cunha and four colleagues survey one thousand six adult residents of a Rio de Janeiro community marked by chronic urban violence. They ask how hard residents perceive primary health care to be to reach. Each respondent rated four standardized hypothetical scenarios and reported violent events experienced in the past year. The study links those perceptions to social characteristics and to direct exposure to violence, an evidence gap in highly vulnerable settings.

Exposure proved frequent: roughly three in ten participants reported threats of harm, about a quarter reported being slapped, and similar shares reported being pushed or restrained. Men were significantly more likely than women to report being punched or kicked. Despite this burden, statistical tests found few differences between social groups in how difficult the care scenarios seemed. The authors contribute a rare quantified picture of perceived access where violence is a daily determinant of health inequity.
pmc-13619311:
Sun and colleagues present in 2026 ProST, a computer framework that identifies spatial domains in spatial transcriptomics data. Spatial domains are regions of tissue with coherent biology, and the data map gene activity while keeping each measurement's location in the tissue slice.

Earlier methods chased clustering scores while neglecting whether the regions drawn actually match tissue architecture, and they largely ignored the microscope image sitting beside the gene data. ProST instead uses the stained tissue image as a prompt, guiding the learning toward morphology while filtering out irrelevant visual noise, and it sharpens how image features are extracted. Across several public datasets the method beat existing approaches at drawing domains, visualizing structure, and inferring spatial trajectories. It also filled in missing gene expression values better in the benchmark comparisons the authors report. The code is freely available.
pmc-13619811:
Carina Mara Souza and four colleagues report a forensic case from southeastern Brazil where insects helped investigators read a woman's death. Her body was found outdoors, and flies and beetles colonizing it carried timing clues. One blow fly species gave the team a way to estimate the postmortem interval, the time since death, based on how long insects had been active on the body.

A second fly species was bred from the corpse, and the authors note that its development data still need building out before it can anchor estimates elsewhere. Feeding by the flies and by a carrion beetle also left marks on the body. Such insect-made damage can be mistaken for injuries suffered before death, so the authors stress knowing each species' biology and behavior. Careful species identification, they argue, keeps entomology evidence from misleading a case.
pmc-13622911:
Benjamin Torner and colleagues tested how blade shape affects blood-pump performance and blood safety. Rotodynamic blood pumps must work reliably across varied flows, yet blade-shape effects on pumping power and blood damage were little mapped. Their 2026 study combined computer and bench tests on three pumps, varying leading-edge shape and blade thickness.

Leading-edge shape barely mattered, shifting efficiency and blood-damage scores by under 3 percent. Blade thickness mattered far more under overload, with thinner blades lifting efficiency by up to 22 percent while barely changing blood damage. Torner and colleagues advise putting edge shape second and tuning thickness against manufacturing limits.
pmc-13623011:
Marie K Plaisy heads a multicentre study tracking fatty liver growth in people living with HIV across low- and middle-income countries. Fat in the liver, called steatosis, can progress to liver damage, and HIV care teams see it as patients age. The study followed adults at nine clinics in Africa, the Americas, and the Asia-Pacific region.

From 2020 to 2023, the team enrolled people aged forty or more who had taken HIV therapy for six months, measured liver fat with a scan-based method over thirty-six months. Of 923 people analysed, one in five showed progression, most of them new cases. Progression ran higher in the Asia-Pacific and the Americas than in Africa. Being overweight, having type 2 diabetes, and having raised blood fats each raised the odds, and long use of one drug class added risk for women. The authors urge liver monitoring in HIV care.
pmc-13624311:
Zhinan Wu and colleagues hunt for drug targets in abdominal aortic aneurysm, a silent ballooning of the body's main artery that kills when it bursts and has no medicine to slow it. Suspicion has grown around ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death, inside immune cells crowding the weakened wall. The team examined a protein, NCOA4, feeding this process by recycling the cell's iron store.

The protein ran high in wall macrophages from aneurysm patients and in mice given a hormone inducing the disease. Mice lacking the gene resisted aneurysm formation, and silencing it in macrophages eased wall damage and inflammation. The protein partners with a transcription factor to switch on an enzyme making a cholesterol product, which pushes macrophages toward activation and iron-driven death. Blocking the enzyme with nanoparticles slowed the disease in mice. The authors flag both the pathway and the blood product as leads.
pmc-13625211:
Giulia Gotti and colleagues review what sets apart people who leave a suicide note from those who do not. Notes are rare first-person records of a suicidal crisis, yet only a minority of deaths involve one, so the team asked whether writers stand for the whole group. Their search of two databases, run to June 2026 under standard review rules, gathered thirty-three comparison studies.

Across social, clinical, and personal measures, no clear line separated writers from non-writers, and findings often clashed. The firmest difference lay in method: writers more often used non-violent means such as poisoning or gas. The authors suggest note-leaving may hinge on the circumstances of the act, and perhaps on having enough order of mind to write, rather than on a distinct inner profile.
pmc-13625711:
Sonja Großmann, Petra Waldegger, Tina Deutinger, and Werner Zwerschke study a little-known matrix protein, SNED1, and what it does for fat tissue stem cells. These adult stem and progenitor cells renew fat and seed new fat cells, guided by the scaffold of proteins around them. SNED1 is secreted into that scaffold, yet its role in human white fat was unclear, so the team lowered its levels in cultured cells and watched their behavior.

With SNED1 knocked down, the cells renewed themselves less, multiplied more slowly, and turned into fat-storing cells less readily. The losses spanned all three jobs that keep fat tissue healthy across life. The authors read SNED1 as a working partner between scaffold and stem cell, one that helps hold stemness and the choice to grow or mature.
pmc-13626711:
Mathilde Sola and a twelve-strong team release NeighborFinder, an R package that maps the microbes living nearest to one chosen species. Most network tools rebuild the whole community web from abundance data, a heavy job when a researcher cares about a single germ's direct partners. Their method runs penalized, cross-checked regressions around the target species, with filters tuned to microbiome data, and reads out an interpretable local network.

On simulated cohorts of a few hundred to a thousand samples, the tool recovered true neighbors with top marks for accuracy. It runs on the public CRAN archive with data and code posted openly. For hypothesis-led work on gut and soil communities, a fast local lens may beat a slow global map, and it can sit beside existing tools rather than replace them.
pmc-13629111:
Peng Ge and four colleagues built machine learning models to predict dangerous fungal infections in children being treated for leukaemia, published in 2026. These children face high infection risk because their disease and chemotherapy suppress immunity, and early prediction could speed up protective treatment.

Working from 247 young patients, the team trained five algorithms on clinical data, imaging features, or both, then checked the winner in a fresh group of sixty-one children. A support vector machine fed both data types performed best by a clear margin, outscoring three radiologists of differing experience. Chest findings such as pleural thickening, low white cell counts, and hormone treatment carried the most predictive weight. The authors present the model as decision support, not a replacement for clinicians.
pmc-13630411:
Hu and colleagues build in 2026 a lipid nanoparticle, a tiny fat bubble for drug delivery, that attacks cancer on two fronts at once through ferroptosis, the iron-driven cell death. Combining gene silencing with an iron-recycling trick in one particle had not been done.

The particle swaps a standard fat for arachidonic acid and carries two cargos. One is iron in its ferric form; the other is a small RNA that silences GPX4, the enzyme that normally cleans up toxic oxidized fats. Inside cancer cells, abundant hydrogen peroxide keeps regenerating the reactive ferrous form of iron. That both drives the lethal fat oxidation and helps the RNA escape to do its silencing at lower doses. In mice bearing a human eye cancer graft, the particles suppressed tumor growth with good safety.
pmc-13632611:
Igor de Almeida and four colleagues asked how often psychology papers name the country their work concerns. Most psychological research draws on Western, educated, wealthy populations yet speaks as if it covered all humanity. Social psychology should be the field least guilty of that habit. The team examined titles and abstracts from sixty-nine social psychology journals across three decades, 1990 to 2020, tracking mentions of nations and regions over three decades.

Cultural awareness stayed strong in journals devoted to culture or international and local topics. It stayed nearly absent in theory, review, and business-focused journals. Western places still earned the most mentions, while some other regions appeared inflated in narrow contexts. The authors warn that psychology's theories cannot claim to be general until culture becomes a central part of research design rather than an afterthought. Their audit gives the field a baseline for judging future progress.
pmc-13633411:
M M Bilodeau and K M Quigley produced the first broad estimate of how many eggs Indo-Pacific corals release in a single spawning season. Reproductive output decides how well reefs resist damage and recover, yet nobody had added it up across the region. The pair combined measured egg counts with trait-based estimates for missing species. They covered two hundred seventy-seven species from fifty-five genera, then scaled by regional coral cover.

Their total came to roughly three quintillion eggs for one spawning period. A few genera, led by Isopora and Acropora, contributed a wildly outsized share. Branching and massive growth forms together supplied about half of all eggs. Rankings by area, colony, and region agreed poorly: a top producer at one scale may look ordinary at another. The authors offer the map as a guide for choosing species that anchor reef recovery.
pmc-13637211:
RuiQi Liu and six colleagues published this 2026 review of whether handgrip squeezing exercises lower blood pressure equally for everyone. The training, holding a steady grip against resistance, has proven pressure-lowering effects. Most trials mixed very different patients, though. The team searched twelve databases for controlled trials and sorted participants by starting pressure: normal, high-normal, or hypertensive. Twenty trials with six hundred twenty-six people qualified.

Across all groups, training cut the top pressure number meaningfully and the bottom number by a smaller margin. Gains concentrated in the high-normal group, where both numbers fell significantly. People starting at normal pressure also gained on the top number. Age worked against the effect in one subgroup, with older participants gaining less on the bottom number, though few studies fed that estimate. The authors present grip training as best aimed at people whose pressure is creeping up but not yet high.
pmc-13638011:
Eric Wu and five colleagues describe the synthesis and crystal structure of a fully fluorinated silver complex. Silver ions bind nitriles readily, and the team wondered whether a fluorinated aryl nitrile would give a two-coordinate or four-coordinate product. Reacting a silver salt carrying a bulky fluorinated aluminate anion with excess perfluorobenzonitrile settled the question. The crystals hold two independent copies of the complex in each repeating unit.

Each silver center binds four nitrile ligands in a distorted tetrahedral arrangement. Most silver-nitrogen bonds cluster tightly, yet one ligand on each center stretches noticeably longer and bends far from straight, a distortion the authors document carefully. The bulky anions sit in the gaps with no close contact to the silver. Fluorine-fluorine contacts lace the packing, and solution fluorine NMR matched the solid structure. The work extends knowledge of weakly coordinating anions and exotic cation chemistry.
pmc-13639011:
Selena S Li and seven colleagues published a 2026 proteomic study of donor hearts kept alive on a perfusion machine before transplant. Perfusing hearts donated after circulatory death has widened the donor pool, but such hearts face higher rejection and failure rates.

The team measured more than eleven thousand proteins in fluid from twenty human hearts during perfusion. Inflammatory signals such as interleukin-6 rose steadily the longer perfusion lasted, and the pattern appeared again in a second human group and in pig hearts. The results suggest that limiting perfusion time or calming this inflammation might protect graft quality.
pmc-13639511:
Al-Amaan Mohamed Mirzan and Roberto Dina evaluated computer-assisted diagnosis for pancreatic fine-needle aspiration cytology in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Pancreatic cancers are deadly and hard to diagnose, with ultrasound-guided needle sampling plus microscope review as the standard, yet pathology staffing is short. Computer tools promise faster screening, but their overall accuracy in this setting was unclear. The authors searched five databases from 2010 to May 2025 and pooled results with bivariate models.

Ten studies qualified. At the level of single images, pooled sensitivity reached 91 percent and specificity 92 percent, while at the patient level sensitivity was 85 percent and specificity 91 percent. Heterogeneity ran high, driven by retrospective designs and shifting reference standards. Pathologists get near-expert accuracy for clear-cut cases with a clear warning: single-center training, selection bias, and uneven thresholds mean prospective multicenter validation on whole-slide workflows must come before routine use.
pmc-13642611:
Yuhui Cai and eight colleagues present a 2026 study of a layered material stack that can tune its own heat radiation in two infrared bands. Most surfaces radiate heat broadly and passively, which limits thermal camouflage, sensing, and infrared energy control.

The stack combines graphene, two-dimensional boron nitride, and a lithium vanadium oxide layer. Coupling between plasmons and lattice vibrations produced five hybrid branches and narrow emission in two mid-infrared windows. Oscillator models matched simulations closely and let the team extract coupling strengths. Making the boron nitride thicker strengthened confinement and splitting, pointing to compact, reconfigurable thermal sources.
pmc-13645511:
Peng Du and four colleagues present a theory paper on how chatty artificial intelligence may reshape identity formation in emerging adulthood. Young adults increasingly ask conversational models who to become, and the authors argue this changes the structure of selfhood, not only its content.

Working from Dialogical Self Theory, they describe the model as a synthetic position inside the self: endlessly flexible, frictionless, only pretending to push back, and authored elsewhere. Habitual use can hand it the self's integrating job, leaving a person richly voiced yet un-authored. The paper turns that claim into testable predictions and sketches measures using a recent Chinese graduating cohort.
pmc-13647711:
Otabek Pulatov and nine colleagues study whether starting an SGLT2 inhibitor during the hospital stay cuts readmission for heart failure patients, in a 2026 cohort. Guidelines elevated these drugs to top-tier therapy for weakened-heart failure in 2022, yet prescribing lagged. Records covered 438 patients discharged from four NYU Langone hospitals between January 2023 and January 2026. The main analysis focused on 221 patients whose hearts pumped at forty percent or less.

About twenty-eight percent of patients started the drug in hospital, and uptake in the weak-heart group had climbed sixfold since an earlier survey. Those patients returned within thirty days far less often than untreated peers, and the gap survived statistical weighting designed to mimic a trial. One gap stood out: patients with a previous heart failure admission started the drug least often. The authors argue hospitals should close that paradox, since prior admission marks the patients with most to gain.
pmc-13649411:
Flavia Costanzi and eight colleagues tested whether platelet-rich plasma, made from a woman's own blood, helps embryos implant after repeated failures. All women in the study had a normal womb lining width, so low width could not explain their losses. Two hundred thirty women took part at one centre from late 2023, with 110 choosing the plasma wash and 120 serving as controls.

Pregnancy rates were far higher in the plasma group, and the gap held after the team adjusted for other factors. Live birth rates were higher too. Since women chose their own group rather than being assigned by chance, bias may remain. The authors call for firmer trials to confirm the benefit.
pmc-13649511:
Xue Zhou and four colleagues compare liver cancer trends in China and the world from 1990 to 2021, in a study published in 2026. They used a global burden dataset that spans 204 lands and lands' data, and they pushed forecasts out to 2035.

World case counts more than doubled, yet rates per head fell over the three decades. Liver harm from hepatitis B drove much of the past burden, and its share shrank. In its place, fatty liver disease and alcohol drove a growing share. China cut its rates more steeply than the world pace, though its case counts still doubled as the population aged. The authors tie the shift to wealth and lifestyle change, and they urge plans that match each cause.
pmc-13649711:
Tanjun Zhao and five colleagues present a single-cell gene atlas of the purple sea urchin's change from larva to juvenile, published in 2026. This shift in body plan is a risky bottleneck for the species, which is prized in China yet falling in the wild and hard to farm at scale.

Cells from both life stages were split apart and read one by one. Eight cell types emerged, from gut and skin cells to nerve, muscle, immune, and skeleton-making cells. The map gives a base for probing how the switch between a two-sided larva and a fivefold adult is run. The authors also note the work may aid both farming and control of grazing damage to seaweed beds.
pmc-13650011:
Haihong Zhang and two colleagues ask whether the short videos that patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease watch are tied to how severe their breathing symptoms feel. In China, short video apps draw huge daily audiences, and patients often meet health claims there, so the team separated what people watch from how long they watch.

The survey covered 207 outpatients with confirmed disease across several centers in the first half of 2025. Symptom burden was measured with a standard breathing questionnaire. Videos about general health preservation went with worse symptoms, while exercise videos went with milder symptoms, and total viewing time alone showed no independent link. Trust in the videos showed a curved pattern that the authors treat with caution. Their point is that content type matters more than minutes watched.
pmc-13652511:
Alexander Tyagunov and six colleagues ask whether early surgery actually helps patients with adhesive small bowel obstruction. Blockages caused by internal scar tissue can settle without an operation, yet doctors lack firm rules for when waiting becomes dangerous. The multicenter study looked back at 143 patients and compared surgery within twelve hours, later surgery. Treatment without surgery, separating cases where the bowel was strangulated from those where it was not.

About half the patients had an operation, most of them started through keyhole surgery. Outcomes for early surgery were no better than for the delayed approach, and the gap was clearest in older patients, who fared worse with rushed intervention. The findings push back on the habit of operating as fast as possible and support a monitored trial of nonoperative care for selected patients, with surgery held in reserve.
pmc-3693611:
Ghasemi and Zahediasl write a guide to normality tests for non-statisticians doing statistical analysis. Statistical errors are common in the scientific literature; about half of published articles contain at least one, they note. Many procedures, namely parametric tests, assume data follow a normal distribution, and their validity depends on it.

Their guide explains how to check that assumption and what to do when it fails. It compares common tests in plain language for working researchers. Better checking protects medical and biological findings from resting on broken assumptions.  Examples use medical data throughout, matching the audience most prone to these errors.
pmc-4205511:
Tavakol and Dennick wrote a guide in 2011 to Cronbach's alpha, a statistic used across health and education research. Alpha is reported as a measure of how well the items in a test or questionnaire hang together. It appears in a huge share of survey-based studies, often with little explanation.

Their paper makes sense of what alpha does and does not show. It explains the ideas behind the number and the limits readers should keep in mind. A high alpha alone does not prove a scale is sound, a point the guide stresses. Students and reviewers use the paper to judge questionnaire quality with more care.
pmc-4935811:
Bronte, Brandau, Chen, and many co-authors wrote recommendations in 2016 on myeloid-derived suppressor cells. These cells, known as MDSC, are a mixed population that expands in cancer and other chronic inflammatory conditions. They suppress immune responses, which can help tumors escape attack.

Different labs described these cells in different ways, which blocked comparison of results. The authors name the main problems and propose a short set of must-report items for MDSC studies in mice and humans. Shared standards for naming and characterizing the cells let studies build on each other. That order is needed before MDSC can be targeted reliably in cancer treatment.
pmc-5940111:
Morgan Levine, Ake Lu, Austin Quach, and coauthors built a new epigenetic marker of aging in 2018. Earlier markers were trained to predict a person's age in years. The authors reasoned that health measures would track true biological aging better.

Their marker, built from chemical marks on DNA plus clinical measures, predicts time to death and disease more strongly. It also separates people aging fast from those aging slowly at the same age. Such a tool could test whether a treatment truly slows aging. Trials of anti-aging ideas need outcomes like this to be convincing.
pmc-8026611:
Daolin Tang and co-authors reviewed in 2020 ferroptosis, a form of cell death driven by iron that was first described in 2012. Cells can die through several distinct programs, and ferroptosis stands apart because it depends on iron and on the buildup of damaged fats in cell membranes. Interest in the process climbed quickly in the years after its naming.

The review lays out the two major routes that can trigger ferroptosis and the molecular machinery along each. It then examines what this death pathway means for health, including its roles in cancer and tissue injury. Because cancer cells can be pushed into ferroptosis, the pathway has drawn attention as a possible new angle for treatment.
pope-essay-on-criticism-1711:
Alexander Pope was only twenty-three when An Essay on Criticism appeared in 1711. Pope, a Catholic shut out of university and office, had taught himself the classics at home. The poem made his name at once and has never gone out of print.

Written in crisp heroic couplets, the essay teaches how to judge poetry: study nature, learn the ancients, and beware of pride and fashion. Famous lines urge that a little learning is a dangerous thing, and that to err is human, to forgive divine. Generations of writers learned their taste from Pope's manual. It remains the clearest statement of neoclassical poetics in English.
prester-john-pg611:
John Buchan's Prester John opens with Davie Crawfurd remembering, as if it were yesterday. His first sight of the man on the Kirkcaple shore, and how little he knew how big the moment was with destiny. The full contents map the destiny: the journey to the winter veld, drums beating at sunset, Captain Arcoll's tale. Treasure-hunting, the cave of the Rooirand, the drift of the Letaba, and Davie carrying the collar of Prester John itself.

Later chapters bring Inanda's kraal, a last sight of the Reverend John Laputa, a second climb of the crags. A great peril and a great salvation, and an uncle's gift many times multiplied. Buchan dedicated the tale to Lionel Phillips as a medley of ways and wars from a lover of the fairest country under the stars. This telling is the classic text entire.
punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-158-19:
Charivaria leads the Punch of February 11, 1920, in volume 158, with its usual run of one-paragraph jokes built from the week's papers. Burglars, boxers, and foreign courts give the column its material this time.

Lady Beecham says she would telephone for help if a burglar entered, while Miss Iris Hoey says she would recite Shakespeare at him, a plan the column treats as cruelty. A German artist faces a libel case over a drawing of the former Crown Prince as a baboon. Nine thousand food officials in Petrograd and the rumoured Dempsey and Carpentier fight round out the sport and politics of the page.
recollections-of-the-private-life-of-nap: Volume eleven of Constant's Private Life of Napoleon Bonaparte comes, in these pages, with a publisher's header and no more. The header gives the full title, the author's name, and English as the language of the text. It is not joined by any page of the memoir itself: readers find neither a first chapter nor a table of contents for this part. Only the series facts can be stated here, the eleventh part of a long life told by Napoleon's valet.
roget-thesaurus-english-words-phrases-19:
Peter Mark Roget, a London doctor with a passion for order, published his Thesaurus in 1852 after decades of private lists. The 1911 edition is the classic form, the one scholars cite. Roget arranged English words by meaning rather than by spelling.

His system sorts the whole vocabulary into six great classes and 1,000 numbered idea groups. Writers use it to find the right word by starting from the thought. Roget's name became the word for the book itself, copied by many rivals since. Few reference works have shaped daily writing so quietly and so completely. Roget kept adding to his lists almost until his death at ninety.
rolland-jean-christophe-cannan-vol2-1911:
Jean-Christophe in Paris forms the second volume of Romain Rolland's great novel cycle, in Gilbert Cannan's translation of 1911. It holds books five through seven: The Market-Place, Antoinette, and The House. Christophe, now a grown composer, leaves Germany and tries his luck in the French capital.

Paris at first dazzles and then disgusts him with its buying and selling of art. He finds true friends, among them the devoted Olivier family, and honors the memory of Antoinette. Work, poverty, and loyalty shape these middle years. Rolland uses the city to test his hero's ideals against the market. The volume deepens the cycle's portrait of the artist in modern Europe.
rousseau-emile-foxley-1911:
Rousseau raised a child on paper in Émile, the treatise-novel Barbara Foxley translated for the Everyman line in 1911. Émile grows up guided by nature rather than books, learning from things themselves and from the results of his own acts. Schooling, Rousseau argues, mostly ruins what nature builds well in a child.

One long section, the Profession of Faith of the Savoyard Vicar, sets out a simple, heartfelt creed of its own. That passage helped get the book condemned at its birth, even as its teaching on childhood spread across Europe. Modern ideas of childhood and learning still trace lines back to Émile's pages.
saadi-bustan-hart-edwards-1911:
Saadi, the thirteenth-century Persian poet of Shiraz, wrote the Bustan, meaning The Orchard, as a long poem on right living. Edwards's 1911 English rendering presents the work to modern readers in clear prose form. The Bustan stands as the companion volume to Saadi's famous Gulistan.

Ten chapters treat justice, kindness, humility, love, and the duties of kings and dervishes in turn. Tales of rulers, slaves, and saints carry the lessons, each closed by a pointed moral. For centuries Persian schoolchildren learned ethics and statecraft from these pages, and the poem still anchors Persian moral teaching.
scheible-das-kloster-vol11:
Johann Scheible issued band eleven of Das Kloster in 1849, holding cells forty-one through forty-four. Only one band now stood between this one and the end of the great set. The anthology's German subtitle, worldly and spiritual, had proved true in every sense.

Spell books and grimoires fill these cells, with Faust books and Höllenzwänge in close attendance. Folk charms, passed down in speech and scrap print, gain firm type at last. The chapbooks, too, keep coming, tales and wonders from the cheap stalls. Band eleven shows Scheible's stock unthinned near the close: the rescue of old print still ran at full pace.
schreiner-woman-and-labour-1911:
Olive Schreiner published Woman and Labour in 1911 in London. Schreiner, the South African novelist of The Story of an African Farm, had worked on the book for years and lost a longer draft. The published part became her feminist classic.

Schreiner argued that modern industry had taken women's old work out of the home, leaving leisured women as parasites on men's labor. She demanded that women win back a share in all fields of work, not as a favor but as a right. Her image of the leisured woman, ornamental and dependent, stung readers across the English-speaking world. The book shaped suffrage-era thought on women and work.
selenka-pithecanthropus-schichten-java-1:
Emil Selenka planned a great dig in Java to restudy the beds where Dubois found his ape man. He died before the trip, and his wife led the work in his name. Max Blanckenhorn joined her, and their joint memoir came out in German in 1911.

The team dug the Trinil beds once more and set out their rocks and beast bones in full. Their work tests where the ape man's bones lay and what age the beds must bear. The book is the first full site study of the most famed find in the field.
sepharial-kabala-of-numbers-1911:
Sepharial was the pen name of Walter Gorn Old, a Theosophist and astrologer of wide output. His Kabala of Numbers, published in 1911, is a manual of numerology and gematria from the Theosophical era. Gematria assigns numbers to letters and reads names and words by their sums.

Sepharial teaches how to turn a name into its number, judge its force, and apply the same art to dates, places, and events. He draws on Hebrew tradition, Greek practice, and the occult teaching of his own circle. The book served the revival's students as their handbook for the hidden arithmetic of words.
sepharial-manual-occultism-1911:
Sepharial was the pen name of Walter Gorn Old, a famed occult scribe. His Manual of Occultism came out in 1911. The book packs the whole field of hid arts in one stout tome. It was made as a desk book for the keen new hand.

Star lore, palm lines, name sums, and seals each get a short course. Ways to tell fate by cards, lots, and signs fill the last parts. Sepharial writes in a brisk, plain hand with no wasted words. The book is a fine snap shot of the occult trade in its Edwardian prime.
sepharial-second-sight-1911:
Sepharial's Second Sight, published in 1911, studies clairvoyance, the claimed power of seeing what the senses cannot reach. He divides his subject into natural second sight and induced clairvoyance, trained by practice. The book surveys both with an occultist's sympathy and a reporter's care.

Scottish Highland seers, crystal gazers, and modern psychics all pass through his chapters with their cases and claims. Sepharial weighs the evidence for a faculty beyond the five senses and finds much of it, in his judgment, hard to dismiss. The study preserves the period's best case for second sight as its believers made it.
simmel-philosophische-kultur-1911:
Simmel gathered his essays as Philosophical Culture in German in 1911. The volume is his most readable book, the one where his gift for finding deep meaning in surface things shines brightest. Simmel wrote essays the way other philosophers wrote systems, one bright subject at a time.

The pieces treat Rodin the sculptor, Goethe the poet, the handle of a vessel, fashion, and the inner life of the modern city. Money, which his great Philosophy of Money had analyzed, returns here in essay form. Each piece begins with something small and opens onto the whole structure of modern culture. The book shows why Simmel's lectures drew crowds in Berlin: he made sociology an art form. Readers new to Simmel are still advised to start with these essays.
tales-and-novels-of-j-de-la-fontaine-vol:
Volume 11 of The Tales and Novels of J. de La Fontaine holds the author's preface to the second book of his tales, with Friar Philip's Geese and Richard Minutolo. The preface is a small classic of the set, since La Fontaine uses it to defend his whole manner.

These are the last works of this style that will come from his pen, he begins, and so his last chance to vindicate the boldness and privilege he has assumed. He refuses to apologize for loose rhymes, lines that run over, or vowels left unmerged, the small carelessnesses he would not allow himself in another style. The tales that follow, of a friar's flock of geese and a Neapolitan schemer, show the freedom he claims in action.
the-bride-of-the-nile-volume-11:
Volume 11 of The Bride of the Nile, by Georg Ebers, opens at Chapter XVII in a prison. Paula passes a fearful night in a small, dreadfully hot cell where she and Betta are shut up. She can't sleep. When she does close her eyes, yells and clanking chains from the common prison wake her. Above her a fellow sufferer paces his room, even more restless than she.

At midnight the noise in the great hall stops, and soft sounds of a lute drift down from the cell above. Paula rises and stands at her barred window to listen, glad of any turn of thought. Her heart stands still: the voice is Orion's. The warder speaks his name, they talk of her dead uncle, then drop to whispers. She presses her face to the hot bars and calls up, soft, then louder: Orion, Orion!
the-caxtons-a-family-picture-volume-11:
Pisistratus speaks again in Part XI of The Caxtons, his family's story told as his own. The household of his scholar father forms the tale's home ground. From it, he rides out into the world and reports back in long, reflective chapters.

The narrator rides outside the Cambridge Telegraph coach without speaking a single word. Fellow riders, he thinks, must rate his learning in dead languages very high. He turns the ride into a long praise of silence, calling it a cloak like sleep. Silence, he argues, covers schemes, hopes, fears, ambition, and despair, and stretches from the human heart to the grave.
the-confessions-of-jean-jacques-rousseau:
Book XI of Jean Jacques Rousseau's Confessions stands here as volume XI of the twelve-book set, privately printed for members of the Aldus Society at London in 1903. Eloisa had been long in the press and still had not appeared at the end of 1760, yet it was already famous.

Madam de Luxembourg had spoken of it at court, and Madam de Houdetot at Paris. Houdetot got leave for Saint Lambert to read the manuscript aloud to the King of Poland, who was delighted by it. Duclos, who had also read the work, spoke of it at the academy. The booksellers of the Rue Saint Jacques and of the Palais Royal were beset by people asking when it would be published. When it came out at length, its success answered, contrary to custom, to the expectation built before it.
the-empire-annual-for-girls-1911: The Empire Annual for Girls, for 1911, was edited by A. R. Buckland and printed in London. Only the title page is present here. It lists the writers, among them Lady Catherine Milnes-Gaskell, Mrs. Creighton, and Mrs. G. de Horne Vaizey. It also names Agnes Giberne and Edith C. Kenyon. Coloured plates and sixteen black-and-white pictures are promised. No tale or article text appears.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-: Dated March 17, 1898, No. 11 of Vol. 2 of The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. It is also numbered No. 71 of the whole run. Only front matter is present here. It gives the masthead and a publisher's notice of rates. The same rates stand here as in the number before this one. A year costs $1.50, and six months seventy-five cents. Foreign subscriptions cost $2.25. Binding into four parts each year costs thirty-five cents a part.
the-history-of-don-quixote-volume-1-part:
Volume 1, Part 11 of Don Quixote comes from Cervantes, in Ormsby's English rendering. Chapter twenty-nine treats the droll device and method used to free the love-stricken knight from the severe penance he had imposed on himself. The opening closes a traveler's sad tale.

A speaker ends the true story of sad adventures and asks the listeners to judge whether the sighs and lamentations they heard were warranted. The company in the Sierra must now plan how to draw Don Quixote out of his chosen penance. Cervantes mixes pity with plotting, as rescue takes the form of a staged device.
the-last-of-the-barons-volume-11:
Edward Bulwer Lytton labels the portion in this record Book Eleven of his Warwick novel. Chronicles place Warwick and Clarence entry into London just before October 6, when leaders escort a restored King in blue velvet to thanksgiving at St Paul. The proclamation of a changed dynasty meets quiet public acceptance.

Lytton stresses restraint in victory, with only the Earl of Worcester executed among major figures. Worcester had impaled twenty men after Warwick flight to France, a cruelty that left him hated. Master Adam Warner also rises in this book, as greatness seeks wisdom beside a fragile throne.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, June 6, 1829, No. 374, illustrates Holland House in Kensington. Kensington has drawn interest since William III became the palace's first royal tenant, but Holland House merits the especial notice here. Sir Walter Cope built it in 1607, and his son-in-law Henry Rich, Earl of Holland, greatly improved it. Its general form is that of a half H.

Inigo Jones designed the stone piers at the court's entrance, carrying the arms of Rich and Cope. Francis Cleyne decorated the interior, and the Gilt Room survives in its original state, its wainscot charged with cross crosslets and fleurs-de-lis. A punning motto plays on the name Rich. The Earl of Holland was twice made prisoner in his own house, first by Charles I in 1633 and later by Parliament. Readers get a Jacobean mansion read through heraldry, painting, and its owner's arrests.

Clifton above Bristol fills the Mirror's No. 390, dated Saturday, September 19, 1829. Clifton is called the Montpellier of England, associated with all that is delightful in nature. The engraving shows the winding Avon, sublime rocks, and the opposite shore's picturesque scenery. Cottage comforts cluster into a village beside the cliff until the eye reaches crescents and terraces art has reared on the brow above.

The village stands a mile west of Bristol, commanding prospects over the city and the ships moving on the Avon's tides. Across the river, Somersetshire farmland rises four or five miles to Dundry Hill and its tower. The tower serves as a weather prophet: mist-hidden it threatens rain, clear at morning it promises a fine day. Clifton's salubrious air has drawn the wealthy, and freestone building covers the hill. Readers get a spa suburb praised as landscape, climate, and real estate at once.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, September 12, 1829, No. 389, illustrates Sion House on the Thames at Isleworth, opposite Richmond gardens. Its whitened towers and battlemented roof are known to every river traveller, the article says. The house takes its name from a Bridgetine nunnery founded by Henry V at Twickenham in 1414 and removed here in 1432. The convent numbered sixty nuns, an abbess, thirteen priests, four deacons, and eight lay brethren.

The inmates were neither sinless nor spotless, and irregularities made Sion among the first great houses suppressed by Henry VIII. Its yearly value was reckoned at 1,944 pounds and change. Henry confined his queen Catherine Howard there from November 1541 until three days before her execution in February 1542. Edward VI then granted the site to his uncle, the Duke of Somerset. Readers follow one riverside seat from nuns to a condemned queen.
the-old-man-of-the-sea-ship-s-company-pa:
W. W. Jacobs wrote The Old Man of the Sea as part of his Ship's Company tales. George Wright, a young man courting a lady, asks the old sailor Mr. Kemp to pose as his rich uncle from New Zealand. Wright has a rival for the lady, and a wealthy uncle who might leave him money could tip the balance.

Kemp admits he has borrowed money before and never paid it back, which Wright waves aside. The plan is for Kemp to enjoy borrowed cash, then sail home on a sudden letter, promising to return in a year. Jacobs builds the comedy on Kemp's honesty about his own failings.
the-parisians-volume-11:
Book XI of Edward Bulwer-Lytton's The Parisians opens with a reflection on love's disappointments. The narrator describes counting on a private meeting with the beloved, only to meet at last amid common company, where nothing wished for can be said. Worse, a subtle feeling warns that the beloved herself has changed.

Graham Vane feels that change in Isaura before he even sits beside her at table. Her touch, her voice, and the missing glow in her smile all tell him. Around them, excited talk fills the room, and the lovers sit silent. The scene turns on glances and tokens rather than words.
the-phrenological-journal-and-science-of: The Phrenological Journal and Science of Health, 1911. The health journal. This book preserves that periodical. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
the-present-picture-of-new-south-wales-1: D. D. Mann's The Present Picture of New South Wales was sold in London in 1811 by John Booth. Mann calls himself many years resident in the colony. It was illustrated with four coloured views of Sydney drawn on the spot, plus a plan of the colony from actual survey. The pages shown carry the title page and a long contents summary of the first chapter. It runs from the colony's discovery and Governor Phillip's departure through lost cattle and a playhouse. Convict unrest and a newspaper's founding appear.
the-stokesley-secret-pg3411:
Charlotte M. Yonge's family story appears here in the same 1902 Macmillan edition, paired with Countess Kate, that a companion record also carries, and the opening is identical in both. Five-year-old David Merrifield sits perched on a big Latin dictionary. From that seat he can reach the tea-table. He asks how a pig can pay the rent.

Around him his brothers and sisters grumble over bread that Sam renames bread and scrape, since the butter shows only in the little holes. Susan pleads the slice's case while Miss Fosbrook pours tea and counsels the deserted children, as Henry calls them, not to grumble, opening a tale of a household managing without its parents.
the-tragical-history-of-doctor-faustus-f: A sibling record of Marlowe's Doctor Faustus, this one follows the quarto of 1616 rather than the 1604 text used by its companion, both edited by Alexander Dyce.
